data.title: P-values, Hypothesis Tests & Better Empirical Practice
data.excerpt: Test a specific claim against a stated model and learn what a p-value measures: how surprising the data would be if that model were true. Put it alongside effect size, uncertainty and study design; a value below 0.05 is not proof, practical importance or the chance that a claim is false.
data.objectives:
State null and alternative hypotheses and identify one- or two-sided tests.
Interpret a p-value conditionally on a null model, study design and analysis assumptions.
Calculate a simple test statistic and connect p-values with effect sizes and interval estimates.
Explain Type I error, Type II error, power, multiplicity and the role of preregistration.
Separate association, prediction, causality, uncertainty and practical or economic importance.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Start with a question, design and null model","body":"A test should follow a question, not replace one. Define the estimand, unit, population, outcome, time window and comparison. The null hypothesis H₀ is a precise reference claim, such as a mean abnormal return μ equal to 0 percentage points; the alternative H₁ describes a departure, such as μ not equal to 0 for a two-sided test. A design determines what observations can be compared, while assumptions describe how the test statistic behaves if H₀ is true. Random assignment can support causal interpretation; an observational event study usually describes an association unless stronger identification assumptions hold. A p-value is evidence about compatibility with this specified model, not a verdict about reality.

Begin by writing the comparison in the units that a reader can audit. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose the estimand is the difference in mean monthly spending between two customer groups, measured in US dollars per customer during January 2026. If group A averages $42 and group B $39, the estimated difference is $42 − $39 = $3 per customer per month. A null of zero says the population difference is $0 per customer per month for the defined groups and period; it does not say every customer spends equally. A survey sample may support an association, but it does not by itself show that membership caused spending. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST — Use and Interpretation of P-Values’ in the linked sources.

A useful design can make the null reflect a decision threshold rather than merely zero. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a retailer pre-specifies the estimand as the population change in fulfillment cost per order, in US dollars per order, after a routing rule; negative values mean savings. If the minimum worthwhile saving is $0.50, a one-sided test can set H₀: μ = −$0.50 (or, for a conservative decision rule, μ ≥ −$0.50) against H₁: μ < −$0.50. Imagine the sample estimate is −$0.80 per order with standard error $0.20 per order. The standardized distance from the boundary is t = [−0.80 − (−0.50)]/$0.20 = −$0.30/$0.20 = −1.5, so a normal one-sided approximation gives p ≈ 0.067. At α = 0.05, this is insufficient evidence that savings reach the $0.50 threshold; it does not prove that savings are absent. The calculation also assumes independent observations and a suitable standard-error model; repeated orders from the same customer or warehouse would require dependence-aware uncertainty, and the routing rule’s observational comparison would still not establish causality without a credible design.

A null hypothesis becomes meaningful only after the comparison is fully specified. Suppose a synthetic analyst asks whether average account-opening time differs between two service channels in March, measured in minutes per completed application. The null could be H₀: μonline − μbranch = 0 minutes, with a two-sided alternative. That statement does not assert identical times for every application; it concerns the defined population mean difference. The sampling design determines which applications are represented, while the model determines how a statistic behaves under the null. If the question instead asks whether online service is faster, the alternative is directional and must be chosen before inspecting results. Design and estimand therefore come before the p-value.","takeaway":"A p-value inherits the question, design, null model and assumptions used to produce it.","formula":"H₀: μ = 0; H₁: μ ≠ 0","practice":{"question":"For a two-sided test of mean abnormal return, what does H₀: μ = 0 mean?","hint":"Identify μ and the units.","solution":"It is the reference claim that the population mean abnormal return is zero percentage points for the defined population, window and design."}},{"title":"Compute and interpret a p-value","body":"A test statistic puts an estimate on a scale of standard errors from the null value. Suppose an illustrative sample estimates a mean abnormal return of 2.4 percentage points with standard error 1.2 percentage points. With μ₀ = 0, the statistic is t = (2.4 − 0) / 1.2 = 2.0. In a simple normal approximation, a two-sided p-value is about 0.0455. The correct reading is: if the null model and its assumptions were true, results at least this extreme would occur about 4.55% of the time. It is not P(H₀ true), not the probability the result happened by chance, and not a 95.45% probability of causality.

Suppose an illustrative employment programme is estimated to raise an employment rate by 2.4 percentage points, with a standard error of 1.2 percentage points. If the null model says the effect is zero, the estimate is 2.4 ÷ 1.2 = 2 standard errors from zero. A two-sided p-value is the probability, assuming that null model and the test’s assumptions, of getting a test statistic at least this far from zero in either direction; a value near 0.046 is one possible result. The steps are: state the null, calculate the estimate’s distance from it in standard-error units, then measure how much of the null reference distribution is at least as extreme.

That 0.046 is not a 4.6% chance that the programme has no effect, and it says nothing by itself about whether a 2.4-point change is worth the cost. The interpretation also depends on the design, model and analysis being reported. If researchers tried many outcomes or specifications and show only the smallest p-value, the single-test calculation hides the search. Report the estimate, units, interval, design and analysis choices together. The ASA statement and NIST interpretation guide linked below explain why a threshold such as 0.05 is not a verdict.

The tail calculation becomes clearer when the statistic is treated as a distance, not a score for truth. Illustrative synthetic example: an estimated change in a default rate is −1.5 percentage points, with a standard error of 0.75 percentage points, under a zero-change null. Then t = (−1.5 − 0) / 0.75 = −2.0; for a two-sided test, both tails count, so the p-value is approximately 0.046 under a normal reference distribution. This says that results at least 2 standard errors from zero would occur about 4.6% of the time if the model were correct. It does not establish a causal reduction or account for unreported analyses. For a fuller treatment, see ‘American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values’ in the linked sources.

Consider two illustrative, synthetic evaluations with the same standardized mean difference, 0.30 SD units, but different sample sizes. Under H₀: effect = 0 and a two-sided normal reference, with n = 100 the lab’s calculation is z = 0.30 × √100 = 0.30 × 10 = 3.00, giving p = 2[1 − Φ(3.00)] ≈ 0.0027. With n = 25, it is z = 0.30 × √25 = 0.30 × 5 = 1.50, giving p ≈ 0.1336. Thus the estimated magnitude is unchanged, while the larger sample makes the same signal more precisely measured and therefore less compatible with the null model. The p-value has not become an effect-size measure: 0.30 SD still requires a substantive interpretation in the outcome’s original units and context. This comparison assumes independent observations and a suitable normal approximation. If observations are clustered—such as workers within firms—the nominal n can overstate information; standard errors should reflect that dependence, or the displayed p-values can be too small. These values are synthetic demonstrations, not observed evidence or causal estimates.

A standardized statistic is a distance with a sign, while a two-sided p-value uses distance in either direction. Consider a clearly labelled synthetic estimate that average processing time is 3 minutes below a null value of 0 difference, with standard error 1.5 minutes. The statistic is t = (−3 − 0) ÷ 1.5 = −2. The minus sign records the direction; the magnitude is 2 standard errors. Under a normal reference distribution, a two-sided p-value is about 0.046. Its conditional wording is essential: if the null model and assumptions held, results at least this far from zero would occur about 4.6% of the time. It is not the chance that the null is true.","takeaway":"The p-value is a conditional tail probability under H₀, not a probability assigned to H₀ itself.","formula":"t = (estimate − null value) / standard error","practice":{"question":"Using the example, calculate t when the estimate is 2.4 percentage points, μ₀ is 0 and the standard error is 1.2 percentage points.","hint":"Subtract the null value, then divide by the standard error.","solution":"t = (2.4 − 0) / 1.2 = 2.0. The units cancel because both numerator and denominator are percentage points."}},{"title":"Read intervals and effect size together","body":"A p-value gives one aspect of evidence; an estimate and interval show magnitude and uncertainty. Continuing the illustrative example, 2.4 percentage points ± 1.96 × 1.2 percentage points gives an approximate 95% interval from 0.048 to 4.752 percentage points under the normal approximation. That interval is compatible with a small positive effect and with a much larger one, so practical importance remains a substantive question. Compare it with a pre-specified materiality threshold, such as 1 percentage point, and report units. A result can be statistically detectable but too small to matter after fees, risk or implementation costs; a meaningful effect can be imprecisely estimated.

Illustrative synthetic example — Suppose a randomly assigned job-search support programme is evaluated using participants’ annual earnings 12 months after enrolment. The estimated difference between the offered and comparison groups is £600 per worker per year, with a standard error of £250. Relative to a zero-effect null, the test statistic is 600 ÷ 250 = 2.4, giving an approximate two-sided normal p-value of 0.016. A rough 95% interval is £600 ± 1.96 × £250, or about £110 to £1,090 per worker per year. The estimate is positive and the interval excludes zero, but it spans effects below and above a pre-specified practical benchmark of £500 per year. Thus the data are fairly incompatible with zero under this model, while the programme’s economically meaningful size remains uncertain.

An interval and p-value can describe sampling evidence and precision; they cannot alone establish that the programme caused the earnings difference, that the effect lasts beyond 12 months, or that benefits exceed delivery costs. A key check is whether assignment was genuinely random and whether attrition, clustering by training centre, or unequal follow-up could change the standard error or comparison; compare results with reasonable design-appropriate analyses. Avoid saying that p = 0.016 means a 1.6% chance the null is true, or that the interval has a 95% probability of containing the fixed effect. The “American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values” and “NIST — Use and Interpretation of P-Values” in the linked sources below explain these cautions.

A useful habit is to compare an interval with a decision-relevant benchmark in the same units. Illustrative synthetic example: a policy estimate is an additional 18 minutes of weekly exercise per participant, with a standard error of 10 minutes. An approximate 95% interval is 18 ± 1.96 × 10 = 18 ± 19.6 minutes, or about −1.6 to 37.6 minutes per week. The estimate is positive, but the interval includes almost no change and effects above half an hour. If the practical benchmark is 30 minutes per week, the interval crosses it, so the study does not pin down whether that target is reached. This evidence alone does not prove the policy caused exercise changes or that benefits exceed costs. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 7: Inference for Numerical Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example — Suppose an estimated price elasticity of demand is −0.40, with standard error 0.15. A normal-approximation 95% interval is −0.40 ± 1.96 × 0.15 = [−0.694, −0.106]. If a firm raises price by 5%, the local constant-elasticity approximation predicts quantity falling by 0.40 × 5% = 2.0%; the interval implies a fall between 0.106 × 5% = 0.53% and 0.694 × 5% = 3.47%. With synthetic baseline sales of 100,000 units per month at £20 each (£2,000,000 monthly revenue), the point prediction gives revenue of £20 × 1.05 × 100,000 × 0.98 = £2,058,000, a £58,000 increase. Using the interval endpoints, revenue ranges from £2,000,000 × 1.05 × 0.9653 = £2,027,130 to £2,000,000 × 1.05 × 0.9947 = £2,088,870 per month. This translation shows why a statistically informative elasticity still requires a demand-model assumption, stable customer mix, no competitor response, and a check that a 5% change is local enough; the interval does not guarantee realized revenue.

A small p-value can coexist with an effect too modest for a decision. Suppose a synthetic audit estimates that a reminder increases on-time payment by 0.4 percentage points, with standard error 0.1 points. The approximate 95% interval is 0.4 ± 1.96 × 0.1, or 0.204 to 0.596 percentage points. This interval excludes zero under the stated model, yet a policy threshold of 1 percentage point lies above its entire range. The statistical evidence is fairly precise about a small positive association, not evidence of reaching the operational target. If assignment was not randomized, the result remains non-causal. Report the outcome definition, units, interval, design, and threshold together rather than letting the p-value carry the conclusion.","takeaway":"Report direction, magnitude, interval width and practical thresholds—not only a significance label.","formula":"estimate ± critical value × standard error","practice":{"question":"Does the illustrative interval [0.048, 4.752] percentage points prove the effect is economically important?","hint":"Compare the interval with a meaningful threshold and consider costs.","solution":"No. It indicates uncertainty about a positive mean under the stated model, but importance requires a domain threshold, costs, risk and context."}},{"title":"Why 0.05 is not a cliff","body":"The ASA advises against treating statistical significance as a binary discovery switch. A p-value of 0.049 and one of 0.051 provide closely related evidence, not opposite truths. The cutoff α = 0.05 is a planning convention that, for a specified procedure, controls the long-run Type I error rate when H₀ is true; it does not measure effect size or truth. “Fail to reject” is not proof of no effect. A small p-value can reflect a tiny effect in a huge sample, while a practically important effect can have a wide interval in a small or noisy sample. Explain uncertainty continuously and avoid cliff language.

Treat nearby p-values as a graded evidential difference, then inspect magnitude and precision. Illustrative synthetic example: Study A estimates a wage gain of $0.20 per hour with p = 0.049; Study B estimates $0.21 per hour with p = 0.051. The estimates differ by only $0.01 per hour, and rounding or modest model changes could affect the displayed p-values. Calling A “real” and B “no effect” creates a discontinuity unsupported by those numbers. The dollar amounts are not automatically useful: over 160 work hours, $0.20 per hour corresponds to $0.20 × 160 = $32 per month before taxes, assuming that schedule. Neither p-value proves causality, and neither assesses the worker’s costs or long-run consequences. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Wasserstein, Schirm & Lazar (2019) — Moving to a World Beyond p < 0.05’ in the linked sources.

Use the lab’s standardized-effect control to see why precision, not just magnitude, moves a p-value. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a productivity assessment has a standard deviation of 20 points and an estimated difference of 0.30 SD, equivalent to 0.30 × 20 = 6 points. With n = 100 independent observations under the lab’s normal approximation, the null-model statistic is z = 0.30 × √100 = 3.00; a two-sided p-value is approximately 2[1 − Φ(3.00)] = 0.0027. Keeping the same estimated 6-point difference but using n = 25 gives z = 0.30 × √25 = 1.50 and p ≈ 0.1336. The estimate and its practical interpretation did not change; the smaller sample made random uncertainty larger. These calculations assume the standardized statistic is appropriate and observations provide the stated information; dependence, non-normality, or a biased comparison can invalidate the approximation. Even the smaller p-value would describe incompatibility with a zero-effect model, not proof that a program caused the productivity difference or that six points is economically worthwhile.

A threshold can simplify a decision rule without creating a discontinuity in the underlying evidence. Imagine two synthetic studies estimating the same waiting-time difference: Study A reports p = 0.049 and Study B p = 0.051. If their estimates and intervals are nearly identical, assigning “effect” to A and “no effect” to B exaggerates a tiny numerical distinction. The cutoff may be useful for a pre-specified action, but it does not measure magnitude, replicability, or practical value. A result just above 0.05 may reflect limited precision, while a result below it may describe a negligible change. Examine the estimate, interval, design, and analysis search. “American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values” supports this context-first interpretation.","takeaway":"Use thresholds for decisions only in context; do not turn 0.05 into a universal truth boundary.","practice":{"question":"What can a p-value above 0.05 mean besides “there is no effect”?","hint":"Think about precision and power.","solution":"The estimate may be imprecise, the sample may be small, noise may be high, or the design may be weak. Non-rejection is not proof that the effect is exactly zero."}},{"title":"Power, errors and study design","body":"Before collecting data, specify a practically meaningful effect, expected variability, sample size, α and the test direction. Type I error means rejecting a true H₀; Type II error means failing to reject a false H₀. Power is 1 − β, the probability of detecting a chosen alternative under the design. Larger samples, lower noise, larger effects and better measurements generally increase power, but power is not a guarantee for one study. A low-powered study may miss a meaningful effect, while a very large study can detect a negligible one. Design quality and measurement validity matter before arithmetic. A credible power calculation should also reflect attrition, clustering or repeated observations when those features are expected.

Power is easiest to communicate with a target effect and a probability scale. Illustrative synthetic example: before a survey, researchers define a meaningful improvement of 4 percentage points in the share completing training and plan a design with β = 0.20. Power = 1 − β = 1 − 0.20 = 0.80, or 80%, for detecting that specified 4-point improvement under the planned assumptions. It does not mean an 80% chance that the eventual estimate is correct. If only 60% of sampled people respond, the effective sample may be smaller and power may fall; nonresponse can also introduce bias that more observations do not automatically fix. The 4 percentage points describe a difference in rates, not a 4% relative increase. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 6: Inference for Categorical Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic planning example: suppose an economist wants to detect a standardized training effect of d = 0.50 SD with two equal-sized randomized groups, using a two-sided α = 0.05 test and 80% power. Under a normal approximation, the required number per arm is n = 2(z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀)²/d² = 2(1.96 + 0.842)²/0.50² = 62.8, so round up to 63 participants per arm (126 analyzed participants). If the analyst anticipates 20% attrition, enrollment should be ceil(63/0.80) = 79 per arm, or 158 total; rounding up matters because fractional people cannot be enrolled. This calculation treats the SD as known, assumes independent observations, equal allocation, a correctly specified outcome, and a normal approximation. Clustering, unequal variances, noncompliance, or a smaller true effect would require a larger or richer calculation. The p-value lab can show how a standardized effect and n change a two-sided tail area, but that tail area is not itself a guarantee that the planned study will achieve 80% power.

Power is tied to a particular alternative, so it is not one permanent attribute of a study. Suppose a synthetic two-group design plans to detect a 5-percentage-point difference in completion rates and has β = 0.25 under its assumed sample size and variability. Its power for that specified difference is 1 − 0.25 = 0.75, or 75%. For a smaller 2-point difference, the power would generally be lower; for a larger difference, generally higher, all else equal. Attrition can reduce effective information, while unequal group sizes can increase uncertainty. Neither 75% power nor a later non-significant result states the probability that a hypothesis is true. State the target effect, alpha, outcome scale, and design assumptions whenever reporting power.","takeaway":"Power concerns a specified effect and design; it is not the probability that a finding is true.","formula":"power = 1 − β; α = long-run Type I error rate under H₀","practice":{"question":"If β = 0.20 for a specified effect and design, what is the power?","hint":"Power is one minus β.","solution":"Power = 1 − 0.20 = 0.80, or 80%. This is conditional on the chosen effect, model, sample size and assumptions."}},{"title":"Multiplicity and the search process","body":"Testing many outcomes, firms, subgroups, event windows or model specifications changes the chance of a small p-value. Even if each test uses α = 0.05, a collection of tests can produce at least one apparently unusual result by chance. Optional stopping, trying alternatives and reporting only favorable results can make nominal error rates misleading. Pre-register primary outcomes, hypotheses, stopping rules and analysis choices when feasible. Disclose all tested analyses, distinguish confirmatory from exploratory work, and use a multiplicity method when the question requires control of family-wise error or false-discovery rate. Transparency lets readers judge how much search occurred before the headline result was selected.

Multiplicity can be shown with a simple probability calculation. Illustrative synthetic example: imagine 20 independent tests, each using a 5% cutoff, while every null hypothesis is actually true. The probability of no false positive is approximately 0.95^20 ≈ 0.358, so the probability of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.358 = 0.642, or about 64.2%. Independence is a simplifying assumption, and dependence can change the number, but searching still matters. If an analyst examines 20 monthly event windows and highlights the one with p = 0.04, that p-value describes the selected window’s calculation, not the whole search process. Disclosure, preregistration, or an appropriate adjustment is needed; the arithmetic does not prove every finding is false. For a fuller treatment, see ‘American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values’ in the linked sources.

A practical way to act on a disclosed search is the Holm step-down procedure. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose four pre-specified null hypotheses concern four different outcomes, and their valid two-sided p-values are 0.003, 0.018, 0.041 and 0.20. First sort them from smallest to largest, then compare the jth value with α/(m−j+1), using α = 0.05 and m = 4. The thresholds are 0.0125, 0.0167, 0.0250 and 0.0500: 0.003 passes the first comparison, but 0.018 exceeds 0.0167, so the step-down sequence stops and only the first hypothesis is rejected. This controls the family-wise error rate at 5% under the procedure’s assumptions, rather than pretending that four unadjusted 5% tests form one 5% decision rule. The calculation does not establish that the first outcome is economically important or causal: report its effect estimate, uncertainty, outcome units, design, and whether the family was defined before looking at results. If the outcomes were selected after seeing the data, adjustment alone cannot recreate preregistration or remove selection bias.

The family of tests must be defined before choosing how to address multiplicity. Suppose an analyst has one primary outcome and four secondary outcomes, each tested at a nominal 5% level. A reader should know whether the five questions form one confirmatory family, whether the secondary analyses were exploratory, and whether any outcome was selected after seeing results. Bonferroni’s simple illustration would compare each p-value with 0.05 ÷ 5 = 0.01 if strong family-wise control were desired, though other procedures may suit the goal and dependence structure. This adjustment does not repair biased sampling or a poor outcome definition. It changes how evidence is judged after a search. Preregistration and complete reporting make the search visible instead of hiding it.","takeaway":"A p-value is only as honest as the analysis search that produced it.","practice":{"question":"Why should an event study disclose that 20 windows were examined before one p-value was reported?","hint":"Consider selection and false discoveries.","solution":"Searching many windows increases the chance of finding a small p-value by chance. Disclosure supports appropriate interpretation and possible multiplicity adjustment."}},{"title":"Association, prediction and causality","body":"A p-value can quantify incompatibility with a null model for an association, but it cannot identify a causal mechanism by itself. Prediction asks how well an outcome can be anticipated for new cases; causality asks what would change under an intervention. Confounding, reverse causality, selection and time trends can create associations in financial data. Random assignment can support causal comparison for the assigned population; observational regression needs explicit identification assumptions. Report the target population, data-generating process, timing, missingness and robustness checks. A statistically detectable relationship may predict poorly out of sample, and a predictive relationship need not be causal or actionable.

Separate the unit of prediction from the unit of causal change. Illustrative synthetic example: across 100 synthetic firms, an observational regression finds that each additional 1 percentage point of quarterly sales growth is associated with 0.3 percentage points higher quarterly return. The arithmetic says a 2-point sales-growth difference corresponds to 0.3 × 2 = 0.6 percentage points of fitted return difference, not that changing sales growth would cause a 0.6-point return. Industry conditions could influence both variables, and an average association may predict poorly for a new firm. A causal claim would need a design or assumptions addressing confounding, timing and selection. The units are percentage points of return, not percent probability and not a guaranteed dollar gain. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST — Use and Interpretation of P-Values’ in the linked sources.

A useful prediction check is to freeze the model before looking at future outcomes. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a researcher uses eight earlier firms to fit next-quarter return from sales growth, then evaluates four later firms. The four model errors (predicted minus realized return) are 0.4, −0.6, 0.8 and −0.2 percentage points, so the test-set mean squared error is (0.4² + (−0.6)² + 0.8² + (−0.2)²)/4 = 1.20/4 = 0.30 pp², and RMSE is √0.30 = 0.55 pp. A simple benchmark that predicts the training-period mean has errors 0.7, −1.1, 1.0 and −0.9 pp: MSE = 3.51/4 = 0.8775 pp² and RMSE ≈ 0.94 pp. The model therefore improves this small synthetic test by about 0.39 pp of RMSE, a predictive result—not evidence that sales growth causes returns. A time-ordered split avoids using future information; repeated periods are needed to assess stability, and trading costs or decision thresholds determine whether a 0.39 pp improvement is economically useful.

The same coefficient can be useful for prediction while remaining unsuitable for a causal story. Imagine a synthetic credit model in which a one-point increase in an observed risk score is associated with a 0.6-percentage-point increase in default probability. For a borrower whose score is 5 points higher, the fitted difference is 5 × 0.6 = 3 percentage points, assuming linearity and the observed range. That is a predicted contrast between cases, not the change caused by raising one borrower’s score. Income, debt, and lender selection may influence both score and default. Predictive validation asks whether forecasts work for new cases; causal identification asks about interventions and counterfactuals. A p-value addresses model compatibility, not either question by itself.","takeaway":"Statistical evidence, prediction and causal claims answer different questions and require different support.","practice":{"question":"Does p = 0.03 for an event-study coefficient prove the disclosure caused the return?","hint":"Separate model compatibility from identification.","solution":"No. It is evidence against the specified null under the event-study assumptions. Causality requires a credible design and assumptions that address confounding and timing."}},{"title":"Beyond statistical significance: transparent conclusions","body":"A responsible conclusion combines the estimate, units, interval, p-value, design, assumptions, analysis search and practical threshold. State what was planned, what was exploratory, which outcomes were missing and whether results are robust to reasonable alternatives. The ASA principles emphasize that scientific conclusions should not depend only on crossing a threshold, that p-values do not measure the probability a hypothesis is true, and that context and transparency matter. Connect evidence to uncertainty and decision consequences without presenting a financial recommendation. “Beyond Statistical Significance” is a useful theme here: the goal is richer reasoning, not replacing one ritual with another. Readers should be able to audit the path from question to conclusion.

A transparent conclusion can be written as a compact audit trail. Illustrative synthetic example: a randomized pilot estimates a reduction of 6 percentage points in missed appointments, with a 95% interval from −11 to −1 percentage points and p = 0.02. Report the outcome unit, follow-up period, assignment rule, missing-data handling and whether this was the pre-specified primary outcome. The interval suggests reductions from 1 to 11 percentage points are compatible with the analysis, while the sign convention must be stated clearly. It does not show that savings exceed programme costs, that the effect persists after six months, or that the result generalizes to other clinics. A reader should also see exploratory outcomes and deviations from plan, rather than only the favorable headline. For a fuller treatment, see ‘American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a pre-specified evaluation estimates a standardized outcome difference from n = 25 independent units, with the outcome expressed in standard-deviation units. Assume the simple normal approximation used by the lab is reasonable under a null of zero difference. First compute the standard error as 1/√25 = 0.20 SD; then z = 0.30/0.20 = 1.50. A two-sided null tail is approximately p = 2[1 − Φ(1.50)] = 0.134, so this sample does not make the estimate unusual at α = 0.05. The approximate 95% interval is 0.30 ± 1.96(0.20) = [−0.092, 0.692] SD. That range includes a small negative effect, no effect, and a potentially meaningful positive effect; it therefore signals imprecision, not proof of no difference. Before changing policy, report the estimand, unit of analysis, missing outcomes, and whether the normal/independence assumptions hold. If assignment was observational, this uncertainty calculation still describes an association under the model, not a causal effect.

A transparent conclusion should allow a reader to reconstruct the claim from the reported quantities. For a synthetic evaluation, write: “The assigned message changed enrollment by 3 percentage points over three months; the 95% interval was −1 to 7 points, and the primary outcome was pre-specified.” Then state attrition, assignment, missing outcomes, and whether the analysis was exploratory. The interval includes a small decrease, no change, and a moderate increase, so the evidence is not precise about direction or practical size. If assignment was credible, the design supports an intention-to-treat interpretation for the eligible population; it still does not establish persistence or financial benefit. This reporting style is richer than “significant” or “not significant” and keeps each claim calibrated.","takeaway":"Transparent, effect-focused reporting is more informative than a binary p < 0.05 claim.","formula":"Evidence report = estimate + interval + p-value + design + assumptions + practical context"}]
data.case_study: Consider an illustrative event study of a new disclosure format and a diversified firm's 3-day abnormal return. The analyst pre-specifies H₀: μ = 0 percentage points, a two-sided alternative, a market-adjustment model, a 3-day window and a materiality threshold of 1 percentage point. The sample estimate is 2.4 percentage points with a standard error of 1.2, giving t = 2.0 and an approximate two-sided p-value of 0.0455; the approximate 95% interval is [0.048, 4.752] percentage points. This is not a 95.45% probability that the disclosure caused the return. The interval spans effects below and above the practical threshold, so economic importance remains uncertain. The analyst should disclose whether other windows, firms, outcomes or specifications were tried, account for multiplicity where appropriate, and report missing events and robustness checks. Without randomization or a credible identification strategy, the result is an association under a model, not proof of causality. The numbers are simulated for teaching, not a historical dataset, forecast or investment advice.
data.misconceptions:
p = 0.03 means a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true, or a 97% chance the alternative is true. The p-value is calculated conditional on the null model and assumptions.
p < 0.05 proves an important, useful or causal effect, while p > 0.05 proves no effect. Thresholds do not measure magnitude, practical importance or identification, and non-rejection may reflect low power.
A large sample or narrow interval fixes bias. More observations can reduce random uncertainty but cannot repair selection, confounding, bad measurement or a misspecified design.
Trying many outcomes, windows or specifications leaves the false-positive risk unchanged. Multiplicity, selective reporting and optional stopping can make nominal error rates misleading.
A statistically significant association is automatically a good prediction or investment opportunity. Association, prediction, causality and decision usefulness are distinct claims.

data.title: Regression for Economic Questions
data.excerpt: Regression summarizes how an outcome changes with one or more measured factors, while accounting for the other factors included in the model. Learn to interpret coefficients and predictions, check how well a model fits, and see why a relationship is not automatically a cause—with examples such as wages, prices and policy outcomes.
data.objectives:
Interpret intercepts and slopes in the units of the response and predictor.
Calculate fitted values and residuals, and use diagnostic plots to assess linearity, variance, dependence, leverage and outliers.
Distinguish association, prediction and causal interpretation in financial regression.
Compare confidence intervals for mean responses with prediction intervals for individual outcomes.
Evaluate statistical evidence with effect size, uncertainty, validation performance and practical importance rather than R-squared alone.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Start with a question, units and a fitted line","body":"Regression asks how an outcome changes on average with a predictor. In the simple model, ŷ = b₀ + b₁x, ŷ is the fitted response, x is the predictor, b₀ is the intercept and b₁ is the slope. The slope's units are response units per predictor unit; the intercept is the fitted response when x = 0, which may be outside the useful data range. For an illustrative dataset, x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 2, 3, 5, least squares gives approximately ŷ = 0.33 + 1.50x. At x = 4, the fitted value is 6.33 response units. These numbers are simulated for teaching, not historical evidence.

Read a fitted line as a compact summary of the sample, not as a rule for every person. Imagine a teaching model for weekly earnings: predicted pay = £300 + £25 × years of schooling. At 12 years the model predicts £300 + 12 × £25 = £600; at 13 years it predicts £625. The slope, £25 per year, is the model’s average difference in predicted pay for a one-year difference in schooling over the data being modelled. The £300 intercept is the model’s predicted value at zero years; if the data contain no such cases, it may be only a mathematical anchor rather than a useful real-world prediction.

The line describes a conditional average, so individual people can earn more or less; their residual is observed pay minus predicted pay. A straight-line summary can miss curves, and predictions far outside the observed schooling range are extrapolations. Most importantly, people with more schooling may also differ in family background, prior opportunity or other factors, so the slope is not automatically the causal payoff to an extra year. Check residuals and the sample range, and use a credible design for causal claims. See the NIST regression references and Angrist & Pischke Chapter 3 linked below.

Before fitting, identify what one row represents and keep the time unit fixed. Suppose a synthetic sample records quarterly household spending in dollars and hours worked per week: a fitted line is spending = 420 dollars + 18 dollars per weekly hour. For a household working 30 hours, the arithmetic is 420 dollars + (18 dollars/hour × 30 hours) = 960 dollars per quarter. Raising hours from 30 to 32 changes the fitted value by 2 × 18 = 36 dollars per quarter, not 36 percent. This is an average comparison within the observed range, assuming the linear summary is reasonable and measurements are comparable. It does not show that adding work hours causes spending to rise; income, household size, and other factors may differ. For an introduction to fitting and interpreting a linear regression, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 8: Introduction to Linear Regression’ in the linked sources.

Consider a new illustrative, synthetic fund example with the fitted line ŷ = 0.20 pp + 0.80 (fund pp per market pp) × x, where x is the market’s monthly excess return. If the market return is 1.50%, use percentage points consistently: x = 1.50 pp. The fitted fund excess return is 0.20 pp + 0.80 × 1.50 pp = 1.40 pp. If the synthetic observed fund return is 2.10 pp, its residual is observed minus fitted = 2.10 pp − 1.40 pp = +0.70 pp; the fund exceeded the line’s conditional average for that month. For a market return of −1.00 pp, the fitted value is 0.20 − 0.80 = −0.60 pp, not −0.60%. Thus the slope implies a fitted change of 0.80 pp for each 1 pp change in the market, while the intercept is evaluated at zero market excess return. This assumes both series use the same monthly window and definitions. A residual is unexplained sample deviation, not evidence of a causal mechanism or a reliable next-month forecast; serial dependence, omitted factors and changing volatility may still matter.

A fitted line is easiest to audit when both slope and intercept are translated into the row’s units. Suppose a synthetic model predicts monthly savings in dollars from commute distance in kilometres: ŷ = 120 − 4x. At x = 15 kilometres, ŷ = 120 − 60 = 60 dollars per month. The slope says that a one-kilometre difference corresponds to 4 fewer dollars in fitted savings, on average, within the modelled range; it does not say every commuter changes by exactly that amount. The intercept predicts 120 dollars at zero kilometres, which may be outside the observed data and need not describe a real household. Keep the time period and observational unit visible before interpreting any coefficient.","takeaway":"Name the observational unit, time window and units before interpreting a coefficient.","formula":"ŷ = b₀ + b₁x; b₀ = intercept, b₁ = slope, x = predictor, ŷ = fitted outcome.","practice":{"question":"Using ŷ = 0.33 + 1.50x, what is the fitted outcome when x = 4, and what are its units?","hint":"Substitute x = 4 and keep the response-unit-per-predictor-unit meaning of the slope visible.","solution":"ŷ = 0.33 + 1.50(4) = 6.33, so the fitted outcome is about 6.33 response units. It is a model average, not a guaranteed observation."}},{"title":"Calculate residuals and read what they leave behind","body":"A residual is the observed outcome minus its fitted value: eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ, where yᵢ is observation i and eᵢ is its unexplained remainder under the model. If an observed value is 5.00 and the fitted value is 4.83, the residual is +0.17 response units; the model under-predicted that case. Residual plots should be checked against fitted values, predictors and time order. A curved band suggests nonlinearity, a funnel suggests changing variance, and runs in time suggest dependence. A large residual is not automatically an error: investigate measurement, unusual conditions and influence before deleting it. Least squares minimizes the sum of squared residuals, so extreme residuals receive disproportionate weight.

Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data; monthly units): suppose a simple model uses a town’s average bus fare in January, February and March to predict monthly passenger trips per 1,000 residents. The fitted equation is predicted trips = 12,000 − 300 × fare, where fare is measured in pounds per ride and predicted trips are rides per month. In February, the fare is £2.00 and the observed total is 11,600 rides per 1,000 residents. The fitted value is 12,000 − 300(2.00) = 11,400 rides, so the residual is observed minus fitted = 11,600 − 11,400 = +200 rides per 1,000 residents. The positive residual means February had more trips than this line predicts; it does not by itself explain why.

Use residuals to assess what the fitted line leaves behind, not to prove a policy effect. A useful diagnostic is a residual plot against fitted values, fare or calendar month: a curved pattern suggests that a straight line misses nonlinearity, a funnel shape suggests changing variance, and runs across months may indicate dependence. The calculation also assumes the recorded outcome and fare are measured consistently and that the model form is reasonable over the observed fare range. A common mistake is to call a positive residual a causal impact of cheaper transport; it is only an observed-minus-predicted difference under this model. For diagnostic guidance, see “NIST — Residual Diagnostics” in the linked sources below.

A residual can be compared across cases only when its outcome units are clear. Consider synthetic weekly forecasts of electricity demand in megawatt-hours (MWh): the model predicts 1,250 MWh for week 6, while actual recorded demand is 1,310 MWh. Thus e = 1,310 MWh − 1,250 MWh = +60 MWh, meaning demand exceeded the fitted value by 60 MWh. If another week has a −60 MWh residual, the magnitudes match but the signs show opposite errors. Plotting these residuals in calendar order can reveal a pattern: four positive errors in a row may indicate an omitted seasonal effect. The calculation assumes the same demand definition and forecast horizon for both numbers. It does not identify the cause of the miss or prove a policy effect. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST — Residual Diagnostics’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data): standardizing a residual can make its unusualness comparable across periods with different typical error sizes. Suppose a model predicts a retailer’s weekly online orders as 2,400 orders and the observed total is 2,520, so e = 2,520 − 2,400 = +120 orders. If comparable residuals have an estimated residual standard deviation of 80 orders, the rough standardized residual is 120/80 = +1.5 SD. A second week might have a smaller raw miss—560 observed versus 500 fitted, e = +60 orders—but a residual SD of only 20 orders, giving +60/20 = +3.0 SD; diagnostically, that second miss is more unusual relative to its local noise. First verify that both forecasts use the same horizon and order definition, then inspect the corresponding predictor, calendar position and leverage. This scaling is not a new causal effect or a license to delete a point: residual spread may vary with fitted level, and high-leverage observations can make a fitted line and its residual scale look deceptively reassuring. Treat the numbers as a screening aid, then investigate the data-generating conditions.

Residual signs help diagnose direction, but patterns require looking across observations. Suppose a synthetic model predicts 48 MWh of daily demand and the recorded value is 45 MWh; e = 45 − 48 = −3 MWh, so the model over-predicted by 3 MWh. If the next four cold days all have negative residuals, the run may indicate that temperature, seasonality, or another feature is missing. A single negative residual does not identify which cause matters. In a residual-versus-fitted plot, a widening cloud suggests nonconstant variance, while a curved band suggests a missing nonlinear component. Inspect the measurement definition and calendar order before changing the model or deleting observations. A diagnostic pattern is evidence about model adequacy, not causal evidence.","takeaway":"Residuals reveal systematic structure that the chosen regression form has not captured.","formula":"eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ; eᵢ = residual for observation i, yᵢ = observed outcome, ŷᵢ = fitted outcome.","practice":{"question":"An observed monthly return is 1.2% and its fitted return is 0.8%. What is the residual?","hint":"Subtract fitted from observed, retaining percentage-point units.","solution":"e = 1.2% − 0.8% = +0.4 percentage points. The positive sign means the observation was above the model's fitted value."}},{"title":"Measure fit without mistaking R-squared for truth","body":"R-squared summarizes the fraction of in-sample variation around the outcome mean that the fitted model reduces under its definition. A common form is R² = 1 − SSE/SST, where SSE is the sum of squared residuals and SST is the total sum of squared deviations from the sample mean. If SSE = 12 and SST = 20 in an illustrative exercise, R² = 1 − 12/20 = 0.40, or 40%. That does not mean 40% of a future outcome is guaranteed, that the model is correctly specified, or that the relationship is causal. R-squared can rise when variables are added, even if prediction does not improve. Report effect sizes, uncertainty and out-of-sample error too.

R-squared is dimensionless, so it should not be described as 0.40 dollars or 40 percentage points. With synthetic annual-income data, suppose SST = 500,000,000 dollar-squared and SSE = 350,000,000 dollar-squared. Then R² = 1 − 350,000,000/500,000,000 = 1 − 0.70 = 0.30, or 30 percent. The model explains 30 percent of the in-sample squared variation around the sample mean under this calculation; the remaining 70 percent is not a claim that each person is predicted 70 percent incorrectly. A second model might reach R² = 0.35 yet make worse future predictions if it overfits. Interpretation assumes the sums use the same sample and outcome scale. R-squared does not establish causal impact, unbiased forecasts, or practical value. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 8: Introduction to Linear Regression (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.

To test whether fit travels beyond the estimation sample, use a held-out benchmark rather than reading the plotted line as a promise. Suppose six synthetic monthly fund excess returns (in percentage points) are 2, −1, 3, 0, −2, and 1, while a model’s illustrative predictions are 1, 0, 2, 1, −1, and 2. The prediction errors are 1, −1, 1, −1, −1, and −1 pp, so the test SSE is 6 pp² and the test RMSE is √(6/6) = 1 pp per month. A mean-only benchmark predicts the held-out mean, (2 − 1 + 3 + 0 − 2 + 1)/6 = 0.5 pp; its squared deviations sum to 17.5 pp². A test-set R² defined as 1 − SSE_model/SSE_mean is therefore 1 − 6/17.5 = 0.657, or 65.7%. This is a relative score on these six synthetic observations, not a causal effect or a guaranteed future accuracy rate. With a tiny holdout, one unusual month can change it sharply; choose the split chronologically when forecasting time-ordered returns and do not tune the model using the test values.

R-squared can be calculated correctly and still answer only a narrow question. Suppose a synthetic model has SST = 80,000 dollar² and SSE = 52,000 dollar² on the same 40 observations. Then R² = 1 − 52,000 ÷ 80,000 = 1 − 0.65 = 0.35, or 35%. This dimensionless value summarizes in-sample reduction in squared variation relative to predicting the sample mean. It does not say that each prediction is 35% accurate, nor that 35% of a future household’s income is explained. Compare models using held-out errors and inspect residuals; adding predictors can increase in-sample R² without improving new-case predictions. The coefficient units, uncertainty, data-generating process, and causal design remain separate from this fit statistic.","takeaway":"R-squared is an in-sample summary, not a certificate of correctness, causality or future performance.","formula":"R² = 1 − SSE/SST; SSE = squared residual sum, SST = total squared deviation from the sample mean."},{"title":"Separate mean-response uncertainty from prediction","body":"A confidence interval for the mean response describes uncertainty about the average outcome at a chosen predictor value, while a prediction interval describes where one new individual outcome may fall. The latter is wider because it includes both uncertainty in the estimated mean and the new observation's residual variation. For an illustrative forecast at x = 4, suppose the fitted mean is 6.33 units, its 95% confidence interval is 5.80–6.86, and the 95% prediction interval is 3.90–8.76. These are simulated teaching numbers, not a forecast of an asset. State the confidence level, sampling or time-series assumptions, model specification and data range. Do not extrapolate casually beyond observed x values.

Use the interval type that matches the decision. Suppose synthetic data give a fitted mean monthly revenue of 80,000 dollars for stores receiving 10 advertisements, with a 95% confidence interval of 78,000–82,000 dollars. This concerns the average revenue for comparable stores at that advertising level. A 95% prediction interval of 60,000–100,000 dollars concerns one new store and is wider because store-specific variation is included. The midpoint is 80,000 dollars; its half-width is 20,000 dollars, versus 2,000 dollars for the mean interval. These dollar units refer to one month, not an annual total. The interpretation assumes a suitable model, representative sampling, and stable conditions; 95% does not mean this interval has a 95% chance after calculation. Neither interval proves advertising causes revenue. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 501 — Regression Inference and Prediction Intervals (Lesson 7)’ in the linked sources.

Consider a synthetic weekly-sales regression in which the fitted mean at a discount level observed in the data is 142 units per week. Suppose the residual standard error is 18 units per week, the leverage for this predictor value is h = 0.10, and a teaching approximation uses t = 2.1 for a 95% interval. The confidence interval for the mean is computed as 142 ± 2.1 × 18 × √0.10 = 142 ± 11.95, or approximately 130.0–154.0 units per week. For one new store-week, add the new-outcome noise through √(1 + h): 142 ± 2.1 × 18 × √1.10 = 142 ± 39.64, giving approximately 102.4–181.6 units per week. Thus the prediction interval is wider by design, not because the fitted average changed. This calculation assumes independent, similarly distributed errors and a correctly specified linear mean; seasonality, store differences, or changing variance could make the stated coverage unreliable. The discount coefficient would still be an association unless a credible design supports a causal claim, and the interval should not be used for discount levels outside the observed range.

The difference between the two interval types is a difference in the question, not merely a formatting choice. Suppose a synthetic model gives an average weekly demand of 500 units at a chosen input. A 95% confidence interval for the mean might be 490–510 units, describing the average of comparable cases. A 95% prediction interval for one new case might be 380–620 units because individual demand includes residual variation around that mean. The prediction interval is wider even when the average is estimated precisely. Neither interval should be read as a probability statement about fixed endpoints after calculation, and neither is automatically causal. Confirm the input lies within the observed range, identify the forecast horizon, and select the interval that matches the decision.","takeaway":"Ask whether uncertainty concerns an average response or one new observation; the intervals answer different questions.","formula":"Prediction uncertainty = mean-estimate uncertainty + new-observation noise; exact interval formulas depend on the fitted model."},{"title":"Validate predictions on data the model did not see","body":"A model can fit its training sample yet fail on new periods. Split observations by a defensible design: for time-ordered finance data, train on earlier dates and test on later dates rather than randomly shuffling away temporal structure. Compare test-set metrics such as mean absolute error, which averages absolute prediction errors in outcome units, or root mean squared error, which emphasizes large errors. Inspect whether performance changes across calm and stressed periods. Cross-validation can help tune a model, but repeated tuning against the same test set leaks information. Include fees, timestamps, missingness and the information actually available at prediction time; a good score is not evidence of causality.

For a time-ordered test, calculate errors using only information available before each forecast. Suppose three synthetic test-month sales outcomes are 100, 120, and 80 units, while predictions are 90, 130, and 70 units. Absolute errors are |100−90| = 10, |120−130| = 10, and |80−70| = 10 units, so MAE = (10 + 10 + 10)/3 = 10 units per month. A random split could accidentally let a later market regime influence training, making this score look safer than a chronological test. The metric is on the outcome scale, so it is not 10 percent unless the outcome itself is defined as a percent. This comparison assumes test outcomes are measured consistently. Low MAE shows predictive performance in that test setting, not causality or guaranteed future accuracy. For residual diagnostics and validation practice, see ‘NIST — Residual Diagnostics’ in the linked sources.

A useful second check is to compare a model with a simple benchmark at each chronological forecast origin. Consider four illustrative, synthetic monthly fund excess returns (in percentage points), observed as 0.8, −0.2, 1.4, and −0.5. Suppose forecasts made without using the current month are 0.2, 0.2, 0.4, and −0.3, giving errors y − ŷ of 0.6, −0.4, 1.0, and −0.2 pp. The model’s MAE is (0.6 + 0.4 + 1.0 + 0.2)/4 = 0.55 pp, while its RMSE is √[(0.6² + (−0.4)² + 1.0² + (−0.2)²)/4] = √0.39 ≈ 0.62 pp. A zero-excess-return benchmark has MAE (0.8 + 0.2 + 1.4 + 0.5)/4 = 0.725 pp and RMSE √0.7225 = 0.85 pp, so this tiny test favors the model on both metrics. That comparison is descriptive, not proof of persistence: four months cannot characterize regimes, and the forecast must be formed before outcomes are known. If the decision concerns investable returns, evaluate net-of-fee outcomes separately; lower forecast error does not automatically imply profitable or causal trading advice.

A validation metric needs a denominator, a time ordering, and an outcome unit. Suppose a synthetic chronological test has actual values 50, 70, and 90 units, while predictions are 55, 65, and 84. Absolute errors are 5, 5, and 6 units, so MAE = (5 + 5 + 6) ÷ 3 = 16 ÷ 3 ≈ 5.33 units per test case. This score describes those held-out cases, not a 5.33% error unless the outcome is measured in percent. Training on later observations before testing earlier ones can leak information in time-ordered settings. Repeatedly tuning against the test set also turns it into a development sample. Chronological validation, timestamp discipline, and regime checks make the predictive claim more credible, but they do not establish causality.","takeaway":"Out-of-sample validation estimates predictive usefulness, while design and assumptions determine whether causal claims are credible.","formula":"MAE = (1/n)Σ|yᵢ − ŷᵢ|; n = number of test cases, yᵢ = observed outcome, ŷᵢ = prediction."},{"title":"Association, prediction and causality in a finance example","body":"Consider a deliberately illustrative regression of a diversified fund's monthly excess return on the market's monthly excess return. With market returns −2%, 0%, 2% and fund returns −3%, 1%, 2%, both sample means are 0 percentage points. The sample covariance is 5 percentage-points-squared and market variance is 4, so the slope (often called beta) is b₁ = 5/4 = 1.25 fund percentage points per market percentage point. This tiny simulated sample shows co-movement, not a trading rule. Omitted exposures, fees, changing regimes and measurement choices remain. A regression association may help prediction, but changing the market is not a randomized intervention; causal interpretation needs design or strong identification assumptions.

In a synthetic example, a fund’s monthly excess return is 1 percentage point when the market’s excess return is 2 percentage points, and the fitted intercept is 0 percentage points with beta 0.8 fund percentage points per market percentage point. The fitted fund return is 0 + 0.8 × 2 = 1.6 percentage points, so the residual is 1.0 − 1.6 = −0.6 percentage points. The negative residual is a model error for that month, not a loss caused by the market. Beta summarizes average association over the chosen sample and may change with fees, exposures, or regimes. It does not say that forcing the market up by 1 percentage point would cause the fund to rise 0.8 points. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 3, §§3.1–3.2.3’ in the linked sources.

Suppose, purely illustratively, that a fitted monthly-return model is y-hat = 0.30 + 0.70x, where both fund excess return y and market excess return x are percentage points and the sample mean of x is 0. An illustrative month with x = 1.5 pp therefore has a fitted fund excess return of 0.30 + (0.70)(1.5) = 1.35 pp. To separate uncertainty about an average response from uncertainty for one fund return, assume the residual standard deviation is 1.50 pp, there are n = 36 months, and the centered predictor sum of squares is Sxx = 48 pp². The standard error for the mean response at x = 1.5 is 1.50√[1/36 + 1.5²/48] = 0.41 pp, giving an illustrative 95% mean-response interval of 1.35 ± 1.96(0.41), or 0.55 to 2.15 pp. For one future month, include the extra 1 inside the square root: 1.50√[1 + 1/36 + 1.5²/48] = 1.56 pp, so the approximate prediction interval is −1.70 to 4.40 pp. These calculations assume independent, constant-variance, approximately normal residuals; they describe association and prediction, not a causal market intervention, and can fail under regime changes or extrapolation.

The regression lab’s coral line is a least-squares fit to simulated points, and the implementation labels the chart as association only. Increasing the noise control spreads observations around the line; increasing sample size adds more simulated observations, but neither control turns the line into a causal estimate. Read the slope as fund percentage points per market percentage point for the generated sample, then inspect how much vertical scatter remains. A point far from the line is a large residual, not proof of a trading opportunity or market impact. Because the data are simulated, the display cannot support a historical claim. Even real finance data would require attention to omitted factors, fees, timing, changing regimes, and out-of-sample performance before prediction or causal language.","takeaway":"A coefficient can summarize historical association or aid prediction without proving what would happen under an intervention.","formula":"b₁ = Cov(x,y)/Var(x); Cov = joint variation, Var = predictor variation, b₁ = slope in outcome units per x unit.","practice":{"question":"In the illustrative example, what does beta = 1.25 mean, and what does it not prove?","hint":"Use the percentage-point units and distinguish association from intervention effects.","solution":"Within this tiny simulated sample and model, a 1 percentage-point market move is associated with 1.25 fund percentage points on average. It does not prove a causal effect or guarantee persistence."}},{"title":"Conditional averages are not automatically causal","body":"Ordinary least squares is a best linear summary of observed conditional averages for the regressors and sample that were chosen. The conditional mean E[Y | X = x] may be curved even when a straight line is used to approximate it. A causal interpretation needs an identification argument beyond the regression calculation. Timing matters for controls: adjusting for a post-treatment mediator can remove part of an effect, while conditioning on a collider can create a spurious path. A good fit to observed averages does not supply the missing counterfactual.

A conditional average compares observations that share predictor values; it does not automatically construct a counterfactual. Suppose a synthetic wage model compares workers with and without training while controlling for age. The fitted conditional mean is 24 dollars per hour for trained workers and 21 dollars per hour for comparable untrained workers, a difference of 24 − 21 = 3 dollars per hour. The figure is an association in hourly wage units. Motivated workers may seek training, leaving motivation as an omitted factor, so the 3-dollar difference need not be the causal effect of training. Conditioning on a post-training variable could remove part of an effect. Causal interpretation requires assumptions about selection and timing; fit alone is insufficient. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 05: Linear Regression (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

Consider a synthetic, illustrative policy example in which firms either claim an investment tax credit or do not, and the outcome is next-year investment growth in percentage points. Among credit claimants, 70% are high-prior-growth firms (20 pp average growth) and 30% are low-prior-growth firms (6 pp); among nonclaimants, the shares are 30% and 70%, with corresponding averages of 18 pp and 5 pp. The raw conditional-group gap is therefore [0.70(20) + 0.30(6)] − [0.30(18) + 0.70(5)] = 15.8 − 8.9 = 6.9 percentage points. To compare like with like, apply a common 50–50 high/low mix: the standardized claimant mean is 0.5(20) + 0.5(6) = 13 pp, and the standardized nonclaimant mean is 0.5(18) + 0.5(5) = 11.5 pp, leaving 1.5 percentage points. This change shows how composition can explain much of a conditional average difference; it does not identify the tax credit’s causal effect. The calculation assumes the two prior-growth strata are measured comparably, but unmeasured investment expectations or industry shocks could remain. A credible causal claim would need design or additional identification assumptions, not merely the adjusted gap.

Controls must be classified by timing and role, not collected indiscriminately. Suppose a synthetic training programme affects certification, and certification affects wages. If certification is included as a control after training, part of the programme’s pathway may be removed from the comparison. A different variable, such as motivation, may precede both training and wages and help block confounding if measured adequately. Conditioning on a collider—an outcome of two otherwise separate causes—can instead create a misleading association. The fitted conditional mean remains an observed comparison unless the identifying assumptions justify a counterfactual interpretation. Draw the proposed arrows, label variables as pre-treatment or post-treatment, and explain why each adjustment belongs. A high fit statistic cannot decide this causal question.","takeaway":"Regression summarizes conditional averages; design and control timing determine whether a coefficient is causal.","formula":"E[Y | X = x] is an observed conditional mean; it equals a causal response only under additional assumptions."}]
data.case_study: An educational analyst regresses a diversified fund's monthly excess return on the market's monthly excess return over a clearly defined historical window. The slope, often called beta, describes average co-movement in fund percentage points per market percentage point; the intercept describes the fitted fund excess return when market excess return is zero. The analyst reports coefficient intervals, plots residuals against fitted values and time, checks changing volatility and influential observations, and compares chronological held-out prediction errors. If the market coefficient is statistically detectable, that still does not establish that market movements caused each fund return, that the effect is economically useful after fees, or that it will persist. A small illustrative or simulated dataset can teach the arithmetic but cannot support historical claims. Limitations include omitted factors, benchmark choice, nonstationary regimes, serial dependence, selection, data revisions and look-ahead bias. The exercise supports statistical reasoning, not investment advice or a forecast.
data.misconceptions:
A high R-squared proves the model is right, causal or useful out of sample. It is only an in-sample fit summary under a particular calculation.
A statistically significant slope is automatically economically large or practically useful. Effect size, units, uncertainty, costs and context still matter.
A nonsignificant slope proves the true association is zero. It may reflect limited precision, high noise, low power or a misspecified model.
A fitted line predicts every next point closely. Individual outcomes vary, prediction intervals are wider, and extrapolation can be fragile.
Normal residuals or a good fit establish causation. Causal claims require design and identification assumptions beyond regression output.

The slope is expressed in outcome units per predictor unit and is conditional on the data, model and period used."}
