data.title: Causal Inference, Experiments & Confounding
data.excerpt: Causal inference asks what would have happened to the same people, places or firms under a different policy or treatment. Compare experiments and observational designs, use counterfactual reasoning, and identify the assumptions needed before a difference between groups can be called an effect.
data.objectives:
Explain why association and prediction alone cannot identify a causal effect.
Define counterfactuals, treatment effects and estimands in clear financial examples.
Use random assignment, DAGs and adjustment rules to reason about confounding, mediators and colliders.
Evaluate difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity and instrumental-variable designs through their assumptions.
Separate identification, uncertainty, statistical evidence, practical importance and generalization.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Association is not the missing counterfactual","body":"A causal question asks what would happen to the same unit under two alternatives, such as receiving a budgeting message versus not receiving it. We can observe only one of those potential outcomes for each customer; the unobserved outcome is the counterfactual. A difference in average returns or enrollment is an association until a design makes the comparison credible. Confounding, reverse causality, selection and chance can all create a pattern. Random sampling mainly supports generalization to a population; random assignment mainly supports comparable treatment groups. Define the unit, treatment, outcome, time window and target population before calculating an effect in context.

A useful way to see the problem is to imagine a job-training programme. In an illustrative record, people who attended later earn £25,000 on average and people who did not attend earn £22,000, a raw gap of £3,000. That is a real difference between the observed groups, but it is not yet the programme effect. People who chose training may already have had more time, support or motivation. For each trainee, the key missing comparison is what that same person would have earned at the same time without training.

Causal inference defines the target first—for example, the average effect of offering training to eligible jobseekers—then asks which design can estimate the missing alternative. Random assignment, a policy threshold or a defensible comparison over time can help, but each relies on different assumptions and may answer a different population-level question. A regression adjustment cannot prove those assumptions just by including many variables. The Penn State notes on bias and confounding and the World Bank DIME causal-inference materials linked below give more examples.

An association can persist even when the proposed treatment has no effect. Illustrative synthetic example: among 500 customers, 150 who use a budgeting app save £40 per month, while 350 non-users save £30 per month. The observed difference is £40 − £30 = £10 per month. That £10 is a group contrast, not the amount the same users would have saved without the app. Suppose app users were already saving £8 more per month before download; a simple before-treatment comparison would leave only £2 per month as a rough residual, though changing prices or habits could still matter. The comparison requires a credible design and a defined month. It does not establish causation or persistence. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 507 — Bias and Confounding’ in the linked sources.

Suppose an analyst asks whether a financial-literacy email changes diversified-fund enrollment. In an illustrative synthetic audit, the email offer X and enrollment Y are recorded, but the analyst adjusts for “opened a follow-up adviser call” M. Opening that call may be caused by X (the offer prompts questions) and by an unmeasured concern U (worried customers seek advice): X → M ← U. M is therefore a collider, not a safe control. Conditioning on M can manufacture an association between the randomized offer and U, distorting the offer’s intention-to-treat estimate even though random assignment made X comparable in expectation. Use this diagnostic sequence: state the estimand (the effect of offering the email), draw arrows using pre-treatment knowledge, exclude post-offer variables such as M from the primary adjustment set, and then report any secondary analysis as assumption-dependent. If the goal instead is the effect of actually reading the email, random assignment alone does not identify it because reading is compliance-mediated; that requires additional assumptions and a different estimand. The numbers here are synthetic, and the DAG is a hypothesis to defend, not evidence of an effect.

A raw group difference mixes the target effect with selection whenever people choose exposure. Consider a synthetic comparison of budgeting-app users and non-users: users save £46 per month and non-users save £38, so the observed gap is £8 per month. Suppose a credible pre-treatment record suggests users were already saving £5 more before downloading. Subtracting that baseline gap gives a simple adjusted contrast of £3, but this arithmetic is not automatically causal; prices, trends, measurement, and remaining differences may still matter. The missing counterfactual is each user’s saving in the same month without the app. A randomized offer, credible policy rule, or defensible comparison over time can make that missing outcome more plausible, while a small p-value alone cannot supply it.","takeaway":"A causal claim needs a credible comparison for the outcome that was not observed.","practice":{"question":"Customers who choose a low-fee fund have 2 percentage points higher annual returns than other customers. Is the 2-point difference automatically a causal effect of low fees?","hint":"Ask what else may influence both fund choice and returns.","solution":"No. Financial literacy, income, risk tolerance, account age or asset allocation may confound the association. A randomized fee intervention or a justified quasi-experiment would be needed for a causal interpretation."}},{"title":"Potential outcomes and treatment effects","body":"Let Y(1) denote a unit's outcome if treated and Y(0) its outcome without treatment. The individual effect is Y(1) − Y(0), but it cannot usually be observed directly because one person cannot occupy both conditions at once. An average treatment effect (ATE) is E[Y(1) − Y(0)] for a specified population; a sample estimate is a difference between group means when design assumptions justify it. In an illustrative randomized test, 100 treated customers show 18% enrollment and 100 controls show 12%. The estimated ATE is 18% − 12% = 6 percentage points, not a promise for every customer.

Consider a council deciding whether to offer jobseekers a travel-supported training place. For applicant i, Yᵢ(1) records whether they would be in paid work three months later if offered a place, while Yᵢ(0) records the same applicant’s outcome without the offer. The individual effect Yᵢ(1) − Yᵢ(0) is either −1, 0 or +1 for this binary outcome, but only one potential outcome is observed. A randomized offer can estimate an average effect for the eligible group; it cannot reveal both outcomes for each person. This is a constructed example, not programme data.

Consider a council deciding whether to offer jobseekers a travel-supported training place. For applicant i, Yᵢ(1) records whether they would be in paid work three months later if offered a place, while Yᵢ(0) records the same applicant’s outcome without the offer. The individual effect Yᵢ(1) − Yᵢ(0) is either −1, 0 or +1 for this binary outcome, but only one potential outcome is observed. A randomized offer can estimate an average effect for the eligible group; it cannot reveal both outcomes for each person. This is a constructed example, not programme data. See Matheus Facure’s Chapter 02, “Randomised Experiments,” in the linked sources below.

Potential outcomes clarify why an average treatment effect is a population summary rather than a personal guarantee. Illustrative synthetic example: 80 applicants are randomly offered coaching and 80 are not. After six months, 28 offered applicants and 20 controls are employed. The offer-group rate is 28/80 = 35%, and the control rate is 20/80 = 25%, so the estimated intention-to-treat effect is 35% − 25% = 10 percentage points. Some may gain, remain unchanged, or be harmed; the group average does not reveal which person belongs to which category. Randomization supports the comparison if assignment is followed and outcomes are measured consistently. It does not reveal both potential outcomes for any applicant or guarantee this 10-point effect elsewhere. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 02: Randomised Experiments (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

An estimand check starts by fixing the outcome scale. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose 500 eligible small firms are randomly offered a bookkeeping subsidy and 500 receive usual information; after 12 months, 75 offered firms and 100 comparison firms have entered insolvency. The risk is 75/500 = 0.150, versus 100/500 = 0.200. The intention-to-treat risk difference is 0.150 − 0.200 = −0.050, or 5 percentage points fewer insolvencies per 100 firms offered the subsidy. The risk ratio is 0.150/0.200 = 0.75: the offered group’s observed risk is 75% of the comparison risk, a 25% relative reduction. The absolute and relative statements answer different questions. With random assignment, consistent outcome measurement, and limited differential attrition, this contrast estimates the average effect of the offer for these eligible firms over 12 months. It does not show that every firm benefited, identify who would be protected in both counterfactual worlds, or establish effects outside the eligibility rules. If take-up is incomplete, calling this the effect of receiving the subsidy changes the estimand and requires further assumptions.

A potential-outcomes table is useful even when its missing cells cannot be filled. Suppose four applicants have employment indicators under an offer and no offer: (1,0), (1,1), (0,0), and (0,1), where each pair is written as (Y(1), Y(0)). Their individual effects are +1, 0, 0, and −1, so the average effect in this tiny synthetic population is (1+0+0−1)/4 = 0. The offer helps one person and harms another while producing no average effect. In real data, only one entry from each pair is observed; randomization helps recover the average contrast, not the hidden pairing. Thus an ATE can be informative without predicting any applicant’s personal outcome.","takeaway":"Name the estimand and population; an average effect is not an effect for every person.","practice":{"question":"In the illustrative test above, what is the estimated effect in percentage points, and what does randomization contribute?","hint":"Subtract the control rate from the treatment rate, then distinguish identification from precision.","solution":"The estimate is 6 percentage points (0.18 − 0.12). Random assignment makes treatment independent of baseline characteristics in expectation, supporting a causal comparison within the eligible population; it does not guarantee a large effect, eliminate sampling uncertainty or prove generalization."}},{"title":"Randomized experiments and implementation","body":"Random assignment balances observed and unobserved pre-treatment factors in expectation, so a treatment-control contrast can identify an intention-to-treat effect when outcomes and assignment are measured correctly. Check compliance, attrition, interference between customers and whether the treatment was delivered as planned. Suppose a message is assigned to 200 customers per arm, but only 160 treated customers actually view it. The assignment effect still answers the policy question of offering the message; it is not automatically the effect among viewers. Report the assignment rule, exclusions, missing outcomes, uncertainty interval and practical threshold. Statistical significance alone does not establish useful practical impact.

Implementation determines whether an experiment estimates an offer effect or an effect of actually receiving treatment. Synthetic example: 300 customers per arm are assigned a budgeting webinar. In the offer arm, 210 attend; enrollment is 27% among all 300 offered customers, versus 22% among 300 controls. The intention-to-treat estimate is 27% − 22% = 5 percentage points. Dividing 5 points by the 70% attendance rate gives about 7.14 points, but that is not automatically a valid treatment-on-the-treated effect: non-attenders may differ from attenders, and assignment can affect behavior even without attendance. Assume assignment is random, outcomes are recorded for all 600 customers, and contamination is limited. The result concerns offering one webinar over the stated follow-up period, not guaranteed long-run enrollment. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 02: Randomised Experiments (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

One useful implementation choice is to prespecify a baseline outcome or prognostic score for precision, without treating adjustment as a substitute for randomization. Illustrative synthetic example: 100 customers per arm receive either an investing lesson or a neutral message. The follow-up outcome is monthly saving, measured in dollars per month; its mean is $70 in the offer arm and $64 in control, so the unadjusted intention-to-treat difference is $70 − $64 = $6 per month. Suppose a pre-specified linear ANCOVA uses a financial-literacy score measured before assignment, with baseline means 60 (offer) and 56 (control), and an estimated slope of $0.50 per score point. The illustrative adjusted contrast is $6 − $0.50 × (60 − 56) = $4 per month. This does not claim the message caused only $4: the baseline imbalance can be chance, and the slope and model are assumptions used to improve precision. Report both contrasts, uncertainty calculated for the chosen model, and the adjustment rule. Never adjust for lesson attendance or another post-assignment variable, because doing so can change the intention-to-treat estimand or induce bias.

Assignment and receipt are different treatment variables. Imagine 100 people are randomly offered a budgeting message, 70 view it, and 30 do not; the control group receives no message. If enrollment is 24% among all offer-assigned people and 20% among controls, the intention-to-treat contrast is 4 percentage points. It answers what would happen if the program were offered through this assignment process. The 70% viewing rate does not justify dividing four by 0.70 and calling the result a universal effect of viewing. Viewing may depend on attention, access, or prior interest, and the offer itself may change behavior. Record assignment, exposure, deviations, and missing outcomes separately before interpreting the estimate.","takeaway":"Randomization helps identification, while implementation and measurement determine which effect was actually estimated."},{"title":"DAGs: confounders, mediators and colliders","body":"A directed acyclic graph (DAG) records a causal story with arrows. If financial literacy affects both message exposure and saving, it is a confounder; adjusting for it can block a non-causal backdoor path when measured before treatment. A mediator lies on the treatment-to-outcome pathway: controlling for message-induced confidence can remove part of the total effect. A collider is caused by two variables; conditioning on account approval, caused by both income and a promotional offer, can create a spurious association. Adjustment is not a checklist. Choose variables from timing and mechanism, and state what effect—total or direct—you intend to estimate.

In an illustrative apprenticeship study, prior work experience may affect both enrolment and later earnings, making it a plausible confounder. A current job type could instead sit on the pathway from training to earnings; controlling for it would remove part of the total effect. Restricting the sample to applicants who received an interview can also be risky if both training and unmeasured motivation affect interview receipt: selection on that shared consequence may create a misleading association. Draw the assumed arrows before choosing controls, and state whether the target is a total or direct effect. These pathways are hypotheses for a design, not empirical findings.

In an illustrative apprenticeship study, prior work experience may affect both enrolment and later earnings, making it a plausible confounder. A current job type could instead sit on the pathway from training to earnings; controlling for it would remove part of the total effect. Restricting the sample to applicants who received an interview can also be risky if both training and unmeasured motivation affect interview receipt: selection on that shared consequence may create a misleading association. Draw the assumed arrows before choosing controls, and state whether the target is a total or direct effect. These pathways are hypotheses for a design, not empirical findings. See Matheus Facure’s Chapter 04, “Graphical Causal Models,” in the linked sources below.

A DAG helps distinguish a variable worth adjusting for from one that creates bias when conditioned on. Illustrative synthetic example: among customers with matched account age, 60% offered coaching open a savings account, compared with 50% not offered. If prior financial literacy raises both the chance of receiving coaching and account opening, literacy is a confounder; adjusting for it may make the comparison more credible. If coaching first increases a savings plan, that plan is a mediator, so controlling for it would remove part of the total coaching effect. If analysts keep only customers approved for a loan, and both coaching and income affect approval, approval is a collider. That 10-point gap need not be causal. These are hypothetical pathways, not observed facts; timing and measurement must support the graph. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Harvard — Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs’ in the linked sources.

Suppose, purely illustratively, that a lender wants the effect of offering a budgeting tool on on-time repayment, and prior income is the only measured pre-treatment confounder. In a synthetic dataset, 50% of eligible borrowers are in a lower-income stratum: the tool-group repayment rates are 40% (lower) and 80% (higher), while comparison rates are 30% and 75%. Standardize both groups to the same 50–50 income mix: the tool mean is 0.5(0.40) + 0.5(0.80) = 0.60, and the comparison mean is 0.5(0.30) + 0.5(0.75) = 0.525, so the standardized contrast is 0.075, or 7.5 percentage points. This calculation is preferable to a raw gap when group composition differs, but it is not automatically causal. Before labeling 7.5 percentage points an effect, check that income was measured before the offer, every stratum has support in both groups, treatment assignment is as-if random within strata (or exchangeability is otherwise credible), outcomes are defined identically, and the tool does not alter which borrowers remain observed. A post-offer repayment behavior would be a mediator, not a routine adjustment variable.

Use the timing of a variable as a first diagnostic, not as a substitute for causal reasoning. In a synthetic lending example, income is measured before an information email and influences both email receipt and repayment; it is a plausible confounder. Confidence measured after the email may carry part of the email’s total effect to repayment, so adjusting for confidence targets a different direct-effect question. Approval, caused by income and the email, is a collider: selecting only approved applicants can make income and email receipt associated even if they were unrelated among all applicants. The same variable name can occupy different roles in different studies. Draw arrows, state the estimand, and justify each adjustment with mechanism and timing.","takeaway":"Adjust for justified pre-treatment confounders, not automatically for every measured variable.","practice":{"question":"A promotion affects account approval, and income also affects approval. Why can restricting analysis to approved accounts bias the promotion-return relationship?","hint":"Identify what kind of DAG node approval may be.","solution":"Approval is a collider on paths from promotion and income. Conditioning on it can open a non-causal path between promotion and income, making the groups differ in income for a design-created reason. The exact bias depends on the full data-generating process."}},{"title":"Difference-in-differences and thresholds","body":"Difference-in-differences (DiD) compares before-to-after change in a treated group with change in a comparison group. In an illustrative policy, treated firms move from 10% to 16% adoption, while controls move from 8% to 10%. The DiD estimate is (16 − 10) − (10 − 8) = 4 percentage points. Its key assumption is parallel trends: absent treatment, both groups would have changed similarly. Inspect pre-period trends, anticipate spillovers and account for staggered timing. Regression discontinuity instead compares units just above and below a cutoff; it needs no precise manipulation and continuity of potential outcomes at the threshold. Neither design becomes causal merely because its p-value is small.

Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data; weekly employment rate, measured in percentage points over two quarters): suppose a town introduces a subsidized bus pass in Quarter 2 for Northside residents, while similar Southside remains a comparison area. Northside employment is 54% in Q1 and 60% in Q2, a +6 percentage-point change. Southside is 52% and 55%, a +3-point change. Difference-in-differences = (60−54)−(55−52) = 6−3 = 3 percentage points. The estimate says Northside employment improved 3 points more than the comparison area after the subsidy, under the design assumptions. The Q2 gap is 5 points (60−55), but that is not the DiD; Northside’s own 6-point increase also includes changes shared by both areas.

Difference-in-differences can identify an average policy effect when the comparison group provides a credible counterfactual trend; it cannot by itself prove that the subsidy caused the entire post-period difference or that every resident benefited. The key check is parallel trends: inspect several pre-policy quarters and plot both areas, looking for similar movements before Q2; a placebo policy date can provide an additional diagnostic. Watch for spillovers, such as Southside residents using the passes, or different employment measurement across areas. A common mistake is to call Northside’s 6-point before-to-after rise the treatment effect, ignoring the comparison change. See “World Bank DIME — Causal Inference and Quasi-Experimental Methods” in the linked sources below.

A threshold design identifies a local comparison, not automatically a policy effect for everyone. Illustrative synthetic example: a grant is offered to firms scoring at least 70 on an eligibility index. Firms just below the cutoff have a 52% three-month adoption rate, while firms just above have 59%; the jump is 59% − 52% = 7 percentage points. Because the groups are close to 70, the comparison can be credible if firms cannot precisely manipulate scores and other determinants change smoothly at the cutoff. The 7-point estimate applies near score 70, for this grant and three-month period; it need not apply to firms scoring 40 or 95. A small sample or a narrow score window can also make the estimate imprecise. For a fuller treatment, see ‘World Bank DIME — Causal Inference and Quasi-Experimental Methods’ in the linked sources.

With staggered adoption, calculate cohort-specific contrasts before pooling them. Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data): Region A adopts a training subsidy in Q2; its monthly earnings rise from $2,000 in Q1 to $2,120 in Q2, while a not-yet-treated comparison rises from $1,800 to $1,880. A's DiD is ($120 − $80) = $40 per worker-month. Region B adopts in Q3; from Q2 to Q3 its earnings rise from $1,500 to $1,590, while the comparison rises from $1,880 to $1,950, giving ($90 − $70) = $20 per worker-month. If the estimand is the equal-weight average across these two adoption cohorts, it is ($40 + $20)/2 = $30 per worker-month—not the difference between the final regional levels. This calculation requires parallel trends separately in each comparison window, no anticipation before adoption, no spillovers into the comparison, and consistent earnings measurement. A pooled regression that treats already-subsidized regions as controls for later adopters can mix treatment effects into the counterfactual; define the cohort and time weights explicitly. The result remains an average for these cohorts and windows, not automatically an effect for regions that adopt earlier, later, or never.

Difference-in-differences can be read as a counterfactual subtraction. Suppose treated firms rise from 50 to 58 units and comparison firms rise from 48 to 53. The treated change is 8 units; the comparison change is 5, so the contrast is 8−5 = 3 units. The implied untreated treated-group endpoint is 50+5 = 55, and the observed endpoint is 58; their gap is again 3. This reconstruction makes the assumption visible: the comparison change stands in for what treated firms would have experienced. If pre-policy movements differ, the 55-unit counterfactual is questionable. A discontinuity estimate has a different scope: it compares units near a cutoff, not all firms.","takeaway":"Quasi-experimental credibility comes from explicit, testable design assumptions, not from the label or sample size.","practice":{"question":"Using the adoption rates above, calculate the DiD estimate and state its central identifying assumption.","hint":"Compute each group's change first.","solution":"Treatment change is 6 points; control change is 2 points; their difference is 4 percentage points. The central assumption is that, without the policy, the treated group would have followed the control group's change on average (parallel trends), subject to no problematic spillovers or simultaneous shocks."}},{"title":"Instrumental variables, uncertainty and transport","body":"An instrumental variable (IV) changes treatment but affects the outcome only through that treatment. A credible IV requires relevance, an exclusion restriction and an appropriate independence story; these are substantive assumptions, not outputs of a regression. In a toy example, an encouragement raises fund adoption by 0.50 (50 percentage points) and raises average saving by 0.02 dollars per dollar of income, so the Wald estimate is 0.02 ÷ 0.50 = 0.04, or 4 cents per dollar for compliers under the design. Report uncertainty, first-stage strength, treatment version, target population and limits on transport. A causal estimate can be internally credible yet practically small or externally narrow.

An instrumental variable can estimate an effect for compliers when its assumptions are plausible, but the arithmetic and target must be stated carefully. Illustrative synthetic example: an encouragement is randomly sent to 200 customers; 40 adopt a savings plan, versus 20 of 200 not encouraged. Adoption rises 40/200 − 20/200 = 20% − 10% = 10 percentage points. Average monthly deposits rise from £18 to £20, a difference of £2 per month. The Wald estimate is £2 ÷ 0.10 = £20 per month per full-unit adoption effect, interpreted for compliers under the model. This requires relevance, independence, and no direct effect of encouragement on deposits except through adoption. It does not prove a £20 increase for every customer or transport to another product, month, or population. For a fuller treatment, see ‘World Bank DIME — Causal Inference and Quasi-Experimental Methods’ in the linked sources.

Use the Wald ratio by keeping the two intention-to-treat effects in their native units. Illustrative synthetic example: among 400 eligible borrowers, a randomly assigned reminder produces repayment-plan enrollment for 160 people (40%) versus 100 (25%) under no reminder, so the first stage is 0.40 − 0.25 = 0.15, or 15 percentage points. Suppose mean annual interest paid is $108 in the reminder group and $112.50 in the control group; the reduced form is $108 − $112.50 = −$4.50 per borrower-year. Dividing gives −$4.50 ÷ 0.15 = −$30 per borrower-year per one-unit increase in enrollment: under the IV assumptions, compliers who enroll because of the reminder pay $30 less annual interest on average. The negative sign indicates lower interest, not a loss. This is not $30 for every borrower: always-enrollers and never-enrollers are not identified by this instrument. The interpretation also requires no direct reminder effect on interest, no spillovers, and a sufficiently strong first stage; report an interval because sampling error in both stages can make a ratio unstable.

The IV lab separates three quantities that are easy to mix up. Let an encouragement increase adoption by 0.40 units and increase saving by 0.12 outcome units. The Wald ratio is 0.12/0.40 = 0.30 outcome units per adoption unit. The numerator is the reduced-form encouragement effect on saving; the denominator is the first-stage effect on adoption. This ratio is not an effect for everyone unless the instrument assumptions support that interpretation. It is typically local to compliers, people whose adoption responds to encouragement. A direct path from encouragement to saving would enter the numerator without entering the denominator, changing the ratio. A weak denominator also magnifies noise, so first-stage strength and uncertainty belong beside the estimate.","takeaway":"Identification assumptions determine what a design can claim; uncertainty and scope determine how useful that claim is."}]
data.case_study: Consider an educational brokerage experiment using deliberately illustrative, simulated numbers. Eligible customers are randomly offered either a low-cost index-fund education message or a neutral message. After three months, 18% of 200 offered customers enroll in a diversified fund, compared with 12% of 200 controls: the intention-to-treat difference is 6 percentage points. Before interpreting it, check that assignment was concealed, exposure was recorded, outcomes were measured consistently, attrition was balanced and customers could not contaminate one another. The estimate answers the effect of offering this message to this eligible population during this period; it does not estimate a universal effect or fund performance. A voluntary-choice comparison would be confounded by literacy, income, risk tolerance and account age. A small p-value would not prove the message caused enrollment, establish financial benefit or make the effect practically important. Pre-specify a meaningful enrollment threshold, report an interval, disclose deviations and consider whether behavior persists. This is a teaching example, not investment advice.
data.misconceptions:
A significant regression coefficient proves causation. Identification comes from design and assumptions, not the p-value.
Adjusting for every available variable always removes bias. Mediators, colliders and post-treatment variables can introduce bias.
More data solve systematic confounding. Sample size reduces some noise, not structural bias.
Random assignment guarantees perfect balance and universal generalization. Balance is probabilistic, and transport depends on the population, treatment and context.
A non-significant result proves no effect, while a significant result proves a useful effect. Precision, effect size, practical thresholds and design credibility must be assessed separately.

Generalization still depends on the sampling frame and context."}

data.title: Economic Time Series & Market Data
data.excerpt: Time series follow an economy or market across dates—for example, inflation, unemployment, output or prices. Learn to spot trends, persistence and changing volatility, make and assess forecasts, and distinguish predicting a movement from explaining what caused it.
data.objectives:
Distinguish price levels, differences and returns.
Interpret stationarity, autocorrelation and volatility clustering.
Compare backward-looking realized volatility with option-implied VIX.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Respect order and transform the series","body":"Financial observations are ordered in time, so shuffling can destroy information. A price level Pₜ is the quoted value at time t; a first difference is Pₜ − Pₜ₋₁. A simple return is (Pₜ/Pₜ₋₁) − 1, while a log return is ln(Pₜ/Pₜ₋₁), where ln is the natural logarithm. For illustrative prices 100, 102, and 99, the two simple returns are 2.00% and −2.94%; wealth changes by 1.02 × 0.9706 − 1 = −1.00%. The log returns add to ln(99/100), about −1.005%. Stationarity means mean, variance and dependence are broadly stable; it is an assumption to check, not a guarantee from using returns.

A useful check is to distinguish a one-period change in currency units from a proportional return. Suppose an illustrative synthetic asset moves from $80 to $84 over one month: the difference is $84 − $80 = $4 per share, while the simple return is 84/80 − 1 = 0.05, or 5%. If it then moves to $81, the next return is 81/84 − 1 = −0.0357, or −3.57%, not −3%. The two-month wealth factor is 1.05 × (81/84) = 1.0125, so cumulative return is 1.25%. This calculation assumes prices are comparable and excludes dividends, fees, and splits. A positive first return does not imply a positive final return. For a fuller treatment, see ‘FRED — Measuring uncertainty and volatility with FRED data’ in the linked sources.

To connect returns to a risk measure without confusing level changes and dispersion, consider this explicitly synthetic five-session window of daily simple returns: +2%, −1%, 0%, +3%, and −2% (the entries are +2, −1, 0, +3, and −2 percentage points). First compute the window mean: (2 − 1 + 0 + 3 − 2)/5 = 0.4 percentage points per day. Subtracting that mean gives deviations 1.6, −1.4, −0.4, 2.6, and −2.4; their squared sum is 17.2 percentage-points-squared. The rolling sample variance is therefore 17.2/(5−1) = 4.3, and the sample standard deviation is √4.3 ≈ 2.07 percentage points per day. If an analyst annualizes this descriptive estimate using √252, the result is 2.07% × √252 ≈ 32.92% per year, under the illustrative assumption of 252 sessions and independent, identically distributed returns with stable variance. This is not a forecast: a different window, denominator, missing session, dividend adjustment, or volatility regime can change it, and annualization does not make clustered risk disappear.

The returns lab’s wealth path shows why a return is not a dollar difference. Start an index at 100, apply a synthetic +4% return, then a −4% return: wealth becomes 100×1.04 = 104 and 104×0.96 = 99.84. The cumulative return is −0.16%, although the two simple returns sum to zero. The log returns, ln(1.04) and ln(0.96), add to ln(0.9984), which corresponds to the same final wealth. A price difference would instead report the index-point changes, +4 and −4. Before calculating, decide whether the series is a price, adjusted price, simple return, or log return; otherwise a correct formula can answer the wrong economic question.","formula":"rₜ = Pₜ/Pₜ₋₁ − 1; ℓₜ = ln(Pₜ/Pₜ₋₁)","takeaway":"Levels, differences and returns answer different questions, and compounding must remain visible.","practice":{"question":"A price moves from 250 to 255 and then to 249. What are the two simple returns and the cumulative return?","hint":"Compute each ratio minus 1, then multiply 1 + r₁ by 1 + r₂ and subtract 1.","solution":"The returns are 255/250 − 1 = 2.00% and 249/255 − 1 ≈ −2.35%. Cumulative return is (1.02)(249/255) − 1 = 249/250 − 1 = −0.40%."}},{"title":"Choose a time scale and avoid spurious patterns","body":"Sampling frequency changes what a chart can reveal. Daily observations may show jumps and gaps; monthly aggregation can smooth them while hiding short-lived stress. A price level that trends upward can produce a high correlation with calendar time even when returns are not predictable. Compare like with like: align timestamps, use adjusted prices when dividends or splits matter, and record whether a value is close, open, yield or return. Missing dates are not automatically zero. A trend or association is not a causal explanation, and patterns found after many date ranges may reflect selection. State the period, frequency and data revisions before modeling.

Illustrative synthetic example — monthly unemployment and job vacancies: Suppose a country records unemployment at 6.0%, 6.2%, and 6.4% in January–March, while vacancies are 2.0%, 2.1%, and 2.2% of the labour force. A simple chart of the three monthly observations shows both series rising; the January-to-March unemployment change is 6.4 − 6.0 = 0.4 percentage points, not 0.4 percent, and the vacancy change is 0.2 percentage points. If we instead average the three months, unemployment is (6.0 + 6.2 + 6.4) ÷ 3 = 6.2%, which describes the quarter but hides the month-by-month timing. The calculation shows why frequency and units must be stated before interpreting a trend or association.

This method can describe how an economic series changes at a chosen frequency, but it cannot establish that rising vacancies caused rising unemployment, nor that the pattern will continue. A key check is to align dates and definitions, inspect a longer pre-specified window, and ask whether the apparent relationship survives a reasonable alternative frequency rather than appearing only after searching many ranges. Do not interpret two upward-sloping levels as evidence of a meaningful causal link: common trends or seasonal timing can create a spurious pattern. Missing months should be investigated, not silently replaced by zero. For the lag-and-dependence diagnostic, see “NIST — Box-Jenkins Model Identification (ACF and PACF)” in the linked sources below.

Aggregation can change both the apparent timing and the units of a relationship. Consider illustrative synthetic weekly sales of 100, 110, 90, and 100 units. The two-week averages are (100 + 110)/2 = 105 units and (90 + 100)/2 = 95 units, so the average falls by 10 units, or 9.52% relative to 105; this is not the same statement as a 20-unit drop from 110 to 90. If a monthly report uses those averages, it cannot reveal which week contained the movement. The comparison assumes each week is equally weighted; a calendar-day or exposure-weighted average could differ. Aggregation describes timing at a chosen scale but does not establish why sales changed. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST — Box-Jenkins Model Identification (ACF and PACF)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic calculation — suppose five consecutive trading-day log returns are 0.010, −0.005, 0.002, −0.003, and 0.006, expressed as decimal returns rather than percentages. Their mean is (0.010 − 0.005 + 0.002 − 0.003 + 0.006) ÷ 5 = 0.002. The sample variance therefore uses n − 1 = 4: [(0.008)^2 + (−0.007)^2 + 0^2 + (−0.005)^2 + (0.004)^2] ÷ 4 = 0.0000385, so the sample daily standard deviation is √0.0000385 = 0.006205, or 0.6205% per trading day. A conventional annualized volatility is 0.006205 × √252 = 0.0985, or 9.85% per year. This conversion assumes returns have a stable variance and little serial dependence; clustered volatility makes it a rough scale conversion, not a forecast. In practice, compute this within each stated rolling window, keep the n − 1 denominator consistent with the lab’s rolling sample SD, and report the window length and 252-trading-day convention. Changing the window or using calendar-day scaling can change the estimate without any underlying price change.

Aggregation is a filter, not a neutral presentation choice. Consider synthetic daily returns of +2%, −2%, +2%, and −2%. The four-day arithmetic average is 0%, but wealth ends at 100×1.02×0.98×1.02×0.98 = 99.920016, a −0.079984% cumulative result (about −0.08%). If these observations were replaced by two two-day compounded returns, each block would be 0.9996 (−0.04%), so the block series preserves the loss while hiding the alternating daily signs. A monthly average could hide a short stress episode altogether. Align frequencies before comparing variables, document how observations are aggregated, and investigate missing dates. A smooth low-frequency plot describes less timing detail; it does not establish a stronger relationship or a causal mechanism.","takeaway":"Frequency, definitions and missingness can change the question before any model is fitted.","practice":{"question":"Why should a missing market date usually not be filled with a zero return without checking the source?","hint":"Ask what the missing date represents and how the return interval is defined.","solution":"It may be a holiday, outage or error. Filling zero can distort volatility, autocorrelation and cumulative calculations; inspect the source first."}},{"title":"Look for dependence in direction and magnitude","body":"Autocorrelation measures linear association between a series and its lagged values. For returns rₜ, lag-1 autocorrelation compares rₜ with rₜ₋₁; a value near zero means little linear directional dependence, not complete independence. Examine absolute returns |rₜ| or squared returns rₜ² as well. Volatility clustering means large moves tend to be near other large moves, even when the next return's sign remains hard to predict. For a rolling window of n observations, the sample standard deviation sₜ summarizes recent spread but changes when n changes. A rolling statistic is descriptive and overlapping, so persistence needs careful uncertainty assessment for careful interpretation.

Separate signs from sizes with an illustrative synthetic sequence of daily returns: +1%, −1%, +1%, −1%. The signs alternate, so a simple directional rule based on yesterday’s sign would be wrong every time in this tiny sample. Yet the absolute returns are 1%, 1%, 1%, and 1%, showing constant magnitude rather than a cluster of large and small moves. Now compare +0.2%, −2.0%, +0.3%, −2.2%: signs still alternate, while magnitudes are 0.2%, 2.0%, 0.3%, and 2.2%, suggesting alternating size rather than independent variation. Autocorrelation calculated on four observations is highly uncertain and may be distorted by the pattern. This evidence supports description, not a causal mechanism or reliable forecast. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST — Box-Jenkins Model Identification (ACF and PACF)’ in the linked sources.

Consider this explicitly illustrative synthetic five-session window of daily returns: +0.4%, −0.6%, +3.0%, −2.5%, and +0.7%. First compute the window mean: (0.4 − 0.6 + 3.0 − 2.5 + 0.7)% ÷ 5 = 0.2%. The squared deviations from that mean are 0.04, 0.64, 7.84, 7.29, and 0.25 percentage-point-squared, totaling 16.06. The rolling sample SD therefore equals √(16.06 ÷ (5 − 1)) = 2.00 percentage points. If an analyst reports an annualized convention, 2.00% × √252 ≈ 31.8% per year, assuming 252 trading sessions and that this scaling is an informative summary; it is not a prediction of next year’s volatility. Dividing by 5 instead would produce 1.79 percentage points, the population-style SD, which is not the lab’s rolling sample-SD convention. The two large moves make the estimate jump even though their signs differ. Before comparing this backward-looking figure with VIX, align annualization, dates, and return units; otherwise a unit mismatch can look like economic disagreement. A five-session estimate is also too short to diagnose persistent clustering reliably.

A rolling standard deviation has two moving parts: the observations included and their distance from that window’s own mean. In a synthetic five-day return sequence of 0.2%, 0.1%, 0.3%, 2.0%, and 1.8%, a two-day window ending on day five contains 2.0% and 1.8%. Its mean is 1.9%; deviations are 0.1% and −0.1%, giving sample standard deviation about 0.14 percentage points. A window ending on day three contains 0.1% and 0.3%, with the same spread. The level of returns differs, but the local volatility is similar. Changing the window changes the question, and overlapping windows reuse observations. A high rolling line describes recent magnitude, not the sign of tomorrow’s return.","formula":"ρ₁ = Corr(rₜ, rₜ₋₁); sₜ = √[Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ(rᵢ − r̄)²/(n − 1)]","takeaway":"Dependence in volatility magnitude is different from predictable return direction.","practice":{"question":"If returns have near-zero autocorrelation but squared returns have positive autocorrelation, what is a reasonable description?","hint":"Separate the sign of the return from the size of the move.","solution":"The data show little linear predictability in return direction but persistence in movement magnitude, consistent with volatility clustering. This is sample association, not a guaranteed forecast."}},{"title":"Measure realized volatility with explicit units","body":"Realized volatility summarizes variation observed after returns occur. For n daily returns rᵢ, compute their sample standard deviation s and, under a simplifying convention, annualize it as s√252, where 252 is an illustrative count of trading days per year. If daily s is 1.25%, annualized volatility is 1.25% × √252 ≈ 19.84%. This conversion assumes the return scale and dependence structure make square-root-of-time reasonable; volatility clustering, jumps and serial dependence can weaken it. Report the window, estimator, annualization convention and distribution treatment. Realized volatility is an estimate of historical variability, not a bound on future losses or a measure of expected return.

The sample standard deviation requires centering returns before measuring spread. For illustrative synthetic daily returns of 1%, 2%, and 3%, the mean is (1% + 2% + 3%)/3 = 2%. Deviations are −1%, 0%, and +1%; their squared sum is 0.0001 + 0 + 0.0001 = 0.0002 in decimal-return-squared units. Dividing by n − 1 = 2 gives 0.0001, and the square root is 0.01, or 1% per day. Under the stated 252-session convention, annualized volatility is 0.01√252 ≈ 0.1587, or 15.87% per year. This tiny sample is only illustrative: it does not estimate a stable future risk level, expected return, or maximum loss. For a fuller treatment, see ‘FRED — Measuring uncertainty and volatility with FRED data’ in the linked sources.

Consider a five-session window of explicitly synthetic daily returns: −2%, 1%, 0%, 3%, and −1%. Their mean is (−2 + 1 + 0 + 3 − 1)% ÷ 5 = 0.2% per session. In percentage-point units, deviations from that mean are −2.2, 0.8, −0.2, 2.8, and −1.2; the squared deviations sum to 14.80 percentage-points-squared. The sample variance is 14.80 ÷ (5 − 1) = 3.70 percentage-points-squared, so the rolling sample SD is √3.70 = 1.92 percentage points per session. Expressed as a decimal, 0.0192√252 ≈ 0.305, or 30.5% annualized under the lesson’s simple convention. For a $10 million position, 1.92% is a one-session standard-deviation scale of about $192,000, not a predicted loss or a guaranteed range. If the calendar contains a holiday, keep the window at five observed sessions rather than inserting a zero return; otherwise the denominator and spread change for a data-management reason. The volatility line in the lab should therefore be read as a backward-looking, window-dependent magnitude estimate on its right-hand scale, not as the signed return bars or a forward VIX measure.

Annualization translates a daily dispersion measure under a stated convention; it does not add information about future shocks. If a synthetic sample has daily standard deviation 0.50%, the square-root-of-252 calculation gives 0.0050×√252 ≈ 0.0794, or 7.94% annualized. The number is in annual return units, while the input is in daily return units. If the daily observations are strongly dependent or volatility clusters, multiplying by √252 may not describe the actual annual dispersion. A sample standard deviation also depends on whether returns are centered and whether the denominator is n−1. Report the window, return definition, estimator, and annualization rule; otherwise two analysts can quote different “annual volatility” values from the same prices.","formula":"σ̂ₐₙₙ ≈ s_daily√252","takeaway":"Annualization is a stated modeling convention, not a law that makes volatility forecasts exact.","practice":{"question":"A 20-session sample has daily standard deviation 0.80%. Under the simple 252-day convention, what is the annualized value?","hint":"Multiply 0.0080 by the square root of 252, then express the result as a percentage.","solution":"0.0080√252 ≈ 0.1270, or about 12.70% annualized. This is conditional on the convention and the sample being informative of the intended horizon."}},{"title":"Separate realized and implied measures","body":"Realized volatility is computed from observed returns over a selected historical window. VIX is derived from prices of S&P 500 index options and is commonly presented as an option-implied measure for approximately the next 30 days, under CBOE's methodology and market assumptions. They use different information, horizons and constructions, so they can diverge without either being a calculation error. A simple comparison should align dates and units, document the rolling window and avoid treating correlation as causation. VIX reflects risk-neutral option pricing information and may include risk premia; it is not a guaranteed forecast of future realized volatility. Neither series is a trade signal or investment advice.

A comparison must keep the horizon and scale visible. Suppose, illustratively and synthetically, a 20-session calculation reports 18% annualized realized volatility on June 1, while VIX is quoted at 24% annualized that day. The gap is 24% − 18% = 6 percentage points, and the ratio is 24/18 ≈ 1.33, so the implied quote is about one-third higher in annualized percentage terms. This does not mean the next 30 calendar days will have exactly 24% volatility: VIX is derived from option prices and reflects pricing assumptions and risk premia, while realized volatility summarizes a selected past window. Different day counts, windows, or market closures can also matter. For a fuller treatment, see ‘FRED — CBOE Volatility Index (VIXCLS)’ in the linked sources.

To audit a rolling estimate, work from the daily units before annualizing. Suppose, purely as a synthetic illustration, the latest five log returns are +1, −2, +3, 0, and −1 percentage points. Their mean is (1 − 2 + 3 + 0 − 1)/5 = 0.2 percentage points. The squared deviations from that mean are 0.64, 4.84, 7.84, 0.04, and 1.44, summing to 14.80 percentage-points-squared. Because the lab describes a rolling sample SD, divide by n − 1 = 4: the variance is 3.70 percentage-points-squared and the daily realized SD is √3.70 = 1.92 percentage points per trading day. If an analyst reports an annualized figure using 252 trading days, convert 1.92 percentage points to 0.0192 and multiply by √252, giving about 0.305, or 30.5% per year. Dividing by five instead would describe a population-style SD and yield a different number. As the window rolls, one observation leaves and another enters; this is a backward-looking summary, not a guarantee about the next return or its sign. Keep the denominator, window, return definition, and annualization convention in the audit trail.

A gap between VIX and realized volatility can be decomposed before it is interpreted. In a synthetic comparison, trailing realized volatility is 15% annualized and VIX is 21% annualized. The difference is 6 percentage points, while the ratio 21/15 = 1.40 says the VIX quote is 40% higher on that scale. Neither calculation says that realized volatility will become 21% or that the 6-point gap is a forecast error. Realized volatility summarizes a selected past return window; VIX incorporates option prices and a forward horizon with pricing premia. Align the observation date, annualization convention, and horizon first. Then describe co-movement as association, not evidence that one measure causes the other.","takeaway":"Before comparing volatility measures, match their horizon, units, construction and information set.","practice":{"question":"Why could VIX rise while a trailing 20-day realized-volatility estimate remains low?","hint":"Compare forward-looking option prices with a backward-looking window.","solution":"Option prices can incorporate expectations or risk premia about near-term turbulence before that turbulence appears in the trailing sample. The measures answer different questions and need not move together immediately."}},{"title":"Model time series with humility","body":"Time-series models use order, lags and assumptions about how the data-generating process changes. A stationary-looking return series can still have structural breaks, changing volatility, heavy tails or dependence across assets. Test robustness across reasonable windows, frequencies and transformations, and reserve later observations for out-of-sample evaluation. Distinguish association from prediction: a lagged variable may improve forecast accuracy without proving a mechanism. Distinguish prediction from causality: an intervention claim needs design and identification assumptions. Also separate statistical detectability from practical importance; a tiny improvement may not cover transaction costs, and a wide interval may make a large-looking estimate uncertain. Simulated examples are teaching devices, not historical evidence.

A simple train-test comparison shows why validation matters. In an illustrative synthetic exercise, a benchmark has a test mean absolute error of 1.30 percentage points, while a lagged model has 1.24 percentage points; the apparent improvement is 1.30 − 1.24 = 0.06 percentage points, or about 4.6% relative to 1.30. If the same model reduced training error from 1.10 to 0.70 percentage points but was tested only once, the training gain could reflect overfitting. The test result is descriptive for that sample and forecast horizon; it does not prove a causal mechanism, durable profitability, or performance in another regime. Costs, uncertainty intervals, and repeated evaluation choices still matter. For a fuller treatment, see ‘FRED — Measuring uncertainty and volatility with FRED data’ in the linked sources.

Suppose, purely illustratively, that a five-session window contains daily returns of −2%, 1%, 0%, 3% and −1%. Their mean is (−2 + 1 + 0 + 3 − 1) / 5 = 0.2%, so the squared deviations sum to 4.84 + 0.64 + 0.04 + 7.84 + 1.44 = 14.80 percentage-points-squared. A rolling sample variance divides by 5 − 1 = 4, giving 3.70, and the sample SD is √3.70 = 1.92 percentage points per day. If an analyst reports an annualized scale under an independent, roughly constant-volatility convention, convert 1.92 percentage points to 0.0192 and multiply by √252: 0.0192 × 15.875 ≈ 0.305, or 30.5% per year. This is a rescaling, not evidence that volatility is constant or that a year’s loss will be 30.5%. The window ending today includes today’s return; tomorrow’s window drops the oldest observation, so adjacent rolling estimates overlap and are not independent. Before comparing this backward-looking figure with VIX, align dates, horizon and annualization convention; otherwise a numerical gap may be a timing or units mismatch rather than a market change.

A forecast comparison should preserve the direction of time. Suppose a synthetic benchmark predicts monthly inflation with test mean absolute error 0.90 percentage points, while a lagged model records 0.86. The absolute improvement is 0.04 percentage points, and relative improvement is 0.04/0.90 ≈ 4.4%. That calculation is meaningful only for the untouched test period and stated horizon. Choosing the model after inspecting that same period would make the comparison optimistic. A lower error also does not identify why inflation moves, and it may be too small to matter operationally. Use an earlier training period, a later holdout, realistic decision costs, and repeated or rolling evaluation. Forecast skill is evidence about prediction under those conditions, not causation or guaranteed persistence.","takeaway":"A useful time-series result must survive assumptions, validation and an economic-importance check.","practice":{"question":"A model's forecast error falls by 0.02 percentage points, but trading costs are 0.10 percentage points. What should be concluded?","hint":"Compare the predictive change with the decision's units and costs.","solution":"The statistical improvement may be practically unhelpful because it is smaller than the stated cost. Check uncertainty and stability before claiming value; forecast accuracy does not imply causality."}}]
data.case_study: Use an explicitly illustrative workflow for learners rather than inventing a historical finding. Imagine an analyst downloads daily S&P 500 close data and FRED VIXCLS for a stated five-year window, verifies dates and units, calculates daily log returns, and computes a 20-session rolling standard deviation. The analyst plots returns, absolute returns, squared returns and both volatility measures, then reports whether large moves cluster and how the two measures co-move. The rolling estimate is backward-looking; VIX is option-implied for a forward horizon, so differences are expected. The analyst should test sensitivity to window length, missing dates, adjusted versus unadjusted prices, annualization convention and a possible regime break. Any correlation is descriptive association, not evidence that VIX causes realized volatility, and a forecast improvement may be too small to matter after costs. Results depend on data quality, model choices and market regimes. It does not establish a trading edge or constitute investment advice.
data.misconceptions:
A trending price series means returns are predictable. Trends in levels and return predictability are different.
Volatility clustering predicts the sign of the next return. It describes magnitude/dependence in variance.
VIX and rolling realized volatility are interchangeable. Their timing and construction differ.
