data.title: Kernel Density Estimation & Local Smoothing
data.excerpt: Kernel density estimation draws a smooth curve to summarize where observations are concentrated, without relying on fixed histogram bins. Compare smoothing settings to see how too much or too little smoothing can hide peaks, exaggerate noise and change the apparent tails.
data.objectives:
Explain how kernel density estimation places and averages a small kernel around each observation.
Describe how kernel choice and bandwidth change the estimated density, including the bias–variance trade-off.
Interpret density values, modes, and interval probability without confusing height with probability.
Connect joint and conditional density estimates to Nadaraya–Watson and local polynomial regression.
Recognize boundary and high-dimensional limitations and use a rule of thumb as a starting point, not a verdict.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"From a histogram to a smooth density","body":"A histogram groups observations into bins, so its appearance can change when the bin width or starting point changes. Kernel density estimation (KDE) instead centers a small, smooth function on every observation and adds the contributions. For observations x₁,…,xₙ and bandwidth h, a common one-dimensional estimate is f̂ₕ(y) = (1/(n h)) Σᵢ K((y − xᵢ)/h). Here K is the kernel shape and h controls its width. If K integrates to one, the estimate is a density: its total area is approximately one, while its height has units of 1/(the measurement unit).

Illustrative synthetic economic example (January–June 2025): suppose four fictional workers’ job-search durations, measured in weeks, are 2, 3, 3, and 5. To show the mechanics without hiding the calculation, use a uniform kernel K(u)=0.5 when |u|≤1 and 0 otherwise, with bandwidth h=1 week. At y=3 weeks, the observations at 2, 3, and 3 are within one bandwidth, while 5 is not, so f̂₁(3)=[0.5+0.5+0.5+0]/(4×1)=0.375 per week. The estimate is a smoothed description of concentration around three-week job searches: its height is density per week, not the probability of exactly three weeks. Probability for an interval would be represented by area under the curve over that interval.

A KDE can summarize where the selected job-search durations are concentrated and can make skewness or multiple local clusters easier to inspect than a single histogram, but it cannot establish the population distribution, explain why searches last longer, prove a policy caused a difference, or forecast an individual’s next duration. Treat bandwidth as a decision to check: compare a narrow, medium, and wide value, inspect whether apparent peaks persist, and consider boundary leakage because durations cannot be negative. A common mistake is reading a tall density value as a probability at one exact continuous duration; use area over a range instead. For implementation details and bandwidth context, see “Scikit-learn User Guide — Density Estimation” in the linked sources below.

KDE is especially useful when bin boundaries are arbitrary. Suppose five synthetic monthly commuting costs are 40, 42, 43, 60, and 61 currency units, and compare the local contribution at y=42 currency units using a uniform kernel with h=2 currency units. The standardized distances are (42−40)/2=1, (42−42)/2=0, (42−43)/2=−0.5, (42−60)/2=−9, and (42−61)/2=−9.5. With K(u)=0.5 for |u|≤1, the density is [0.5+0.5+0.5+0+0]/(5×2)=0.15 per currency unit. This height describes concentration near 42, not the chance of one exact cost. It also does not show why costs differ or support a causal claim. For implementation details, see “Scikit-learn User Guide — Density Estimation” in the linked sources.

To turn a KDE into a decision quantity, integrate it over the relevant return range rather than reading a curve height. Consider an explicitly illustrative synthetic sample of four daily changes, measured in percentage points: −1.0, 0.0, 0.5, and 1.5. With a Gaussian KDE and bandwidth h = 0.5 percentage points, the estimated probability of a non-positive change is the average of four standard-normal cumulative probabilities: [Φ((0−(−1.0))/0.5) + Φ((0−0.0)/0.5) + Φ((0−0.5)/0.5) + Φ((0−1.5)/0.5)]/4 = [Φ(2)+Φ(0)+Φ(−1)+Φ(−3)]/4 ≈ (0.9772+0.5000+0.1587+0.0013)/4 = 0.4093, or about 40.9%. Thus the smoothed sample assigns roughly four in ten days to returns at or below zero, conditional on this bandwidth and sample—not a population frequency or forecast. The Gaussian kernel also assigns some mass beyond any finite boundary; for genuinely bounded outcomes, inspect boundary bias or use a suitable transformation. Changing h changes this area, so report it alongside the smoothing choice.

A KDE’s normalization explains why doubling the sample does not automatically double its total area. For the lab’s Gaussian kernel, each observation contributes exp(−0.5u²)/(n h √(2π)), where u is its distance from x in bandwidth units. With n = 10 and h = 0.5 percentage points, the multiplier before the exponential is 1/(10×0.5×√(2π)) ≈ 0.0798 per percentage point. Summing ten components gives an integrated curve near one over the full real line; a displayed finite range or numerical grid can leave small area outside or error. The vertical axis is density per percentage point, not a count or point probability. The bandwidth’s unit is on the horizontal scale. Scikit-learn User Guide — Density Estimation gives implementation context.","formula":"f̂ₕ(y) = (1 / (n h)) Σᵢ K((y − xᵢ) / h)","takeaway":"A KDE is a sum of little contributions centered on the observed data; it does not create new observations.","practice":{"question":"If returns are measured in percentage points, what does the vertical axis of a one-dimensional density plot represent?","hint":"A density is normalized by area, so its units are the inverse of the horizontal-axis units.","solution":"It is density per percentage point, not a probability at one exact return. Probability is represented by area over a range of returns."}},{"title":"What the kernel contributes","body":"A kernel is a weighting function. The supplied lecture describes a symmetric kernel with integral one, mean zero, and finite variance; common positive choices include Gaussian, triangular, and Epanechnikov shapes. In a standard positive-kernel KDE, nearby observations contribute more than distant ones. The kernel's exact shape usually matters less than the bandwidth, though shape and support affect smoothness and edge behavior. Higher-order kernels can use zero or negative weights to reduce some smoothing bias, but the resulting estimate may dip below zero and is less intuitive; they are not the default beginner choice.

The kernel shape determines how quickly influence fades, even when the bandwidth is fixed. Consider three synthetic hourly wages, measured in currency units: 10, 12, and 16, and estimate at y=12 with h=4 currency units. The standardized distances are −0.5, 0, and 1. A triangular kernel K(u)=1−|u| for |u|≤1 gives weights 0.5, 1, and 0, so the unnormalized contributions are 0.5, 1, and 0; the observation at 16 is just at the support edge and contributes zero. A Gaussian kernel would give it a small positive contribution instead. Thus kernel choice changes local emphasis, while h sets the distance scale. This comparison is descriptive, assumes comparable wage measurements, and does not identify a wage-setting mechanism. For a reference implementation, see “SciPy Reference — gaussian_kde” in the linked sources.

To see the normalization and units, use an illustrative synthetic sample of four monthly inflation changes, measured in percentage points: −1, 0, 1, and 2, with Gaussian bandwidth h = 1 percentage point. At y = 0, the KDE is [φ(1) + φ(0) + φ(1) + φ(2)]/(4 × 1 pp), where φ(0) ≈ 0.39894, φ(1) ≈ 0.24197, and φ(2) ≈ 0.05399. The result is (0.24197 + 0.39894 + 0.24197 + 0.05399)/4 ≈ 0.23422 per percentage point. That is a density height, not a 23.422% chance of exactly zero inflation. For an interval, integrate the same four shifted normal kernels: the estimated probability of 0 ≤ Y ≤ 1 pp is [Φ(2)−Φ(1) + Φ(1)−Φ(0) + Φ(0)−Φ(−1) + Φ(−1)−Φ(−2)]/4 ≈ [0.13591 + 0.34134 + 0.34134 + 0.13591]/4 = 0.23863, or 23.863%. The calculation assumes comparable measurements and treats the sample as descriptive; changing h changes both local height and interval area allocation, while the full mixture still integrates to one over the whole real line.

Compact-support and Gaussian kernels differ most clearly at a distant point. Suppose synthetic costs are 10, 12, and 18 currency units, the target is y = 12, and h = 4. The standardized distance for 18 is (12 − 18) ÷ 4 = −1.5. A triangular kernel defined only for |u| ≤ 1 assigns it weight zero, whereas a Gaussian kernel assigns a small positive weight. The nearby 10 and exact 12 observations still contribute more under either rule. Thus a kernel changes how influence fades, but the bandwidth determines the measurement scale for “nearby.” This comparison is descriptive and synthetic; it does not explain cost differences. SciPy Reference — gaussian_kde documents Gaussian-kernel implementation details.","formula":"u = (y − xᵢ) / h  ·  nearby observations receive larger K(u)","takeaway":"The kernel says how each point fades with distance; the bandwidth decides what counts as nearby.","practice":{"question":"A symmetric kernel is centered on an observation. Which observation contributes more to the estimate at y: one very close to y or one far away?","hint":"Think about the kernel's weight as distance from its center grows.","solution":"The nearby observation usually contributes more. A Gaussian kernel never becomes exactly zero, while a compact-support kernel eventually gives distant points zero weight."}},{"title":"Bandwidth is the main smoothing decision","body":"A small h creates narrow bumps: genuine local structure may appear, but random wiggles can look like extra modes. A large h merges nearby features and can hide multiple peaks. This is the bias–variance trade-off: extra smoothness often raises smoothing bias while reducing sample-to-sample roughness. One familiar univariate normal-reference starting point is Silverman's rule h ≈ 1.06 s n⁻¹ᐟ⁵, where s is the sample standard deviation and n the number of observations. It is a rule of thumb, not a universal optimum; cross-validation and subject-matter checks can lead to a different choice. Compare several plausible bandwidths before telling a story about the number of modes.

Bandwidth sensitivity can be made concrete with the rule h≈1.06s n⁻¹ᐟ⁵. For a synthetic sample of n=32 quarterly inflation rates measured in percentage points, suppose the sample standard deviation is s=2 percentage points. Since 32^(−1/5) is approximately 0.5, the starting bandwidth is 1.06×2×0.5=1.06 percentage points. A bandwidth near 0.5 percentage points would show finer variation; one near 2 percentage points would merge features roughly two percentage points apart. These are smoothing distances, not inflation changes or probabilities. The calculation assumes the normal-reference rule is a reasonable starting approximation; it does not prove normality, select the true population bandwidth, or establish economic causes of peaks. Compare validation results and plots before interpreting modes. This is a univariate normal-reference rule, not a universal optimum. Defaults vary: SciPy’s gaussian_kde uses Scott’s factor by default, and its Silverman factor is a multivariate rule rather than this exact univariate formula. For the normal-reference derivation, see “Hyndman et al. — Normal Reference Rule for Kernel Density Estimation” and “Bruce Hansen — Kernel Density Estimation (normal-reference rule)”; for SciPy’s default, see “SciPy Reference — gaussian_kde.”

To turn a KDE into an interval summary, integrate the kernels rather than reading the curve’s height. Consider this explicitly synthetic example of eight daily return changes, in percentage points: −1.0, −0.6, −0.2, 0.1, 0.3, 0.8, 1.1, and 1.5, with Gaussian bandwidth h = 0.4 percentage points. For the interval [0, 1] percentage point, the estimated mass is (1/8) Σᵢ[Φ((1−xᵢ)/0.4) − Φ((0−xᵢ)/0.4)], where Φ is the standard-normal CDF. The eight kernel contributions are approximately 0.006, 0.067, 0.307, 0.586, 0.733, 0.669, 0.398, and 0.106; they sum to 2.873, so division by n gives 0.359, or 35.9% estimated mass. This is not the observed fraction in the interval (3/8 = 37.5%) and is not a probability that the next return will land there: smoothing reallocates weight across the boundaries. The calculation assumes these observations represent the target return distribution and that Gaussian smoothing is defensible. Recompute it for alternative h values; a materially different 35.9% figure signals bandwidth sensitivity, not a contradiction in the arithmetic.

Bandwidth sensitivity is easiest to inspect by holding observations fixed and changing only h. Suppose a synthetic return sample has two tight clusters near −1 and +1 percentage points. With h = 0.25 pp, the KDE may show two narrow peaks plus small wiggles; with h = 1.5 pp, the clusters can blend into a single broad mound. Neither view is automatically the truth: the first can follow sampling noise and the second can erase meaningful separation. The lab’s bandwidth control is measured in percentage points, not probability or return. Compare plausible settings, report the selected rule, and avoid counting modes mechanically. Scikit-learn User Guide — Density Estimation discusses bandwidth choice.","formula":"Univariate Gaussian normal-reference starting point: h ≈ 1.06 s n⁻¹ᐟ⁵; software defaults vary.","takeaway":"Bandwidth is measured in the same units as the data and can change the story; always inspect sensitivity.","practice":{"question":"Your KDE shows four small peaks with a very narrow bandwidth, but only one broad mound with a wider bandwidth. What should you conclude?","hint":"Ask whether the apparent structure is stable across reasonable smoothing choices.","solution":"Do not treat either curve as a verdict. The narrow curve may overfit sample noise and the wide one may oversmooth real subgroups. Show sensitivity, check the observations and use a defensible bandwidth rule or validation criterion."}},{"title":"Read the curve as a density, not a probability","body":"A density curve's height is not the probability of observing that exact continuous value. Probability over an interval is the area under the density across that interval. A high peak indicates that observations are concentrated nearby relative to other regions; it does not mean that the peak value is common as an exact outcome. KDEs can reveal skewness, multiple clusters, and tail shape that a single mean conceals. Near a hard boundary—such as a nonnegative duration—symmetric kernels can place some mass outside the allowed range, so consider boundary-aware methods or state the limitation.

To translate height into probability, use area and keep the horizontal units visible. Suppose a synthetic KDE for annual portfolio returns has an average estimated density of 0.08 per percentage point from −1% to 1%. The interval width is 1−(−1)=2 percentage points, so a simple rectangle approximation gives probability 0.08×2=0.16, or 16%. This is not the probability of an exact 0% return; a single point has zero width on a continuous scale. The 16% is only an approximation to the KDE area, conditional on the sample and smoothing choice. It does not guarantee that future returns follow the curve or establish that a portfolio policy caused returns. Boundary and tail behavior should be checked separately. For density-estimation details, see “SciPy Reference — gaussian_kde” in the linked sources.

For a concrete, synthetic calculation, take the lab’s first six displayed return changes, −2.80, −2.45, −2.20, −1.95, −1.72, and −1.48 percentage points, and evaluate the KDE at x = −2.50 percentage points with bandwidth h = 0.50 percentage points. The Gaussian estimate is f(x) = (1/n)Σ[exp(−(x−xᵢ)²/(2h²))/(h√(2π))], so its units are density per percentage point. Here n = 6 and the six component contributions are approximately 0.1111, 0.1323, 0.1111, 0.0726, 0.0394, and 0.0166 per percentage point; adding them gives f(−2.50) ≈ 0.4831 per percentage point. This is a height, not a 48.31% probability: an interval probability still requires integrating the curve over a range. As a bandwidth diagnostic, keeping these six synthetic observations fixed but changing h to 0.70 pp lowers the calculated height at −2.50 pp to about 0.4217 per pp, illustrating smoothing rather than a change in the observations. The result describes this selected sample only; it is not a forecast or causal estimate, and the truncated displayed range can omit tail area.

Use a small interval to translate a density height into an approximate probability, while keeping units explicit. Suppose a synthetic KDE is about 0.12 per percentage point throughout the interval from −0.5 to 0.5 percentage points. Its width is 1 percentage point, so the rectangle approximation to area is 0.12 × 1 = 0.12, or 12%. The 12% refers to a return in that interval, not an exact return of 0%. If the density were 0.12 per decimal return instead, the unit conversion would matter: one percentage point equals 0.01 decimal units. Boundary leakage can also distort a KDE for nonnegative durations. SciPy Reference — gaussian_kde explains the density object; area, not height, carries probability.","takeaway":"Use area for interval probability, and remember that smoothing can leak across real data boundaries.","practice":{"question":"A density curve is tallest near a 0% return. Does the curve's height give the probability of an exact 0% return?","hint":"A single point has zero area on a continuous scale.","solution":"No. The height is density per unit, not point probability. The probability of a range around zero is the area over that range."}},{"title":"Joint and conditional densities add a second variable","body":"For paired observations (xᵢ, yᵢ), a bivariate KDE can place a two-dimensional kernel at each point. With separate bandwidths hₓ and hᵧ, a product-kernel form is f̂(x,y) = (1/(n hₓ hᵧ)) Σᵢ Kₓ((x−xᵢ)/hₓ)Kᵧ((y−yᵢ)/hᵧ). The resulting surface describes joint concentration. Integrating over one variable gives a marginal density; dividing the joint density by the relevant marginal gives a conditional density. A density surface can show a relationship that a single correlation number misses, but estimates become data-hungry as dimensions increase—the curse of dimensionality.

A joint density keeps both variables paired, while a conditional density focuses on one variable at a specified level of the other. Using synthetic observations of training hours per month and hourly earnings in currency units—(2, 15), (4, 16), (4, 20), and (8, 25)—the subset at exactly 4 training hours has earnings 16 and 20, whose simple average is (16+20)/2=18 currency units per hour. A conditional KDE would smooth around 4 hours rather than automatically treating these two points as the whole population. The marginal earnings density would ignore training hours entirely. This comparison assumes the measurements are on compatible scales and enough nearby pairs exist; it does not prove that extra training causes higher earnings. For density-estimation guidance, see “Scikit-learn User Guide — Density Estimation” in the linked sources.

Consider this explicitly synthetic illustration of a conditional KDE for hourly earnings y (currency units per hour) near x = 5 monthly training hours. Suppose the paired observations are (3,18), (4,20), and (6,24), and use a Gaussian x-bandwidth hₓ = 1 hour. Their unnormalized proximity weights are exp(−2) = 0.1353, exp(−0.5) = 0.6065, and 0.6065, so the normalized weights are approximately 0.100, 0.450, and 0.450. A local conditional mean is therefore (0.100×18 + 0.450×20 + 0.450×24) currency units per hour = 21.60 currency units per hour; it is a weighted summary, not a causal return to training. If hᵧ = 2 currency units per hour and we ask for density at y = 22, the Gaussian kernel values are about 0.0270, 0.1210, and 0.1210 per currency unit, producing f̂(22|5) ≈ 0.112 per currency unit after weighting. That height is not a probability; an interval probability requires integrating over an earnings range. Results depend on both bandwidths, the local data supply, and the assumption that nearby x-values provide relevant comparisons. The three points are illustrative, not observed earnings, and this paired extension is not the lab’s one-variable return chart.

A marginal density can hide pairing that a joint display retains. Imagine synthetic observations of market return and fund return: (−2, −1), (−1, 0), (1, 1), and (2, 0), all in percentage points. The fund-return marginal sees values −1, 0, 1, and 0 but forgets which market value accompanied each one. A joint KDE keeps those pairs and can reveal that the fund tends to be higher when the market is positive, while also showing the unusual final pair. A conditional density asks a narrower question, such as the fund-return distribution near market return 2. More dimensions require more data and stronger scaling choices. Scikit-learn User Guide — Density Estimation covers joint and conditional density concepts.","formula":"f̂(x,y) = (1 / (n hₓ hᵧ)) Σᵢ Kₓ((x−xᵢ)/hₓ) Kᵧ((y−yᵢ)/hᵧ)","takeaway":"A second variable changes a curve into a surface; more dimensions require much more data.","practice":{"question":"You want to see how the distribution of fund returns changes with market returns. Which object is more relevant: the marginal density of fund returns alone or a conditional density given market returns?","hint":"The question asks about fund returns at different levels of another variable.","solution":"A conditional density of fund returns given market returns directly answers the question. A joint density can also display both variables together; a marginal density alone omits their pairing."}},{"title":"Kernel regression estimates a local conditional mean","body":"The lecture connects density estimation to the Nadaraya–Watson estimator. At a chosen x, it computes a weighted average of nearby outcomes: m̂(x) = Σᵢ wᵢ(x)yᵢ, where wᵢ(x) = K((x−xᵢ)/h) / Σⱼ K((x−xⱼ)/h). The weights add to one, so this is a local mean rather than a density. Small bandwidths focus tightly on neighbors; large ones average broadly. This nonparametric curve can describe a nonlinear conditional mean without choosing one global straight line, but it is an association estimate, not a causal effect.

The Nadaraya–Watson calculation is transparent when kernel weights are supplied. Suppose three synthetic firms have advertising spending of 1, 2, and 5 thousand currency units and sales growth of 4%, 6%, and 10%, respectively. At x=2 thousand currency units, use illustrative kernel weights 0.25, 1, and 0.05. Their total is 1.30, so normalized weights are 0.25/1.30, 1/1.30, and 0.05/1.30. The estimate is (0.25×4%+1×6%+0.05×10%)/1.30=5.77% approximately. The output remains in percent because it is a weighted average of percentage outcomes. It describes a local conditional mean, not the effect of increasing advertising by one thousand currency units; confounding and extrapolation remain concerns. For implementation details on kernel regression, see “statsmodels — KernelReg” in the linked sources.

Consider a synthetic retail example in which x is a store’s discount, measured in percentage points, and y is weekly sales measured in thousand currency units. To estimate mean sales at a 10-point discount, suppose three illustrative observations are (8, 120), (10, 150), and (13, 240), with supplied kernel weights 0.25, 1.00, and 0.10. First add the weights: 0.25 + 1.00 + 0.10 = 1.35. Normalize them to 0.1852, 0.7407, and 0.0741 (approximately), then compute the local mean: (0.25×120 + 1.00×150 + 0.10×240) / 1.35 = 204/1.35 ≈ 151.11 thousand currency units per week. The estimate is therefore a conditional mean in y-units, not a slope or a forecast for one store. A useful diagnostic is to repeat the calculation with a wider bandwidth: more distant stores receive material weight, so the estimate may move toward a broader market average. Near the edge of the observed discount range, weights are inherently one-sided, making boundary bias plausible; avoid treating the curve as reliable extrapolation beyond the available x values.

Normalization in Nadaraya–Watson regression keeps the output on the outcome scale. Suppose three synthetic firms have inputs 1, 3, and 6 thousand currency units, outcomes 2%, 5%, and 11%, and kernel weights at x = 3 of 0.2, 1.0, and 0.1. Total weight is 1.3; the weighted outcome is 0.2×2 + 1.0×5 + 0.1×11 = 6.5 percentage-point-weight units, so the estimate is 6.5 ÷ 1.3 = 5%. Normalized weights sum to one, and the output remains percent. It is a local conditional average near input 3, not the causal effect of spending another thousand units. If nearby weights change, the estimate changes despite fixed outcomes, so report bandwidth and data support. Scikit-learn User Guide — Density Estimation provides related nonparametric context.","formula":"m̂(x) = Σᵢ wᵢ(x)yᵢ  ·  wᵢ(x) = K((x−xᵢ)/h) / Σⱼ K((x−xⱼ)/h)","takeaway":"KDE estimates where data concentrate; Nadaraya–Watson estimates a locally weighted average outcome.","practice":{"question":"Why do the Nadaraya–Watson weights include a denominator that sums all kernel weights?","hint":"Compare the weights with shares that should add to one.","solution":"The denominator normalizes the local weights to sum to one, making the estimate a weighted mean of nearby y values."}},{"title":"Local polynomials and a careful workflow","body":"Local polynomial smoothing fits a small polynomial near each target x, weighting observations by distance. Degree zero is the local-constant Nadaraya–Watson idea; higher degrees can adapt to local slopes and often reduce boundary bias. The supplied lecture also sketches semiparametric regression, which combines a structured linear component with a smooth component for other covariates. These tools add flexibility, not automatic truth: results depend on bandwidth, sample size, covariate scaling, edge behavior, and model design. In practice, plot the raw points, label units, compare bandwidths, check boundary behavior, and keep descriptive association separate from prediction and causal claims.

A local polynomial can correct a straight-line fit’s edge behavior, but the data near the edge still matter. Imagine synthetic weekly delivery times of 2, 3, 4, and 5 days with satisfaction scores of 80%, 78%, 75%, and 70%. At x=2 days, a local constant fit may average nearby scores and flatten the endpoint. A local linear fit instead estimates a local slope: using the first two points, the change is (78−80)/(3−2)=−2 percentage points per day, so one illustrative one-day extrapolation predicts 82% at x=1 day. That prediction is outside the observed range and should not be treated as evidence. Local polynomial degree, bandwidth, and edge support must be reported; the curve is associational and does not prove faster delivery causes satisfaction. For kernel-regression implementation details, see “statsmodels — KernelReg” in the linked sources.

Consider an illustrative, synthetic wage-growth diagnostic rather than observed data. To estimate monthly wage growth at an unemployment rate of x₀ = 6 percentage points, suppose four nearby observations are (x, y) = (4, 2.4%), (5, 1.8%), (7, 1.0%), and (9, 0.2%), where y is percent per month. With a Gaussian bandwidth h = 2 percentage points, use weights wᵢ = exp[−(xᵢ−6)²/(2h²)]: approximately 0.607, 0.882, 0.882, and 0.325. Fit yᵢ = a + b(xᵢ−6) by weighted least squares. The weighted sums give Σw = 2.696, Σw(x−6) = −0.239, and the fitted coefficients are a ≈ 1.442% per month and b ≈ −0.433 percentage points of wage growth per one percentage-point increase in unemployment. Thus the local estimate at 6% is 1.44%, while the local-constant (Nadaraya–Watson) weighted mean would be 3.992/2.696 ≈ 1.480%. The small difference reflects slope adjustment, not causality. Recheck sensitivity to h and sparse support; this is interpolation near 6%, not a license to extrapolate beyond the observed range.

At a boundary, local polynomial flexibility can tempt an analyst into unsupported extrapolation. Suppose synthetic observations pair delivery time 3, 4, and 5 days with satisfaction 76%, 74%, and 71%. A simple local slope from the first two points is (74 − 76) ÷ (4 − 3) = −2 percentage points per day. Extending that line to 2 days gives an illustrative 78%, but 2 days lies outside the observed support. The arithmetic is valid as a line extension, not as evidence that a faster delivery would cause 78% satisfaction. Report the boundary, degree, bandwidth, and available nearby data. Scikit-learn User Guide — Density Estimation describes smoothing methods, while design determines causal meaning.","takeaway":"Flexible smoothing is useful when the shape is unknown, but each added degree of freedom needs data and diagnostics.","practice":{"question":"A local-polynomial curve bends around the observations. Does that establish that changing x would cause y to change along that curve?","hint":"Separate the shape of an observational fit from the design that supports intervention claims.","solution":"No. It estimates a conditional relationship. Causal interpretation still needs a credible experimental or observational identification design and its assumptions."}}]
data.case_study: A risk analyst compares simulated daily returns for two hypothetical funds: one may contain a single broad cluster, while the other may have a quiet center and a separate shock-prone group. The analyst overlays a histogram and KDE, labels returns in percent, and compares a narrow, medium, and wide bandwidth before describing any peaks. The curve is a smoothed description of the selected sample—not a forecast, a guaranteed tail bound, or evidence that one fund caused another outcome. For an interval such as returns below −2%, the relevant probability-like summary is area over that range under the estimated density, conditional on the data and smoothing choice. All figures are educational and do not represent a recommendation.
data.misconceptions:
A density height is not the probability of one exact continuous observation.
A KDE's peaks are not guaranteed population subgroups; bandwidth can create or hide them.
The kernel shape is not the only choice—bandwidth often changes the estimate more.
A smooth conditional curve does not prove a causal relationship or forecast the next return.
Higher-order or multivariate smoothing is not automatically more accurate, especially with small samples.

data.title: A Starter Toolkit for Statistical Analysis
data.excerpt: Learn the practical steps behind a trustworthy analysis: organise a dataset, check variable types and missing values, calculate summaries, and make clear charts. Use spreadsheets and introductory Python to keep the work reproducible, so results can be checked and updated.
data.objectives:
Choose a spreadsheet or a code-based workflow to match the size, repeatability, and complexity of a task.
Recognize rows, columns, types, units, and missing values in a dataset before analyzing it.
Use pandas, NumPy, and Matplotlib for basic data inspection, summaries, and plots.
Keep raw data, transformations, formulas, and outputs traceable and reproducible.
Check whether a statistical result answers the question and respects the data's limitations.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Pick the tool for the job","body":"A spreadsheet is useful for a small, visible table and quick checks, provided formulas, units, and filters are clear. A script is a better fit when the same steps must run repeatedly, data are large, several files must be joined, or every transformation needs an audit trail. Python is a free general-purpose option; the pandas library provides labeled Series and DataFrame structures, NumPy supplies array operations, SciPy contains statistical routines such as gaussian_kde, and Matplotlib makes plots. R is another widely used statistical environment. The tool cannot repair a biased sample or a poorly defined variable.

A way to choose is to compare the cost of one run with the cost of repeating it. Suppose a spreadsheet check takes 12 minutes per file and a documented script takes 90 minutes to write, then 8 minutes per file thereafter. For 10 files, the spreadsheet takes 10 × 12 = 120 minutes, while the script takes 90 + (10 × 8) = 170 minutes, so the spreadsheet is faster initially. For 20 files, the totals are 240 minutes versus 90 + 160 = 250 minutes; at 23 files, the script takes 274 minutes versus 276 minutes, so the reusable workflow is just faster. These are illustrative, synthetic times, not measured performance. The calculation does not prove the script is more accurate; definitions and checks still matter. For a fuller treatment, see ‘pandas User Guide — 10 Minutes to pandas’ in the linked sources.

When a recurring workflow combines files, make the denominator explicit before choosing a summary command. Suppose two illustrative, synthetic payroll extracts use the same currency-per-hour unit: file A has 8 observed workers with a mean wage of $4.00/hour, and file B has 2 observed workers with a mean of $10.00/hour. If the estimand is the mean across all 10 observed workers, do not average the two file means: that would give ($4.00 + $10.00)/2 = $7.00/hour and gives each file equal weight. Pool the numerators instead: (8 × $4.00 + 2 × $10.00)/(8 + 2) = $52/10 = $5.20/hour. A script can retain each file’s observed count, sum, and unit metadata, then assert that the pooled denominator is 10 before writing the result. This calculation assumes each observed worker contributes one equal-weight observation and that the files measure the same wage concept; survey weights, duplicated workers, or different target populations require a different estimand and documented weighting rule. The numbers are synthetic, not observed wages.

Tool choice can be framed as a repeatability and error-control decision rather than a contest between software brands. A small synthetic table of 12 rows may be easiest to inspect in a spreadsheet, where formulas are visible beside values. If the same cleaning must run on 200 monthly files, a script can apply one recorded rule consistently and preserve a log. Neither route answers whether the rows represent the intended population. Before choosing, specify the task size, expected repetitions, joins, missing-data decisions, and review needs. pandas User Guide — 10 Minutes to pandas describes labeled table operations; NumPy Reference — Statistical Functions covers numerical summaries; Matplotlib — Pyplot Tutorial covers plotted output.","takeaway":"Choose a workflow for transparency and repeatability, not because one tool makes a result automatically correct.","practice":{"question":"You need to rerun the same cleaning and charting steps monthly on 40 files. What is a good default workflow?","hint":"Think about the cost of repeating manual actions and the value of a saved procedure.","solution":"Use a documented script or a carefully structured spreadsheet process with saved formulas. For many files and recurring work, a script is usually easier to rerun and review."}},{"title":"Make a small data dictionary","body":"For each column, record its name, meaning, type, unit, source, and missing-value convention. Each row should describe one observational unit, and each variable should use consistent definitions. Dates need a declared time zone and frequency; returns need a stated price and adjustment rule; a blank cell should not silently mean zero. A data dictionary makes it easier to spot when an amount is stored as text, a percentage is represented as a decimal, or a category code is being treated as a measured quantity.

A dictionary should also make scales unambiguous when a calculation combines columns. Imagine two illustrative, synthetic observations: a price of 80 currency units and a discount recorded as 0.15. If the discount is a decimal proportion, the discounted price is 80 × (1 − 0.15) = 68 currency units. If another file records the same discount as 15 percent, converting 15 percent ÷ 100 = 0.15 gives the same 68 currency units. But treating 15 as a proportion would produce 80 × (1 − 15) = −1,120 currency units, an obvious unit error. The dictionary should state currency, percentage scale, reference date, and whether the amount is nominal or real. This check prevents coding mistakes, but it cannot validate the economic definition itself. For pandas table inspection and column metadata, see ‘pandas User Guide — 10 Minutes to pandas’; economic definitions must be justified from the relevant data source.

A useful dictionary test is to compute an economic rate two ways and ask which estimand the rows support. Consider an illustrative, synthetic file with one row per month for a shop: revenue is 100, 120, and 130 currency units, while labor hours are 20, 10, and 10 hours. The typical-month mean of monthly revenue per hour is (100/20 + 120/10 + 130/10) ÷ 3 = (5 + 12 + 13) ÷ 3 = 10 currency units per hour. If the question is the rate across all recorded labor time, first aggregate the numerator and denominator: (100 + 120 + 130) ÷ (20 + 10 + 10) = 350 ÷ 40 = 8.75 currency units per hour. The difference is not a coding error; the first weights months equally, whereas the second weights hours equally. Record the row unit, period coverage, whether revenue is nominal or inflation-adjusted, and the denominator's definition. Also verify that a month is not duplicated or split across files before calculating either rate; otherwise the chosen estimand can be silently changed.

A data dictionary should identify both storage format and interpretation. Suppose a synthetic column called rate contains 0.03, while another file contains 3. If the first means a decimal rate and the second means percent, standardization requires 3 ÷ 100 = 0.03 before combining them. If 3 instead means three percentage points of a different measure, the conversion would be wrong despite matching labels. Record the numerator, denominator, unit, reference period, missing-value code, and whether the measure is a level or change. This prevents silent scale errors but cannot decide whether the economic concept is valid. pandas User Guide — 10 Minutes to pandas supports inspecting labeled columns; the definitions must come from the data source.","takeaway":"Well-named columns and explicit units prevent many errors before any test or model is run.","practice":{"question":"A return column stores 0.025 in one file and 2.5 in another. What must you check before combining them?","hint":"They may encode the same value using different scales.","solution":"Check the source definitions and units. One may store a decimal proportion and the other percent; standardize the representation and document the conversion before combining."}},{"title":"Load and inspect with pandas","body":"A pandas DataFrame is a labeled two-dimensional table; a Series is a labeled one-dimensional column. Start by loading the file, inspecting the first rows and data types, checking missingness, and confirming the date range. Use an explicit path and keep the original file unchanged. This first pass is about understanding what arrived—not making every column numeric or deleting every incomplete row. If you need to share code, include the package and version assumptions or a reproducible environment file.

Inspection can be treated as a small audit with explicit counts. Suppose an illustrative, synthetic CSV has 240 rows representing daily observations over 12 months, and `df['price'].isna().sum()` returns 6. The observed non-missing count is 240 − 6 = 234 daily prices, not 240 complete records. If the six gaps are spread across six different dates, a time-series calculation may need those dates retained and marked missing rather than silently deleting rows. Checking `df['date'].min()` and `max()` might show 2025-01-01 through 2025-12-31, but that range alone does not prove every calendar day is present. The count and date meaning must agree. These numbers are illustrative and synthetic; the procedure does not establish data accuracy or representativeness. For a fuller treatment, see ‘pandas User Guide — 10 Minutes to pandas’ in the linked sources.

After the structural pass, validate a measurement convention before summarizing returns. Consider an explicitly illustrative, synthetic three-row extract whose strings are `2%`, `-1%`, and `3%`. Parse the date column with `pd.to_datetime(..., errors='coerce')`, then count invalid dates and duplicate dates; a duplicate month is not automatically a second independent observation and should be resolved from the data documentation. For the return column, the percent signs mean the numeric decimals are 0.02, −0.01, and 0.03, so the arithmetic mean is (0.02 − 0.01 + 0.03)/3 = 0.013333…, or 1.333% per month. If these are consecutive holding-period returns, the cumulative simple return is (1 + 0.02)(1 − 0.01)(1 + 0.03) − 1 = 0.040094, or 4.0094% over the three months. The mean and compounded total answer different questions; neither should be relabeled as an annual rate without an explicit annualization assumption. These values are synthetic, and the check still depends on documented timing, consistent units, and no unrecognized missing or duplicated periods.

A preview is a starting point, not a data-quality certificate. Imagine a synthetic CSV with 100 rows, six blank prices, and a date column imported as text. The non-missing price count is 100 − 6 = 94, but the date endpoints may still look plausible in the first five displayed rows. Parse dates explicitly, inspect dtypes, count missing values, check duplicate dates, and compare the observed keys with the expected calendar. Keep blanks as missing until their meaning is established; do not coerce them to zero merely to satisfy a calculation. The procedure describes the file’s structure, not its accuracy or representativeness. pandas User Guide — 10 Minutes to pandas documents the inspection workflow.","code":"import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('returns.csv')
print(df.head())
print(df.dtypes)
print(df.isna().sum())","takeaway":"Inspect structure, types, and missingness before running summaries.","practice":{"question":"Why is df.head() not enough to verify that a date column was imported correctly?","hint":"A few displayed values do not reveal the underlying data type or the full time range.","solution":"Also inspect column types, date parsing, missing values, and the minimum and maximum dates. A plausible-looking preview can still hide text dates or gaps."}},{"title":"Summarize with NumPy and pandas","body":"Use summary commands as checks, not as substitutes for a plot or a definition. Pandas describe() provides common numeric summaries, value_counts() helps inspect categories, and NumPy offers array-based calculations such as mean, standard deviation, covariance, and correlation. Verify the axis and missing-value policy for each operation. For sample variance, many functions use degrees-of-freedom adjustment; state whether you want a population or sample estimate. A one-line output cannot tell you whether the observations are independent, selected, or measured in the right units.

Illustrative example: suppose a DataFrame contains a synthetic town series for average weekly rent, measured in pounds, from January through June 2025: £410, £430, £450, £470, £490 and £550. After checking that the column is numeric and has six non-missing monthly observations, pandas can report count, mean, minimum and maximum, while NumPy calculates the mean as (410 + 430 + 450 + 470 + 490 + 550) ÷ 6 = £466.67 per week. Using sample variability, `np.std(rent, ddof=1)` is about £49.67 per week. The mean describes the average month in this six-month window; the standard deviation indicates how much the monthly values vary around that average. The £550 observation is worth checking rather than silently deleting.

A NumPy or pandas summary can describe the recorded months and calculate the requested statistic, but it cannot show that the series represents every renter, establish why rents changed, or forecast July 2025. Before interpreting it, check the date range, missing-value count, consistent pound-per-week units, and whether each row represents one month rather than one household; for paired statistics, also verify that both variables use the same months. Do not mistake a standard deviation for a standard error, or treat pandas’ default as automatically answering the question: confirm the degrees-of-freedom and missing-data choices. The practical details in “pandas User Guide — 10 Minutes to pandas” and “NumPy Reference — Statistical Functions” in the linked sources below support this workflow.

Different summaries answer different questions. Consider illustrative, synthetic weekly sales in currency units: 100, 110, 120, and 300. The mean is (100 + 110 + 120 + 300) ÷ 4 = 157.5 currency units, while the median is (110 + 120) ÷ 2 = 115 currency units. The 185-unit gap between them signals that the high week pulls the mean upward; neither number is automatically the “typical” week. If the 300 value is a genuine promotion week, removing it would change the question rather than repair the data. If it is a transcription error, document the correction and retain the original. These values are illustrative and synthetic. The summaries describe these four weeks only and do not establish a cause for the high sales or justify a forecast. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NumPy Reference — Statistical Functions’ in the linked sources.

For a paired summary, compute covariance from centered values rather than reading a single matrix entry as a causal result. As an illustrative synthetic example, take four monthly market excess returns x = −2, 0, 1, 3 percentage points and corresponding fund excess returns y = −1, 1, 1, 5 percentage points. Their means are x̄ = 0.5 pp and ȳ = 1.5 pp. The cross-products of deviations are (−2.5)(−2.5) + (−0.5)(−0.5) + (0.5)(−0.5) + (2.5)(3.5) = 15 pp², so the sample covariance is 15 ÷ (4 − 1) = 5 pp². The denominator n − 1 is appropriate when estimating from a sample; dividing by n answers a population-descriptive question instead. Here, positive covariance means months with above-average market returns tend to coincide with above-average fund returns in this tiny window. It is scale-dependent, so compare strength with correlation: the sample standard deviations are about 2.08 pp and 2.52 pp, giving r ≈ 5 ÷ (2.08 × 2.52) = 0.95. These synthetic values do not identify a market-caused fund response; check pairing, time alignment, and whether four months can support the intended claim.

A summary command should be checked against the estimand and denominator it actually used. Suppose a synthetic column records weekly rents of 900, 1,000, 1,100, and one missing value, all in currency units. The observed mean is (900 + 1,000 + 1,100) ÷ 3 = 1,000 currency units, not 750 from silently inserting zero and dividing by four. A sample standard deviation also needs a denominator convention, while a paired statistic needs matching weeks in both columns. After computing, inspect a plot and the missingness rule. NumPy Reference — Statistical Functions describes available numerical operations, but a correct function call cannot determine whether missing means unavailable or truly zero.","code":"x = df['monthly_return'].dropna()
summary = x.describe()
r = df[['fund_return', 'market_return']].corr()","takeaway":"A correct computation still needs the right variables, paired sample, units, and assumptions.","practice":{"question":"A function returns a correlation matrix for three columns. What should you check before interpreting an entry?","hint":"Consider the paired observations and the variable definitions behind that cell.","solution":"Check that columns use compatible periods and units, missing data are handled as intended, the entry refers to the intended paired sample, and a scatterplot supports the linear interpretation."}},{"title":"Plot and label with Matplotlib","body":"A chart is part of the analysis workflow. Use a histogram or box plot for a single variable, a scatterplot for paired variables, and a line plot only when the horizontal order is meaningful. Matplotlib's figure and axes interface supports labeled titles, axes, legends, and multiple panels. Include units, data period, transformations, and whether values are observed or simulated. Avoid truncating an axis in a way that exaggerates a difference, and do not rely on color alone to distinguish groups.

Labels should let a reader reconstruct the comparison without guessing the scale. Suppose an illustrative, synthetic chart compares a savings rate rising from 4 percent to 6 percent. The absolute change is 6 − 4 = 2 percentage points, while the relative change is (6 − 4) ÷ 4 = 0.50, or 50 percent. A y-axis labeled only “change” could make these distinct statements appear interchangeable. Write the unit and denominator in the label or caption, such as “Savings rate (percent of monthly income)” and “2024–2025.” If the chart uses decimal values, 0.04 and 0.06, say so or format ticks as percentages. The figures are illustrative and synthetic, not historical observations. A clear plot shows association or difference but cannot establish why the rate changed. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matplotlib — Pyplot Tutorial’ in the linked sources.

When a time plot contains a missing period, the visual connection itself can become an unstated assumption. Consider illustrative, synthetic quarterly unemployment rates measured as percent of the labor force: Q1 = 5.0%, Q2 = 5.4%, Q3 = missing, and Q4 = 5.8%. First preserve Q3 as a missing value and keep the x-axis at quarterly spacing; do not relabel the remaining three rows as consecutive observations. If Matplotlib connects Q2 directly to Q4 after dropping the missing row, a reader may mistake the segment for a one-quarter movement. The observed endpoint difference is 5.8 − 5.4 = 0.4 percentage points over two quarters, not 0.4 points in one quarter. A linear interpolation would imply Q3 = (5.4 + 5.8) ÷ 2 = 5.6%, or 0.2 percentage points per quarter, but that is a modeled value, not an observation. Plot it separately with a distinct marker or dashed line and label “imputed.” The relative endpoint increase is 0.4 ÷ 5.4 ≈ 7.4%, a different denominator from the percentage-point change; neither calculation explains why unemployment changed.

A labeled axis prevents a common percentage-versus-percentage-point error. Suppose a synthetic savings rate rises from 8% to 10%. The absolute change is 10 − 8 = 2 percentage points; the relative change is 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25, or 25%. A chart caption should identify which statement the visual supports, along with whether stored values were 0.08 and 0.10 or displayed as 8 and 10. Include the outcome definition, time window, denominator, and whether points are simulated. If the vertical axis begins at 7%, the visual may emphasize a small movement, so show the scale honestly and explain any deliberate zoom. Matplotlib — Pyplot Tutorial covers labels and axes; it does not supply economic interpretation.","code":"import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df['monthly_return'].plot(kind='hist', bins=20)
plt.xlabel('Monthly return (decimal)')
plt.ylabel('Count')
plt.show()","takeaway":"A readable chart makes the variables, units, and denominator visible.","practice":{"question":"A histogram has no horizontal-axis unit label. What important interpretation could be lost?","hint":"A return can be encoded as a fraction, percent, or percentage-point value.","solution":"The reader may confuse decimals with percentages or compare values on an incompatible scale. Label the variable and unit explicitly."}},{"title":"Keep the analysis reproducible","body":"Save raw inputs separately from cleaned outputs, keep transformations in formulas or code, and state file sources, dates, software versions, assumptions, filters, and missing-data rules. Use clear names, version control when appropriate, and a fresh run from source data to check that the final result is repeatable. For an exploratory project, record both the intended question and any patterns discovered after looking. For a confirmatory test, do not silently tune the method until it produces the answer you hoped for. Code is an audit trail only if another person can see the inputs and choices it depends on.

A reproducible workflow should make both the input and the transformation testable. Suppose an illustrative, synthetic file contains 50 rows of monthly costs in currency units. A cleaning rule converts text “£12.50” to 12.50 currency units and removes 2 rows explicitly marked “missing,” leaving 50 − 2 = 48 usable rows. If a later rerun leaves 47 rows, the changed count is a warning to compare the raw file, rule, and software environment rather than overwrite the earlier result. Save the raw 50-row input, the rule, and the output date; record whether missingness means unavailable rather than zero. Reproducibility makes a calculation traceable, but it does not make the sample unbiased or the measurement valid. For a fuller treatment, see ‘pandas User Guide — 10 Minutes to pandas’ in the linked sources.

Treat a rerun as a comparison of records, not just a comparison of final means. For an illustrative, synthetic toolkit run, suppose the manifest stores rows = 40, missing-rate target = 15%, seed = 327 + 40×19 + 15×43 = 1732, and the code version. The target implies an expected 40×0.15 = 6 missing values, but a random draw might produce 4, 7, or another count; the realized count is not evidence that the control failed. First rerun the unchanged raw input and environment, then compare the row count, missing-value mask, observed count, and mean in standardized units. If the mask is unchanged but the mean differs, inspect numeric parsing or the averaging rule; if the mask changes, inspect the seed, random-number calls, and library versions. Do not replace gaps with zero: that would alter both the observed count and the estimand from the mean among available entries. Finally, save the manifest beside the output and report that the chart is simulated, so repeatability is distinguishable from accuracy or representativeness.

A fresh-run check can reveal hidden state that a saved notebook conceals. Suppose an illustrative synthetic analysis starts with 30 rows, marks 4 as missing, and produces 26 usable observations. After reopening the project from raw input, a rerun produces 25 because one cleaning rule changed from “blank” to “blank or zero.” The discrepancy is a diagnostic signal: compare the raw file, rule text, package versions, and output log before choosing a result. Preserve the original 30-row input, the exact transformation, and the reason zeros are values rather than missing records. pandas User Guide — 10 Minutes to pandas supports transparent table workflows, but reproducibility still depends on inputs, ordered steps, and documented assumptions.","takeaway":"Reproducibility is a documented path from input to result—not merely a saved screenshot or notebook.","practice":{"question":"A notebook produces a chart only because it refers to a file on your laptop and uses hidden state from earlier cells. Is it reproducible for a colleague?","hint":"Ask whether the colleague can recreate the input and run steps in order.","solution":"Not yet. Share or document the input source, clean environment or package versions, file paths, and ordered steps, then test the notebook from a fresh session."}}]
data.case_study: A learner receives monthly return data in a CSV. They use pandas to inspect the date, data types, and missing rows; they verify whether returns are decimals or percentages; and they compare a summary table with a histogram and a time plot. A small NumPy calculation checks the covariance with a benchmark, while a labeled Matplotlib chart shows the sample window and units. The learner preserves the raw CSV and saves a reproducible script with the data source and cleaning decisions. The example is a tool workflow, not a trading signal or investment advice.
data.misconceptions:
A spreadsheet or programming library cannot fix a poor sample or unclear measurement definition.
A preview of the first few rows does not verify every type, unit, or missing value.
One command's default missing-value or variance convention may not match the analysis question.
A chart without units and time scope can be easy to misread even when the code runs.
A saved notebook is not reproducible if its inputs, environment, or hidden state are missing.

data.title: From Research Question to Credible Estimate
data.excerpt: Turn a broad economic question into a specific outcome, comparison, population and time period before estimating anything. Learn to define the effect you want to measure, choose a design that creates a credible comparison, and state assumptions and checks clearly.
data.objectives:
State a target population, outcome, treatment and time horizon.
Distinguish a descriptive contrast from a causal effect.
Choose a design and list its identifying assumptions before estimating.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Write down the question before the model","body":"Suppose a city offers a job-training programme and wants to know whether it raises participants’ earnings one year later. Define who is eligible, what counts as participation, which earnings measure is used, and the follow-up date. These choices define the population, treatment and outcome. A vague question such as ‘does training work?’ cannot be answered by one coefficient until those details are made explicit.

A useful question also fixes the unit of analysis and the comparison’s time boundary. For example, ask whether the programme changes monthly after-tax earnings in euros during months 10–12 after enrolment, among residents eligible on 1 January, rather than asking whether it improves lives. Illustrative synthetic example: if the outcome is three-month earnings, a participant earning €6,300 has an average of €6,300 ÷ 3 = €2,100 per month; the same calculation must be applied to every person before comparing group means. This defines a measurable outcome, but it does not establish that training caused any difference: participants may differ in motivation or prior earnings. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Hernán & Robins — Causal Inference: What If (authors’ open book)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: measure outcome as monthly earnings in euros one year after eligibility. Suppose the programme group averages €2,400 and the comparison group €2,000, so the raw group gap is €2,400 − €2,000 = €400 per month. Do not label that gap the programme effect yet. Write the decomposition as raw gap = causal effect + selection bias. If a defensible design or sensitivity analysis implies that pre-existing differences would have made the programme group earn €150 more even without training, the implied effect is €400 − €150 = €250 per month. The sign matters: positive selection bias makes the raw gap too large; negative selection would make it too small. This calculation is an interpretation conditional on the €150 assumption, not a discovery of it from arithmetic. Random assignment makes the offer independent of potential outcomes in expectation, so the intention-to-treat effect is identified under suitable follow-up and measurement conditions. Actual take-up can remain selective; an effect of participation therefore needs additional instrumental-variable assumptions and is generally interpreted for compliers. Report the target population and estimand alongside the €250 figure, and test whether attrition, different earnings definitions, or a different follow-up window changes the result; precision cannot repair a biased counterfactual.

A well-defined estimand can be tested against every later choice. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose the target is the change in monthly after-tax earnings, in euros, for residents eligible on 1 January, measured during months 10–12 after enrolment. “Earnings” still needs a rule: include wages only, or wages plus benefits? If one resident has €7,200 over those three months, the monthly outcome is €7,200 ÷ 3 = €2,400, provided all residents use the same window. Next specify whether treatment means an offer, enrolment, or completed attendance. These are different interventions. A precise question does not create a counterfactual, but it prevents a coefficient about one outcome and population from being presented as an answer about another.","takeaway":"A precise estimand starts with a population, intervention, outcome and time horizon.","practice":{"question":"A report compares average earnings of graduates and non-graduates. What is missing before calling the difference a programme effect?","hint":"Ask whether the two groups would have had the same outcomes without the programme.","solution":"The comparison lacks a defensible counterfactual design. Eligibility, selection into training, baseline differences and the causal estimand must be specified."}},{"title":"Name the counterfactual","body":"For each eligible person, imagine two potential outcomes: earnings if they participate and earnings if they do not. Only one is observed for that person, so the unobserved alternative is the counterfactual. An average treatment effect compares the mean of these potential outcomes in a stated target population. The gap between treated and untreated people is not automatically that effect when participation is selective.

Potential outcomes become clearer when the treatment contrast is written for one person before averaging. Illustrative synthetic example: resident A would earn €2,400 per month with training and €2,100 without it, so A’s individual effect is €2,400 − €2,100 = €300 per month; resident B might have €1,900 under either option, giving €0 per month. We cannot observe both outcomes for the same resident, so an average treatment effect is assembled across people using a credible comparison. If the target population has equal numbers of A-like and B-like residents, the illustrative average is (€300 + €0) ÷ 2 = €150 per month. This arithmetic is not evidence that training caused €150; selection or unequal composition can distort observed group differences. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Cunningham — Causal Inference: The Mixtape (Yale University Press)’ in the linked sources.

Suppose an illustrative synthetic evaluation records average monthly earnings of €2,900 for programme participants and €2,000 for eligible nonparticipants: the raw gap is €900 per month. Before calling that an effect, write the lab’s decomposition, observed gap = target causal effect + selection bias. If, purely as a synthetic sensitivity assumption, the selection component is €350 per month—for example, participants would have earned €350 more even without training—then the implied target effect is €900 − €350 = €550 per month. The subtraction is on one outcome scale and uses the same eligible population, time window, and earnings definition in both terms. A negative bias would instead mean participants started with lower untreated earnings, so subtracting it would increase the implied effect. This calculation is only an accounting illustration, not an identification strategy: the €350 would need support from a credible comparison, such as random assignment or defensible quasi-experimental assumptions. If that component is guessed, the result is sensitivity analysis, and the effect may apply only to the eligible population represented by the comparison—not to every worker or to a different follow-up horizon.

The counterfactual is easiest to protect when the comparison is written before looking at outcomes. Illustrative synthetic example: for four eligible residents, the no-training earnings outcomes would be €1,800, €2,200, €2,400, and €2,000, while the corresponding training outcomes would be €1,950, €2,200, €2,550, and €1,950. The individual differences are €150, €0, €150, and −€50; their average is (€150 + 0 + €150 − €50) ÷ 4 = €62.50 per month. In real data, each person contributes only one potential outcome, so this table is a teaching device, not an observable calculation. A group gap can differ from €62.50 if participation selects people with different untreated earnings.","takeaway":"Causal inference is a comparison with an unobserved alternative, not merely a difference between observed groups.","formula":"ATE = E[Y(1) − Y(0)]; Y(1) and Y(0) are potential outcomes under treatment and no treatment."},{"title":"Choose an identification strategy","body":"A randomized offer, a policy threshold, an external instrument, or a well-supported comparison over time can create different routes to a counterfactual. Each design answers a somewhat different question and needs its own assumptions. Random assignment supports a direct comparison on average; an instrument or threshold often identifies an effect for a narrower group near the source of variation.

Illustrative synthetic example: A city randomly offers a 12-month job-training place to 200 eligible unemployed residents, offering it to 100 and not offering it to 100. After 12 months, 70 people in the offer group and 60 in the no-offer group are employed. The intention-to-treat estimate is 70/100 − 60/100 = 0.10, or 10 percentage points: the average difference associated with being offered the programme. Suppose 80% of the offer group and 20% of the comparison group actually attend, a first-stage difference of 0.60. A simple Wald calculation is 0.10 ÷ 0.60 = 0.167, or 16.7 percentage points per additional participant induced by the offer. All quantities are employment rates at the same one-year horizon.

The randomized offer can identify the average effect of being offered training for these eligible residents, provided assignment was implemented as planned and outcome measurement and follow-up are comparable. The Wald result may identify a local effect for compliers, not the effect for every attendee, and it additionally needs relevance, an exclusion restriction, and no treatment switching that reverses the assignment pattern. Check take-up by assignment, baseline balance, missing 12-month outcomes, and possible spillovers before interpreting it. Do not call the 10-percentage-point ITT a 10% increase, or treat the 16.7-point complier estimate as universal. The linked sources below, including “Angrist & Pischke — Mastering ’Metrics (Princeton University Press),” provide further guidance on matching designs to counterfactuals.

Identification is about why two observed groups can stand in for the missing counterfactual, not merely about choosing a named estimator. Illustrative synthetic example: a benefit rule grants an extra €120 per month to applicants scoring at least 50 points. Among applicants within one point of the cutoff, those scoring 49 receive €0 and those scoring 50 receive €120; the raw discontinuity is €120 per month. A regression-discontinuity estimate would interpret that jump as local only if applicants cannot precisely manipulate scores and other outcomes change smoothly at 50. The comparison does not automatically reveal the effect for applicants scoring 80, nor does it prove every euro of the jump was caused by the benefit if another policy also starts at the cutoff. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke — Mastering ’Metrics (Princeton University Press)’ in the linked sources.

For a separate illustrative synthetic example, suppose a voluntary wage-support programme has an observed post-programme monthly earnings gap of €280: participants average €1,480 and non-participants €1,200. That €280 is a descriptive contrast, not yet the programme effect. Suppose a credible pre-treatment comparison or sensitivity analysis supports the assumption that, without the programme, participants would have earned €180 more per month because they entered with stronger prior earnings. Writing the decomposition explicitly gives observed gap = causal effect + selection bias, so €280 = effect + €180 and the implied effect is €100 per participant per month. The sign matters: positive selection inflates the raw gap; subtracting it prevents that baseline advantage from being credited to treatment. This calculation is conditional on the €180 counterfactual assumption, not a substitute for random assignment or another identifying design. If plausible selection bias ranged from €100 to €250, the corresponding effects would range from €180 to €30 per month, even though the raw gap stays €280. Report the estimand, time unit, and sensitivity range rather than presenting €100 as universal or causal for people outside this comparison.

A design should be selected from the way treatment actually varies. Illustrative synthetic example: a benefit begins at a score of 50, and applicants scoring 49 receive €0 while those scoring 50 receive €120. The discontinuity is €120 at the boundary, but its causal interpretation is local. Ask three separate questions: can applicants manipulate the score precisely, do other policies also change at 50, and are outcomes smooth through the cutoff absent the benefit? A regression-discontinuity estimate is then about applicants near 50, not automatically those scoring 80. The research-design lab shows a schematic decomposition of effect, selection bias, and observed gap, not evidence about these RD assumptions; moving its controls cannot validate them. “Angrist & Pischke — Mastering ’Metrics (Princeton University Press)” gives further design guidance.","takeaway":"Pick a design because of how treatment varies, not because a particular estimator is familiar."},{"title":"Pre-specify checks and communicate scope","body":"Before interpreting estimates, record the data source, sample rules, comparison group, outcome construction, uncertainty method and planned sensitivity checks. Ask what could violate the design: selective take-up, anticipation, spillovers, measurement changes or a policy concurrent with treatment. Report the population and period to which the result applies. A careful estimate can be useful even when it does not generalize everywhere.

A pre-specified missing-data rule prevents researchers from quietly changing the target after seeing results. Illustrative synthetic example: a study begins with 250 people per arm and observes 225 treated and 200 comparison outcomes at month 12, so observed follow-up rates are 225 ÷ 250 = 90% and 200 ÷ 250 = 80%. If average monthly earnings are €2,400 for observed treated people and €2,200 for observed comparison people, the observed contrast is €200 per month, but it need not equal the full-sample contrast because missingness may depend on earnings. Report the units, dates, attrition by arm, and a sensitivity analysis; comparable follow-up is an assumption, not a guarantee. The contrast remains associational unless the design supports causality. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke — Mostly Harmless Econometrics (Princeton University Press)’ in the linked sources.

Use a sensitivity calculation to separate what the data show from what the design must justify. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose eligible people offered a programme earn €2,650 per month on average at follow-up, while the comparison group earns €2,400; the raw gap is €2,650 − €2,400 = €250 per month. Now write an explicit selection-bias scenario: if people accepting or being offered the programme would have earned €100 more even without it, then the implied effect under that scenario is €250 − €100 = €150 per month. The sign matters: positive selection bias makes the raw gap too large, whereas a −€100 bias would imply €250 − (−€100) = €350 per month. These are not observed facts or a causal estimate; they are a transparent sensitivity range built from an assumption about the counterfactual. Record who the bias refers to, the outcome definition and follow-up month, then ask whether €100 is substantively plausible. The design lab’s target-effect-plus-selection-bias decomposition makes the same accounting visible, but changing a slider cannot validate the assumed bias or extend the result beyond the eligible population.

A missing-data rule should say what happens before anyone sees the treatment contrast. Illustrative synthetic example: 300 people are assigned to each arm, with 270 treated and 255 comparison outcomes observed at follow-up. Retention is 270 ÷ 300 = 90% in treatment and 255 ÷ 300 = 85% in comparison, a five-percentage-point retention difference. If observed monthly earnings average €2,500 and €2,300, their contrast is €200, but that number describes observed cases unless a justified analysis addresses missing outcomes. Compare missingness by arm and inspect whether the outcome itself predicts being observed. Also preserve the target population, date, units, and planned sensitivity rules. Precision around a selected subset cannot repair informative attrition or a changed estimand.","takeaway":"Transparent design choices make a result easier to challenge, reproduce and use responsibly."},{"title":"The same design can identify different target effects","body":"Imagine a city offers job training, but some invited residents decline and some uninvited residents find another course. The outcome difference by original invitation is the intention-to-treat effect. Dividing that outcome difference by the invitation's effect on take-up can identify a local average treatment effect for people whose participation changed because of the invitation, but only under the IV assumptions. A threshold design is local to people near its cutoff; a difference-in-differences design targets a treated group's change relative to a credible comparison trend. These are not automatically estimates of one universal effect. State who, what treatment contrast, outcome, and horizon the number describes before comparing estimates.

Changing the target effect can change the answer even when the data are unchanged. Illustrative synthetic example: an invitation raises course take-up from 20% to 50%, a 30-percentage-point increase, and raises employment at month 6 from 40% to 46%, a 6-percentage-point ITT. Using the stated formula, the Wald ratio is 6 ÷ 30 = 0.20, or 20 percentage points of employment per additional participant induced by the invitation. That number is a complier-scale effect, not a 20% increase and not necessarily the effect for voluntary attendees who would participate without an invitation. It also relies on instrument relevance, exclusion, and monotonicity; the arithmetic alone cannot verify them. Always state percentage points, the six-month horizon, and the complier population. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Chs. 1–2’ in the linked sources.

Use the lab’s decomposition to diagnose why a raw gap can mislead. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose the treatment would raise the six-month outcome by 2.0 outcome units for a clearly defined target population, but people who self-select into treatment would have been 0.8 units lower even without treatment. With selection bias defined as treated-minus-comparison potential outcomes under no treatment, the observed gap is target effect + bias = 2.0 + (−0.8) = 1.2 outcome units. A naive comparison therefore understates the target effect by 0.8 units; it is not evidence that the programme delivered only 1.2 units. Reverse the sign and the same 2.0-unit effect plus +0.8 units of positive selection produces a 2.8-unit observed gap, overstating the effect. The calculation is an accounting identity, not an identification strategy: the unobserved no-treatment difference cannot be learned from the gap alone. Before interpreting a comparison, ask which design supplies that counterfactual, whether treatment timing and outcome measurement match the target, and whether the resulting estimate applies to the stated population rather than merely to a selected subgroup.

Two estimates can disagree because they answer different counterfactual questions, not because one arithmetic step is wrong. Illustrative synthetic example: an invitation raises course participation from 25% to 55%, a 30-percentage-point first stage. Employment rises from 48% to 54%, a 6-point intention-to-treat contrast. The Wald ratio is 0.06 ÷ 0.30 = 0.20, or 20 percentage points per additional participant induced by the invitation. The numerator concerns assignment; the ratio concerns compliers under instrumental-variable assumptions. It is not a 20% increase, nor necessarily the effect among people who would volunteer without an invitation. State the outcome horizon, the denominator’s scale, and the population whose behaviour changed. The design, not the estimator label alone, determines scope.","takeaway":"A method's source of variation helps define the estimand; the estimator name alone does not say who the result is about.","formula":"ITT = E[Y|Z=1] − E[Y|Z=0]; under IV assumptions, LATE = ITT / (E[D|Z=1] − E[D|Z=0]).","practice":{"question":"A policy team wants the effect of completing training, but only the invitation was randomized. Which effect can be estimated directly from assignment?","hint":"Keep the original randomized variable separate from take-up.","solution":"The intention-to-treat effect of the invitation is directly estimated by comparing outcomes by assigned offer. The effect of completing training requires additional IV assumptions and generally applies to compliers, not automatically to everyone."}}]
data.case_study: A local authority evaluates a voluntary employment programme. The first task is to define an eligible population and earnings outcome, then map how the offer and take-up occurred. The comparison design—not a significance threshold—determines what effect can be defended.
data.misconceptions:
A regression adjustment does not create random assignment.
A statistically precise estimate can still target the wrong population or outcome.
An estimate from one design need not apply to people far from its comparison group.
