data.title: Regression Discontinuity Designs
data.excerpt: Regression discontinuity uses a cutoff in a policy rule—such as an eligibility score—to compare units just above and below it. See how different assignment rules work, check whether people can manipulate the score, and understand why the result usually applies only near the cutoff.
data.objectives:
Distinguish sharp and fuzzy regression discontinuity.
Explain continuity and no-precise-manipulation assumptions.
Interpret local estimates and test sensitivity to bandwidth and specification.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"A threshold can create a local comparison","body":"Suppose a training grant is offered when a score reaches 70. People scoring 69.8 and 70.2 may be similar in many ways, while their probability of receiving the grant changes at the rule. A discontinuity in outcomes at 70 can be attributed to the offer only if other determinants of outcomes do not also jump there and units cannot precisely sort around the cutoff.

Illustrative synthetic example (weekly earnings, 2025): a city uses an eligibility score of 70 to offer a training grant. Among 1,000 applicants scoring 69.5–69.9, 41% receive the grant and average earnings three months later are £320 per week; among 1,000 scoring 70.0–70.4, 61% receive it and average earnings are £350 per week. The grant-receipt probability therefore jumps by 0.61 − 0.41 = 0.20, or 20 percentage points, while the earnings outcome jumps by £350 − £320 = £30 per week. In this fuzzy regression-discontinuity example, the Wald ratio is £30 ÷ 0.20 = £150 in weekly earnings per additional recipient induced by eligibility near the cutoff. The £30 discontinuity is the effect of eligibility (the reduced form); the £150 ratio concerns receipt under the additional design assumptions. These figures are synthetic, not programme evidence.

A fuzzy regression-discontinuity design can estimate a local effect for applicants near score 70 when potential outcomes would change smoothly through the cutoff, applicants cannot precisely manipulate their scores, eligibility changes grant receipt, and the exclusion and monotonicity assumptions are defensible. It cannot automatically describe workers far from the threshold or prove a nationwide effect. Check whether the score distribution shows bunching around 70 and whether baseline characteristics also jump there; use those as diagnostics, not proof that all assumptions hold. Do not interpret the £30 eligibility discontinuity as the effect for every grant recipient, or the £150 local estimate as an effect for all workers. For the institutional logic and local interpretation, see “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 6, §§6.1–6.2” in the linked sources below.

Illustrative synthetic example: a housing voucher uses an income-score cutoff of 50 points. In a window from 48 to 52, 200 households just below average 2.4 months of stable housing during the next 12 months, while 200 just above average 2.7 months. The outcome difference is 2.7 − 2.4 = 0.3 months per household. If voucher receipt rises from 10% to 30%, eligibility’s first-stage jump is 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.20, or 20 percentage points. A fuzzy Wald calculation is 0.3 ÷ 0.20 = 1.5 additional months per induced recipient. This local interpretation requires smooth untreated outcomes and no precise score sorting; it does not establish effects for all households. For a fuller treatment, see “Cunningham — Causal Inference: The Mixtape (Yale University Press)” in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic diagnostic: suppose a municipal hiring credit is assigned at score 50, and the outcome is employment six months later, in percentage points. Fit separate local linear lines on each side and evaluate both at the cutoff—not at the average score in each group. With a score bandwidth of 2 points, imagine the fitted left-hand limit is 58 percentage points and the right-hand limit is 64 percentage points. The discontinuity is therefore 64 − 58 = 6 percentage points, meaning an eligibility jump in employment probability near score 50, not a six-percent increase. Re-estimating with bandwidth 4 gives fitted limits of 55 and 62 percentage points, so the corresponding jump is 62 − 55 = 7 percentage points. The positive sign is reassuring, but the one-point change signals sensitivity to which observations and trend shape are used; it is not a reason to select the estimate. Report both specifications, inspect the score density and predetermined outcomes, and ask whether untreated employment would plausibly vary smoothly through 50. These values are explicitly synthetic, and neither estimate automatically applies to applicants far from the threshold or establishes a causal effect without those assumptions.

A threshold comparison has two distinct jumps to read. Imagine an eligibility indicator rising from 0.30 just below a score cutoff to 0.50 just above it, while an outcome rises from 72 to 78 illustrative units. The first stage is 0.50 − 0.30 = 0.20, or 20 percentage points; the reduced-form outcome jump is 6 units. Dividing gives a fuzzy-RD Wald ratio of 6 ÷ 0.20 = 30 outcome units per additional recipient induced by eligibility. That ratio is local and needs exclusion and monotonicity; it is not the effect for every recipient. If treatment changes from zero to one exactly at the threshold, the first stage is 1 and the reduced form is the sharp-RD effect. These are synthetic calculations, not programme evidence.","takeaway":"RD compares observations close to a threshold where treatment probability changes."},{"title":"Sharp and fuzzy assignment differ","body":"In a sharp design, everyone on one side receives treatment and everyone on the other side does not. In a fuzzy design, crossing the threshold changes the chance of treatment but does not determine it perfectly. The fuzzy design uses threshold eligibility as an instrument for actual treatment and inherits the additional IV conditions. State whether the target is the effect of eligibility or treatment receipt.

Illustrative synthetic example: among 100 applicants immediately below a score cutoff, 0 receive a fee waiver; among 100 immediately above, all 100 receive one. Treatment probability changes by 100/100 − 0/100 = 1.00, or 100 percentage points, so this is sharp RD. In a different synthetic programme, 84 of 100 below and 94 of 100 above receive tutoring: 0.94 − 0.84 = 0.10, or 10 percentage points, making it fuzzy. If test scores rise by 4 points across that cutoff, the reduced-form jump is 4 points, while the Wald ratio is 4 ÷ 0.10 = 40 test-score points per induced participant. The ratio needs exclusion and monotonicity; it is not automatically the average effect for every participant. For a fuller treatment, see “Angrist & Pischke — Mastering ’Metrics (Princeton University Press)” in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a benefit-eligibility score has a cutoff at 0, and the outcome is monthly earnings measured in currency units. Within a deliberately narrow window, estimate the untreated-side trend as Y₀ = 50 + 4x and the treated-side trend as Y₁ = 50 + 4x + 2.5, where x is score units. Evaluate both fitted lines at the threshold rather than comparing averages from distant applicants: the left limit is 50 currency units per month, the right limit is 52.5, so the sharp-RD discontinuity is 52.5 − 50 = 2.5 currency units per month. At x = 0.5, the same lines predict 52 and 54.5; their difference remains 2.5 because the illustrative slopes are equal. If widening the bandwidth changes the estimated jump substantially, that is a sensitivity warning: curvature, other threshold changes, or a different local population may be entering. The 2.5-unit interpretation is a local causal effect only if potential outcomes would have been continuous at the cutoff and applicants could not precisely sort around it; otherwise it is a descriptive jump.

Read the assignment mechanism before choosing the estimand. In a synthetic sharp design, 250 applicants below a cutoff have zero treatment receipts and 250 above have 250 receipts, so receipt probability changes from 0.00 to 1.00, a 100-percentage-point first stage. If average outcomes are 48 below and 53 above, the reduced-form jump is 5 outcome units, which is also the sharp local treatment contrast under the design assumptions. In a synthetic fuzzy design, receipt changes from 0.40 to 0.70, a 0.30 first stage, while outcomes change from 48 to 53; the Wald ratio is 5 ÷ 0.30 = 16.67 units per induced recipient, rounded to two decimals. The figures are illustrative, and fuzzy interpretation requires continuity, exclusion, and monotonicity.","takeaway":"The assignment rule determines which RD estimand and assumptions apply."},{"title":"Choose the local window responsibly","body":"The estimate can change with the bandwidth, polynomial order and weighting near the cutoff. Show the score-outcome relationship on both sides, use transparent and restrained functional forms, and report sensitivity across reasonable bandwidths. A very wide window may rely on distant comparisons; a very narrow one may be imprecise. These choices should be motivated rather than selected for a preferred result.

Bandwidth choice changes which observations define “near” the cutoff. Illustrative synthetic example: with a score cutoff of 60, a narrow window of 59–61 contains 80 observations and estimates a wage jump of $18 per week; a wider window of 55–65 contains 600 observations and estimates $11 per week. The wider estimate may be more precise because 600 exceeds 80, but it compares people farther apart in score and may depend more on curve shape. The difference is $18 − $11 = $7 per week, not evidence that either estimate is true. Report bandwidth, counts, uncertainty, and alternatives. Smoothness near the cutoff is needed, and polynomial flexibility cannot repair a discontinuity in another determinant. These figures are illustrative and synthetic. For a fuller treatment, see “Matheus Facure — Ch. 16: Regression Discontinuity (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)” in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic calculation: recenter the running score so the cutoff is x = 0, then fit separate local lines, y = α_L + β_Lx below and y = α_R + β_Rx above. Within a ±0.5-score window, suppose the left line has α_L = 2.80 outcome units and β_L = 0.40 outcome units per score unit, while the right line has α_R = 4.10 and β_R = 0.90. The RD contrast compares the two limits at x = 0: τ̂ = α_R − α_L = 4.10 − 2.80 = 1.30 outcome units. Comparing predictions at x = −0.5 and x = +0.5 would instead give 2.80 − 0.40(0.5) = 2.60 and 4.10 + 0.90(0.5) = 4.55, a 1.95-unit gap that also reflects movement along the score slopes. Refit the centered specification at ±0.3 and ±0.8 score units and report how τ̂ changes; this is a sensitivity check, not a reason to select the largest jump. Causal interpretation still requires untreated outcomes and relevant covariates to vary smoothly through the cutoff, with no precise sorting. These numbers are illustrative and synthetic; the estimate is local to the threshold.

A responsible bandwidth comparison changes one design choice at a time and records what it changes. Consider a synthetic cutoff at score 40. A window from 39.5 to 40.5 contains 100 observations and gives a fitted jump of 2.4 wage units; a window from 38 to 42 contains 500 observations and gives 1.8 wage units. The difference is 0.6 units, calculated as 2.4 − 1.8, but neither number wins merely because it is larger. The narrow window is more local; the wide window has five times as many records (500 ÷ 100 = 5) and may be more precise, while asking more of the fitted curves. Report both sides, uncertainty, specification, and counts. These are synthetic outputs, not empirical evidence.","takeaway":"Bandwidth analysis reveals the trade-off between locality and precision."},{"title":"Probe the threshold story","body":"Check whether the running variable bunches at the cutoff, whether baseline covariates jump, whether outcomes change at placebo thresholds and whether another policy uses the same rule. These checks can expose threats but cannot prove that no unobserved factor changes at the cutoff. The estimate is local to units near the threshold and need not represent everyone eligible for the policy.

Diagnostics provide evidence about assumptions, not automatic proof. Illustrative example: in a synthetic sample of 500 applicants, 246 lie just below a cutoff and 254 just above, so counts differ by 254 − 246 = 8 applicants; that imbalance is not clear bunching. Suppose average prior GPA is 3.10 below and 3.12 above: the difference is 0.02 GPA points, which may be sampling noise. A placebo cutoff at 40 produces a 0.01-point outcome jump, whereas the real cutoff produces 0.15 points; the contrast is informative but not conclusive. Check rules, density plots, covariates, and placebo locations. Manipulation, another policy at the same score, or measurement error can still undermine causal interpretation. The estimate remains local and need not apply to distant applicants. For a fuller treatment, see “Edward Rubin — EC 607: Lecture 10: Regression Discontinuity (license not stated; link only)” in the linked sources.

A useful sensitivity calculation is to recompute the discontinuity, rather than treating one window as definitive. Suppose, purely illustratively, that a scholarship cutoff is score 0 and the outcome is first-year credits completed (credits). Fit separate local lines using applicants within 2 score units, then evaluate both lines at score 0: if the below-cutoff prediction is 28.4 credits and the above-cutoff prediction is 31.9 credits, the local jump is 31.9 − 28.4 = 3.5 credits per applicant. Now widen the window to 5 score units; the corresponding predictions might be 27.6 and 32.6 credits, giving 5.0 credits. These numbers are synthetic, not observed data. The change, 1.5 credits, is a warning that observations farther from the threshold or curvature may be influencing the fit; it is not evidence that either estimate is correct. Report the bandwidth, polynomial order, and standard-error method alongside the estimate, and inspect a plot. A causal reading still requires that potential outcomes vary smoothly at the cutoff and that applicants cannot precisely sort around it; otherwise this arithmetic is only a conditional local contrast.

Treat threshold diagnostics as stress tests for a story about assignment. In a synthetic diagnostic, suppose a running-score histogram has 98 applicants in the bin just below the cutoff and 102 just above; the four-applicant difference is not, by itself, proof of manipulation. Suppose a pre-treatment income mean is $2,410 below and $2,425 above, a $15 level difference. A placebo cutoff elsewhere produces a 0.2-unit outcome jump, while the policy cutoff produces 1.1 units; the latter exceeds the placebo by 0.9 units, but this comparison still cannot rule out another rule changing at the threshold. The RD lab’s simulated observations are explanatory, not measured data. Use density, covariate, placebo, and institutional checks together, and keep the estimate local.","takeaway":"RD is persuasive when institutional details support a clean local comparison."},{"title":"The bandwidth trades locality against precision","body":"Suppose a scholarship rule changes at a score of 75 and estimated enrolment rises by 6 percentage points just at that threshold. This is evidence about applicants close to 75, not automatically about those far below or above it. A narrower bandwidth compares more similar scores and can reduce reliance on a broad functional-form extrapolation, but it leaves fewer observations and usually increases uncertainty. A wider window adds information while asking the fitted curves to describe more distant units. Show the cutoff, observations on each side, the chosen local specification, uncertainty, and sensitivity to reasonable bandwidths. Smooth covariates and no visible bunching can support the design story, but do not prove every continuity assumption.

Imagine a scholarship offered to applicants scoring at least 75. Just below the cutoff, 60% enrol; just above it, 66% enrol. The 6-percentage-point jump is the basic discontinuity. The comparison is persuasive when applicants close to 75 are otherwise alike and crossing 75 changes eligibility, while other influences on enrolment move smoothly through the score. It is not a comparison of every eligible applicant with every ineligible applicant; distant scores may represent very different people.

A bandwidth decides how close to 75 the analysis stays. A narrow window makes the applicants more alike but leaves fewer observations and a noisier estimate; a wide window adds precision but may compare less similar people and depend more on the model’s shape. Check whether scores bunch at the cutoff, whether pre-policy characteristics also jump, and whether the result is sensitive to reasonable windows. The estimate is local to applicants near 75, and a smooth graph cannot prove every assumption. See Angrist & Pischke Chapter 6 and the linked regression-discontinuity references.

A bandwidth sets the population being compared. Illustrative synthetic example: for a score cutoff of 75, a ±2-point window contains 120 applicants and gives an enrolment jump of 5 percentage points, while a ±8-point window contains 720 applicants and gives 3 percentage points. The narrower estimate compares scores from 73 to 77, whereas the wider includes 67 to 83; the sample is six times larger (720 ÷ 120 = 6), but the wider comparison may involve less similar applicants. A percentage-point jump is not a percent increase: 5 percentage points means, for example, 60% to 65%, not a 5% relative change. Treat differences across windows as sensitivity evidence, not as permission to choose a preferred result. Continuity and no precise manipulation remain necessary, and the result is local rather than universal. For a fuller treatment, see “Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)” in the linked sources.

Consider how the local fitted lines turn a bandwidth choice into a precise estimand. Illustrative synthetic example: within scores 74–76, suppose the below-cutoff fit is Ŷ₋ = 58.4 + 0.8(score − 75) percentage points and the above-cutoff fit is Ŷ₊ = 64.9 + 1.1(score − 75) percentage points. Evaluating both equations at the threshold sets score − 75 = 0, so the estimated jump is Ŷ₊(75) − Ŷ₋(75) = 64.9% − 58.4% = 6.5 percentage points. The slopes have units of percentage points per score unit; they adjust for different local trends, so this is not merely the difference between two unadjusted group averages. As a sensitivity check, a wider synthetic ±3-score window might produce fitted intercepts of 58.0% and 63.7%, giving 5.7 percentage points (63.7 − 58.0), not evidence that either window is automatically correct. Report the chosen window, polynomial order, and uncertainty, and ask whether results change materially. A causal reading still requires that potential outcomes vary smoothly at 75, scores are not precisely manipulated, and crossing the threshold changes eligibility rather than another contemporaneous rule.

In the RD lab, the mint vertical lines mark the selected local window around a cutoff, while the synthetic points outside that window do not define the displayed local comparison. With the jump control at 1.5 outcome units and bandwidth at 0.7 score units, the diagram should be read as a local discontinuity, not a population average. If a teaching change sets bandwidth to 0.4, the window narrows to scores within 0.4 of the cutoff; setting it to 1.0 includes a broader neighborhood. The control changes the comparison region, not the underlying causal assumptions. A stable-looking jump across windows is reassuring sensitivity evidence, whereas a moving jump signals specification dependence. All plotted values are simulated illustrations, and continuity plus no precise manipulation remain necessary.","takeaway":"The local window is part of the RD design: explain its bias–precision trade-off and keep the claim local to the cutoff.","formula":{"question":"An RD estimate is stable near a score cutoff. Can it be reported as the average effect for all scholarship applicants?","hint":"Identify which units supply the comparison.","solution":"Not without additional assumptions. The design directly compares units near the cutoff, so broad generalization beyond that local group needs separate evidence."}}]
data.case_study: A scholarship is assigned to applicants with a score above a published threshold. Compare applicants near the cutoff, inspect score manipulation and baseline discontinuities, and describe the estimate as a local effect around that score.
data.misconceptions:
An RD estimate is usually local to the cutoff, not a whole-population average.
A plot that looks smooth cannot verify every continuity assumption.
In fuzzy RD, eligibility and actual treatment are not interchangeable.

data.title: Panel Data, Fixed Effects & First Differences
data.excerpt: Panel data track the same people, firms or regions over time, helping separate lasting differences from changes within a unit. Learn how fixed effects and first differences work, what they cannot control for, and why repeated observations must be handled carefully.
data.objectives:
Identify the unit and time dimensions of panel data.
Interpret entity and time fixed effects.
Recognize time-varying confounding and the need to cluster dependence appropriately.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Follow the same units over time","body":"A panel follows the same people, firms, schools or regions across multiple periods. Repeated observations let an analyst distinguish persistent differences between units from changes within a unit. The data structure also creates dependence: observations from one unit often share unobserved factors across time, so ordinary independent-observation formulas may understate uncertainty.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose two stores are observed for January and February, with sales measured in dollars per week. Store A rises from $1,000 to $1,100, a change of +$100; Store B falls from $800 to $760, a change of −$40. The panel records two units × two months, or four store-month observations, but the two observations from each store may share persistent management or neighborhood conditions. Comparing changes within stores avoids treating A’s higher starting level as a February effect. Still, a simple change comparison does not establish causality: a February festival could affect stores differently. Missing one store-month also changes the comparison and may create attrition bias. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose two municipalities report an employment index in three periods, with a transport subsidy beginning only for municipality A in period 3. A records 102, 104 and 112 index points; the comparison municipality B records 98, 100 and 102. First difference each unit across periods 1 to 3: A changes by 112 − 102 = 10 points, while B changes by 102 − 98 = 4 points. The difference-in-changes is therefore 10 − 4 = 6 index points. In a model y_it = α_i + βD_it + λ_t + u_it, differencing removes the municipality effect α_i; subtracting B’s change also removes a common two-period time movement (2 index points per period here, as in the lab’s shared-shock illustration). The 6-point contrast can be read as the treatment effect only if, absent the subsidy, A would have followed B’s trend, and neither municipality anticipated treatment. A time-varying industry closure affecting A alone would remain in u_it and could bias the contrast; fixed effects do not automatically remove it. These values are invented for calculation, not observed evidence, and the index points are not percentages unless the index is explicitly defined that way.

Panel notation tells you what is repeated and what can be compared. A dataset with 5 municipalities observed in 4 years has 20 municipality-year rows, but only 5 unit histories; each history may carry a persistent local shock across years. If one municipality is missing in year 4, the balanced count falls from 20 to 19, and that missingness is not harmless if service changes predict observation. A within-unit change subtracts a unit’s earlier outcome from its later outcome, removing a stable baseline but not a new factory closure or targeted investment. The panel lab is a three-period group-mean illustration rather than an individual fixed-effects regression. Use its controls to separate a common shock from a treatment effect, and do not infer causality from repeated rows alone.","takeaway":"Panel data add a within-unit time dimension; they do not automatically solve endogeneity."},{"title":"Entity fixed effects remove stable differences","body":"An entity fixed-effects model allows each unit to have its own constant baseline. This absorbs characteristics that do not change over the observed period, such as persistent geography or a stable historical legacy. It cannot remove a time-varying confounder that changes alongside treatment, and it cannot estimate effects of variables that never vary within a unit.

Illustrative synthetic example: imagine two factories measured in output units per day over two quarters. Factory A produces 100 then 110 units; Factory B produces 70 then 75. Their changes are +10 and +5 units, while the 30-unit starting gap is not evidence about those changes. An entity fixed effect gives each factory its own baseline, so a stable location advantage can be absorbed. However, if A also installed new machinery only in quarter two, the coefficient on an investment indicator can mix the machinery effect with other simultaneous changes. Fixed effects require within-factory variation: a constant ownership category has no separate slope to estimate. The arithmetic describes an adjusted comparison, not proof that machinery caused output. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 14: Panel Data and Fixed Effects (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic calculation: suppose two retail stores are observed for three months, with weekly sales y measured in $1,000s and advertising x measured in $1,000s. Store A has (x, y) = (0, 10), (1, 14), (2, 18); Store B has (0, 8), (2, 13), (4, 18). To remove each store’s stable level, subtract its own mean: A’s means are x̄ = 1 and ȳ = 14, giving demeaned pairs (−1, −4), (0, 0), (1, 4); B’s means are x̄ = 2 and ȳ = 13, giving (−2, −5), (0, 0), (2, 5). The within estimator is β = Σ(x−x̄ᵢ)(y−ȳᵢ) / Σ(x−x̄ᵢ)² = 28/10 = 2.8: an additional $1,000 of advertising is associated with $2,800 of weekly sales within a store, under this illustrative model. This interpretation requires no time-varying sales driver to move with advertising; common month shocks should be represented by time effects, and dependence across repeated observations calls for store-clustered inference when there are enough clusters. The calculation is not causal evidence by itself.

Entity fixed effects can be pictured as giving every unit its own intercept. Consider a synthetic two-period panel: harbor firm H has output 130 then 134 units per day, while inland firm I has 100 then 103. H starts 30 units higher, but its within-firm change is +4 and I’s is +3; the stable starting gap is not the slope on a changing input. If a location indicator is constant for each firm, demeaning makes it constant zero within firm, so its separate coefficient is not identified. If an energy subsidy begins only for H in period two while electricity prices also fall there, fixed effects cannot distinguish those changes without more design information. The arithmetic is illustrative, not causal evidence. See “Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)” for the within-unit perspective.","takeaway":"Fixed effects control for time-invariant unit attributes, not every unobserved cause."},{"title":"Time effects capture common shocks","body":"Adding time fixed effects absorbs shocks shared across units in a period, such as a national business-cycle change. With both entity and time effects, treatment effects are identified from remaining within-unit changes relative to common period shifts. The analyst still needs a credible comparison and should inspect whether treatment timing tracks other changing local conditions.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose three counties are observed in 2023 and 2024, with outcome equal to the employment rate in percentage points. County A rises from 62% to 65% (+3 points), while counties B and C rise from 60% to 61% and from 58% to 59% (+1 point each). The average outcome rises from 60.0% to 61.7%, a common increase of about 1.7 points. A time effect removes that year-wide movement: A's adjusted change is about 3 − 1.7 = 1.3 points, while the average control change is about 1 − 1.7 = −0.7 points. In a two-way fixed-effects model, the coefficient uses these within-county changes after accounting for the common year shock, not the counties' different baseline employment levels.

Time effects can absorb shocks shared by all observed counties in a period, such as a nationwide change in demand, but they cannot remove a shock affecting only one county or a county-specific trend. A useful diagnostic is to inspect several pre-policy periods for similar trends and to cluster uncertainty at the county level when repeated observations within counties may be dependent; the lab's controls and results should be read with those design choices visible. Fixed effects do not by themselves prove that a coefficient is causal, and a time-effect coefficient is not the effect of “time” itself. For assumptions and panel-data treatment, see “Wooldridge — Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data (MIT Press)” and “Matheus Facure — Ch. 14: Panel Data and Fixed Effects (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)” in the linked sources below.

Illustrative synthetic example: consider three regions’ unemployment rates, measured in percentage points, before and after a nationwide tax change. Their rates move 8 to 7, 6 to 5, and 4 to 3: every region falls by 1 percentage point. A time effect absorbs that common −1-point movement, so the residual change attributable to region-specific variation is 0 points for each region before considering treatment. If a treated region instead falls from 8 to 6, its extra change is −2 − (−1) = −1 percentage point relative to the common shock. This calculation assumes the shock is genuinely shared and measured comparably. It does not show the tax caused the extra decline; a region-specific recession could remain. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose two otherwise comparable factories report monthly output (thousand units) for January, February, and March. Factory A records 100, 108, and 116; Factory B records 90, 96, and 102. First compute each factory’s change: A gains 8 and then 8, while B gains 6 and then 6. The average period change is therefore 7 thousand units in both intervals, so a month effect can absorb that shared movement. After subtracting the common 7-unit increment, neither factory shows an additional February or March movement: the residual changes are 1 and −1 in each interval, respectively, relative to the period shock. That residual contrast is descriptive, not automatically a treatment effect. Before interpreting it, check whether A simultaneously installed new equipment or changed its product mix; such a factory-specific, time-varying change is not removed by entity or time effects. Also distinguish a common level shift from a common trend: month indicators can absorb each period’s mean shock, whereas extrapolating a trend requires a functional-form assumption. The lab’s shared-shock slider illustrates the former, not proof of parallel trends or causal identification.

Time effects remove a movement shared by every observed unit in the same period, not a unit’s entire trend. Synthetic example: three municipalities have employment rates 70%, 64%, and 58% in year one, then 72%, 65%, and 59% in year two. Changes are +2, +1, and +1 percentage points; the average change is 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33 points. Subtracting that common-year movement gives adjusted changes of +0.67, −0.33, and −0.33 points, respectively. This centering does not prove the first municipality’s extra movement was caused by transport expansion: a municipality-specific investment could remain. In the panel lab, a dashed divider marks treatment after period 2; both group trajectories continue into period 3. Interpret time effects as controls for shared timing.","takeaway":"Two-way fixed effects remove stable unit differences and common time shocks under the model."},{"title":"First differences and design limits","body":"With two periods, subtracting the first observation from the second removes the unit’s stable baseline and is closely related to an entity fixed-effects estimate. With more periods, the exact relationship depends on the model and assumptions. Track attrition, changing definitions, anticipation, treatment reversals and serial dependence. A panel is not automatically a natural experiment.

Illustrative synthetic example: using the formula’s outcome notation, suppose one worker’s monthly earnings are $2,400 in month 1 and $2,550 in month 2, while training exposure D changes from 0 to 1. The first difference is ΔY = $2,550 − $2,400 = $150 per month, and ΔD = 1 − 0 = 1 exposure unit. A two-period comparison therefore removes the worker’s stable baseline, represented by αᵢ; common month effects and other changing factors are not automatically removed. If a month-wide bonus raises everyone’s earnings by $50, the worker’s remaining change is $100 after accounting for that shock. This assumes consistent earnings definitions and comparable periods. The $150 change is not by itself a causal training effect. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Wooldridge — Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data (MIT Press)’ in the linked sources.

Consider this illustrative synthetic panel of county employment, measured in thousands of jobs. County A records 50, 52, and 60 in periods 1, 2, and 3; County B records 40, 41, and 46. A policy starts in County A only in period 3. First difference A across the policy boundary is 60 − 52 = 8 thousand jobs, while B changes by 46 − 41 = 5 thousand jobs. Subtracting these changes gives 8 − 5 = 3 thousand jobs, the difference-in-differences contrast. In a model, differencing removes each county’s time-invariant level: ΔYᵢₜ = Δλₜ + βΔDᵢₜ + Δεᵢₜ (plus differenced covariates when included); it does not remove a county-specific shock that changes over time. The pre-policy changes are 52 − 50 = 2 for A and 41 − 40 = 1 for B, a warning that their trends already differed by 1 thousand jobs. Treating the 3-thousand contrast as a causal policy effect therefore requires a defensible parallel-trends argument, stable measurement, no anticipation, and appropriate uncertainty estimation; the arithmetic alone is descriptive.

First differences make the cancellation of a stable unit effect explicit. Synthetic example: a worker earns $2,800 per month before training and $2,950 after, so ΔY = $2,950 − $2,800 = $150. Training exposure changes from 0 to 1, so ΔD = 1. If a nationwide pay shock adds $40 to everyone, the worker’s change relative to that shared shock is $150 − $40 = $110, assuming the shock is measured correctly. A local promotion worth $25 to this worker would still be inside the remaining $110 unless separately modeled. Thus differencing removes the fixed baseline, not all changing causes. The panel lab labels its display a three-period group-mean DiD contrast, not an individual fixed-effects regression. These values are synthetic and do not establish a training effect.","takeaway":"Repeated measures help describe change, but causal interpretation still rests on design assumptions.","formula":"Yᵢₜ = αᵢ + λₜ + βDᵢₜ + Xᵢₜ′γ + εᵢₜ; αᵢ is the unit effect and λₜ the time effect."},{"title":"Fixed effects and lagged outcomes answer different questions","body":"Unit fixed effects remove stable additive differences and identify coefficients from within-unit changes. A lagged dependent variable instead conditions on the previous outcome to describe a dynamic relationship. In short panels, that lag can be correlated with the transformed error in a fixed-effects model, so the estimator may be biased. Neither approach is a mechanical substitute for the other: choose based on the data-generating story, timing and assumptions, and consider whether treatment changes with time-varying confounders.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a firm’s productivity is 40 units per worker in year 1 and 44 in year 2, while its previous-year productivity is included as a lagged outcome. Fixed effects ask how a change in a predictor within that firm relates to the 4-unit increase; the lag asks whether current productivity is related to the prior 40 units, measured in units per worker. These are different questions, even if both appear in one regression. In a two-year panel, the lagged outcome can be mechanically tied to the transformed error because the first observation supplies the lag and the differencing process reuses information. The example is synthetic and does not establish persistence or causality. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke — Mostly Harmless Econometrics (Princeton University Press)’ in the linked sources.

A useful diagnostic is to write the fixed-effects transformation before interpreting a coefficient. Consider an illustrative synthetic three-year panel for one shop: weekly sales are 100, 110, and 120 units, while advertising spending is 2, 3, and 5 thousand dollars per week. The shop means are 110 units and 10/3 thousand dollars, so the within-unit deviations are sales −10, 0, +10 and advertising −4/3, −1/3, +5/3. The fixed-effects regression uses these deviations (after accounting for any time effects), not the shop’s average sales level; stable location or clientele therefore drops out. A lagged-outcome specification asks a different question: whether this week’s sales depend on last week’s 100 or 110 units, conditional on the included covariates. With only three periods, the lag leaves just two usable transitions, and its transformed lag can be correlated with the transformed disturbance, so a large persistence estimate need not be causal. Treat these numbers as synthetic, and check that advertising timing precedes sales and that changing promotions or demand shocks are not omitted time-varying confounders.

A lagged outcome is a predictor with a time-ordering story; a fixed effect is a way to remove stable unit levels. Synthetic example: a shop’s sales are $9,000 in quarter one and $9,600 in quarter two, while its lagged sales value is $9,000. A fixed-effects question asks how within-shop changes in advertising relate to the $600 change. A dynamic question asks how current sales relate to the prior $9,000, perhaps after other controls. In a short panel, within transformation can correlate a lagged outcome with transformed errors, so adding the lag does not automatically solve persistence or endogeneity. The two quantities have different units and interpretations even when shown in one table. The example is synthetic, not causal evidence; consult “Wooldridge — Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data (MIT Press)”.","takeaway":"Fixed effects remove time-constant unit differences; adding a lagged outcome is a separate modelling choice with its own assumptions."},{"title":"The within transformation shows what identifies a fixed-effects estimate","body":"For each firm, subtract its own time average from each variable. A stable characteristic such as persistent management style then disappears from both the outcome and treatment deviations. The treatment coefficient is identified from how treatment and outcome move within the same firm over time, after any included period effects. A variable that never changes within a firm cannot have its separate coefficient estimated this way. Nor does demeaning remove a time-varying shock that changes alongside treatment, such as a local demand surge that triggers both investment and hiring. Describe the remaining source of treatment variation, not just the phrase ‘fixed effects’.

Subtracting each unit’s own average makes the logic visible. Suppose firm A pays £22 and £24 per hour in two periods; its average is £23, so its demeaned values are −£1 and +£1. Firm B pays £18 and £19; its average is £18.50, so its values are −£0.50 and +£0.50. The stable difference in firms’ usual pay levels disappears when each firm is centred on itself. A fixed-effects slope is learned from changes within firms, not from the fact that A usually pays more than B.

This only removes stable additive differences. If a local demand boom both changes a firm’s training policy and raises its wages, firm fixed effects do not remove that time-varying confounder. A factor that never changes within a firm cannot have its separate effect identified by firm fixed effects, and repeated observations from the same firm are not independent rows for uncertainty calculations. The design and timing still determine whether the coefficient is causal. See Wooldridge and Angrist & Pischke Chapter 5 in the sources linked below.

Synthetic example: take a two-year panel of two cafés, with hourly wages in dollars. Café A pays $15 then $17, so its mean is $16 and deviations are −$1 and +$1. Café B pays $11 then $12, so its mean is $11.50 and deviations are −$0.50 and +$0.50. Demeaning removes the stable $4 starting-pay gap from the transformed outcome; identification comes from paired movements within cafés. If training changes from 0 to 1 at both cafés in the same period while time effects are included, the training indicator is perfectly collinear with that period indicator, so a separate training coefficient cannot be identified. Within transformation does not remove a café-specific demand surge. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 5, §§5.1, 5.3’ in the linked sources.

Consider a synthetic panel of hourly wages where treatment is the number of training sessions received by a store. After removing each store's fixed level, work with four store-period transitions: (ΔD, ΔY) = (1 session, $2/hour), (0, $1/hour), (2, $5/hour), and (1, $3/hour). A simple first-difference regression through the origin gives β = ΣΔDΔY / Σ(ΔD)^2 = (1×2 + 0×1 + 2×5 + 1×3)/(1² + 0² + 2² + 1²) = 15/6 = $2.50 per additional session per hour. The zero-treatment-change transition contributes zero to both sums, so it supplies no slope leverage; averaging the nonzero transition ratios would be a different calculation and need not equal this coefficient. This number is illustrative, synthetic, and descriptive of the specified calculation—not evidence that training caused wages to rise. A causal reading additionally needs plausible no-confounding in changes and appropriate treatment timing; a store-specific demand surge could remain in Δε. Unlike this individual-transition calculation, the panel lab plots group means and subtracts a common period shock, so its displayed contrast is a teaching DiD rather than this fitted coefficient.

Demeaning can be checked with a small arithmetic table. Synthetic example: firm C’s hourly pay is $20 and $23, whose mean is $21.50, producing deviations −$1.50 and +$1.50. Firm D’s pay is $16 and $18, mean $17, producing −$1 and +$1. The firms’ $4 gap in first-period pay is a time-invariant level difference that fixed effects remove; the transformed observations are deviations from each firm’s own mean. If training changes from 0 to 1 for every firm in the same period as a time indicator changes, the transformed training variable is perfectly aligned with the time effect and its separate coefficient cannot be learned. Demeaning also leaves a firm-specific demand boom intact. These numbers are synthetic. The bar over Y means the unit-specific time average, not a population average.

Every included time-varying regressor is demeaned too; a time-invariant regressor becomes zero and is not separately identified by the within transformation.","takeaway":"Fixed-effects identification comes from within-unit changes that remain after removing stable unit differences and included time effects.","formula":"Yᵢₜ − Ȳᵢ = β(Dᵢₜ − D̄ᵢ) + (Xᵢₜ − X̄ᵢ)′γ + (εᵢₜ − ε̄ᵢ), when time effects are excluded; otherwise include the demeaned period-effect term too."},{"title":"Nearby units can share changing shocks","body":"Unit and time fixed effects remove stable unit differences and common period shocks, but they do not necessarily remove a time-varying shock shared by neighbouring regions. A plant closure, transport disruption or local epidemic can affect nearby units differently over time and leave spatially correlated residuals. Map residual patterns and describe plausible cross-unit links; if spatial dependence is material, use an estimator and uncertainty method matched to the specific lag, error or spillover process. Fixed effects alone do not identify those mechanisms.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose two adjacent districts report bus ridership in passenger trips. District A rises from 1,000 to 1,200 trips and District B rises from 800 to 1,000 after a shared rail outage redirects passengers. Both changes are +200 trips per week, so a time effect captures a common +200-trip shift, but it does not reveal whether a district-specific policy mattered. If the outage affects A by +300 and B by +100 because routes differ, the average common shift is +200 and deviations are +100 and −100 trips. Nearby residual movements can still be correlated, making independent standard errors too small. This synthetic arithmetic is descriptive, not causal evidence. Mapping routes and using dependence-appropriate uncertainty remain necessary. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 14: Panel Data and Fixed Effects (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: let monthly job vacancies in District A move from 500 before a transport project to 565 afterward, while neighboring District B moves from 420 to 455. The changes are 65 and 35 vacancies per month. Suppose a nationwide hiring recovery contributes +30 vacancies in each district; subtracting that common period component leaves +35 in A and +5 in B, so the difference in residual changes is 30 vacancies per month. That 30 is not automatically the project effect: a nearby factory closure could have redirected applicants toward A, contributing +25 there and +5 in B, leaving only a residual +10 in A in this illustrative decomposition. The arithmetic is descriptive and synthetic, not observed evidence. The key assumption for a fixed-effects interpretation is that no other district-specific change covaries with project exposure; neighboring spillovers directly threaten it. If many adjacent districts show co-moving residuals, treat geography as part of the dependence structure—using geographically appropriate clustering or a spatial model—and report the estimand and uncertainty method rather than relying on independent standard errors.

Spatial proximity can create dependence after fixed effects. In a synthetic bridge-closure example, Town A gains 180 bus trips and Town B gains 60; the mean change is (180 + 60) ÷ 2 = 120 trips. Deviations from that common-period mean are +60 and −60. A time effect removes the mean movement but not linked town-specific deviations; one road serves both markets. Treating residuals as independent can make uncertainty too small. A map or route network can suggest a spillover mechanism, but visible correlation alone is not its causal estimate. The panel diagram’s common highlighted period cannot show neighborhood-specific shocks. Match clustering or spatial methods to the dependence process, as emphasized in “Angrist & Pischke — Mostly Harmless Econometrics (Princeton University Press)”.","takeaway":"Two-way fixed effects do not automatically absorb changing spatially correlated shocks."}]
data.case_study: A panel of municipalities records employment before and after a public-transport expansion. Municipality effects absorb stable local traits and year effects absorb shared shocks, but changing industry mix or targeted investment may still confound the comparison.
data.misconceptions:
Fixed effects do not control for unobserved factors that change over time.
A unit fixed effect does not identify the coefficient of a time-invariant regressor.
Panel structure alone does not justify a causal claim.

data.title: Robust, Clustered & Design-Based Inference
data.excerpt: A standard error describes how much an estimate might vary, but the right calculation depends on how data were collected, assigned and grouped. Learn when robust or clustered methods are useful, why groups—not just rows—can determine precision, and how few independent groups limit confidence.
data.objectives:
Distinguish heteroskedasticity-robust from cluster-robust standard errors.
Choose clustering levels based on assignment and dependence.
Explain small-cluster limits and design-based randomization inference.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Uncertainty follows the data-generating design","body":"A coefficient estimate summarizes a sample, and its uncertainty depends on how observations could vary across repeated samples or assignments. If outcome noise changes with income or firm size, homoskedastic formulas may be inappropriate. Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors adjust the variance calculation without changing the fitted coefficient, subject to large-sample conditions.

Robust standard errors change the estimated uncertainty, not the fitted relationship. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a regression estimates that one additional weekly training hour is associated with $18 in weekly earnings; the conventional standard error is $4 and the heteroskedasticity-robust standard error is $6, each measured in weekly-earnings dollars per additional training hour. The coefficient remains $18 in those same slope units. A rough 95% interval changes from $18 ± 1.96×$4 = $18 ± $7.84, or $10.16 to $25.84 in weekly-earnings dollars per additional training hour, to $18 ± 1.96×$6 = $18 ± $11.76, or $6.24 to $29.76 in the same units. These intervals describe an association, not a causal training effect. Robustness does not remove omitted-variable bias, reverse causality, or small-sample problems. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Wooldridge — Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data (MIT Press)’ in the linked sources.

Consider an illustrative synthetic minimum-wage study with 12 states, 20 workers per state, and policy assigned at the state level: there are 240 worker rows but only 12 assignment clusters. Suppose the within-state intracluster correlation is ρ = 0.20. Using the lab’s equal-size approximation, the design effect is 1 + (m − 1)ρ = 1 + (20 − 1)(0.20) = 4.80, so the approximate effective sample size is 240/4.80 = 50 independent-observation equivalents. The corresponding standard-error multiplier is √4.80 ≈ 2.19. Thus, if an illustrative coefficient were $2.00 per hour and the independence-based standard error were $0.10 per hour, a cluster-aware approximation would be about $0.219 per hour; a rough 95% interval would be $2.00 ± 1.96($0.219) = $2.00 ± $0.429, or $1.57 to $2.43 per hour. This calculation changes precision, not the coefficient or its causal validity. With only 12 states, asymptotic cluster-robust approximations may be unreliable; use small-cluster corrections or assignment-based randomization inference when the policy assignment mechanism is known, and do not treat worker count as a substitute for independent states.

Robust standard errors and clustered standard errors answer different dependence questions. Synthetic example: a regression coefficient for one extra training hour is $12 per week. If the conventional standard error is $3 and a heteroskedasticity-robust value is $5, the coefficient stays $12; a rough 95% interval using 1.96 is $12 ± 9.80, or $2.20 to $21.80. Robustness changes the uncertainty calculation for unequal variance, not omitted-variable bias or reverse causality. If training was assigned by state, workers within one state may share policy shocks, so clustering by state addresses a different dependence structure than merely allowing unequal individual variances. The interval is a synthetic normal approximation, not an empirical finding. Report the assignment unit, cluster count, estimator, and design limitations together rather than choosing the narrowest interval.","takeaway":"Robust inference is about uncertainty calculations, not a repair for a biased design."},{"title":"Cluster where outcomes can move together","body":"If a policy is assigned by school district, outcomes for pupils in one district can share shocks. Treating every pupil as independent may overstate information. Cluster-robust uncertainty often groups observations at the level of assignment or a justified dependence structure. The number of clusters—not just the number of rows—matters for accuracy.

Clustering matters because averaging many correlated records does not reduce uncertainty as quickly as averaging independent records. Illustrative synthetic example: four stores each report monthly sales changes of 2, 4, 6, and 8 percentage points after a regional promotion, so the row-level mean is (2+4+6+8) ÷ 4 = 5 percentage points. If each store has 100 customers, there may be 400 customer rows, but only four store-level shocks in this simplified comparison. A customer-level standard error would implicitly treat repeated customers as independent; a store-clustered calculation allows each store’s residual movement to be shared. The 5-percentage-point mean is descriptive and does not prove the promotion caused the change; seasonality or store selection could explain it. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Cameron & Trivedi — Microeconometrics: Methods and Applications (Cambridge University Press)’ in the linked sources.

Consider this illustrative synthetic minimum-wage calculation: suppose six states are the assignment clusters, each contributing 30 workers, so N = 6 × 30 = 180 worker observations. Assume the within-state correlation of hourly-wage outcomes is ρ = 0.25 and cluster sizes are equal. The lab’s design-effect approximation gives DEFF = 1 + (m − 1)ρ = 1 + (30 − 1)(0.25) = 8.25. Thus the equivalent independent sample size is N/DEFF = 180/8.25 ≈ 21.8, not 180, and the uncertainty multiplier is √8.25 ≈ 2.87. If an independence-based standard error were illustratively $0.50 per hour, the corresponding approximation would be $0.50 × 2.87 ≈ $1.44 per hour; the coefficient’s wage unit does not change. Because treatment was assigned by state, clustering by state matches the assignment and shared shocks, whereas clustering by worker would not create six independent policy assignments. Finally, six clusters is a small-cluster setting: a cluster-robust formula may be unreliable in conventional large-cluster approximations, so few-cluster corrections or randomization inference based on the known assignment rule deserve consideration. These numbers are teaching assumptions, not observed wage data.

The cluster level should follow shared assignment or shared shocks. Synthetic example: five clinics report patient recovery changes of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 percentage points after a common referral campaign. Their mean change is (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5) ÷ 5 = 3 percentage points. If each clinic contributes 80 patient records, the file contains 400 rows but only five clinic-level outcome environments in this simplified illustration. Patient records within a clinic may share staff, scheduling, and local demand, so row count exaggerates independent information. The 3-point mean is descriptive and not a causal campaign effect. In the lab’s cluster schematic, colored observations sit inside cluster boxes to show shared structure; the visual grouping is a reason to ask whether clustering belongs at that level or another justified level.","takeaway":"The cluster level should reflect the assignment and dependence process, not whichever choice produces a smaller p-value."},{"title":"Few clusters need extra care","body":"Cluster-robust variance estimates can perform poorly when the number of independent clusters is small, especially with unbalanced group sizes or high-leverage clusters. Report cluster counts and consider appropriate small-sample corrections, randomization-based inference or a wild cluster bootstrap where justified. No correction can create independent assignment units that the design did not provide.

Illustrative synthetic example (six-month employment outcome): a city assigns job-search support by employment centre, with 12 centres serving 40 jobseekers each; six centres receive the offer and six do not. At follow-up, 55% of people in offered centres and 50% in comparison centres have found work, an observed difference of 5 percentage points. People served by the same centre may share caseworkers, local vacancies, and other shocks, so their outcomes need not be independent. If the average cluster size is m = 40 and the within-centre correlation is illustratively ρ = 0.05, the simple equal-cluster design-effect approximation is 1 + (m − 1)ρ = 1 + 39 × 0.05 = 2.95. With 480 individual records, dividing by that factor gives a rough independent-observation equivalent of 480 ÷ 2.95 ≈ 163; the assignment still occurred in only 12 centres.

The design-effect calculation is an intuition aid, not an exact standard error or a replacement for analysis at the assignment level. With only 12 randomized centres, report cluster-aware uncertainty and use an appropriate small-sample correction or randomization-based check; do not treat 480 people as 480 independent assignments. Verify how centres were randomized, inspect centre-level balance and sizes, and describe whether the target is the effect of the offer or of actual participation. A 5-point observed gap alone cannot establish a policy effect or precision. See “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 8, §§8.1–8.3” and “Edward Rubin — EC 607: Lecture 11: Inference and Clustering (license not stated; link only)” in the linked sources below.

Few clusters make tail probabilities and corrections fragile, even when each has many people. Synthetic example: an intervention is assigned to 8 clinics, with 4 treated and 4 untreated; clinic-level outcome changes, in percentage points, are 3, 7, 1, and 5 for treated clinics and 0, 2, 4, and 2 for controls. The treated average is (3+7+1+5) ÷ 4 = 4 percentage points, while the control average is (0+2+4+2) ÷ 4 = 2 percentage points, giving a 2-point gap. That gap is not necessarily precise: eight assignment units leave limited information for estimating a reference distribution. A correction or wild cluster bootstrap may help when justified, but neither creates more clinics or guarantees valid inference. This is not evidence of a causal effect without credible assignment assumptions. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 8, §§8.1–8.3’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a state-level policy is evaluated in six states, three treated and three comparison states, with employment rates recorded as state percentages. The treated states report 61%, 58%, and 64%, while comparison states report 55%, 54%, and 57%. If the estimand is the average effect across states, first average within each assignment arm: treated = (61 + 58 + 64) ÷ 3 = 61.00%, comparison = (55 + 54 + 57) ÷ 3 = 55.33%, so the state-average gap is 5.67 percentage points. But if the estimand is the effect for a randomly selected worker, state sizes should determine weights. With treated-state sizes 100, 300, and 100, the treated worker-weighted rate is (100×61 + 300×58 + 100×64) ÷ 500 = 59.80%; with comparison sizes 100, 100, and 300, the corresponding rate is (100×55 + 100×54 + 300×57) ÷ 500 = 56.00%, giving 3.80 percentage points. These are different targets, not a calculation error. Either way, inference still has only six independent assignment clusters; weighting does not create more clusters, and causal interpretation requires credible state-level assignment assumptions.

The cluster lab exposes why many rows cannot replace few assignment units. Its equal-size teaching setting uses m = 20 records per cluster, so with within-cluster correlation ρ = 0.20 the design effect is 1 + (20 − 1)×0.20 = 1 + 3.8 = 4.8. If there are 12 clusters, the illustrative total is 12×20 = 240 records and the rough effective record count is 240 ÷ 4.8 = 50. The cluster-aware standard-error multiplier is the square root of 4.8, approximately 2.19, not 4.8; the former concerns standard errors, the latter a variance-style design effect. This is an equal-size heuristic, not an exact estimator. Twelve clusters still mean twelve assignment units, so small-sample or randomization-based inference may be needed.","takeaway":"Thousands of observations within a handful of clusters are not thousands of independent policy assignments."},{"title":"Use the design to guide inference","body":"In a randomized study, randomization inference can evaluate how the estimate would vary under the assignment mechanism, if that mechanism is known and the null is clearly stated. In observational studies, inference must also acknowledge model uncertainty and identification assumptions. State the estimator, variance method, clustering level and limitations together.

Randomization inference follows the actual set of assignments rather than relying only on a large-sample approximation. Illustrative synthetic example: 6 districts are assigned 3 offers and 3 non-offers, and the observed district-average employment rates are 60%, 55%, 50% for offered districts versus 52%, 50%, 48% for non-offered districts. The observed difference is (60+55+50) ÷ 3 − (52+50+48) ÷ 3 = 55% − 50% = 5 percentage points. A sharp-null randomization check would repeatedly reassign exactly 3 of 6 districts, recompute this difference, and compare the observed 5-point gap with that reference distribution. It requires a known assignment mechanism and a clearly stated null; it does not automatically adjust for noncompliance or establish generalization beyond the districts studied. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke — Mostly Harmless Econometrics (Princeton University Press)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a minimum-wage change is assigned to 4 of 8 states, with 100 workers observed in each state. First reduce each state to its pre–post employment-rate change: the treated states show +2, +1, +3, and 0 percentage points, while the four comparison states show +1, −1, 0, and 0 percentage points. The treated mean change is (2+1+3+0)/4 = 1.5 percentage points; the comparison mean is (1−1+0+0)/4 = 0, so the difference is +1.5 percentage points. The 800 worker rows do not turn this into an 800-unit assignment experiment: treatment was assigned at the state level, and workers in a state can share policy exposure and economic shocks. Under a sharp null of no effect and a known rule assigning exactly 4 of 8 states, enumerate all C(8,4) = 70 treated-state assignments, recompute the state-mean difference each time, and locate +1.5 in that reference distribution. This supports design-based inference for these states; it does not solve spillovers, noncompliance, or generalization beyond them.

Randomization inference starts with the assignments the design actually permits. Synthetic example: four districts are assigned two offers and two non-offers, with offered outcomes 58% and 54% and non-offered outcomes 51% and 49%. The observed difference is (58 + 54) ÷ 2 − (51 + 49) ÷ 2 = 56% − 50% = 6 percentage points. Under a sharp null, enumerate or repeatedly sample assignments that choose exactly two of four districts, recompute the same difference, and compare 6 points with that reference distribution. This procedure uses district-level assignment, not 80 individual rows if each district has 20 people. It does not repair noncompliance, confounding in an observational assignment, or limited generalization. The numbers are synthetic; “Angrist & Pischke — Mostly Harmless Econometrics (Princeton University Press)” supplies the design-based rationale.","takeaway":"The uncertainty method should be chosen before inspecting which one gives the preferred conclusion."},{"title":"Cluster where assignment and shocks are shared","body":"Suppose a programme is assigned to 30 schools, with 20 pupils observed in each. There are 600 pupil records but only 30 independently assigned school-level units. If pupils in a school share teachers, neighbourhood shocks, or the same treatment, their errors can move together; treating all 600 as independent can make uncertainty look too small. A simple equal-size intuition is the design effect 1 + (m − 1)ρ, where m is pupils per school and ρ is within-school correlation. With few schools, ordinary cluster-robust standard errors can themselves be unreliable, so report the number and size of clusters and use inference appropriate to the assignment design, such as randomization-based or small-sample methods when justified.

The design-effect expression gives a quick scale check for how within-school similarity changes effective information. Illustrative synthetic example: 20 pupils per school and an assumed within-school correlation of ρ = 0.10 give 1 + (20−1)×0.10 = 1 + 1.9 = 2.9. Thus 600 pupil records from 30 schools have a rough independent-observation equivalent of 600 ÷ 2.9 ≈ 207 pupil records, not 600 independent school assignments. The units are records for this heuristic; the assignment information remains 30 schools. This calculation is illustrative and synthetic, not an estimated historical correlation or an exact variance. It does not say that clustering always widens uncertainty by exactly 2.9, nor does it identify a treatment effect. A valid analysis still needs the assignment rule and an appropriate estimator. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)’ in the linked sources.

Consider an illustrative synthetic wage-policy regression with 12 states, 20 workers per state, and treatment assigned at the state level. Suppose the estimated policy effect is $2.00 per worker-hour and an independence-based standard error is $0.40 per worker-hour. Using the cluster lab’s equal-size settings ρ = 0.20 and m = 20, the design effect is 1 + (20 − 1)(0.20) = 4.8, so the corresponding standard-error multiplier is √4.8 ≈ 2.19. The illustrative cluster-aware standard error is therefore $0.40 × 2.19 ≈ $0.88 per worker-hour, not $0.88 per state. A normal-approximation interval would be $2.00 ± 1.96($0.88), or approximately $0.28 to $3.72 per worker-hour. Because only 12 states supply independent assignments, that interval is a rough illustration, not a final reported interval: use a small-cluster correction or randomization-based inference when the state assignment mechanism supports it. The calculation changes uncertainty, not the point estimate, and it cannot repair omitted policy confounders or justify treating workers as independently assigned.

Read the cluster lab’s controls as a two-part information calculation. With 12 clusters and ICC ρ = 0.20, its fixed m = 20 approximation gives design effect 1 + 19×0.20 = 4.8 and approximate effective n = 12×20 ÷ 4.8 = 50. The plotted cluster-aware standard-error multiplier is √4.8 ≈ 2.19 times the naive bar, because standard error is a square-root scale. Raising the cluster count changes how many groups are shown and changes the effective-n calculation; raising ICC increases dependence while leaving the nominal row count fixed. These controls are a teaching approximation with equal cluster sizes, not a fitted survey estimate. The 50 effective records do not mean there are 50 independent assignments: the design still supplies 12 clusters. Use the assignment rule and shock structure to justify inference.","takeaway":"The number of rows is not the number of independent treatment assignments; choose inference at the design's shared-variation level.","formula":"Equal-cluster-size intuition: design effect ≈ 1 + (m − 1)ρ; this is not a substitute for a design-specific variance estimator.","practice":{"question":"If treatment is assigned to schools, which count is more relevant to the independent assignment information: 600 pupils or 30 schools?","hint":"Use the unit that received the assignment.","solution":"The 30 schools. Pupils within a school may provide outcome detail, but they do not create 600 independent school-level assignments."}},{"title":"Sampling clusters and assignment clusters play different roles","body":"A district can be a primary sampling unit because it was selected from a survey frame, an assignment cluster because a policy lottery happened at district level, or both. Survey weights and design-based variance estimation describe how sampled units represent the population; cluster-robust causal inference addresses shared treatment assignment or residual shocks. The correct variance method follows the actual sampling and assignment process, and the target population still follows the estimand. Do not assume that calling a variable ‘cluster’ resolves both questions.

Separate the question “who represents the population?” from “who received the treatment decision?” Illustrative synthetic example: a survey samples 2 districts from a population of 10, then samples 50 workers per selected district; survey weights may be 10 ÷ 2 = 5 at the district-selection stage. If a wage subsidy is instead assigned by firm, with 20 firms represented inside those districts, firm-level assignment—not the district sampling count—determines the natural treatment-dependence cluster. The survey estimate and its design-based variance concern population representation, while the policy comparison concerns shared assignment and shocks. Mixing them can produce a neat-looking but mismatched standard error. Neither weighting nor clustering cures nonresponse, selection bias, or confounding. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Cameron & Trivedi — Microeconometrics: Methods and Applications (Cambridge University Press)’ in the linked sources.

Consider an illustrative synthetic wage-policy study with 8 states and 20 workers observed per state (160 worker rows). Suppose the policy is assigned at the state level and, for teaching, within-state correlation is ρ = 0.25. The equal-size design effect is 1 + (m − 1)ρ = 1 + 19 × 0.25 = 5.75, so the corresponding effective sample size is approximately 160 ÷ 5.75 = 27.8 independent observations—not 160. If the outcome’s illustrative individual-level standard deviation is $2 per hour, an independence calculation gives a standard error of $2/√160 = $0.158 per hour; multiplying by √5.75 gives about $0.379 per hour under this approximation. The larger uncertainty reflects shared state shocks, not a change in the wage unit. However, only eight states supply assignment-level information, so ordinary cluster-robust asymptotics may be unreliable. A state-level randomization or permutation procedure, or a small-cluster correction justified by the design, should be considered; neither can repair nonrandom policy assignment, omitted confounding, or a sampling frame that misses relevant workers. The numbers are synthetic, and the calculation is diagnostic rather than a causal estimate.

Sampling and treatment dependence can point to different cluster variables. Synthetic example: a survey selects 3 districts from 12, giving a first-stage selection-weight intuition of 12 ÷ 3 = 4, then samples 40 workers per selected district. If a wage subsidy is assigned independently by firm and 18 firms appear inside those districts, firm—not district—is the natural treatment-assignment level for shared policy shocks. The district selection affects population representation and survey variance; firm assignment affects treatment comparison and residual dependence. A weight of 4 cannot create random treatment, and clustering by district cannot automatically solve firm-level assignment dependence. Neither method cures nonresponse or unmeasured confounding. Keep the target population, sampling process, assignment process, and variance estimator explicitly separate.","takeaway":"Sampling design and treatment assignment can create different sources of dependence."}]
data.case_study: A minimum-wage policy changes at the state level, while a dataset contains many workers per state. The analysis should explain why states are the assignment units and how the limited number of states affects precision.
data.misconceptions:
Robust standard errors do not correct omitted-variable bias or poor measurement.
Clustering by an arbitrary variable is not a universal safeguard.
A large row count cannot compensate for very few independent clusters.
