data.title: Matching, Weighting & Propensity Scores
data.excerpt: Matching and weighting make programme and comparison groups more alike on measured characteristics, such as earlier earnings or age. Learn to check whether the groups overlap and are balanced, understand propensity scores, and make clear that unmeasured differences can still distort a causal claim.
data.objectives:
Define propensity scores and common support.
Use matching or weighting to balance observed covariates.
Explain why balance cannot rule out unmeasured confounding.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Compare units with similar observed histories","body":"If people choose whether to join a job programme, participants may differ from non-participants before treatment. Matching pairs or weighting can make the measured covariate distributions more similar, such as age, education and prior earnings. The causal interpretation still requires that these measured variables capture all confounding needed for the comparison.

Illustrative synthetic example: In January 2025, six similar households apply for a housing-voucher programme. Three receive a voucher (treated) and three do not (comparison). Before the programme, match each treated household to a comparison household using observed monthly income and household size: for example, a treated household earning £1,800 per month with four members is paired with a comparison household earning £1,820 with four members. Twelve months later, monthly rent burden is 35%, 38% and 30% for the treated households, versus 42%, 40% and 34% for their matched comparisons. The matched differences are −7, −2 and −4 percentage points; their average is (−7 − 2 − 4) ÷ 3 = −4.33 percentage points. This is an adjusted observed contrast, not automatically the voucher’s causal effect.

A matching calculation can establish that the selected treated and comparison observations are more comparable on the measured variables used by the method; it cannot establish that motivation, landlord access or other unmeasured factors are balanced. Check standardized differences and the distributions of pre-program income and household size after matching, and inspect whether every treated household has a plausible comparison rather than relying on a large numerical weight. Avoid saying that a −4.33-percentage-point matched difference proves vouchers caused the reduction, or that a propensity score makes treatment random. The result needs conditional exchangeability and adequate overlap for its intended target population. See “Matheus Facure — Ch. 10: Matching (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)” in the linked sources below.

A useful matching workflow is to define a distance using only pre-treatment information, then check whether the pairing is substantively plausible. Illustrative synthetic example: match two applicants on age and prior monthly earnings. Applicant A is age 30 with £2,400 earnings; candidate controls are age 29 with £2,450 and age 42 with £2,410. The first is closer on both measures, so it is the more defensible match; the age gap is 1 year and the earnings gap is £50 per month, rather than 12 years and £10 per month. This comparison describes observed similarity, not a guaranteed counterfactual. It assumes the selected covariates capture relevant pre-treatment differences; unmeasured health or motivation could remain imbalanced. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 10: Matching (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a voucher study targets the average effect for applicants who received an offer (the ATT), and three non-recipient households have estimated voucher propensities of 0.50, 0.25, and 0.20. Give each treated household weight 1, and each comparison household weight p/(1−p): 1, 0.25/0.75 = 0.333, and 0.20/0.80 = 0.25. If their observed monthly rent-burden reductions are 9, 7, and 6 percentage points, the weighted comparison mean is (1×9 + 0.333×7 + 0.25×6) ÷ (1 + 0.333 + 0.25) = 12.831 ÷ 1.583 = 8.11 percentage points. If the treated mean is 10.00 percentage points, the weighted ATT contrast is 10.00 − 8.11 = 1.89 percentage points, not 1.89 percent. This is only a reweighted observed contrast: causal interpretation needs conditional exchangeability, correct propensity models, and overlap. A propensity near 0.95 would give a comparison weight of 19, so one observation could dominate; inspect weight distributions and consider a pre-specified trim, recognizing that trimming changes the represented applicant population.

The matching lab’s balance plot is about signed standardized mean differences, where zero means no measured difference on that covariate. Suppose its illustrative controls show a largest initial absolute SMD of 1.00 and a remaining imbalance share of 0.25. The implied post-adjustment maximum absolute SMD is 1.00×0.25 = 0.25, still not zero. If assumed common-support overlap is set to 80%, that gauge is a teaching input, not an observed propensity-score diagnostic. A lower SMD supports measured comparability, while the 20% outside the stated overlap may change the target population if trimmed. Matching cannot balance unmeasured motivation or landlord access merely because the plot looks improved. These lab values are synthetic; causal interpretation still requires adequate overlap and conditional exchangeability.","takeaway":"Matching and weighting balance observed information; they do not randomize treatment."},{"title":"The propensity score is a balancing summary","body":"The propensity score is the probability of treatment given observed pre-treatment covariates. Under suitable conditions, conditioning on it can balance those measured covariates between treatment groups. Estimate it using variables measured before treatment and based on substantive knowledge; including post-treatment outcomes or mediators can introduce bias.

The propensity score is on a probability scale from 0 to 1, not a predicted outcome or a treatment effect. Illustrative synthetic example: a fitted model gives three people probabilities of programme participation of 0.20, 0.55 and 0.80. A treated person with score 0.55 is compared with control people near 0.55 because their observed pre-treatment profiles imply similar treatment-selection chances. If the treated scores average (0.20 + 0.80) ÷ 2 = 0.50 and two controls score 0.45 and 0.55, the control average is (0.45 + 0.55) ÷ 2 = 0.50, so this simple check shows score balance. It does not show that outcomes would have been equal without treatment, and model misspecification can leave covariate imbalance. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 11: Propensity Scores (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose four households have estimated participation scores e of 0.25, 0.75, 0.25 and 0.75. The first two received the voucher and recorded 8 and 10 months housed; the latter two did not and recorded 5 and 7 months. For an inverse-probability-weighted ATE, assign treated weight 1/e and control weight 1/(1−e): the treated weights are 4 and 1.333, while the control weights are 1.333 and 4. Normalize within arm rather than comparing raw weighted sums. The weighted treated mean is (4×8 + 1.333×10)/(4 + 1.333) = 8.50 months, and the weighted control mean is (1.333×5 + 4×7)/(1.333 + 4) = 6.50 months; the estimated contrast is therefore 2.00 months. This calculation targets the combined population represented by the ATE weights, not necessarily the treated group. It is only illustrative, not observed data: credible interpretation still requires correctly specified pre-treatment scores, positivity, and no unmeasured confounding. A score near 0 or 1 would create a large weight, so inspect overlap and consider whether trimming changes the target before trusting precision.

Think of the propensity score as a compact description of selection into treatment, not as a shortcut to the outcome. Illustrative synthetic example: four treated households have scores 0.30 and 0.70 repeated twice, while four controls have scores 0.25, 0.35, 0.65, and 0.75. The treated mean is (0.30 + 0.70 + 0.30 + 0.70) ÷ 4 = 0.50; the control mean is 2.00 ÷ 4 = 0.50. Equal means alone do not show equal distributions: the controls include values near each treated score, but another sample could hide separation behind the same average. Inspect covariate balance and overlap, use only pre-treatment predictors, and remember that unmeasured motivation can remain. See ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 11: Propensity Scores (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ for the balancing logic.","takeaway":"A propensity score is a model for treatment assignment, not a probability that the causal claim is true."},{"title":"Check overlap and balance","body":"After matching or weighting, inspect standardized differences and distribution plots for each important covariate. Check whether treated units have plausible comparison units and whether weights become extreme. Limited overlap means the data provide weak support for comparisons in some regions; trimming changes the target population and should be reported.

Balance diagnostics should be read in the units of the diagnostic, not as outcome evidence. Illustrative synthetic example: before weighting, mean baseline income is £1,900 per month for 40 treated households and £1,600 per month for 60 controls; after weighting, the means are £1,850 and £1,820, a difference of £30 per month. That improvement is encouraging for this measured variable, but also inspect age, household size, and the full distributions. Suppose one treated household has propensity score 0.98 while the nearest controls are 0.40 and 0.45: overlap is weak even if a weighted table looks balanced elsewhere. Large weights may make the effective sample size much smaller than the nominal sample size. These checks do not prove no hidden confounding or establish causality. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Hernán & Robins — Causal Inference: What If (authors’ open book)’ in the linked sources.

Consider a different illustrative, synthetic diagnostic for pre-program rent burden, measured in percentage points of monthly income. Suppose the treated mean is 52 and the comparison mean is 44; assume each group’s SD is 10 and 14 percentage points. Using the simple pooled-SD approximation, the denominator is sqrt((10² + 14²)/2) = sqrt(148) = 12.17 percentage points, so the standardized mean difference is (52 − 44)/12.17 = +0.66 SD units. After reweighting, suppose the means become 49 and 48 while these illustrative SDs remain 10 and 14: the new SMD is (49 − 48)/12.17 = +0.08 SD units. The movement toward zero is evidence that this measured covariate is more comparable, not evidence that voucher assignment is as-good-as-random. Before interpreting the improvement, inspect whether the weights concentrate on a few households and whether the treated and comparison rent-burden distributions actually overlap; similar means can hide separated tails. Also state whether the weighting targets the treated population, the combined sample, or another population, because the same reweighting can change the estimand. The pooled-SD shortcut is a summary choice, not a universal balance threshold.

A balance table and an overlap check answer different questions. Illustrative synthetic example: after weighting, average age is 41.2 years in the treated group and 41.0 in controls, a 0.2-year difference, while the largest standardized difference for education is 0.18 standard deviations. Those summaries concern measured variables; neither tells you whether every treated person has a credible comparison. If treated scores occupy 0.85–0.95 but controls stop at 0.60, the high-score region lacks support even when overall means align. Trimming may improve comparability, yet the estimate then describes a narrower population. Report retained units, weight distribution, and effective sample size, not only a pleasing table. These are synthetic diagnostics, not evidence of a housing-voucher effect. ‘Hernán & Robins — Causal Inference: What If (authors’ open book)’ explains why identification needs more than observed balance.","takeaway":"A good balance diagnostic is necessary for the observed covariates, but not sufficient for identification."},{"title":"State the assumptions and target","body":"A weighted estimate may target the average effect for all eligible units, for treated units, or another population depending on the weights. State that target and the conditional-exchangeability assumption: after adjusting for measured covariates, there are no remaining common causes of treatment and outcome. Use sensitivity analysis to show how hidden confounding could change conclusions.

Always name the population behind an estimate and the assumption linking adjustment to causality. Illustrative synthetic example: among 100 eligible households, 40 receive a programme. A treated-group target asks about those 40 households; a population target asks about all 100. If their estimated mean rent burdens are 32% and 36%, the adjusted contrast is 32% − 36% = −4 percentage points, but the interpretation differs by target. Conditional exchangeability requires that, within measured covariate patterns, treatment assignment is unrelated to potential outcomes; overlap requires plausible treated and untreated units in those patterns. A sensitivity analysis might report how strong an unmeasured factor would need to be to erase 4 percentage points. Neither calculation proves the assumption or guarantees transportability to a new year. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Hernán & Robins — Causal Inference: What If (authors’ open book)’ in the linked sources.

For a treated-population (ATT) estimand, inverse-odds weighting can make the untreated group resemble the treated group on measured covariates. Illustrative synthetic example: give each treated household weight 1, and give an untreated household with estimated propensity score e the weight e/(1−e). Suppose three untreated households have rent-burden outcomes of 6, 9, and 11 percentage points and scores 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75; their weights are 1/3, 1, and 3. The weighted untreated mean is [(1/3)×6 + 1×9 + 3×11] / [(1/3)+1+3] = 44/4.333… = 10.15 percentage points. If the three treated households’ mean is 12.00 percentage points, the weighted ATT contrast is 12.00 − 10.15 = 1.85 percentage points, interpreted for treated households—not all eligible households. Before trusting it, inspect covariate balance and common support, because a score near 1 creates a large control weight; here the weight 3 already makes one observation influential. The calculation still relies on conditional exchangeability and correctly specified scores; neither is established by balance alone.

An adjusted contrast is incomplete until its population and identifying assumption are named. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a voucher estimate is −3 percentage points for treated households but −2 percentage points for all eligible households. The first statement concerns recipients; the second concerns the wider eligible population, so the numerical difference is 1 percentage point despite the shared outcome scale. Conditional exchangeability asks whether measured pre-voucher covariates suffice to remove common causes of treatment and outcome; overlap asks whether both treatment states appear within those covariate patterns. Sensitivity analysis can vary plausible hidden differences, but cannot verify them. Do not silently generalize a treated-group result to untreated applicants or another city. See ‘Hernán & Robins — Causal Inference: What If (authors’ open book)’ for target-population reasoning.","takeaway":"The target population and no-unmeasured-confounding assumption belong beside the estimate."},{"title":"Weighting choices define which population the contrast describes","body":"Matching or weighting can make treated and comparison units more alike on measured pre-treatment covariates, but different weights answer different target-population questions. For example, weighting comparison units to resemble the treated group supports an effect-on-the-treated target under conditional exchangeability and overlap; other weights may target an average effect for a broader population. Units with almost no comparable counterparts receive extreme weights or no credible match. Show balance after weighting, overlap, influential weights, and the effective sample size. Trimming unsupported regions may improve stability, but it also changes who the estimate represents and must be reported as a target-population choice.

A weight is not merely a technical correction; it changes how observations contribute to the target average. Illustrative synthetic example: three control households have monthly incomes of £1,500, £2,500, and £4,000, with weights 1, 2, and 4. Their weighted control income is (1×£1,500 + 2×£2,500 + 4×£4,000) ÷ (1+2+4) = £22,500 ÷ 7 = £3,214.29 per month. The £4,000 household therefore contributes four times as much as the £1,500 household. This may represent a deliberately chosen target, but an extreme weight can make the estimate sensitive to one observation and reduce effective sample size. If no controls resemble £4,000, increasing its weight cannot create information. The contrast remains dependent on measured-confounding and overlap assumptions, not proof of a causal effect. For propensity-score weighting, overlap, and the role of extreme weights, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 11: Propensity Scores (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

A useful stability check is the effective sample size (ESS), calculated after choosing the target population. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose four comparison households receive normalized weights 1, 1, 2, and 4 to represent the treated target. The total weight is 8, and the sum of squared weights is 1² + 1² + 2² + 4² = 22, so ESS = (Σw)²/Σw² = 8²/22 = 64/22 ≈ 2.91 households. Although four households appear in the weighted calculation, their unequal influence gives precision closer to roughly three equally weighted observations, not four; the ESS is a diagnostic, not a literal replacement sample. Multiplying every weight by the same constant leaves a normalized weighted mean unchanged and also leaves this ESS unchanged, because the scale cancels. By contrast, trimming the weight of the fourth household would usually raise ESS while excluding or down-weighting part of the target population. An analyst should therefore report the weighting rule, retained overlap, ESS, and whether the estimand is ATT, ATE, or another explicitly defined target. Even a comfortable ESS cannot address unmeasured confounding or justify extrapolation beyond common support.

Weighting changes the arithmetic of an average, so inspect whose observations receive influence. Illustrative synthetic example: three comparison households have monthly rent burdens of 20%, 30%, and 50%, with weights 1, 1, and 3. The weighted mean is (20 + 30 + 150) ÷ 5 = 40%, whereas the unweighted mean is 100 ÷ 3 = 33.33%. The high-burden household contributes three times as much as either other household because the target emphasizes similar units. That may be intentional, but it makes the estimate sensitive to one record. A weight cannot supply a missing analogue; truncation may stabilize results while changing the represented population. Report the weighting rule, units, denominator, and effective sample size. This calculation is synthetic, not an empirical effect. See ‘Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 3, §§3.3.1–3.3.3, 3.4.1’.","takeaway":"Balance is about measured covariates; the weighting rule and overlap determine the target population and the remaining assumptions.","formula":{"question":"A treated group has no comparable controls for the highest baseline-risk units. What should an analyst not do?","hint":"Ask whether a weight can create information where no comparison exists.","solution":"Do not hide the lack of overlap behind a large weight or extrapolate without qualification. Report the unsupported group and state how any trimming changes the target population."}}]
data.case_study: To assess a housing voucher pilot, balance pre-program income, household composition and prior housing instability. Report overlap and the population the weights represent; unmeasured differences in application motivation may remain.
data.misconceptions:
A balanced table does not prove the absence of hidden confounding.
The propensity score is not itself an outcome model or a causal effect.
Extreme weights can make an estimate unstable and change its effective target.

It cannot verify the assumption that all relevant confounders were measured."}

data.title: Synthetic Control for Comparative Case Studies
data.excerpt: When one region or institution adopts a policy, synthetic control builds a comparison by weighting similar places that did not. Learn to judge how well the comparison matched before the policy, which places contribute to it, and what placebo checks can—and cannot—show about a single case.
data.objectives:
Explain the donor pool and weighted synthetic comparison.
Assess pre-treatment fit and predictor selection.
Use placebo and sensitivity analyses while respecting single-treated-unit limits.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Construct a comparison from donor units","body":"When one region adopts a policy and no single comparison region is persuasive, synthetic control combines untreated units using weights chosen to match the treated unit before adoption. The result is a data-driven comparison, not a guarantee of causal validity. The donor pool must be unaffected by treatment and sufficiently similar on relevant pre-policy histories.

A useful way to read the weights is as a recipe for one counterfactual observation. Illustrative synthetic example: three donor regions have 2023 housing starts of 80, 100, and 120 homes per 10,000 residents, with weights 0.20, 0.50, and 0.30. The synthetic value is (0.20 × 80) + (0.50 × 100) + (0.30 × 120) = 16 + 50 + 36 = 102 homes per 10,000 residents. The weights sum to 1.00, so the units remain homes per 10,000 residents rather than homes. This construction describes a weighted benchmark; it does not prove that the benchmark would share every future shock. Donors must be untreated and plausibly comparable. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Cunningham — Causal Inference: The Mixtape (Yale University Press)’ in the linked sources.

To diagnose whether a reported gap is large relative to construction error, compute pre-policy RMSPE (root mean squared prediction error) before interpreting the post-policy path. Illustrative synthetic values: across four pre-policy periods, treated outcomes are 10, 12, 11, and 13 outcome units, while the synthetic series is 10.2, 11.8, 11.3, and 12.7. The errors are −0.2, 0.2, −0.3, and 0.3 units; squaring gives 0.04, 0.04, 0.09, and 0.09, whose mean is 0.065, so RMSPE = √0.065 ≈ 0.255 outcome units. If the three post-policy gaps are 1.0, 1.3, and 1.1 units, their average gap is 1.13 units, about 1.13 ÷ 0.255 ≈ 4.4 times the pre-policy RMSPE. That ratio flags a visually substantial departure in this teaching example, but it is not a p-value or proof of an effect. Re-estimate after excluding each influential donor, and compare the treated ratio with analogous ratios from placebo-treated donors; concurrent policies or a poorly chosen donor pool can still explain the divergence.

A synthetic control is a weighted recipe, so first check what the recipe preserves. Illustrative synthetic example: donor regions report unemployment rates of 4%, 6%, and 8%, with weights 0.25, 0.50, and 0.25. The constructed rate is 0.25×4 + 0.50×6 + 0.25×8 = 1 + 3 + 2 = 6%. Because weights sum to 1, the result remains a rate, not a count or an unstated percentage-point change. A high-weight donor matters greatly, and a donor affected by policy or spillovers is not a valid untreated building block. Matching one predictor in one year is insufficient: inspect the entire pre-policy path and relevant predictors. This arithmetic is synthetic; any post-policy gap remains descriptive until design assumptions are defended. See ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 15: Synthetic Control (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’.","takeaway":"Synthetic control constructs a weighted comparison, but institutional knowledge still defines a credible donor pool."},{"title":"Pre-treatment fit is the first check","body":"Plot the treated and synthetic outcome paths before the intervention and summarize the gap. Poor pre-treatment fit signals that the constructed comparison does not reproduce the treated unit’s prior trajectory. A good fit is helpful but does not prove that unobserved post-policy shocks would have matched.

Illustrative example: suppose City A introduces a bus-fare subsidy in 2022, and annual public-transit employment is measured as jobs per 1,000 working-age residents from 2018 through 2023. Use three unaffected donor cities, with weights 0.50, 0.30, and 0.20. In 2021 their rates are 62, 60, and 63, so the synthetic rate is 0.50 × 62 + 0.30 × 60 + 0.20 × 63 = 61.6 jobs per 1,000. If City A’s observed rate is 61.5, the pre-treatment gap is 61.5 − 61.6 = −0.1 jobs per 1,000. Repeat this calculation for every pre-2022 year and inspect the path, not just one number. A small, stable gap suggests the weighted comparison tracks City A before the subsidy; it does not yet establish an effect afterward.

Before interpreting a post-2022 gap, synthetic control can show whether the donor-weighted path resembles the treated city during the pre-policy period, but it cannot prove the unobserved no-subsidy path or establish a population-wide effect from one treated case. Check the pre-treatment plot and summarize gaps; then inspect whether donor weights are concentrated in one city and whether excluding that donor changes the fit. A key assumption is that donors are not affected by the subsidy or related spillovers, and predictors should be chosen before searching for a favourable post-policy result. Do not call a post-policy difference the subsidy’s causal effect merely because it is large. As explained in “Matheus Facure — Ch. 15: Synthetic Control (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)” in the linked sources below, placebo comparisons are references, not randomization.

Fit should be assessed across periods, not selected from the most convenient year. Illustrative synthetic example: a treated county’s quarterly vacancy rates are 6.0% and 6.4% in two pre-policy quarters, while its synthetic rates are 5.8% and 6.1%. The gaps are 6.0 − 5.8 = 0.2 percentage points and 6.4 − 6.1 = 0.3 percentage points; the mean absolute gap is (0.2 + 0.3) / 2 = 0.25 percentage points. That small summary is useful, but a plot may reveal a trend or an outlier hidden by averaging. The calculation does not establish that post-policy movements are causal, because unmeasured shocks may differ. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 15: Synthetic Control (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative calculation (synthetic values, not observed data): suppose a treated region and its weighted donor combination have four pre-policy gaps, defined as treated minus synthetic outcome, of +0.20, −0.10, +0.30, and 0.00 jobs per 1,000 residents. The root mean squared prediction error (RMSPE) is sqrt[(0.20² + (−0.10)² + 0.30² + 0.00²) / 4] = sqrt(0.035) ≈ 0.187 jobs per 1,000 residents. If the average post-policy gap over two periods is +1.20 jobs per 1,000, the descriptive post/pre ratio is 1.20 / 0.187 ≈ 6.4. This ratio says the post-policy divergence is large relative to the model’s typical pre-policy discrepancy; it is not a p-value, confidence interval, or causal effect. First verify that the pre-period gaps do not show a systematic trend, then check whether one donor supplies most of the weight and recompute the diagnostic after excluding it. A ratio can look impressive when pre-fit is almost perfect, so report the raw post-policy gap and its units as well. The interpretation still requires unaffected donors, no anticipation or spillovers, and no concurrent shock that selectively changes the treated region.

Pre-treatment fit is a falsification-style check on whether the donor recipe can reproduce the treated path before policy. Illustrative synthetic example: quarterly vacancy rates for a treated city are 5.0%, 5.4%, and 5.2%; the synthetic path is 5.1%, 5.3%, and 5.3%. The signed gaps are −0.1, 0.1, and −0.1 percentage points, and the mean absolute gap is (0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1) ÷ 3 = 0.1 percentage points. That summary is useful, but it can hide a pattern if gaps alternate or widen over time, so plot each period. A close pre-policy path supports the comparison’s plausibility; it does not reveal the unobserved no-policy path after adoption. The lab’s curves are simulated, not city data. Report the pre-policy window, donor weights, and concurrent shocks. See ‘Cunningham — Causal Inference: The Mixtape (Yale University Press)’.","takeaway":"A convincing post-policy gap is hard to interpret if the pre-policy paths already diverge."},{"title":"Inspect donors and modelling choices","body":"Show which donor units receive weight, whether any are unusually influential, and how the fit changes when one donor or predictor is removed. Exclude units exposed to the same policy or spillovers. Avoid choosing predictors after looking for a large post-treatment gap. These decisions affect the counterfactual and must be documented.

Sensitivity analysis asks whether the conclusion depends on a particular donor or modelling decision. Illustrative synthetic example: a synthetic index uses weights 0.60, 0.25, and 0.15, and the post-policy index gap is 8 index points. Removing the 0.60-weight donor and re-estimating with the remaining donors gives a gap of 3 index points. The change, 8 − 3 = 5 index points, signals influential-donor dependence, not an automatic correction. If a predictor is measured in dollars per household, do not silently treat it as comparable to a percentage; scaling and predictor definitions matter. Document the donor exclusion and the pre-policy window before interpreting results. This exercise cannot show which specification is true or eliminate confounding. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Causal Inference: The Mixtape — open first-edition text’ in the linked sources.

Use a fit-scaled placebo check before treating a large gap as persuasive. Suppose, purely illustratively, a treated country’s pre-policy emissions gaps from its synthetic control (in million tonnes of CO₂ per year) are +0.2, −0.1, +0.3, and −0.2. The pre-period RMSPE is √[(0.2²+0.1²+0.3²+0.2²)/4] = √0.045 ≈ 0.21 million tonnes per year. If the three post-policy gaps are +1.1, +1.0, and +1.3, the post RMSPE is √[(1.1²+1.0²+1.3²)/3] = √1.30 ≈ 1.14 million tonnes per year, so the post/pre ratio is 1.14/0.21 ≈ 5.4. Next, reassign the intervention label to each eligible donor and calculate the same ratio, using the identical pre- and post-period definitions. A treated ratio of 5.4 is more informative if most placebo ratios are near 1, but it is not a p-value and does not establish causality. Discarding poorly fitting placebos can make the ranking look stronger, so set a transparent pre-fit rule in advance; also report the raw gaps because a high ratio can result from an unusually tiny denominator.

Sensitivity analysis should reveal whether one donor or one modelling decision carries the result. Illustrative synthetic example: a post-policy gap is 4.5 employment-index points with donors weighted 0.55, 0.30, and 0.15. Removing the 0.55-weight donor and rebuilding the comparison gives 2.0 points, a change of 2.5 points. That movement is evidence of influential-donor dependence, not proof that either specification is correct. Ask why the donor was influential: it may uniquely match pre-policy trends, or it may share a shock that makes it unsuitable. Repeating the exercise after excluding spillover-exposed donors and after changing the pre-policy window makes the design transparent. Never choose predictors after inspecting the preferred post-policy gap. The lab’s adjustable paths are teaching simulations, not measured policy outcomes. See ‘Causal Inference: The Mixtape — open first-edition text’.","takeaway":"The donor pool and predictor choices are part of the design, not invisible software defaults."},{"title":"Use placebos as a reference, not a magic test","body":"Applying the same procedure to untreated donor units can show whether the treated unit’s post-policy gap is unusually large relative to placebo gaps. Results are most informative when placebo units have comparable pre-treatment fit and the treated unit is not an extreme outlier simply because it has a much larger sample. With one treated case, uncertainty and generalization remain limited.

A placebo comparison is a ranking device, not a p-value that automatically solves a single-case design. Illustrative synthetic example: the treated unit’s post-policy gap is 12 percentage points, while four untreated placebo gaps are 2, 4, 7, and 15 percentage points, measured over the same one-year period. Three of four placebo gaps are smaller than 12, so the treated gap ranks fourth among five units; 75% of the placebo gaps are smaller. That ranking is descriptive and sensitive to the small placebo count, unequal pre-policy fit, and different outcome volatility. It does not prove a treatment effect or justify generalizing to all regions. Apply the same outcome units and time window to every unit. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 15: Synthetic Control (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

A useful refinement is to scale each unit’s post-policy discrepancy by its own pre-policy root mean squared prediction error (RMSPE), so a large raw gap is not mistaken for an unusual change when the synthetic match was already poor. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose the treated unit has pre-policy RMSPE 0.5 outcome units and post-policy RMSPE 2.0 outcome units; its deterioration ratio is 2.0 ÷ 0.5 = 4.0. Compute the same ratio for every placebo using the identical pre- and post-period windows. If the placebo ratios are 1.2, 1.8, 2.6, and 5.0, the treated ratio exceeds three of four, but not the largest; that is a descriptive rank, not a probability that the policy worked. Before ranking, inspect whether any denominator is near zero, because tiny pre-fit error can make a modest post-gap look enormous. Also report the raw outcome-unit gap alongside the ratio: scaling improves comparability, but it cannot repair donor contamination, anticipation, or a structurally different treated unit.

A placebo exercise asks whether untreated units produce similarly large gaps when treated as if exposed. Illustrative synthetic example: the treated gap is 9 index points, and five placebo gaps are 1, 3, 4, 8, and 12. Four are smaller than 9, so the treated case ranks fifth of six by magnitude; this is descriptive ordering, not a p-value. Interpretation also requires comparable pre-policy fit, outcome units, time windows, and attention to donor size or volatility. A poorly matched placebo can exaggerate unusualness, while a small placebo pool gives a coarse reference. The diagram labels its post-policy gap descriptive, and the lab’s curves are simulated. Placebos do not randomize one case or establish a population-wide effect. See ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 15: Synthetic Control (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’.","takeaway":"Placebo comparisons can calibrate evidence but do not turn one case into a randomized experiment."},{"title":"Compare placebo units only when their pre-policy fit is comparable","body":"A post-policy gap for the treated region is easier to interpret when the weighted donors tracked it closely before the policy. Applying the same procedure to untreated donor units can show whether the treated gap is unusual, but a donor with a very poor pre-policy match is not a fair placebo comparator. Report pre-policy fit for each placebo, the treated unit's place in that distribution, donor weights, and sensitivity to removing influential donors or changing the pre-policy window. With one treated case, this is a structured comparison rather than a large-sample experiment; uncertainty and generalization remain limited.

Before comparing post-policy gaps, put placebo units on a common fit scale. Illustrative synthetic example: the treated region has a pre-policy root mean squared gap of 0.4 percentage points, while three placebo regions have 0.5, 0.6, and 2.0 percentage points. If the analysis keeps placebo units with fit no larger than twice the treated value, the cutoff is 2 × 0.4 = 0.8 percentage points, so the first two placebo regions qualify and the third does not. This rule is a transparent screening choice, not a universal threshold. It changes the reference distribution and may discard informative evidence; report it alongside the original results. Comparable fit improves interpretation but cannot remove spillovers or hidden shocks. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Causal Inference: The Mixtape — open first-edition text’ in the linked sources.

A useful second diagnostic is to scale each post-policy gap by that unit’s own pre-policy root mean squared gap, rather than ranking raw gaps alone. Use the ratio R = |post-policy gap| / pre-policy RMS gap; the numerator and denominator are both in outcome units, so R is unit-free. Illustrative synthetic values make the calculation concrete: suppose the treated region’s gap is 1.20 outcome units and its pre-policy RMS gap is 0.30, giving R_T = 1.20 / 0.30 = 4.00. A placebo region with a 0.90-unit gap but a 0.30-unit pre-fit error has R_P = 3.00, whereas another with a 1.00-unit gap and 0.80-unit pre-fit error has R_P = 1.25. The raw gaps alone would make the latter look more unusual; the scaled ratios reverse that impression because its baseline mismatch was larger. Treat this as a descriptive diagnostic, not a p-value or causal proof. If a pre-fit RMS gap is zero or extremely small, the ratio becomes undefined or unstable; report the raw gap too and use a pre-specified minimum denominator or a separate sensitivity analysis.

Placebo gaps should be compared on a common scale of pre-policy credibility, not simply sorted by their post-policy size. Illustrative synthetic example: the treated unit’s pre-policy root mean squared gap is 0.3 outcome units. Three placebo units have fit values 0.4, 0.6, and 1.1; using a transparent screen of no more than twice the treated fit gives a cutoff of 2×0.3 = 0.6, so only the first two qualify. The screen is an analyst’s choice, not a universal law, and excluding the third changes the reference distribution. Report results with and without the screen, plus the reasons for any donor exclusion. A comparable fit does not rule out spillovers, concurrent policies, or different shocks. The lab’s pre-fit control is a simulated teaching input, not an estimate. See ‘Causal Inference: The Mixtape — open first-edition text’.","takeaway":"Placebo gaps are informative only alongside comparable pre-treatment fit and a transparent donor pool."}]
data.case_study: A country introduces a large carbon levy while comparable countries do not. Build a synthetic comparison from unaffected countries, examine pre-policy emissions fit and test sensitivity to donor exclusions and concurrent climate policies.
data.misconceptions:
Synthetic control is not automatically randomized or bias-free.
Poor pre-treatment fit undermines the post-treatment comparison.
Placebo distributions do not remove all uncertainty in a single treated case.

data.title: Binary, Count & Limited Outcomes
data.excerpt: Many economic outcomes are not unrestricted numbers: employment is yes or no, clinic visits are counts, and spending may be zero for many people. Learn which models fit these patterns and how to report results as probabilities, expected counts or amounts people can interpret.
data.objectives:
Compare the linear probability, logit and probit models.
Interpret marginal effects rather than relying only on odds ratios.
Recognize count, censoring and two-part outcome structures.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Start with the outcome’s support","body":"A binary outcome such as employment is zero or one. A count such as clinic visits is a non-negative integer. Expenditure may include many zeros and a long right tail. The outcome type guides model choice, but a more complex model is not automatically better; the target may be an average probability change, a predicted count or the amount spent conditional on spending.

Support means the set of values an outcome can take, and it determines what an average represents. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose five households report 0, 0, 1, 2, and 5 clinic visits during one calendar month. Their mean is (0+0+1+2+5) ÷ 5 = 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6 visits per household-month, while the median is 1 visit; the long upper tail matters. A binary employment indicator instead has units of people in work (yes/no), so its mean is a proportion: 3 employed out of 5 equals 3/5 = 0.60, or 60 percent. These summaries do not establish why outcomes differ, and a model still needs a clearly defined population and period. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Cameron & Trivedi — Microeconometrics: Methods and Applications (Cambridge University Press)’ in the linked sources.

A probability-scale slope and a logit-index slope must be translated before they can be compared. Illustrative synthetic example: take a baseline placement probability of 40% at predictor index x = 0. With an LPM slope of 0.12, moving to x = 1 gives 0.40 + 0.12(1) = 0.52, a 12 percentage-point increase; moving to x = −2 gives 0.16, still inside [0,1] for this range. For a logit with the same 40% baseline and index slope 0.80, first compute the baseline log-odds log(0.40/0.60) ≈ −0.405. At x = 1 the index is −0.405 + 0.80 = 0.395, so the predicted probability is 1/[1 + exp(−0.395)] ≈ 0.597, or 59.7%. The comparable change from x = 0 is therefore about 19.7 percentage points, not 0.80 points. Because the logit effect varies with baseline risk, report predicted probabilities or marginal effects at relevant x values. Also check the whole policy-relevant range: an LPM can leave [0,1] outside the plotted range, while a logit stays bounded; neither calculation alone establishes a causal placement effect without a credible design.

Outcome support tells you what a model’s prediction is allowed to mean. Illustrative synthetic example: five clients make 0, 1, 2, 2, and 7 appointments in a month. The mean is 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4 appointments per client-month, while the median is 2; 7 pulls the mean upward without making appointments continuous. For employment recorded as 0 or 1, four employed people among five give 4 ÷ 5 = 0.80, or 80 percent, a probability-scale summary. These outcomes have different supports and units. A count model must consider exposure time and eligibility, while a binary model concerns an event definition and window. The diagram’s count bars are illustrative frequencies, not measured service use. Complexity cannot replace a clear estimand or credible design. See ‘Cameron & Trivedi — Microeconometrics: Methods and Applications (Cambridge University Press)’.","takeaway":"Model the variable and the policy question, not a textbook label."},{"title":"Compare linear probability and nonlinear links","body":"A linear probability model is easy to interpret: a coefficient of 0.04 is a four-percentage-point conditional difference, though predictions can fall outside zero and one and variance is not constant. Logit and probit map a linear index into probabilities between zero and one. Their coefficients are on a latent scale, so show average marginal effects or predicted probabilities for policy interpretation.

Illustrative synthetic example: a city employment office follows 400 unemployed adults for six months and records placement as 1 if a person starts a job and 0 otherwise. Suppose a linear probability model compares people offered text-message appointment reminders with those not offered them, holding the stated controls fixed. If the reminder coefficient is 0.04, calculate 0.04 × 100 = 4 percentage points: the model predicts a conditional placement probability four points higher for the offer group. A logit model may instead predict 0.40 placement probability without the reminder and 0.46 with it for a specified person; 0.46 − 0.40 = 0.06, or 6 percentage points. Report these probabilities, the six-month horizon and the 400-person analysis sample, not only a logit coefficient.

Neither comparison alone establishes that reminders caused placement: that requires a credible assignment or other design, and both models summarize conditional associations under their specifications. Check that fitted linear probabilities stay between 0 and 1, use suitable robust uncertainty for its unequal error variance, and examine whether the logit contrast changes across baseline covariates; report an average marginal effect when the audience needs a sample-wide summary. A common mistake is to read a logit coefficient of 0.04 as a four-percentage-point increase: it is a log-odds change, and the probability effect depends on the starting values. For model interpretation and limits, see “Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)” in the linked sources below.

A useful comparison holds the covariates and time horizon fixed, then examines fitted probabilities rather than coefficient labels. Illustrative synthetic example: for two otherwise specified applicants over a three-month follow-up, a linear probability model predicts 0.72 with training information and 0.65 without it; 0.72 − 0.65 = 0.07, or 7 percentage points. If a logit model gives 0.70 and 0.76 for the same comparison, the contrast is 0.06, or 6 percentage points. Both are probability-scale statements, but neither is automatically causal: assignment, omitted variables, and model specification still matter. A linear prediction of 1.04 would mean 104 percent, an impossible probability, whereas the logit link avoids that boundary violation. Predictions also depend on the chosen covariate values and stated three-month period. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)’ in the linked sources.

To turn a nonlinear-link coefficient into a local probability statement, differentiate the inverse-logit rather than multiplying the coefficient by 100. Illustrative synthetic calculation using the lab’s default settings: let the baseline probability at predictor index x = 0 be p = 0.40 and let the logit index slope be β = 0.80 per index unit. The local marginal effect at x = 0 is p(1 − p)β = 0.40 × 0.60 × 0.80 = 0.192 probability units per index unit, or 19.2 percentage points per one-unit increase, holding the other covariates and outcome horizon fixed. This is a local derivative, not a universal effect: evaluating the same curve gives p(−1) = 23.1% and p(1) = 59.7%, so moving from −1 to 1 changes the prediction by 36.7 percentage points, not 2 × 19.2 = 38.4 points. The difference arises because the logistic curve flattens near zero and one. The contrast remains a model-based conditional association unless a credible assignment design supports a causal interpretation; report the covariate values and horizon with any marginal effect.

One logit coefficient can imply different probability changes because the logistic curve is steepest near its middle. Suppose the same synthetic model has coefficient 0.8 for a one-unit training indicator, with other covariates held fixed. From baseline probability 0.10, adding 0.8 to the log-odds gives logistic(logit(0.10) + 0.8) ≈ 0.198, an increase of 9.8 percentage points. From baseline 0.50, logistic(0.8) ≈ 0.690, an increase of 19.0 points; from baseline 0.90, the predicted probability is about 0.952, an increase of 5.2 points. The coefficient stays constant while conditional changes vary. Average marginal effects average such changes over a specified sample. These synthetic predictions are not causal effects without a credible design.","takeaway":"Report meaningful probability changes rather than treating a logit coefficient as a percentage-point effect."},{"title":"Choose a count model and inspect its limits","body":"Poisson regression links the expected count to predictors and can be useful even when the variance is not exactly equal to the mean if inference is robust. Overdispersion or unobserved heterogeneity may motivate alternatives such as negative binomial models. If many observations have zero use because they are not eligible or do not participate, distinguish a structural participation process from a count process only when the data and question support it.

Count models describe non-negative integer events, but their fitted mean is not necessarily a person’s most likely count. Illustrative synthetic example: four patients have 0, 1, 1, and 6 visits over a six-month period. The sample mean is (0+1+1+6) ÷ 4 = 2 visits per patient-six-months, while the variance around that mean is much larger than it would be for clustered counts. A Poisson model uses predictors to estimate an expected count; robust inference can protect standard errors when the mean–variance equality is doubtful, but it does not repair a badly chosen mean function. Negative binomial modeling may capture extra dispersion, yet it still does not prove that a predictor causes visits. Check exposure time, eligibility, excess zeros, and whether counts are comparable across people. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Cameron & Trivedi — Microeconometrics: Methods and Applications (Cambridge University Press)’ in the linked sources.

When people are observed for different lengths of time, compare rates rather than raw counts. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a comparison group averages 3 appointments during 6 person-months of eligibility, giving a rate of 3 ÷ 6 = 0.50 appointments per person-month. A Poisson specification can write E[Y_i|X_i,t_i] = t_i exp(X_iβ), or equivalently include log(t_i) as a fixed offset. If an appointment-system indicator has β = 0.20, its rate ratio is exp(0.20) ≈ 1.221, so the modeled rate is about 22.1% higher—not 0.20 additional appointments and not a 20-percentage-point probability change. Holding exposure at six person-months, the illustrative expected count changes from 6(0.50) = 3.00 to 3.00 × 1.221 ≈ 3.66 appointments; this is an expectation, not a guarantee for an individual. Before interpreting it, verify that eligibility time is measured consistently, that the offset is not itself affected by the system, and that residual dispersion or dependence does not make Poisson uncertainty misleading. The rate ratio remains associational unless a credible design supports a causal reading.

A boundary value can arise from recording limits or from a genuine zero, and those mechanisms imply different questions. Illustrative synthetic example: an insurer records monthly claims above $10,000 as exactly $10,000. A reported $10,000 could conceal $10,500 or $25,000, so the observed value is top-coded rather than a true amount. Separately, four households spend $0, $15, $40, and $80 on a service; the mean is $135 ÷ 4 = $33.75 per household-month, and zero may represent nonparticipation rather than censoring. A two-part model can separate the probability of any spending from positive spending, whereas a Tobit-style restriction links both through one latent process. Choose from the data-collection story and estimand, not from the presence of zeros alone. Neither model establishes causality. See ‘Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)’.","takeaway":"Check the observed distribution and assumptions before choosing a count model."},{"title":"Censoring and selection need different stories","body":"A top-coded income is censored because values above a limit are recorded at that limit; expenditure with many true zeros is not automatically censored. Tobit-type models impose a shared latent process for the zero boundary and positive outcome, which may not fit a separate participation decision. Compare predicted outcomes and state the assumptions that connect the observed measure to the model.

The recording mechanism determines the model’s interpretation. Illustrative synthetic example: an income survey records every value above $5,000 per month as $5,000. A reported value of $5,000 could therefore represent $5,200 or $8,000; the observation is censored at a currency threshold, not genuinely equal to $5,000. By contrast, if four households spend $0, $20, $20, and $60 on a service during January, the zeros may reflect nonparticipation; the mean is ($0+$20+$20+$60) ÷ 4 = $25 per household-month, with no censoring implied. A Tobit-style model assumes one latent process connects the boundary and positive values, while a two-part approach can model participation and positive spending separately. Neither structure identifies causes without a credible design, and the $5,000 threshold and January period must be reported. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)’ in the linked sources.

Consider an illustrative synthetic labor-market file with a 12-month follow-up. For a worker who finds a job in month 5, the unemployment duration is recorded as 5 months; for one still unemployed at month 12, the record says 12+ months. The second value is right-censored, not evidence that the spell ended at 12, so a survival analysis should retain that worker’s 12 months at risk and mark the event as unobserved. In a separate wage file, suppose wages are observed only for the 6 of 10 synthetic workers who accepted a job. The four missing wages are not censored wages at a known ceiling: their values are unobserved because employment selection occurred. First define the estimand—time to re-employment for the full worker population or mean wage among employed workers—then ask whether the recording rule is administrative censoring or outcome-dependent observation. A model for censored duration and a selection model answer different questions; neither becomes causal merely because its likelihood fits. Report the follow-up horizon, event definition, and who could enter the wage sample.

Selection and censoring describe different ways outcomes enter a file. Suppose a synthetic study follows 100 job applicants: 60 are employed with average observed wage £2,000, while wages for the other 40 are unavailable. The £2,000 is a mean for employed applicants. If the target is monthly earnings for all 100 and nonworkers are defined to earn zero, the implied mean is 60×£2,000/100 = £1,200; that is a constructed earnings measure, not an observed wage. A recording cap among the 60 workers would instead censor high wages while retaining those people. The first mechanism changes who is observed; the second limits recorded values. State the target and data-collection rule before choosing a selection or censoring model. Neither model alone establishes causality.","takeaway":"Do not use a censored-outcome model merely because the data contain zeros."},{"title":"Translate nonlinear coefficients onto the probability scale","body":"For a binary outcome, a logit coefficient is a change in log odds, not a fixed percentage-point change in participation. If a model predicts a probability rising from 0.40 to 0.46 for a stated comparison, the difference is 0.06, or 6 percentage points. In a logit model that probability contrast depends on the starting covariate values; report predicted probabilities or an average marginal effect and show the population over which it is averaged. A linear probability coefficient is already on the probability scale but can predict outside zero and one and needs appropriate inference. Neither functional form makes the contrast causal without a design that supports that claim.

To communicate a nonlinear model, calculate the contrast on the probability scale at specified covariates or average contrasts across a defined sample. Illustrative synthetic example: for 200 synthetic observations, predicted participation is 0.30 without a subsidy and 0.36 with it at the same stated characteristics. The change is 0.36 − 0.30 = 0.06, or 6 percentage points; it is not 6 percent relative growth, which would be 0.06 ÷ 0.30 = 0.20, or 20 percent. An average marginal effect instead averages observation-specific changes, so its weighting and sample size should be stated. A logit coefficient alone is a log-odds change, and no probability contrast proves causality; treatment assignment and omitted confounding remain concerns. Keep the outcome definition, comparison, and time period explicit. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Gelman, Hill & Vehtari — Regression and Other Stories (Cambridge University Press)’ in the linked sources.

A useful diagnostic is to separate a local marginal effect from a finite change in a predictor. Consider an explicitly illustrative synthetic logit model with log-odds index η = −0.4055 + 0.8x; the intercept is −0.4055 because at x = 0 the baseline probability is 0.40, since ln(0.40/0.60) ≈ −0.4055. The derivative is ∂p/∂x = p(1−p)·0.8, so at x = 0 it equals 0.40×0.60×0.8 = 0.192, or about 19.2 percentage points for a one-unit change locally. That is not the exact effect over a wide move: at x = 1, p = 1/[1+exp(−(−0.4055+0.8))] ≈ 0.597, so moving from x = 0 to x = 1 changes probability by 0.597−0.400 = 0.197, or 19.7 percentage points. At x = −1, p ≈ 0.230, showing why the same coefficient does not imply the same probability change everywhere. These calculations assume the covariate comparison and functional form are meaningful; they describe model predictions, not a causal effect without credible assignment or adjustment.

Linear probability and logit models can produce similar local comparisons while carrying different boundary behavior. Illustrative synthetic example: at one stated covariate value, the linear model predicts 0.62 without an offer and 0.70 with it, a difference of 0.08 or 8 percentage points. A logit model predicts 0.61 and 0.69, a 0.08 difference as well. At more extreme covariate values, the contrasts need not match, and the linear model may predict 1.04 or −0.03, which cannot be a probability. The logit link remains within [0,1], but its coefficient is not itself a probability change. Report predicted probabilities, sample and follow-up period, and use appropriate inference for the linear model’s unequal variance. The interactive limited-outcome curves are simulated teaching objects, not empirical fits. Neither functional form resolves omitted confounding. See ‘Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)’.","takeaway":"Report probability changes at stated covariate values or averaged over a defined sample; do not read log-odds as percentage points.","formula":"0.46 − 0.40 = 0.06 = 6 percentage points.","practice":{"question":"A logit coefficient is 0.06. Does that mean the outcome probability rises by 6 percentage points for everyone?","hint":"Check the scale of the coefficient and whether the probability link is nonlinear.","solution":"No. The coefficient is on the log-odds scale. The probability change depends on baseline covariates; calculate a predicted-probability contrast or marginal effect."}}]
data.case_study: A local employment service studies whether a new appointment system changes the probability of job placement and the number of appointments used. Report probability changes and count-model checks rather than presenting only nonlinear-link coefficients.
data.misconceptions:
A logit coefficient is not directly a percentage-point change in probability.
Many zeros do not by themselves justify a zero-inflated model.
A more flexible likelihood does not fix an ill-defined estimand or confounding.
