data.title: Selection, Attrition & Missing Data
data.excerpt: Missing values and dropouts are not just blank cells; they can change who the data represent and what a result measures. Learn to trace why observations are absent, how selection and attrition can bias an estimate, and which comparisons or sensitivity checks may help.
data.objectives:
Distinguish common missingness mechanisms and sample selection.
Describe attrition and compare observed baseline features.
Use weighting or sensitivity analysis only with explicit assumptions.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Missing rows can change the question","body":"A household survey may miss people who move frequently, a firm database may omit businesses that close, and a trial may lose participants at follow-up. The observed sample then represents a selected group. Describe which units or variables are missing, when they became missing, and whether selection is related to treatment or outcomes.

Start by naming the target population and the unit of analysis before calculating a mean. Illustrative synthetic example: a city wants the average weekly food spending of 12 sampled households, but two households with no internet access are absent. The ten observed amounts, in pounds per week, total £620, so the observed mean is £620 ÷ 10 = £62 per household-week. If the two missing households would each have spent £90, the target-sample mean would be (£620 + £90 + £90) ÷ 12 = £800 ÷ 12 = £66.67 per household-week, a £4.67 difference. This does not prove the missing households spend more; their values are unknown. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Gelman, Hill & Vehtari — Regression and Other Stories (Cambridge University Press)’ in the linked sources.

Use the attrition check to separate an observed contrast from a sensitivity scenario. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose 250 people are assigned an offer and 250 a comparison condition; 20% of the offer group and 10% of the comparison group lack follow-up, so the observed means describe 200 and 225 people, not the original 250-person groups. If the observed outcome gap (offer minus comparison) is +2.0 units, do not silently call it the assignment effect. In the lab’s deliberately simplified scenario, let the unobserved offer-group outcomes be 1.5 units lower than the corresponding unobserved comparison outcomes. The sensitivity adjustment is (1 − 0.20) × (−1.5) = −1.20 units, giving an adjusted gap of 2.00 − 1.20 = +0.80 units. This is not a recovered truth: it is conditional on the chosen shift and the lab’s one-sided adjustment, while comparison attrition still warrants inspection. Report assignment counts, observed counts, attrition rates, and the range of plausible shifts; identification would require stronger assumptions or a design addressing differential follow-up.

Before calculating an average, specify whether the denominator is observed cases or the intended sample. Illustrative synthetic example: a survey targets 15 households, but three records are absent. The 12 observed weekly transport costs total £360, so the complete-case mean is £360 ÷ 12 = £30 per household-week. If the missing households would each have cost £50, the target-sample mean would be (£360 + £150) ÷ 15 = £34 per household-week, a £4 difference. Those values are assumed, not recovered observations. Describe when records disappeared, which baseline features predict absence, and whether treatment is involved. A large observed file does not remove selection bias if missingness is systematic. The lab’s rows remain missing, and its sensitivity shift is hypothetical. See ‘Gelman, Hill & Vehtari — Regression and Other Stories (Cambridge University Press)’.","takeaway":"Missingness is about the data-collection process, not just blank cells in a spreadsheet."},{"title":"State the missingness assumption","body":"Missing completely at random means missingness is unrelated to observed or unobserved data. Missing at random allows it to depend on observed information after conditioning on that information. Missing not at random still depends on unobserved values after adjustment. These labels are assumptions about how data went missing, not properties that can usually be diagnosed from observed data alone.

Illustrative synthetic example: consider 100 apprentices surveyed about monthly earnings in June 2025, measured in pounds. Age group is recorded for everyone, but earnings are observed for only 80 people: 45 of 50 younger apprentices, whose observed mean is £1,800, and 35 of 50 older apprentices, whose observed mean is £2,200. The complete-case mean is (45×£1,800 + 35×£2,200) ÷ 80 = £1,975 per month. If we assume missing at random given age, the response probabilities are 0.90 and 0.70, so inverse-probability weighting gives [45×£1,800÷0.90 + 35×£2,200÷0.70] ÷ [45÷0.90 + 35÷0.70] = £2,000 per month. The weighted result rebalances observed apprentices to the original age-group counts; it is conditional on that assumption.

This calculation can estimate the average June 2025 monthly earnings for all 100 apprentices only if, after conditioning on recorded age and any other included predictors, response is unrelated to the unobserved earnings; that is the missing-at-random assumption. It cannot prove that assumption from the observed file, recover earnings for a person who never responded, or establish a causal programme effect. Check response rates and baseline characteristics by age group and treatment or offer status, and look for adequate overlap rather than relying on extreme weights. A common error is to treat the £2,000 as automatically more truthful than £1,975: weighting changes the estimand under a model, not the underlying evidence. For broader discussion, see “Hernán & Robins — Causal Inference: What If (authors’ open book)” in the linked sources below.

A useful diagnostic is to compare response rates across recorded groups, while remembering that such comparisons cannot test dependence on an unrecorded value. Illustrative synthetic example: among 40 urban and 60 rural applicants, outcomes are observed for 32 urban and 42 rural applicants. Response rates are 32 ÷ 40 = 0.80, or 80%, and 42 ÷ 60 = 0.70, or 70%; the gap is 10 percentage points, not 10 percent. A missing-at-random analysis could adjust for urban/rural status, but only if those recorded categories capture the relevant response differences. It does not justify claiming that unobserved outcomes match observed outcomes within each category, nor does it establish a causal effect. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Hernán & Robins — Causal Inference: What If (authors’ open book)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic sensitivity check: suppose 100 people are offered training and 100 are in the comparison group. Offer-group attrition is 20%, so 80 offer outcomes are observed; comparison attrition is 10%, so 90 comparison outcomes are observed. If the observed monthly earnings means are £54 and £50, the complete-case gap is £4 per month, but reconstructing the assigned-group means requires assumptions about the 30 missing earnings values. Set the comparison missing mean to £50 and let the offer missing mean be £50 + δ, where δ is the assumed offer-minus-comparison difference among missing people. The all-assigned gap is [(80×54 + 20×(50+δ)) − (90×50 + 10×50)] ÷ 100 = £3.20 + 0.20δ per month. Thus δ = −£10 gives £1.20, δ = £0 gives £3.20, and δ = £10 gives £5.20. This range is a sensitivity analysis, not a discovered effect: it changes the estimand from observed responders to everyone assigned and depends on plausible missing-outcome values. Random assignment could support a causal offer effect only with appropriate design and interpretation; attrition assumptions remain central.

MCAR, MAR, and MNAR describe assumptions about the observation process, not labels proved by a response-rate table. Illustrative synthetic example: among 50 younger and 50 older workers, outcomes are observed for 45 younger and 35 older workers. Response rates are 45 ÷ 50 = 90% and 35 ÷ 50 = 70%, a 20-percentage-point difference. MAR could be plausible if recorded age and other observed predictors explain the response gap and no remaining dependence involves unobserved outcomes. MNAR remains possible if unusually low earners are less likely to respond within age groups. Weighting or imputation produces model-based results, not newly observed wages. Check overlap before weighting, and vary plausible unseen outcomes. The diagram says MAR/MNAR assumptions cannot be verified from observed outcomes alone. See ‘Hernán & Robins — Causal Inference: What If (authors’ open book)’.","takeaway":"Observed patterns can challenge assumptions but cannot reveal every unobserved missing value."},{"title":"Account for selective observation","body":"If follow-up depends on measured baseline variables, inverse-probability weights can reweight observed participants toward the target population under a correct observation model and adequate overlap. Extreme weights signal limited information. Multiple imputation can represent uncertainty under a stated missing-at-random model, but neither method automatically corrects unmeasured selection.

Weighting is easiest to understand as a duplication rule that restores representation, not as extra information. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose 50 eligible people include 30 low-risk and 20 high-risk people, but observed follow-up includes 24 low-risk and 8 high-risk people. Their response probabilities are 24 ÷ 30 = 0.80 and 8 ÷ 20 = 0.40, so observed high-risk cases receive weight 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.5, while low-risk cases receive 1 ÷ 0.80 = 1.25. The weighted counts are 24×1.25 = 30 and 8×2.5 = 20, totaling 50. This re-creates group totals only under a correct observation model and adequate overlap; it cannot repair unmeasured selection or prove causality. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)’ in the linked sources.

Consider a synthetic job-training follow-up with 200 people offered training and 200 comparison people. Among offer-group responders, mean monthly earnings are $2,200; among comparison responders, they are $2,000. Response rates are 85% and 70%, respectively, so the complete-case gap is $200 per month, but that is not automatically the effect for everyone assigned. For a transparent sensitivity calculation, suppose comparison-group nonresponders would average the observed comparison mean, $2,000, and let δ be the offer-group nonresponder mean minus $2,000. The offer-group population mean under this scenario is 0.85($2,200) + 0.15($2,000 + δ) = $2,170 + 0.15δ, while the comparison mean is $2,000; hence the adjusted contrast is $170 + 0.15δ per month. If δ = $400, the contrast is $230; if δ = −$400, it is $110. These are illustrative synthetic assumptions, not recovered outcomes. Report the response rates, denominator, and δ range explicitly: if plausible values cross zero or reverse the conclusion, the result is sensitive to attrition rather than securely identified.

Inverse-probability weighting restores representation only for differences captured by the observation model. Illustrative synthetic example: a target has 40 low-risk and 20 high-risk people, but observed follow-up includes 32 low-risk and 6 high-risk people. Response probabilities are 32 ÷ 40 = 0.80 and 6 ÷ 20 = 0.30, giving weights 1.25 and approximately 3.33. Weighted counts are 32×1.25 = 40 and 6×3.33 ≈ 20, so observed groups reproduce target totals approximately. High-risk cases exert much more influence, making estimates unstable if their outcomes are few or extreme. This adjustment assumes recorded risk groups suffice and each target group has positive response probability; it cannot correct unmeasured selection. Report weighted and complete-case results, response rates, and effective sample size. The scenario is synthetic, not an evaluation finding. See ‘Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)’.","takeaway":"Weighting and imputation rely on assumptions that should be explained in plain language."},{"title":"Show sensitivity and preserve denominators","body":"Report the starting sample, exclusions, missing outcome rates by group and reasons for loss where known. Compare complete-case estimates with defensible alternatives. For missing-not-at-random concerns, show how results would change under plausible departures from the main assumption. Keep denominators visible so a reader can see who contributes to each estimate.

A sensitivity analysis can translate an assumption about missing outcomes into a transparent range. Illustrative synthetic example: an evaluation starts with 100 treated and 100 control people; observed success counts are 54 of 80 treated and 50 of 90 control people. Complete-case rates are 54 ÷ 80 = 67.5% and 50 ÷ 90 = 55.6%, a difference of 11.9 percentage points. If every missing treated person succeeded and every missing control person failed, rates become (54+20) ÷ 100 = 74% and 50 ÷ 100 = 50%, a 24-point difference. These are bounds under extreme, explicitly stated assumptions, not observed results; they do not identify a causal effect if missingness is related to treatment response. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 2, §2.1; Ch. 3, §3.2’ in the linked sources.

A different check is to standardize observed outcomes to the baseline mix that was assigned, rather than letting differential follow-up redefine the target population. Illustrative synthetic example: each arm starts with 120 people, two-thirds in a lower-risk stratum and one-third in a higher-risk stratum. In the offer arm, follow-up is observed for 72 of 80 lower-risk people, with 36 successes, and 20 of 40 higher-risk people, with 12 successes. The stratum-specific rates are therefore 36/72 = 50% and 12/20 = 60%; applying the assigned shares gives (2/3)(0.50) + (1/3)(0.60) = 53.3%. In the comparison arm, the corresponding observed counts are 64 of 80 with 24 successes and 36 of 40 with 18 successes, giving 37.5% and 50%, so standardization gives (2/3)(0.375) + (1/3)(0.50) = 41.7%. The standardized difference is 11.7 percentage points, versus 48/92 − 42/100 = 10.2 points using unweighted complete cases. This adjustment is defensible only if, within treatment and baseline stratum, follow-up is unrelated to the missing outcome (a MAR-style assumption); inspect whether the strata are sufficiently predictive and report sensitivity if that assumption is doubtful.

A missing-outcome sensitivity analysis should show how an explicit scenario changes the estimand, while keeping assigned denominators visible. Illustrative synthetic example: 120 treated people produce 78 observed successes from 90 observed outcomes; 120 controls produce 60 successes from 100 observed outcomes. Complete-case rates are 78 ÷ 90 = 86.7% and 60 ÷ 100 = 60.0%, a 26.7-percentage-point difference. If all 30 missing treated outcomes fail and all 20 missing control outcomes succeed, full-denominator rates become 78 ÷ 120 = 65.0% and 80 ÷ 120 = 66.7%, reversing the contrast to −1.7 percentage points. These are assumed bounds, not observed results or causal estimates. Present intermediate scenarios and explain whether conclusions depend on extreme unseen outcomes. See ‘Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 2, §2.1; Ch. 3, §3.2’.","takeaway":"A sensitivity analysis makes the role of missing-data assumptions visible instead of silently treating observed cases as everyone."},{"title":"Conditioning on who is observed can change the estimand","body":"Suppose a training programme can affect whether a person is employed, and wages are recorded only for employed people. Comparing wages among observed workers conditions on a status that may itself be changed by treatment. The result is then about selected observed workers, not automatically the programme's effect on earnings for everyone offered training; selection can also open a non-causal association between treatment and unobserved determinants of employment. Report employment and wage outcomes separately where possible, retain the assigned groups and denominators, and explain any bounds or sensitivity analysis used for wages that are unobserved. Accurate wage measurement among workers does not solve the missing counterfactual for those not working.

When treatment affects employment, report employment itself before discussing wages among workers. Illustrative synthetic example: 100 people are assigned to training and 100 to control. Employment is 70 of 100 in training and 60 of 100 in control, so the employment difference is 70% − 60% = 10 percentage points. Among employed people, average monthly wages are £2,100 for 70 trainees and £2,000 for 60 controls, a £100 monthly difference. The wage comparison is conditional on different selected groups: training may have brought additional people into work. It therefore is not automatically the programme’s effect on everyone’s potential wage, including those not employed. Wage units are pounds per month, and this association alone does not establish causality. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Hernán & Robins — Causal Inference: What If (authors’ open book)’ in the linked sources.

A useful sensitivity check is to bound an outcome rather than silently fill in missing cases. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose the outcome is a 0–10 training-test score, with 18% of the offer group and 12% of the comparison group missing. Among observed cases, the means are 7.2 and 5.8, so the observed-case gap is 7.2 − 5.8 = 1.4 score points. Keep the assigned denominators: the offer-group overall mean is 0.82(7.2) + 0.18mₒ = 5.904 + 0.18mₒ, while the comparison mean is 0.88(5.8) + 0.12m𝚌 = 5.104 + 0.12m𝚌, where mₒ and m𝚌 are unknown missing-case means. Using only the known 0–10 range, the smallest gap sets mₒ = 0 and m𝚌 = 10: 5.904 − 6.304 = −0.400 points. The largest sets mₒ = 10 and m𝚌 = 0: 7.704 − 5.104 = 2.600 points. Thus the data alone permit a −0.4 to 2.6 point range, not a precise effect. If assignment was randomized, this can be an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis; otherwise it is descriptive, not causal. The lab’s attrition and unseen-outcome controls illustrate the same logic, but their values are teaching assumptions, not observed data.

When treatment changes an intermediate status, restricting analysis to that status can compare different compositions. Illustrative synthetic example: 100 people receive training and 100 do not. Employment is 68% among trainees and 58% among controls, a 10-percentage-point difference. Among those employed, monthly wages average £2,300 for 68 trainees and £2,200 for 58 controls, a £100 difference. The wage comparison is conditional on employment, which training may have changed; it does not describe the average wage effect for the original 200 people, including those not employed. Report employment first, retain assigned-group denominators, and state assumptions used to bound unobserved wages. Accurate wage records among workers cannot reveal counterfactual wages for nonworkers. The lab’s adjusted gap is a hypothetical sensitivity scenario, not measured evidence. See ‘Hernán & Robins — Causal Inference: What If (authors’ open book)’.","takeaway":"When observation depends on a post-treatment outcome or status, the observed-case comparison may answer a different question from the policy estimand.","formula":{"question":"If treatment changes who is employed, what is the risk of comparing wages only among currently employed people?","hint":"Ask whether employment is fixed before treatment or can be changed by it.","solution":"Employment is post-treatment and may select different people into the wage sample in each group. The wage comparison among workers need not be the effect for the original assigned population."}}]
data.case_study: A job-training evaluation loses more participants from the control group than from the offer group. Compare attrition and baseline data, report who remains in each analysis, and test how plausible outcome differences among missing participants affect the result.
data.misconceptions:
A large sample does not remove selection bias.
Complete-case analysis is not automatically unbiased.
Imputation or weighting does not reveal outcomes that were never observed without assumptions.

data.title: Heterogeneous Effects & Quantile Regression
data.excerpt: An average effect can hide very different outcomes for different people or places. Learn how subgroup and quantile analyses describe variation across groups or across the outcome distribution, and why searching many subgroups can produce patterns that are not reliable.
data.objectives:
Interpret interactions as conditional differences.
Distinguish subgroup average effects from quantile regression coefficients.
Pre-specify heterogeneity questions and report uncertainty across groups.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"An average can hide variation","body":"A policy can affect people differently because baseline resources, constraints or local conditions differ. The average treatment effect summarises one mean contrast and does not imply that every unit experiences that amount. Before exploring subgroups, name a mechanism and a small number of groups that matter for the decision.

Consider two synthetic regions receiving the same job-training policy. Region A’s average monthly earnings rise from 2,000 to 2,080 currency units, an increase of 80 currency units per worker. Region B rises from 1,500 to 1,560, an increase of 60 currency units. If the regions contain 50 and 150 workers, the pooled average increase is (50×80 + 150×60)/(50+150) = 13,000/200 = 65 currency units per worker per month. That 65-unit average does not describe either region exactly, and it could hide still wider variation within each region. The comparison assumes earnings are measured on the same monthly scale and groups were defined before treatment; it does not establish that the policy caused the changes without a valid design. For a fuller treatment, see “Cameron & Trivedi — Microeconometrics: Methods and Applications (Cambridge University Press)” in the linked sources.

Suppose a randomized childcare-subsidy offer is evaluated with baseline care access defined in advance. In a synthetic example, parents with high access have participation of 62% without the offer and 68% with it, so their subgroup average effect is 68 − 62 = 6 percentage points. Parents with low access move from 41% to 53%, giving 12 percentage points. The interaction contrast asks whether those effects differ: (53 − 41) − (68 − 62) = 12 − 6 = 6 percentage points, not whether one subgroup’s separate test is significant and the other is not. If 40% of the target population has high access and 60% low access, the corresponding standardized average is 0.40×6 + 0.60×12 = 9.6 percentage points; changing those population shares changes the overall estimand, not the subgroup effects. These figures are illustrative and synthetic, not observed outcomes. For a causal interpretation, random assignment must be credible within the pre-specified groups, participation must be measured on the same follow-up window, and uncertainty for the 6-point interaction should be reported directly. This interaction is a probability-scale contrast; a quantile-regression coefficient would answer a different distributional question.

A pooled effect is a weighted average and can conceal subgroup contrasts. Illustrative synthetic example: a childcare subsidy raises monthly earnings by £120 for 30 parents with limited access and by £40 for 70 parents with reliable care. The pooled increase is (30×120 + 70×40) ÷ 100 = £6,400 ÷ 100 = £64 per parent-month. That £64 is not the effect for either subgroup. Estimate the direct contrast, £120 − £40 = £80, with uncertainty, rather than declaring heterogeneity because one subgroup is significant and the other is not. Define groups before searching, and distinguish subgroup average effects from quantile coefficients. The forest plot is illustrative. See ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 18: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’.","takeaway":"Heterogeneity is a question about how effects vary, not a licence to search endlessly for significant groups."},{"title":"Read interaction terms carefully","body":"An interaction between treatment and a pre-treatment characteristic allows the treatment contrast to vary across that characteristic. In a linear model, the treatment coefficient may describe the effect at the reference value, while the interaction describes how the slope changes. For nonlinear models, coefficient interactions do not translate directly into probability-scale treatment-effect interactions; compute predictions or marginal effects on the scale of interest.

Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data; January–December 2025): suppose a randomly assigned childcare subsidy is evaluated using monthly hours worked, and baseline childcare access is measured in hours per week before the subsidy. Fit the simple model: predicted subsidy effect = 4 + 0.6 × access. The 4 means 4 additional hours worked per month for a parent with zero recorded access; the interaction coefficient, 0.6, means the estimated subsidy contrast rises by 0.6 monthly work hours for each extra weekly hour of baseline access. At 5 access hours, the predicted effect is 4 + (0.6 × 5) = 7 hours per month; at 15 hours, it is 13 hours. Thus the model describes a 6-hour difference in predicted effects between those profiles, not a claim about every parent.

An interaction can summarize conditional differences and, with a credible randomized or otherwise defensible design, may estimate how an average treatment contrast varies with a pre-treatment characteristic. It cannot by itself prove that access causes the difference, identify each person’s treatment effect, or show that the pattern generalizes beyond the observed access range. Check the units, observed range, reference value, sample sizes, and confidence intervals; calculate predicted contrasts at meaningful access values and inspect whether the lab-style plot is sensitive to reasonable specifications. Do not say that one subgroup “benefits” more merely because its estimate is significant while another is not: test their difference directly. See “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 3, §3.3; Ch. 7, §§7.1–7.2” in the linked sources below.

Centering a modifier can make an interaction easier to interpret without changing fitted predictions. In a synthetic model, the predicted treatment contrast in percentage points is 6 + 0.4 × (baseline score − 50), where score is measured in points. At score 50, the contrast is 6 + 0.4×0 = 6 percentage points; at score 60, it is 6 + 0.4×10 = 10 percentage points. Thus the interaction contributes 4 percentage points across that ten-point difference. This arithmetic describes model-based contrasts, not guaranteed changes for individuals. It assumes the linear specification is reasonable over the stated score range and that baseline score precedes treatment; extrapolating beyond observed scores or reading the interaction as causal requires additional design assumptions. For a fuller treatment, see “Gelman, Hill & Vehtari — Regression and Other Stories (Cambridge University Press)” in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data): suppose a logistic model predicts whether a household takes a training course, with treatment T and a pre-treatment income indicator H (1 for high income). Let the fitted logit be logit[P(Y=1)] = −1.20 + 0.50T + 0.80H − 0.30(T×H). First compute the treated-minus-untreated contrast separately on the probability scale. For H=0, the untreated probability is logistic(−1.20)=0.231 and the treated probability is logistic(−0.70)=0.332, so the predicted contrast is 0.101, or 10.1 percentage points. For H=1, the corresponding linear predictors are −0.40 and −0.10; logistic(−0.40)=0.401 and logistic(−0.10)=0.475, giving 7.4 percentage points. The difference in predicted treatment contrasts is therefore 7.4−10.1 = −2.7 percentage points—not −0.30, because the interaction coefficient is on the log-odds scale. Treat these as model-based average predictions, not individual effects; report uncertainty for the direct contrast of contrasts, and check that probabilities remain plausible over the observed income range. A causal interpretation still requires treatment assignment or other identification assumptions.

An interaction is easiest to explain by evaluating the full contrast at two meaningful modifier values. Illustrative synthetic model: a subsidy changes monthly participation probability by 3 + 0.2 × baseline care-hours, where care-hours are measured per week. At 5 hours, the model contrast is 3 + 1 = 4 percentage points; at 15 hours, it is 3 + 3 = 6 percentage points. The predicted difference across those profiles is therefore 2 percentage points, not 0.2 percentage points. The interaction slope has units of participation percentage points per weekly care-hour. These are model-based synthetic contrasts, not observed effects. Check that 5 and 15 hours lie inside the data range, and report uncertainty for each prediction and their difference. See “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 3, §3.3; Ch. 7, §§7.1–7.2”","takeaway":"Explain the scale and reference group when presenting an interaction."},{"title":"Quantile regression answers a distributional question","body":"Quantile regression models a conditional quantile, such as the median outcome given covariates. Its slope describes how a covariate relates to that conditional quantile under the model. It is not automatically the effect for the same individuals who would occupy a particular rank under both treatment states; treatment-effect distributions require additional methods and assumptions.

Suppose a synthetic quantile regression for monthly household spending (currency units) gives a treatment coefficient of 120 at the 25th conditional quantile and 300 at the 75th, holding listed covariates fixed. The fitted gap between these coefficients is 300 − 120 = 180 currency units per month: the association is larger higher in the conditional spending distribution. This does not say that the same household’s spending effect changes by 180 units when it moves from the 25th to the 75th rank; quantiles describe different conditional locations, not tracked people. Interpretation also assumes the covariates and quantile model are suitable, and uncertainty should be reported for both coefficients and their difference. The result is not causal without an appropriate identification strategy. For a fuller treatment, see “Cameron & Trivedi — Microeconometrics: Methods and Applications (Cambridge University Press)” in the linked sources.

A useful follow-up to the displayed subgroup estimates is to test a contrast directly. Take a synthetic lab setting with total sample size n = 120, average effect 0.8 outcome units, and subgroup spread 0.6 units. The implied subgroup estimates are A = 0.8 − 0.6 = 0.2, B = 0.8, and C = 0.8 + 0.6 = 1.4 units. Using the lab’s illustrative standard error, SE = 1.4/√(120/3) = 0.221 units, each 95% reference interval has half-width 1.96 × 0.221 = 0.434 units. The scientifically targeted comparison is C − A = 1.4 − 0.2 = 1.2 units, not whether C’s interval excludes zero while A’s does not. If the two subgroup estimates were independent with this same SE, SE(C − A) = √(0.221² + 0.221²) = 0.313 units, giving z = 1.2/0.313 = 3.83 and an approximate 95% interval of 1.2 ± 1.96(0.313) = [0.586, 1.814] units. In real data, covariance, unequal sizes, and pre-specified subgroup definitions change this calculation; even a precise contrast is not causal without identification assumptions.

Read a quantile coefficient as a conditional-location comparison, not as a statement about one specially ranked household. Illustrative synthetic output gives a training coefficient of £80 at the 20th conditional quantile and £140 at the 80th, with the same listed covariates. The difference is £140 − £80 = £60 per month between fitted conditional associations. It does not mean one person’s treatment gain rises by £60 when that person moves from the 20th to the 80th percentile; the people and rankings defining those conditional quantiles can differ. Before comparing coefficients, verify that both models use the same outcome units, covariates, sample, and treatment definition. Report interval estimates for each coefficient and their contrast. For the distributional interpretation, see “Cameron & Trivedi — Microeconometrics: Methods and Applications (Cambridge University Press)”","takeaway":"A conditional quantile coefficient is not automatically an individual-level treatment effect."},{"title":"Keep discovery and confirmation distinct","body":"Subgroup analysis can produce many comparisons, especially when analysts try several outcomes, cut points and models. Pre-specify a few policy-relevant contrasts, show confidence intervals and sample sizes, and treat exploratory findings as hypotheses for further study. Where treatment effects differ, report the groups and context rather than implying a universal ranking of people.

Imagine a synthetic analyst tests 20 pre-treatment subgroups, each at a 5% threshold, even though no subgroup truly differs. The simple expected count of false positives is 20 × 0.05 = 1 subgroup, so one apparently “significant” result can arise by chance alone. A confirmation plan might instead pre-specify three contrasts, report each estimate with its 95% confidence interval, and label the other 17 comparisons exploratory. This arithmetic is a warning about multiplicity, not a guarantee that exactly one false positive will occur in one sample. The plan assumes the subgroup definitions and primary outcome are fixed before seeing results; replication or multiplicity-aware methods are still needed. Exploratory patterns cannot by themselves justify causal or universal claims. For multiple-testing and false-discovery-rate context, see “UC Berkeley STAT C141 — Multiple Hypothesis Testing and False Discovery Rate Notes” in the linked sources.

Suppose, purely illustratively, a pre-specified childcare-subsidy analysis estimates a participation increase of 2.0 percentage points for parents with reliable backup care (standard error 0.8 points) and 5.0 percentage points for those without it (standard error 1.0 point). The heterogeneity estimand is the difference in subgroup effects, 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 percentage points—not a comparison of which subgroup has a smaller p-value. If the two subgroup estimates come from disjoint samples and their errors are independent, the standard error of that contrast is √(0.8² + 1.0²) = √1.64 ≈ 1.28 percentage points. A normal-approximation 95% interval is therefore 3.0 ± 1.96 × 1.28, or approximately 0.49 to 5.51 percentage points. This interval describes uncertainty about the difference in average effects, not an effect for a particular parent. Independence is an assumption: with overlapping observations or shared fitted parameters, use the covariance-adjusted variance Var(τ̂₂ − τ̂₁) = Var(τ̂₂) + Var(τ̂₁) − 2Cov(τ̂₂,τ̂₁). Even a positive contrast remains conditional on credible treatment assignment, outcome measurement and pre-specified group definitions.

Multiplicity is a planning problem, not merely a reporting footnote. Illustrative synthetic exercise: an analyst examines 12 pre-treatment cut points, 3 outcomes, and 2 specifications, creating 12 × 3 × 2 = 72 reported opportunities for an apparently unusual result. At a nominal 5% threshold, the simple expected count under a world with no real findings is 72 × 0.05 = 3.6 false positives; this is an expectation, not a prediction that exactly four will appear. A defensible confirmation analysis would name one primary outcome, a small set of cut points, and the interaction contrasts before viewing results. Label the remaining searches exploratory, preserve their denominators, and seek replication. The arithmetic does not establish any causal effect. See “Matheus Facure — Ch. 18: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)”","takeaway":"Transparent subgroup plans reduce selective emphasis and support fair interpretation."},{"title":"Conditional quantiles are not individual treatment effects","body":"A quantile regression can describe, for example, the conditional median of earnings among people with specified observed covariates. A quantile treatment effect instead compares quantiles of potential-outcome distributions under a design that supports a causal contrast. Neither reveals which particular person's treatment effect is large, and a change in a conditional quantile need not equal a change in the marginal population quantile. Name the distribution, conditioning variables, target group and identification assumptions before making a distributional claim.

Use a tiny synthetic example to separate conditional quantiles from individual effects. Under treatment, three comparable covariate profiles have predicted monthly incomes of 2,000, 3,000, and 5,000 currency units; under control, the corresponding conditional predictions are 1,900, 2,900, and 4,800. The middle conditional quantile difference is 3,000 − 2,900 = 100 currency units per month. That 100-unit QTE summarizes a distributional comparison at a stated quantile; it does not identify which person gains 100 units, and rankings could change between treatment and control. The displayed formula requires clearly defined potential-outcome distributions and quantile τ. Causal interpretation additionally requires identification assumptions such as valid treatment assignment; regression adjustment alone does not supply them. For a fuller treatment, see “Cunningham — Causal Inference: The Mixtape (Yale University Press)” in the linked sources.

Consider a pre-specified interaction for the childcare example. Suppose, purely illustratively, a randomized subsidy study estimates a monthly participation-related earnings effect of 120 currency units for parents with high baseline care access and 40 currency units for parents with low access. Code high access as G = 1 and low access as G = 0; in a linear outcome model, the interaction coefficient is the conditional contrast 120 − 40 = 80 currency units per month. If the two subgroup estimates have standard errors of 30 and 25 currency units and their estimation errors are treated as uncorrelated for this illustration, the contrast standard error is √(30² + 25²) = √1,525 ≈ 39.1 currency units per month. A normal-approximation 95% interval is therefore 80 ± 1.96(39.1), or about 3.4 to 156.6 currency units per month. This supports a positive difference under the stated approximation, but it is not an individual treatment effect or a quantile coefficient. The grouping variable must be measured before treatment; random assignment (or a defensible conditional-exchangeability design) is needed for causal interpretation, and unequal variances or correlated estimates require the appropriate covariance-aware standard error.

The notation Q[Y(1), τ] − Q[Y(0), τ] compares two potential-outcome distributions at the same quantile index; it does not pair each treated person with that person’s untreated outcome. Illustrative synthetic distributions at τ = 0.50 have medians of 2,400 and 2,250 currency units per month, giving a quantile contrast of 150 units. A different individual-level effect distribution could produce that same median difference, because people may change rank between treatment states. Causal language additionally requires a design or assumptions identifying both potential-outcome distributions, such as valid assignment and a clearly defined target population. State whether the regression is conditional on covariates or the estimand is marginal. These values are synthetic, not empirical findings. See “Cunningham — Causal Inference: The Mixtape (Yale University Press)”","takeaway":"Quantile regression describes conditional distributions; causal quantile effects require a design and a clearly stated target.","formula":"QTE at quantile τ = Q[Y(1), τ] − Q[Y(0), τ]."},{"title":"Test the difference between groups directly","body":"Imagine a training effect estimate of 0.4 for younger applicants and 0.1 for older applicants. One estimate having a confidence interval that excludes zero while the other does not is not itself evidence that the two effects differ. Estimate the group contrast, often with a pre-specified treatment-by-group interaction, and report its uncertainty and the group sample sizes. Choose characteristics measured before treatment when defining subgroups, and limit the number of comparisons or label them exploratory. A real average-effect difference across groups still does not reveal every individual's treatment effect or establish a universal ranking of who benefits most.

Suppose synthetic training estimates are 0.40 and 0.10 standard-deviation units for Groups A and B. The direct contrast is τA − τB = 0.40 − 0.10 = 0.30 standard-deviation units. If its 95% confidence interval is 0.02 to 0.58, the interval concerns the difference itself, whereas separate intervals for 0.40 and 0.10 concern different questions. A contrast near zero would not prove identical effects if the sample is small; it could reflect imprecision. The calculation assumes both estimates use the same outcome scale, treatment definition, and comparable time period. A statistically detectable contrast still does not establish why groups differ, reveal every person’s gain, or justify ranking all applicants. For a fuller treatment, see “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 3, §3.3; Ch. 7, §§7.1–7.2” in the linked sources.

Consider a synthetic childcare-subsidy example in which the outcome is labour-force participation, measured as a probability. Pre-specify baseline care access as the subgroup indicator, then compare treated and untreated parents within each group. If participation is 35% without and 47% with the subsidy among low-access parents, their estimated effect is 47% − 35% = 12 percentage points. Suppose the corresponding high-access figures are 62% and 68%, giving 6 percentage points. The interaction contrast is therefore 12 − 6 = 6 percentage points: the estimated subsidy effect is larger for the low-access group by six percentage points, not “six percent.” If 40% of the target population is low-access and 60% high-access, the standardized average effect would be 0.40×12 + 0.60×6 = 4.8 + 3.6 = 8.4 percentage points, so subgroup effects need not equal the overall effect. These numbers are illustrative, synthetic values, not observed data. The interpretation requires credible treatment comparisons within both pre-treatment groups, a common outcome definition and adequate sample support; calculate uncertainty for the six-point interaction before making a policy claim.

Separate confidence intervals answer whether each subgroup contrast differs from zero; they do not directly answer whether the contrasts differ from each other. Illustrative synthetic estimates are 0.18 and 0.05 outcome-standard-deviation units for Groups A and B. The planned interaction contrast is 0.18 − 0.05 = 0.13 standard-deviation units. If a direct 95% interval for that contrast is −0.04 to 0.30, the data are compatible with either a small negative or positive difference, even if Group A’s interval excludes zero. Use the same scale, follow-up window, and pre-treatment subgroup rule for both groups, and report their sample sizes. A non-detectable contrast is not proof of equality, nor is the contrast causal without identification. See “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 3, §3.3; Ch. 7, §§7.1–7.2”","takeaway":"Evidence that one subgroup effect differs from zero is not a test that it differs from another subgroup effect.","formula":"Group contrast = τ₁ − τ₂; assess its uncertainty directly rather than comparing two separate significance labels.","practice":{"question":"Group A's estimate is statistically significant and Group B's is not. What additional quantity should be examined before claiming different effects?","hint":"Form the contrast of the estimates.","solution":"Estimate τ_A − τ_B and its uncertainty, such as the interaction contrast from a pre-specified model. Separate p-values do not test equality of effects."}}]
data.case_study: A childcare subsidy may affect labour-force participation differently for parents with different baseline care access. Define groups before analysis, estimate probability-scale contrasts, and report uncertainty without labelling exploratory differences as definitive.
data.misconceptions:
A quantile coefficient does not directly identify the effect for a person at that rank.
A significant subgroup and a non-significant subgroup do not prove their effects differ.
Many data-driven subgroup searches inflate false-positive risk.

data.title: Functional Form, Interactions & Model Checks
data.excerpt: Models simplify the real world, and the shape of that simplification matters. Explore when relationships may be curved or depend on several factors together, how units and plots guide model choices, and how to check whether another reasonable specification changes the conclusion.
data.objectives:
Interpret level, log and polynomial specifications in their units.
Use interactions and indicators without losing the reference category.
Use residual and sensitivity checks to challenge a model.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Keep units attached to every coefficient","body":"A level-on-level slope describes outcome units per one-unit change in a predictor. A log outcome with a level predictor often describes an approximate percentage difference per predictor unit; a log-log slope is an elasticity under the model. These are approximations whose accuracy depends on the change size and transformation. State units before translating coefficients into economic meaning.

Suppose a synthetic wage model predicts weekly pay in dollars as 520 + 18 × training hours. Moving from 6 to 9 hours changes the prediction by 18 × (9 − 6) = 54 dollars per week, not 54 percent. If the outcome were log weekly pay instead, a coefficient of 0.04 on one additional hour would be approximately a 4 percent difference in weekly pay, while 0.04 is not 4 percentage points. For a log-log model, a coefficient of 0.8 would mean an approximately 0.8 percent change in weekly pay for a 1 percent change in hours. These interpretations assume the fitted functional form is reasonable over the stated comparison and do not prove training causes pay changes. For a fuller treatment, see “Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)” in the linked sources.

A quadratic term makes the coefficient on the level term only part of the calculation. Consider this explicitly synthetic model for monthly pay, measured in dollars, where x is years of training: predicted pay = 2,400 + 300x − 20x². The 300 has units of dollars per month per training year, while −20 has units of dollars per month per training-year squared. To compare 8 with 9 years, calculate the change directly: 300(9−8) − 20(9²−8²) = 300 − 20(17) = −40 dollars per month. Indeed, the predictions are 3,520 dollars at x = 8 and 3,480 dollars at x = 9. The local marginal effect is 300 − 40x, so it is −20 dollars per month per additional year at x = 8; the fitted maximum occurs where this equals zero, x = 7.5 years. Thus, do not read 300 as the effect at every training level. This interpretation is descriptive of the fitted curve, not evidence that training causes pay, and the turning point is especially fragile if the data contain few observations near it or the model is extrapolated beyond the observed range.

Transformations change the scale on which a coefficient operates. Illustrative synthetic level model: weekly earnings = 480 + 22 × training-hours, so moving from 4 to 7 hours changes the prediction by 22 × (7 − 4) = £66 per week. In a log-earnings model, a coefficient of 0.03 instead describes an approximate 3% difference per additional training hour, not £0.03 and not 3 percentage points. For an exact finite change in a log model, exp(0.03) − 1 ≈ 0.0305, or about 3.05%, under the model. A log-log coefficient of 0.7 is an elasticity: a 1% predictor increase corresponds to approximately a 0.7% outcome change. These examples are synthetic associations, not causal returns. See “Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)”","takeaway":"Functional form changes the interpretation, so report the variables and units used."},{"title":"Allow curvature when the question calls for it","body":"A squared term can represent a changing slope, such as the association between experience and wages that rises then flattens. The marginal association depends on the value of the predictor, so interpret the combined expression or predicted curve rather than the squared-term coefficient alone. Polynomials can behave erratically outside the observed range, making extrapolation especially risky.

Consider an illustrative synthetic prediction of monthly spending in dollars: 900 + 40x − 2x², where x is income measured in thousands of dollars per month. At x = 5, predicted spending is 900 + 200 − 50 = 1,050 dollars; at x = 6, it is 900 + 240 − 72 = 1,068 dollars, so the one-thousand-dollar income-unit increase adds 18 dollars. The next increase, from x = 6 to x = 7, gives 900 + 280 − 98 = 1,082 dollars, an addition of only 14 dollars. The curve therefore flattens in this range. This is an association-based prediction, not proof that income causes spending, and the pattern may fail outside observed income values. For a fuller treatment, see “Gelman, Hill & Vehtari — Regression and Other Stories (Cambridge University Press)” in the linked sources.

Suppose, purely illustratively, that a synthetic wage model measures hourly pay in dollars and experience x in years: W(x) = 20 + 1.2x − 0.1x². The slope is not 1.2 dollars everywhere; differentiating gives dW/dx = 1.2 − 0.2x dollars per additional year. Thus the model predicts a gain of 0.4 dollars per hour at 4 years, zero marginal change at x = 6, and a decline of 0.4 dollars per hour at 8 years. The turning point is −1.2/[2(−0.1)] = 6 years, where predicted pay is 20 + 7.2 − 3.6 = 23.6 dollars per hour. A discrete check from 5 to 6 years gives W(5) = 23.5 and W(6) = 23.6, an increase of 0.1 dollar per hour; from 6 to 7, W(7) = 23.5, a decrease of 0.1. This is a model-implied association, not a causal return to schooling or experience: omitted ability, cohort differences, and sparse observations near 8 years could change the curve. In the specification lab, compare the quadratic’s lower in-sample error with residual patterns and held-out performance before trusting the turning point.

For a quadratic prediction f(x) = 500 + 12x − 0.5x², the change from x to x + 1 is not always 12 units because the squared term also changes. At x = 4, f(4) = 500 + 48 − 8 = 540; at x = 5, f(5) = 500 + 60 − 12.5 = 547.5, so the increment is 7.5 outcome units. At x = 5 to 6, f(6) = 500 + 72 − 18 = 554, an increment of 6.5 units. The predicted slope is flattening over this range. The calculation uses synthetic outcome units and says nothing about a causal income response. Plot predictions only across supported x values; a quadratic can turn sharply outside the data. See “Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)”","takeaway":"A nonlinear term is a modelling choice that should match the supported data range and theory."},{"title":"Interactions compare conditional slopes","body":"An interaction lets the relationship between one predictor and the outcome depend on another, such as a training association that differs by prior education. With a binary indicator, the main coefficient is tied to its reference group. Show predicted values or marginal contrasts for meaningful combinations, and avoid interpreting one term in isolation.

Illustrative synthetic example: measure monthly earnings in pounds one year after a training course, using training hours and a college-education indicator. Let the reference group be workers without a college education, and suppose the fitted model is predicted earnings = £1,800 + £30 × training hours + £200 × college + £10 × (training hours × college). For a non-college worker completing 4 hours, the prediction is £1,800 + £120 = £1,920 per month. For a college-educated worker, it is £1,800 + £120 + £200 + £40 = £2,160. Thus the training slope is £30 per hour for the reference group and £40 (£30 + £10) for the college group; the predicted group contrast at 4 hours is £240 per month. These numbers are illustrative, not observed estimates.

An interaction can describe conditional associations and predicted differences, but it cannot by itself establish that training caused higher earnings: selection into training, prior ability, local labour demand, and other confounders may remain. Check that the chosen groups and training-hour values are represented in the data, inspect residuals across fitted values and training hours, and compare this specification with a small number of substantively motivated alternatives. A common mistake is to read £30 as the training effect for everyone or £10 as the full earnings gap between groups; each term is conditional on the other variables, and the relevant comparison must combine terms. For model interpretation and specification guidance, see “Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)” in the linked sources below.

Imagine synthetic, illustrative test scores measured in points: score = 60 + 2 × study hours + 5 × tutoring + 1 × (study hours × tutoring), where tutoring is 0 or 1. Without tutoring, 3 study hours predicts 60 + 6 = 66 points. With tutoring, the same 3 hours predicts 60 + 6 + 5 + 3 = 74 points, an 8-point difference. The study-hours slope is 2 points per hour without tutoring and 2 + 1 = 3 points per hour with tutoring. The interaction changes a conditional association; it does not show tutoring caused the score difference, because motivation or prior preparation may differ. Interpret only study-hour and tutoring combinations represented in the sample. For a fuller treatment, see “Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)” in the linked sources.

Consider a synthetic demand model where weekly sales q are measured in units, discount d in percentage points, and household income i in thousands of pounds: q = 120 + 4d − 1.5i + 0.2(di). The marginal association of discount is the derivative ∂q/∂d = 4 + 0.2i units per percentage point. At i = 20, one additional percentage point of discount corresponds to 8 more units per week; at i = 35, it corresponds to 11 more, so the conditional-slope difference is 3 units per percentage point, computed as 0.2 × (35 − 20). For a transparent intercept, center income at £20,000: with i_c = i − 20, the same equation is q = 90 + 8d − 1.5i_c + 0.2(di_c). Now the coefficient 8 describes the discount slope at the meaningful reference income, rather than at zero income. These are explicitly illustrative synthetic values, not observed demand. Check that discounts and incomes lie within the sample’s support; otherwise the slope comparison is extrapolation. The interaction is an association unless a credible design supports a causal pricing claim, and residual or nonlinear-fit checks can reveal misspecification.

With a binary indicator, the main slope belongs to the reference category, while the interaction modifies that slope. Illustrative synthetic model for commuting minutes: predicted employment score = 50 + 1.5 × distance + 4 × rail-access + 0.5 × distance × rail-access. For a worker without rail access, one extra distance unit changes the score by 1.5 points. With rail access, it changes by 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 points. At distance 6, the predicted group gap is 4 + 0.5 × 6 = 7 points, not merely the rail-access coefficient of 4. These are synthetic score units; the interaction is an association unless design assumptions support causality. Confirm that the reference category and distance range are explicit, then inspect residual patterns for both groups. See “Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)”","takeaway":"Name the reference category and show the combined comparison people actually care about."},{"title":"Check specification without chasing a preferred fit","body":"Plot residuals against fitted values, key predictors and time; examine influential observations; and compare a small number of substantively motivated specifications. Changes in coefficients may reveal sensitivity to controls or sample rules. Higher R-squared alone does not demonstrate correct specification, causal identification or out-of-sample value.

Suppose two illustrative synthetic models predict monthly rent in dollars. Model A predicts 1,200 dollars for an apartment, while Model B predicts 1,260 dollars after adding a distance-squared term. A 60-dollar difference is meaningful only relative to the comparison: it is 5 percent of Model A’s prediction because 60 ÷ 1,200 = 0.05, but it is not evidence that Model B is correct. Plotting residuals can reveal whether errors systematically rise with fitted rent; for example, residuals of −20, +15, and +80 dollars at fitted values of 800, 1,200, and 1,600 suggest increasing spread. This check does not establish causality or guarantee future accuracy. Compare motivated specifications using the same sample and outcome definition. For a fuller treatment, see “Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)” in the linked sources.

Use held-out prediction to test whether an apparently useful curve travels beyond the observations that shaped it. For an illustrative synthetic dataset of 30 apartments, split the rows into five folds of six, fit each specification on the other 24 rows, and predict the six held-out rents; keep the folds identical for both models. Suppose the five held-out sums of squared errors (SSE), in dollars squared, are 18, 20, 16, 22, and 19 for the linear model, versus 16, 19, 18, 20, and 17 for the quadratic model. The totals are 95 and 90 dollars squared, so the cross-validated RMSEs are √(95/30) = $1.78 and √(90/30) = $1.73 per apartment-month, respectively. The quadratic model therefore improves held-out RMSE by about $0.05, or roughly 2.7% relative to $1.78, in this synthetic illustration. Because the gain is small and fold-specific errors differ, inspect prediction intervals and sensitivity to the fold assignment before preferring the curve. This checks predictive stability, not causal validity; it also cannot justify extrapolating beyond the observed commute-distance range.

A specification check should ask whether the model misses systematic structure, not whether one line produces the largest fit statistic. Illustrative synthetic residuals at fitted rents of 700, 1,000, and 1,500 pounds are −10, 20, and 90 pounds. Their magnitudes rise from 10 to 90, but one residual at each fitted value cannot establish changing variance; a curved mean pattern or one unusual case could also explain them. Plot residuals against fitted values and predictors, look for repeated spread patterns, and compare models on the same observations and outcome definition. The specification lab’s curves and errors are simulated teaching objects, not measured rents. Better in-sample fit does not certify causal structure or future accuracy. See “Gelman, Hill & Vehtari — Regression and Other Stories (Cambridge University Press)”.","takeaway":"Model checks can reveal trouble, but no single diagnostic certifies a model as true."},{"title":"Trace omitted-variable bias through two relationships","body":"In a simple linear setting, omitting a variable U that affects the outcome can shift the treatment coefficient in proportion to two links: how U predicts the outcome after included controls, and how U is associated with treatment after those controls. If recent unemployment raises take-up of a training programme but lowers later earnings, omitting it can push the training coefficient downward. If prior ability raises both take-up and earnings, omitting it can push the coefficient upward. The sign is not determined by whether a variable sounds important; it depends on both relationships and the conditioning set. A formula is a guide to the direction under a simple model, not a replacement for a causal design or a reason to control for post-treatment variables.

Use the stated approximation with illustrative synthetic slopes: if an omitted factor U has an outcome slope γ = −300 dollars per month per U-unit and a treatment slope δ = 0.2 U-units per treated-status unit, then γ × δ = −300 × 0.2 = −60 dollars per month per treatment-status unit. The simple formula therefore predicts a downward bias of about 60 dollars per month in the treatment coefficient. The units multiply: dollars per month per U-unit times U-units per treatment status equals dollars per month per treatment status. This is a directional diagnostic, not a measured historical estimate and not proof of a causal effect. It relies on the simple model and conditional relationships; changing controls or measurement can change the result. For a fuller treatment, see “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 3, §§3.1–3.2.3” in the linked sources.

A useful diagnostic is to translate the bias into the same units as the reported coefficient. Consider an explicitly synthetic evaluation of a remote-work subsidy: after controlling for observed age and occupation, the earnings gap is +$180 per month, but commute reliability, U, remains omitted. Among comparable workers, subsidy recipients average 0.5 standard deviations higher on U, while a separate conditional outcome relationship assigns U a slope of −$200 per month per standard deviation. The implied omitted-variable component is (0.5 SD) × (−$200/month/SD) = −$100 per month. Because the observed gap equals the target effect plus this component in the additive linear approximation, a bias-corrected descriptive estimate would be +$180 − (−$100) = +$280 per month, not +$80. This arithmetic is illustrative, not an observed estimate: it assumes the U gap and outcome slope refer to the same conditioning set, uses a correctly measured pre-treatment U, and ignores nonlinearities and interactions. A residual plot or a better-fitting curve in the specification lab cannot verify those confounding assumptions; it can only flag model-form problems in the simulated outcome relationship.

The approximation bias(β̂D) ≈ γδ is a sign-and-units exercise conditional on controls. Illustrative synthetic case: an omitted stress measure U has γ = −120 dollars per month per U-unit in the outcome equation and δ = 0.30 U-units per treatment-status unit in the treatment equation. Their product is −120 × 0.30 = −$36 per month per treatment-status unit, predicting downward bias of about $36 in the simplified setting. If both links were positive, the product would instead be positive; if either conditional link were near zero, the bias would be small under this approximation. Do not apply the formula after conditioning on post-treatment variables or changing controls without reconsidering both links. The arithmetic is synthetic, not an empirical estimate. See “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 3, §§3.1–3.2.3”.","takeaway":"The direction of omitted-variable bias depends on both the outcome link and the treatment association, conditional on included controls.","formula":"In a simple one-omitted-variable model: bias in β̂_D ≈ γ × δ, where γ is U's outcome slope and δ is U's treatment slope.","practice":{"question":"An unobserved factor raises programme take-up (δ > 0) but lowers earnings (γ < 0). What direction does the simple omitted-variable-bias formula predict?","hint":"Multiply the signs of the two links.","solution":"The product is negative, so the estimated programme coefficient is biased downward in this simplified setup. The result depends on the stated model and conditional relationships."}}]
data.case_study: A study of commuting time and employment uses a nonlinear relationship because transport access may matter more for some distances than others. Plot predictions over the observed range, define the reference group and avoid extrapolating to unobserved commute distances.
data.misconceptions:
A coefficient cannot be interpreted without units and reference values.
Adding terms until fit improves does not establish causality.
A polynomial fit may be unreliable beyond the observed data range.
