data.title: Applied Macro Time Series & Forecasting
data.excerpt: Use time-series tools to study inflation, unemployment, output and interest rates. Learn how trends and persistence shape forecasts, how shocks may unfold over time, and why predicting a movement is different from proving what caused it.
data.objectives:
Recognize trend, persistence, seasonality and structural change.
Use lagged models and forecast evaluation with time-ordered data.
Interpret dynamic responses and uncertainty cautiously.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Inspect time order and measurement first","body":"Macroeconomic observations are ordered and often revised, seasonal and affected by changes in definitions. Plot levels and changes, record frequency and units, and mark major institutional breaks. A rising nominal series can reflect inflation rather than real growth, while annualising a monthly rate changes the scale. Preserve data vintages when a real-time forecast question matters.

A practical first pass is to distinguish a level, a change, and a rate of change. Suppose an illustrative synthetic price index is 120 in January and 123 in February: the one-month change is 123 minus 120 = 3 index points, while the growth rate is 3 divided by 120 = 0.025, or 2.5 percent. Index points are not currency units, and 2.5 percent is not 2.5 percentage points unless the variable itself is a percentage. If February is later revised to 124, the calculated change becomes 4 points, so a forecast made in March may not reproduce an earlier real-time calculation. This comparison describes measurement and revision, not an economic cause. For a fuller treatment, see “Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)” in the linked sources.

To make a forecast check reproducible, use a rolling origin and freeze the information set at each origin. For an explicitly illustrative synthetic quarterly unemployment rate, suppose the long-run level is 5.0%, the latest vintage reports 6.2%, and a centered AR(1) persistence parameter is φ = 0.75. The one-quarter-ahead forecast is 5.0% + 0.75(6.2% − 5.0%) = 5.9%; the two-quarter forecast is 5.0% + 0.75²(1.2 percentage points) = 5.675%. If the innovation standard deviation is assumed to be 0.4 percentage points, the forecast standard deviations are 0.4 percentage points at one quarter and 0.4√(1 + 0.75²) ≈ 0.50 percentage points at two quarters. A rough normal 95% interval for the second forecast is therefore 5.675% ± 1.96(0.50 percentage points), or about 4.70% to 6.65%. At the next quarter, compare that stored forecast with the newly available observation, then move the origin forward and repeat; do not refit using later revisions when evaluating an earlier forecast. This tests predictive accuracy, not whether persistence caused unemployment or whether the assumed AR(1) form is structurally stable.

Before modelling a macro series, distinguish a level, a difference, and a proportional change. Illustrative synthetic index values are 200 in March and 204 in April. The level difference is 204 − 200 = 4 index points, while the growth rate is 4 ÷ 200 = 0.02, or 2%. If the index is later revised to 205, the same April change becomes 5 points and 5 ÷ 200 = 2.5%. That revision changes a real-time analyst’s information set. Index points are not currency units, and a 2% growth rate is not automatically 2 percentage points. Record vintage, frequency, seasonal adjustment, and definitions before interpreting a movement. This is a measurement illustration, not evidence that any policy caused growth. See “Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)”","takeaway":"Time-series interpretation depends on dates, units, revisions and the measurement process."},{"title":"Separate trend from persistence","body":"A series may move slowly because shocks persist, because it follows a deterministic trend, or because it contains a stochastic trend. Regressing unrelated trending levels can produce a persuasive but spurious relationship. Consider transformations such as growth rates or differences when they fit the question, and state what long-run information those transformations discard.

A useful diagnostic is to compare a level forecast with a change forecast. In an illustrative synthetic series, output is 200 billion currency units in year 1, 204 in year 2, and 208 in year 3. The level rises by 4 billion each year, while the simple growth rates are 4/200 = 2.0 percent and 4/204 = 1.96 percent. A difference of 4 billion currency units highlights an approximately linear trend; a growth rate highlights proportional movement. If a shock raises year-3 output by 8 billion, the level change is 8 billion, but the growth rate is 8/204 = 3.92 percent. Neither comparison alone proves persistence or causality; omitted factors may explain the movement. For a fuller treatment, see “Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)” in the linked sources.

To separate persistence from a level forecast, center the series on a reference mean and model the deviation y_t. Suppose, illustratively with synthetic monthly data, an inflation deviation is y_t = 1.5 percentage points, the AR(1) persistence parameter is φ = 0.80, and the innovation standard deviation is σ = 0.60 percentage points per month. The one-, two-, and three-month conditional mean deviations are 0.80(1.5) = 1.20, 0.80²(1.5) = 0.96, and 0.80³(1.5) = 0.768 percentage points: the shock fades toward zero rather than being added repeatedly. Forecast uncertainty can be built recursively: V₁ = 0.60² = 0.36, V₂ = 0.36 + 0.80²(0.36) = 0.5904, and V₃ = 0.36 + 0.80²(0.5904) = 0.737856, so the standard deviations are 0.60, 0.768, and about 0.859 percentage points. A 95% half-width is 1.96 times each SD, or 1.176, 1.506, and 1.684 percentage points. This interpretation assumes a stable |φ| < 1 process and mean-zero innovations; changing policy regimes or seasonal structure can invalidate it, and forecasting does not identify what caused the initial shock.

Differencing removes a level component, so it changes the question rather than magically solving time dependence. Illustrative synthetic levels are 100, 103, and 106 units in three successive periods. First differences are 3 and 3 units; the second difference is 3 − 3 = 0 units, consistent with a constant linear increment in this tiny example. The level comparison asks about the series’ absolute path, whereas the differenced comparison asks whether period-to-period changes move. A differenced regression can hide a long-run relationship if levels share an equilibrium pattern, while a level regression can be misleading for unrelated trends. Check plots, residual dependence, and the economic meaning of the transformation. These numbers are synthetic and do not establish a causal link between series. See “Wooldridge — Introductory Econometrics (Cengage)”","takeaway":"A high fit between trending series is not evidence that one causes the other."},{"title":"Build forecasts using only past information","body":"A time-ordered training and test split avoids using future observations to predict the past. Compare a simple benchmark with models containing lags or predictors that would have been available at the forecast date. Evaluate errors across multiple forecast origins and show intervals, not just one point prediction. Revisions or data leakage can make a historical backtest look better than a real-time forecast.

Forecast evaluation should mimic the information set at each forecast origin. Consider an illustrative synthetic monthly inflation-rate series measured in percent: a model predicts 2.0 percent for April and the later observed value is 2.6 percent, giving an error of 2.6 − 2.0 = 0.6 percentage points and an absolute error of 0.6 percentage points. A second forecast predicts 1.8 percent for May and the observed value is 1.5 percent, so its error is −0.3 percentage points and absolute error is 0.3. The two-origin mean absolute error is (0.6 + 0.3)/2 = 0.45 percentage points. This score compares predictive accuracy, not causal validity, and two months are far too few for stable conclusions. For a fuller treatment, see “Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)” in the linked sources.

Suppose, purely illustratively, that a monthly unemployment-rate deviation from its long-run mean is +1.2 percentage points at the forecast origin. A zero-mean AR(1) model with persistence φ = 0.75 and innovation standard deviation σ = 0.4 percentage points gives the one-month-ahead mean as 0.75 × 1.2 = 0.90 percentage points, and the two-month-ahead mean as 0.75² × 1.2 = 0.675 percentage points. Uncertainty accumulates new shocks: at horizon 1, variance = 0.4² = 0.16 (percentage points)², so SD = 0.40 percentage points; at horizon 2, variance = 0.16 + 0.75² × 0.16 = 0.25 (percentage points)², so SD = 0.50 percentage points. A rough 95% interval is 0.90 ± 1.96(0.40) = 0.116 to 1.684 percentage points at one month, and 0.675 ± 1.96(0.50) = −0.305 to 1.655 percentage points at two months. These are forecasts of a deviation, not levels or a causal effect. They rely on stable persistence, constant innovation variance, and a zero long-run mean—assumptions to check, not silently import.

A backtest reproduces the information set available when each prediction would have been issued. Illustrative synthetic forecasts for three months are 1.2%, 1.5%, and 1.7%, while observed inflation rates are 1.6%, 1.4%, and 2.0%. Signed errors observed minus predicted are 0.4, −0.1, and 0.3 percentage points; absolute errors are 0.4, 0.1, and 0.3. Mean absolute error is (0.4 + 0.1 + 0.3) ÷ 3 = 0.267 percentage points, approximately. Do not train using revised future values or randomly shuffle time rows. Compare the same forecast origins with a benchmark and retain intervals, not only means. Three synthetic origins are too few for a stable performance claim, and predictive accuracy does not identify a cause. See “Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)”","takeaway":"Forecast evaluation should reproduce when information would actually have been available."},{"title":"Dynamic responses are model-dependent","body":"Distributed-lag and autoregressive models can summarize how outcomes move after a shock. The response depends on lag length, stability, the meaning of the shock and assumptions about simultaneity. HAC standard errors can address certain forms of autocorrelation and heteroskedasticity for inference, but do not make an endogenous shock causal. State the model and show uncertainty across horizons.

A lag coefficient describes conditional association at a particular horizon, not automatically a policy effect. Suppose an illustrative synthetic distributed-lag model predicts a 0.4 percentage-point increase in an unemployment rate after a one-unit shock this month and a 0.2 percentage-point increase next month, with all other included variables held as specified. The cumulative two-month response is 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6 percentage points, not 0.6 percent. If the shock is measured as a 1 percentage-point interest-rate change, the units should be reported as percentage points of unemployment per percentage point of interest rate. This arithmetic is a model summary; it does not establish that the shock was exogenous, nor that concurrent policies were irrelevant. For a fuller treatment, see “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 8, §§8.2–8.3 (serial dependence and inference)” in the linked sources.

To see why the forecast band widens, use an illustrative synthetic AR(1) model, Y_t = 0.8Y_{t−1} + ε_t, with innovation standard deviation σ = 0.6 series units and a final observed value of Y_T = 2 units. The three conditional forecast means are 0.8(2) = 1.6 units, 0.8²(2) = 1.28 units, and 0.8³(2) = 1.024 units: persistence moves the mean toward the model’s zero level, rather than adding 2 units at every date. Forecast variance must also accumulate: at horizon 3 it is σ²[1 + 0.8² + 0.8⁴] = 0.36(1 + 0.64 + 0.4096) = 0.737856 units², so the standard deviation is about 0.859 units. A normal-reference 95% band around the third-step mean is therefore 1.024 ± 1.96(0.859), or approximately −0.660 to 2.708 units. These are conditional model summaries, not observed outcomes; the interval relies on the innovation and stability assumptions, and neither persistence nor a good forecast identifies a causal policy shock. A structural break could make both the decay and the band misleading.

A distributed-lag coefficient should be accumulated only when the model defines comparable response units across horizons. Illustrative synthetic model: a one-unit shock is associated with −0.3 percentage points in employment growth in month 0, −0.1 in month 1, and +0.1 in month 2. The sum is −0.3 − 0.1 + 0.1 = −0.3 percentage points per shock unit. It is not −0.3 percent unless the outcome is explicitly a percent change, and it is not automatically a permanent effect. Sum is conditional on lag specification, stability, and shock interpretation. HAC standard errors may alter uncertainty for serial dependence but cannot make an endogenous shock exogenous. These response numbers are synthetic, not policy evidence. See “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 8, §§8.2–8.3 (serial dependence and inference)”","takeaway":"Dynamic estimates are not causal impulse responses unless the shock identification is defended."},{"title":"An AR(1) forecast mean-reverts toward its long-run mean","body":"For the zero-mean stationary process in this module, yₜ = φyₜ₋₁ + εₜ with |φ| < 1, the h-step conditional mean is φʰyₜ, so it decays toward zero. It is not the last observation plus another copy of its projected value. With innovation variance σ², the h-step forecast variance is σ²(1 + φ² + … + φ²⁽ʰ⁻¹⁾); the band widens with horizon and approaches the long-run variance. A different intercept or deterministic trend changes the long-run mean, so the model specification must be stated.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a country’s monthly unemployment-rate deviation from its long-run average is 1.2 percentage points in January 2025, and an AR(1) model estimates φ = 0.75, with deviations measured in percentage points. The one-month-ahead February forecast is 0.75 × 1.2 = 0.90 percentage points; the two-month-ahead March forecast is 0.75² × 1.2 = 0.675 percentage points; and the three-month-ahead April forecast is 0.75³ × 1.2 = 0.50625 percentage points. Thus, under this model, the unemployment deviation is expected to move closer to zero over time: persistence remains, but its projected size shrinks. These are synthetic calculations, not observed unemployment estimates, and zero represents the stated long-run mean rather than zero unemployment.

The AR(1) method can summarize persistence and produce conditional forecasts, but it cannot establish why unemployment changed, prove that a policy caused the movement, or guarantee that future observations follow the same process. One essential assumption or decision check is stationarity: inspect the series and residual diagnostics, and ask whether the estimated |φ| is below 1 and whether a structural break or changing definition makes that assumption implausible. Compare its rolling, time-ordered forecast errors with a simple benchmark before relying on it. Do not interpret mean reversion as a certainty that unemployment must return on schedule; it is a model-based average path with widening uncertainty. For broader econometric context, see “Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)” in the linked sources below.

Forecast variance can be understood by adding independent innovation contributions, each damped by the autoregressive coefficient. As an illustrative synthetic example, let φ = 0.5 and the innovation standard deviation be 2 percentage points, so σ² = 4 square-percentage-points. For a two-month horizon, the variance is 4(1 + 0.5²) = 4(1.25) = 5 square-percentage-points, and the standard deviation is √5 ≈ 2.24 percentage points. The uncertainty is therefore larger than the one-month standard deviation of 2 percentage points, even though the forecast mean moves toward the long-run mean. This calculation assumes stable dynamics and uncorrelated innovations; it does not guarantee a 95 percent interval or rule out a structural break. For a fuller treatment, see “Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)” in the linked sources.

An additional diagnostic is the persistence half-life: the number of periods needed for the model’s forecast mean to shrink to half its current deviation. For an illustrative synthetic AR(1) with φ = 0.80 and a final observed deviation of −2.5 percentage points from the long-run mean, solve 0.80^h = 0.5: h = ln(0.5) / ln(0.80) ≈ 3.11 periods. The six-period forecast is not halfway again by an informal rule; it is (0.80)^6(−2.5) = 0.262144(−2.5) = −0.65536 percentage points, so the expected deviation retains about 26.2% of its initial magnitude. A negative starting deviation remains negative in the conditional mean because φ is positive, while each future innovation can move the realized series above or below that path. In the interactive lab, changing persistence changes both this decay rate and the uncertainty accumulation, whereas changing the horizon simply asks how far along the same model path to look. The half-life describes model-implied persistence, not a causal effect of a policy or a guaranteed date of recovery; a break or changing measurement definition would invalidate the calculation.

For a zero-mean AR(1), the forecast is φ^h times the last deviation, so the horizon exponent matters. Illustrative synthetic deviation is −2 percentage points with φ = 0.6. One period ahead is 0.6 × (−2) = −1.2 points; two periods ahead is 0.6² × (−2) = 0.36 × (−2) = −0.72 points; three periods ahead is 0.216 × (−2) = −0.432 points. The negative deviation shrinks toward zero, which here denotes the stated long-run mean, not zero unemployment or inflation. The macro lab’s persistence and horizon controls generate a synthetic teaching projection, not a real forecast. Verify |φ| < 1 and investigate breaks or changing definitions before calling the process stationary. The shrinking mean does not mean uncertainty shrinks. See “Stock & Watson — Introduction to Econometrics, 4th edition (Pearson)”","takeaway":"A stationary zero-mean AR(1) forecast moves toward zero; forecast uncertainty accumulates with the horizon.","formula":"E[yₜ₊ₕ | yₜ] = φʰyₜ; Var(errorₜ₊ₕ) = σ² Σⱼ₌₀ʰ⁻¹ φ²ʲ."},{"title":"Serial dependence means monthly rows are not monthly experiments","body":"Inflation or unemployment observed month after month often carries persistent shocks forward. If adjacent errors are correlated, treating each month as an independent observation can make a standard error too small even when the coefficient calculation is unchanged. Heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation-consistent methods can address specified forms of serial dependence for some inferential targets, but the lag window and sample length matter; in a short series, uncertainty can remain substantial. Such standard errors do not repair a structural break, omitted policy change, trend misspecification, or an endogenous shock. Describe the time span and dependence assumptions alongside any interval.

A small effective-information example shows why row count can mislead. Suppose an illustrative synthetic sample has 12 monthly residuals, each measured in percentage points, but adjacent residuals move together because shocks persist. The arithmetic count is 12 rows, yet the 12 rows do not represent 12 independent experiments. If a naive standard error is 0.20 percentage points and serial-correlation adjustment raises it to 0.35 percentage points, an estimate of 0.80 percentage points has naive ratio 0.80/0.20 = 4.0 but adjusted ratio 0.80/0.35 ≈ 2.29. The coefficient is unchanged; uncertainty is not. This adjustment does not fix omitted variables, breaks, or endogeneity, and 12 months remains a short time span. For a fuller treatment, see “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 8, §§8.2–8.3 (serial dependence and inference)” in the linked sources.

Use the forecast origin to separate persistence from new uncertainty. For an illustrative synthetic AR(1) series with zero long-run mean, suppose the last observed value is 2.00 units, persistence is φ = 0.65, the innovation standard deviation is 0.60 units per period, and the horizon is three periods. The one-step, two-step and three-step forecast means are respectively 0.65(2.00) = 1.30, 0.65²(2.00) = 0.845, and 0.65³(2.00) = 0.549 units: the old deviation decays rather than being added repeatedly. The three-step forecast-error variance is 0.60²[1 + 0.65² + 0.65⁴] = 0.576 units², so its standard deviation is √0.576 = 0.759 units. A normal-reference 95% band is therefore 0.549 ± 1.96(0.759), or approximately −0.939 to 2.037 units. The band is a conditional forecast interval, not a confidence interval for a causal policy effect. It also depends on stationarity, a stable φ, correctly specified innovation variance, and no intervening structural break; re-estimation and forecast evaluation should use only information available at each date.

Serial dependence changes the precision calculation. Illustrative synthetic estimate is 0.50 percentage points with a naive standard error of 0.10; its naive ratio is 0.50 ÷ 0.10 = 5.0. Suppose a dependence-robust calculation gives 0.22 percentage points, making the ratio 0.50 ÷ 0.22 ≈ 2.27. The estimate did not move, but the evidence-to-noise ratio did. With only 12 monthly observations, a robust procedure can still be unreliable because the time dimension is short; a lag window is an assumption, not a cure. Check seasonality, breaks, omitted interventions, and the timing of any shock separately. The lab’s series and forecast band are synthetic teaching objects. HAC-style inference addresses specified dependence patterns, not causal identification. See “Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 8, §§8.2–8.3 (serial dependence and inference)”","takeaway":"A long sequence can contain far fewer independent pieces of information than its row count suggests; robust inference does not create causal identification."}]
data.case_study: An analyst studies whether a tax change affected inflation and employment. The series should be plotted, revisions and concurrent policies documented, a time-ordered comparison designed, and any dynamic response reported with its identification assumptions.
data.misconceptions:
A forecast can be useful without identifying a cause.
Differencing can help with trends but changes the question and may remove long-run relationships.
HAC standard errors do not identify an exogenous shock.

data.title: Multilevel Models & Partial Pooling
data.excerpt: Data often come in groups—students in schools, workers in regions or patients in clinics—and small groups can look unusually high or low by chance. Compare one shared estimate, separate group estimates and partial pooling, which balances local information with the overall pattern.
data.objectives:
Recognize grouped data and separate within-group from between-group variation.
Compare complete pooling, no pooling and partial pooling.
Interpret varying intercepts, group-level predictors and the limits of small-group data.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Why a group label can matter","body":"Suppose a labour economist compares earnings across local job centres. People within a centre share local employers and services, so their outcomes may be more alike than outcomes from unrelated centres. A single regression that ignores that grouping can misstate uncertainty or miss meaningful variation. A multilevel model represents both an overall relationship and group-specific departures, while keeping the level of each variable clear.

A group label can change the comparison because observations sharing a workplace, school, or neighborhood may have correlated outcomes. Separate within-office from between-office comparisons. Suppose Office A pays £20 and £24 per hour and Office B pays £26 and £30. The within-office range is £4 in each office, while the difference in office means is £28 − £22 = £6 per hour. Treating all four workers as independent can make uncertainty too small because centre membership is repeated information, not four unrelated contexts. A multilevel model can represent both contrasts while retaining the wage unit (pounds per hour). This structure does not establish that a centre caused wages to differ; worker composition or local employers may explain the association. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Gelman, Hill & Vehtari — Regression and Other Stories (Cambridge University Press)’ in the linked sources.

Suppose, purely illustratively, that eight synthetic observations from Office A imply a mean placement rate of 68 percentage points, while the four-office grand mean is 60 percentage points. Use the lab’s known-variance normal-normal illustration with within-office standard deviation σ = 4 percentage points and between-office standard deviation τ = 2 percentage points. First compute the local-mean precision, n/σ² = 8/16 = 0.5, and the prior (between-office) precision, 1/τ² = 1/4 = 0.25. The weight on Office A’s local estimate is therefore λ = 0.5/(0.5 + 0.25) = 2/3. The partially pooled estimate is 60 + (2/3)(68 − 60) = 60 + 5.33 = 65.33 percentage points, rather than either 68 or 60. Thus the model treats the office as above the overall level while tempering a noisy small-sample contrast. If n rose, λ would increase; if σ rose, it would decrease. This is estimation of a modeled office difference, not evidence that the office caused placement outcomes, and the calculation assumes comparable group sizes and correctly specified variance components; unequal sizes require group-specific weights.

A group label signals shared context, so the effective information is not simply the number of rows. Illustrative synthetic offices each have two workers: Office A wages are £18 and £22 per hour, and Office B wages are £24 and £28. The within-office range is £4 in both places, while the office-mean difference is (26 − 20) = £6 per hour. The £6 comparison mixes office context with worker composition; the £4 range describes within-office variation in this tiny example. Treating four workers as independent and ignoring office shocks can understate uncertainty. A multilevel model can represent common structure and group departures, but it does not make office membership a causal intervention. Check the number of independent offices, not only employees. See “Gelman, Hill & Vehtari — Regression and Other Stories (Cambridge University Press)”.","takeaway":"Grouping is part of the data structure; it is not automatically a causal design."},{"title":"The two extremes: pool everything or nothing","body":"Complete pooling estimates one common group mean and treats observed differences as noise. No pooling estimates each group independently, so a small centre with only a few cases can appear unusually high or low by chance. Neither extreme is ideal when groups are related but not identical. The model should allow differences while sharing information in a way justified by the group structure.

Complete pooling and no pooling answer different descriptive questions. Imagine three synthetic clinics reporting mean waiting times in minutes: 10, 20, and 30, with 2, 10, and 100 patients. Complete pooling gives (2×10 + 10×20 + 100×30) ÷ 112 = 3,220 ÷ 112 ≈ 28.8 minutes, one value for every clinic. No pooling keeps 10, 20, and 30 minutes, but the two-patient mean is especially unstable. A no-pooling ranking may treat a small random fluctuation as a real clinic difference, while complete pooling erases potentially useful differences. These are estimates of waiting time, not evidence that clinic policy caused them. Partial pooling offers an intermediate description under explicit assumptions. For a fuller treatment, see ‘PyMC example — Hierarchical Partial Pooling’ in the linked sources.

Consider an illustrative synthetic wage-outcome example with four regions, each having n = 9 workers. Suppose the within-region standard deviation is σ = 3 outcome units and the between-region standard deviation is τ = 1.5 outcome units; treat both variance components as known, as in the teaching lab. If the synthetic regional mean is 56 and the synthetic grand mean is 50, the partial-pooling weight on the local mean is λ = τ²/(τ² + σ²/n) = 1.5²/(1.5² + 3²/9) = 2.25/(2.25 + 1) = 0.692. The pooled estimate is therefore 50 + 0.692(56 − 50) = 54.15 outcome units: it moves 1.85 units toward the common mean, rather than declaring 56 to be a precise regional level. A region with mean 47 would instead receive 50 + 0.692(47 − 50) = 47.92. Increasing n raises λ because σ²/n falls, so the data receive more weight; increasing τ also raises λ because genuine regional differences are modeled as larger. This is descriptive shrinkage, not evidence that region caused wages, and unequal group sizes require group-specific weights.

Complete pooling and no pooling preserve different information. Illustrative synthetic clinic means are 12, 18, and 30 minutes, with 5, 15, and 80 patients. The pooled mean is (5×12 + 15×18 + 80×30) ÷ 100 = (60 + 270 + 2,400) ÷ 100 = 27.3 minutes. Complete pooling reports 27.3 for every clinic; no pooling reports 12, 18, and 30, even though the five-patient estimate is noisy. Neither result alone separates real clinic differences from sampling variation. Partial pooling can borrow information while allowing departures, provided the group-level distribution and observation model are plausible. These are synthetic waiting-time summaries, not evidence that one clinic’s policy caused shorter waits. A league table should include uncertainty and group sizes rather than rank raw means alone. See “PyMC example — Hierarchical Partial Pooling”","takeaway":"Complete pooling can hide real group variation; no pooling can overreact to noisy small groups."},{"title":"Partial pooling tempers noisy group estimates","body":"Partial pooling estimates an overall level and a distribution of group effects. A group with abundant, precise information stays closer to its own data; a small or noisy group is pulled more toward the overall pattern. This shrinkage is not an arbitrary correction: it follows from the assumed distribution of group effects and within-group uncertainty. The amount of pooling is learned or specified through the model, not chosen to make a preferred ranking.

Illustrative synthetic example (regional employment offices, January–December 2025): suppose Office A placed 8 of 8 referred jobseekers, an observed rate of 100%, while the model’s overall placement rate is 60%. For teaching purposes, let the fitted partial-pooling weight for this small office be w = 0.20, meaning only one-fifth of its noisy local signal is retained. Its adjusted rate is w × 100% + (1 − w) × 60% = 0.20 × 100% + 0.80 × 60% = 68%. A larger Office B might have 640 placements among 800 referrals, or 80%, and an illustrative weight of 0.90, giving 0.90 × 80% + 0.10 × 60% = 78%. The small office moves farther toward the overall pattern because eight cases provide less precise evidence.

Partial pooling can estimate a common level and group-specific differences more stably, but it cannot prove why offices differ, recover unobserved referrals, or turn a modeled placement rate into a causal effect of office management. The calculation above uses deliberately chosen weights; a fitted model would estimate pooling from assumptions about between-office variation and within-office outcome noise. Check group sizes, outcome definitions, convergence or other fit diagnostics, and sensitivity to reasonable distributional choices before ranking offices. Do not interpret shrinkage as proof that Office A’s true rate is 60%, or as evidence that its apparent 100% was entirely luck: it is an uncertainty-aware compromise. See “Gelman, Hill & Vehtari — Regression and Other Stories (Cambridge University Press)” in the linked sources below.

Shrinkage is easiest to understand as a precision-weighted compromise, not as a command to make groups equal. Consider an illustrative synthetic exam score on a 0–100-point scale. A small class has a mean of 90 from 5 students, while the overall mean is 70; suppose an illustrative fitted weight is 0.25. Its partial-pool estimate is 0.25×90 + 0.75×70 = 22.5 + 52.5 = 75 points. A larger class mean of 82 from 100 students, with weight 0.80, becomes 0.80×82 + 0.20×70 = 65.6 + 14 = 79.6 points. The second estimate moves less because its mean is more precise. These weights are synthetic teaching values, not observed evidence, and shrinkage does not prove why classes differ. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Gelman, Hill & Vehtari — Regression and Other Stories (Cambridge University Press)’ in the linked sources.

A useful diagnostic is to recompute the same group mean under two sample sizes while holding the observed mean fixed. Use an illustrative synthetic outcome measured in monthly percentage points: a group mean is 4.2 pp, the observed grand mean is 2.0 pp, the within-group SD is σ = 3 pp, and the between-group SD is τ = 1.5 pp. With n = 9, the known-variance teaching weight is λ = τ²/(τ² + σ²/n) = 2.25/(2.25 + 9/9) = 2.25/3.25 ≈ 0.692. The partially pooled estimate is 2.0 + 0.692(4.2 − 2.0) = 2.0 + 1.522 ≈ 3.52 pp. If a later, equally precise-looking group mean of 4.2 pp came from n = 36 instead, λ = 2.25/(2.25 + 9/36) = 2.25/2.50 = 0.90, so the estimate becomes 2.0 + 0.90(2.2) = 3.98 pp. Thus the same gap receives different borrowing because σ²/n changes. This is a sensitivity calculation, not evidence that the larger group is causally better: unequal variances, missing outcomes, or estimated τ can alter the weight.

Shrinkage should be read as a precision-weighted compromise, not as a verdict that a small group equals the grand mean. Suppose a small office has 3 placements from 3 referrals, an observed rate of 100%, and grand rate of 60%. If a teaching weight is 0.10, its adjusted rate is 0.10×100% + 0.90×60% = 10% + 54% = 64%. A larger office with 72 placements from 100 referrals has an observed rate of 72%; with weight 0.80, its adjusted rate is 0.80×72% + 0.20×60% = 57.6% + 12% = 69.6%. The weights are illustrative, not estimated from these counts. Inspect group sizes, outcome definitions, model fit, and sensitivity to between-group variation before ranking. Shrinkage does not reveal causal reason offices differ. See “Gelman, Hill & Vehtari — Regression and Other Stories (Cambridge University Press)”.","takeaway":"Groups with less information are generally shrunk more, with uncertainty retained."},{"title":"Read a varying-intercept model","body":"A random-intercept model can be written as Yᵢⱼ = α + βXᵢⱼ + uⱼ + εᵢⱼ, where j indexes groups, i indexes people, uⱼ is a group deviation, and εᵢⱼ is an individual deviation. The group effects are commonly modeled as coming from a shared distribution with variance τ². A group-level predictor, such as local unemployment, can explain some between-group variation, but its coefficient is not automatically causal and can mix within- and between-group comparisons if the question is not carefully defined.

In Yᵢⱼ = α + βXᵢⱼ + uⱼ + εᵢⱼ, every term must share Y’s units. Suppose synthetic clinic data measure a patient’s waiting time in minutes, with α = 30 minutes, β = 2 minutes per additional appointment in the queue, uⱼ = −5 minutes for Clinic A, and εᵢⱼ = 3 minutes. For Xᵢⱼ = 4 appointments, the fitted value is 30 + 2×4 − 5 = 33 minutes; adding that patient’s deviation gives 36 minutes. Here uⱼ shifts Clinic A’s intercept, while εᵢⱼ is individual variation. The variance terms τ² and σ² describe spread in squared minutes, not minutes. This model assumes the specified structure and does not show that queue length causes waiting time. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Regression and Other Stories — authors’ book site and chapter resources’ in the linked sources.

To see the mechanics of shrinkage, consider an explicitly synthetic example of four employment offices with equal samples. Suppose the overall mean placement rate is 50%, Office A’s unpooled sample mean is 62%, the within-office standard deviation is σ = 10 percentage points, the between-office standard deviation is τ = 4 percentage points, and n = 16 people are observed in each office. Under the lab’s known-variance normal-normal illustration, the weight on Office A’s local signal is λ = τ²/(τ² + σ²/n) = 16/(16 + 100/16) = 16/22.25 ≈ 0.719. The partially pooled estimate is therefore 50% + 0.719(62% − 50%) = 50% + 8.63 percentage points = 58.63%. It remains above the overall mean, but moves 3.37 percentage points toward it because 16 observations leave sampling noise. Increasing n would reduce σ²/n and raise λ; increasing within-office variation would lower λ. This calculation assumes comparable office sizes, a suitable model, and known variance components; in fitted data, estimating τ and σ adds uncertainty, and the result is not proof that Office A causes better placement.

In Yᵢⱼ = α + βXᵢⱼ + uⱼ + εᵢⱼ, the group term shifts the intercept while the individual term records remaining deviation. Synthetic waiting-time model has α = 25 minutes, β = 1.5 minutes per queued appointment, uⱼ = 4 minutes for Clinic B, and Xᵢⱼ = 6. The fitted group-specific mean is 25 + 1.5×6 + 4 = 38 minutes; if an individual residual is εᵢⱼ = −3 minutes, the predicted individual outcome is 35 minutes. Every additive term is in minutes. By contrast, τ² = Var(uⱼ) and σ² = Var(εᵢⱼ) are in squared minutes, so they describe dispersion rather than waiting time itself. A positive uⱼ is residual group variation under the model, not proof that Clinic B causes delay. See “Regression and Other Stories — authors’ book site and chapter resources”","takeaway":"A group effect describes residual group variation under the model, not a proven group-level cause.","formula":"Yᵢⱼ = α + βXᵢⱼ + uⱼ + εᵢⱼ; Var(uⱼ)=τ² and Var(εᵢⱼ)=σ²."},{"title":"Know what the design can support","body":"Many observations within a handful of groups do not provide the same information as many independent groups. Report both the number of groups and the number of observations per group, inspect whether group sizes are uneven, and check sensitivity to the distributional assumptions. Predictions for an already observed group use its data; predictions for a new group also include uncertainty about the distribution of group effects. A varying-slope model is useful only when the data support group-specific relationships and the added complexity serves the question.

The number of independent groups matters separately from the number of people inside each group. As an illustrative synthetic comparison, 600 workers split across 3 regions means 200 workers per region, whereas 600 workers across 30 regions means 20 per region. The first design may estimate each region’s mean precisely, but it has only 3 independent regional contexts for learning between-region variation; the second supplies 30 contexts, though each regional mean is noisier. For a new region, prediction also includes uncertainty about the distribution of group effects, unlike prediction for an already observed region that uses its data. Unequal sizes and missing groups can change these conclusions. More workers do not automatically create more independent groups or justify causal claims. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Gelman, Hill & Vehtari — Regression and Other Stories (Cambridge University Press)’ in the linked sources.

Consider an explicitly illustrative synthetic wage index with four offices, known within-office SD σ = 2 wage-index units, and assumed between-office SD τ = 1.5 units. Suppose the observed grand mean is 10, and Office A’s mean is 12 from n = 16 workers. Its sampling variance is σ²/n = 4/16 = 0.25, so the normal-normal partial-pooling weight on A’s deviation is λ = τ²/(τ² + σ²/n) = 2.25/(2.25 + 0.25) = 0.90. The pooled estimate is therefore 10 + 0.90(12 − 10) = 11.8 wage-index units: it moves 0.2 units toward the grand mean, rather than declaring the local mean exact. If the same mean came from n = 4, λ would be 2.25/(2.25 + 1) = 0.692, giving 11.38 units, because the local estimate is noisier. These calculations describe modeled office differences, not productivity effects or causes. In the actual lab, σ and τ are teaching inputs and group sizes are equal; with unequal sizes or estimated variance components, uncertainty in those inputs must also be reported.

The pooling lab makes a useful distinction visible: changing Observations per group improves the precision of a local mean, while changing Between-group SD τ changes how much groups are allowed to differ. Suppose two offices each report a 60% placement rate, but one has 10 workers and the other 100. The first rate has much more sampling noise, so partial pooling should move it more toward the overall level; it does not erase the office label. Increasing Within-group SD σ makes both estimates noisier without creating additional independent offices. These are synthetic teaching settings, not measured office outcomes. A model can describe existing offices more confidently than it can predict a genuinely new office.","takeaway":"Distinguish inference about existing groups from prediction for a new group.","practice":{"question":"Two districts have the same observed mean wage, but one mean comes from 8 workers and the other from 800. Which district estimate should usually be pulled more toward the overall mean in a partial-pooling model?","hint":"Compare how much sampling noise each group mean is likely to contain.","solution":"The estimate from 8 workers is usually less precise and is therefore pulled more strongly toward the overall mean, subject to the model’s variance assumptions."}}]
data.case_study: A regional employment service compares job-placement outcomes across 35 offices. Office sizes vary widely. Partial pooling can prevent very small offices from dominating league tables because of chance variation, while retaining evidence that some places may have systematically different outcomes. The estimates describe modeled differences; they do not by themselves explain why offices differ.
data.misconceptions:
Partial pooling does not make every group identical.
Shrinkage is not proof that a group’s true effect equals the overall mean.
A large number of individuals cannot replace information from having more independent groups.
A group-level association is not automatically causal.

Less precise estimates generally receive more shrinkage, conditional on the model."}

data.title: Survey Sampling & Complex Designs
data.excerpt: A national survey is rarely a simple random sample: it may select households in stages, divide them into groups and sample some populations more often. Learn how weights, strata and clusters help produce population-relevant estimates, and how the survey design affects uncertainty.
data.objectives:
Define the target population, sampling frame and unit before interpreting a survey estimate.
Explain why unequal selection probabilities lead to survey weights.
Distinguish stratification, cluster sampling, nonresponse adjustment and design-based uncertainty.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Start with the population, frame and selection process","body":"A survey of household energy costs should say which households, geography and reference period it represents. The sampling frame is the operational list or process from which units can be selected; it can omit eligible households or include outdated records. A probability sample gives each eligible unit a known, non-zero chance of selection under the design. A very large sample cannot repair a frame that systematically excludes the population of interest.

A sampling frame is more than a contact list: it determines which eligible units can enter the sample. Suppose the target is all 1,000 rented homes in a city in March 2026, but the frame lists only 900 homes because 100 newly converted flats are missing. If 90 homes are sampled from the listed 900, each listed home has selection probability 90/900 = 0.10, yet every missing flat has probability 0. The sample can describe listed homes under the design, not automatically all rented homes. A frame audit might compare its count with an independent housing register and record the reference date. This example is illustrative and synthetic; it does not establish actual coverage. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 506 — Sampling Theory and Methods (open course notes)’ in the linked sources.

Consider an illustrative, synthetic labour-market survey of 1,000 firms whose frame covers 600 micro firms and 400 larger firms. Suppose the design selects 60 micro firms (selection probability 0.10) and 80 larger firms (probability 0.20), and the corresponding respondent mean monthly wage is 19 currency units for micro firms and 36 currency units for larger firms. The unweighted respondent mean is (60×19 + 80×36)/140 = 28.71 currency units, but it overrepresents the larger stratum. An inverse-probability estimate of the population total is 60×19/0.10 + 80×36/0.20 = 11,400 + 14,400 = 25,800 currency units across the 1,000 firms; dividing by the known population size gives an estimated mean of 25.80 currency units per firm. Equivalently, the stratum shares are 0.60 and 0.40, so the benchmark calculation is 0.60×19 + 0.40×36 = 25.80. This interpretation requires complete frame coverage, known non-zero selection probabilities, and roughly random selection within each stratum; weighting does not repair nonresponse or biased within-stratum wage reporting.

Before calculating a survey average, write a one-sentence estimand containing population, geography, unit, and reference period. For a synthetic frame of 1,200 eligible apartments, an outdated list containing 1,000 gives 200 units zero inclusion probability; sampling 100 from the listed homes produces a 0.10 chance only for listed homes. A response table cannot reveal the missing apartments unless the frame is audited against another register. Also check whether the unit is an apartment, household, or person, since substituting one changes the target. The large sample-size argument begins after coverage is credible, not before it. See “Penn State STAT 506 — Sampling Theory and Methods (open course notes)”.","takeaway":"Population coverage and selection probabilities matter before sample size does."},{"title":"Weights reflect unequal chances of selection","body":"If unit i has inclusion probability πᵢ, its basic design weight is 1/πᵢ: units selected less often represent more of the population. A Horvitz–Thompson total sums the observed value multiplied by that base weight. Production survey weights may add nonresponse adjustments and calibration to known population totals. These steps can improve representation under their assumptions, but a weight is not a magic correction for unmeasured coverage or response bias; extreme weights can also make estimates less precise.

Illustrative synthetic example (annual household food spending, 2025): A town survey selects four households with unequal inclusion probabilities. Household A has a 0.10 chance and reports £3,000; B has 0.10 and £4,000; C has 0.20 and £2,500; D has 0.20 and £3,500. Their basic design weights are 1/0.10 = 10, 10, 1/0.20 = 5 and 5. The weighted total is 10(£3,000) + 10(£4,000) + 5(£2,500) + 5(£3,500) = £100,000, and the weights sum to 30 represented households. The estimated mean annual spending is £100,000 ÷ 30 = £3,333.33 per household. The unweighted mean, £13,000 ÷ 4 = £3,250, gives each sampled household equal influence even though the design did not give them equal selection chances.

This weighted mean can describe the target town’s 2025 annual household food spending only under the stated sampling and adjustment assumptions; it cannot prove that every household spends £3,333.33, remove coverage gaps, repair inaccurate probabilities, establish causality, or guarantee that nonrespondents resemble respondents. Check that inclusion probabilities are known and non-zero, compare the weighted count (30 in this illustration) with the intended population count, and inspect whether very large weights make the estimate unstable. A common mistake is to treat weights as extra observations or as proof that a survey is representative; they encode who was selected and any documented adjustments, but they do not create information that was never collected. See “Penn State STAT 506 — Sampling Theory and Methods (open course notes)” in the linked sources below.

Unequal weights affect averages through both the numerator and denominator. Consider an illustrative synthetic survey of two income groups in one month: four sampled urban workers each represent 5 workers and report £2,000, while two sampled rural workers each represent 20 workers and report £1,500. The weighted mean is [4(5)(£2,000) + 2(20)(£1,500)] ÷ [4(5) + 2(20)] = £100,000 ÷ 60 = £1,666.67 per worker-month. The raw mean is [4(£2,000) + 2(£1,500)] ÷ 6 = £1,833.33. The difference reflects the designed representation, not a change in anyone’s income. Weights do not prove accurate reporting or remove nonresponse bias. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 506 — Sampling Theory and Methods (open course notes)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data): suppose a labour-force survey samples three strata and records estimated unemployment rates of 4% in stratum A, 8% in B and 15% in C. The sample contains 50, 60 and 40 people, while the target population counts are 5,000, 3,000 and 2,000. Start by checking each base weight: 5,000/50 = 100 for A, 3,000/60 = 50 for B, and 2,000/40 = 50 for C. Treating the within-stratum rates as sample estimates, the estimated unemployed count is 100(50)(0.04) + 50(60)(0.08) + 50(40)(0.15) = 200 + 240 + 300 = 740 people. The weighted population denominator is 5,000 + 3,000 + 2,000 = 10,000, so the estimated unemployment rate is 740/10,000 = 0.074, or 7.4%. An equal-weight average of the three stratum rates would be (4% + 8% + 15%)/3 = 9.0%, which answers a different question because it gives each stratum equal influence rather than each person. Before reporting 7.4%, verify that the population counts and non-zero selection probabilities are appropriate; differential nonresponse or misclassified strata can still bias every weighted component.

To read a weighted estimate, follow its two jobs: expand each observed unit and normalize by the total expansion. In a synthetic sample, two workers with probability 0.25 report $30 per hour and one worker with probability 0.50 reports $18. Their base weights are 4, 4, and 2. The weighted hourly total is 4(30) + 4(30) + 2(18) = $300, while represented workers total 10, giving $30 per hour. The unweighted mean is $26, because the less frequently selected high-wage workers receive too little influence. This calculation assumes correct inclusion probabilities; it does not correct missing coverage, nonresponse, or measurement error. See “Penn State STAT 506 — Sampling Theory and Methods (open course notes)”.","takeaway":"Weights encode a stated selection or adjustment process; report how they were built.","formula":"Base design weight dᵢ = 1/πᵢ; estimated population total = Σᵢ∈sample dᵢYᵢ."},{"title":"Strata and clusters solve different field problems","body":"Stratification partitions the population into groups before selection and samples within each group. It can ensure subgroup coverage and improve precision when units within a stratum are similar on the outcome. Cluster sampling selects groups such as neighbourhoods or schools, often to reduce travel or listing cost. Members of a selected cluster may be similar, so collecting many people in a few clusters can yield less independent information than the row count suggests. A design can use strata and multiple sampling stages together.

Stratification and clustering can produce different information even with the same number of interviews. In an illustrative synthetic design, a city has two strata, east and west, and the analyst samples 30 residents from each: both areas are guaranteed representation. Alternatively, six neighbourhood clusters might be selected and 10 residents interviewed in each, again yielding 60 interviews. If residents within a neighbourhood tend to have similar commuting costs, the cluster sample may contain less independent variation than 60 widely spread selections. Stratification answers “which groups must be represented?”; clustering answers “which groups are selected together?” A design can stratify by region and then cluster by neighbourhood within each region. These counts are examples, not observed data. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 506 — Stratified Sampling’ in the linked sources.

Suppose, purely illustratively, that annual household food spending averages $24,000 in an urban stratum and $12,000 in a rural stratum. If those strata comprise 75% and 25% of the target population, the population-weighted estimate is 0.75 × $24,000 + 0.25 × $12,000 = $21,000 per household-year. A sample containing 60% urban and 40% rural households would instead have the raw mean 0.60 × $24,000 + 0.40 × $12,000 = $19,200, a $1,800 understatement caused by composition. The corresponding calibration factors are 0.75/0.60 = 1.25 for urban respondents and 0.25/0.40 = 0.625 for rural respondents; applying them and dividing by their weighted share total reproduces $21,000. This fixes unequal representation only under the illustrative assumption that each stratum mean is adequately measured; it does not prove nonresponse is ignorable. For uncertainty, suppose 120 respondents came as 8 equal-size neighbourhood clusters of 15 and an illustrative within-cluster correlation was ρ = 0.15. The rough design effect 1 + (15 − 1)ρ = 3.10 gives an effective-size diagnostic of 120/3.10 ≈ 38.7, not 120 independent observations.

Imagine 60 interviews planned for a national commuting survey. Stratifying by urban and rural status and taking 30 from each guarantees both categories appear, even if rural residents are a minority. Selecting six villages and interviewing 10 people in each instead saves travel, but village members may share roads, employers, and weather, reducing independent information. These designs can be combined: stratify by region, then select villages as primary sampling units inside each stratum. The labels answer different questions, so do not call every grouped sample “stratified.” When reading results, identify the stratum variables, cluster identifiers, selection stages, and weights separately. This design distinction is emphasized in “Penn State STAT 506 — Stratified Sampling”.","takeaway":"Strata organize selection across groups; primary sampling units describe clustered selection."},{"title":"Let the sample design govern uncertainty","body":"An unweighted standard error that assumes independent, equally selected observations may not describe a stratified, clustered or unequal-probability sample. Analysts need the released design variables or replicate weights and the documented variance method. For an equal-size cluster illustration, the design effect is approximately 1 + (m − 1)ρ, where m is cluster size and ρ is the within-cluster correlation; real survey design effects depend on the estimator, weights and full design. A design-based standard error describes sampling variation, not confounding in a causal comparison.

The design effect translates dependence into an effective-information warning, not a correction to the point estimate. Using the lesson’s approximation, suppose an illustrative synthetic cluster design interviews m = 8 people per cluster and has within-cluster correlation ρ = 0.20 on a satisfaction score. Then deff ≈ 1 + (8 − 1)(0.20) = 1 + 1.40 = 2.40. If a simple-random-sample standard error were 4 percentage points, the approximate design-aware standard error would be 4√2.40 ≈ 6.20 percentage points, so the uncertainty is wider by about 2.20 percentage points. This does not prove that clusters caused satisfaction or account for unequal weights, stratification, or finite-population corrections. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Zins & Burgard — Considering interviewer and design effects when planning sample sizes (Statistics Canada)’ in the linked sources.

A useful check is to separate stratified sampling variance from the point-estimate calculation. Suppose, purely illustratively, that the target population is 30% stratum A and 70% stratum B, and the outcome is weekly earnings in currency units. If independent within-stratum samples give n_A = 50 with s_A = 12 currency units and n_B = 100 with s_B = 20, the estimated population mean is μ̂ = 0.30ȳ_A + 0.70ȳ_B, while an approximate variance (before finite-population corrections) is (0.30² × 12²/50) + (0.70² × 20²/100) = 0.2592 + 1.9600 = 2.2192 currency-units². Thus SE(μ̂) = √2.2192 ≈ 1.49 currency units, and a normal-reference 95% margin is 1.96 × 1.49 ≈ 2.92 currency units. The squared weights matter: the larger, more variable stratum contributes most of the uncertainty. This calculation assumes independent observations within each stratum and correctly defined stratum shares; if the sample also selects clusters, a PSU-aware variance method must replace this shortcut, and nonresponse adjustment requires its own justification.

The survey lab’s cluster-size and within-cluster correlation controls show why row count alone is incomplete. Using deff ≈ 1 + (m − 1)ρ, a synthetic design with m = 5 and ρ = 0.30 gives 1 + 4(0.30) = 2.20. If an independent-sample standard error were 3 percentage points, the rough design-aware value would be 3√2.20 ≈ 4.45 percentage points. The point estimate has not been multiplied by 2.20; only its variance warning changes. This approximation assumes equal cluster sizes and a suitable estimator. Actual analysis should retain strata, primary sampling units, weights, and the released variance method. “Zins & Burgard — Considering interviewer and design effects when planning sample sizes (Statistics Canada)” gives the relevant planning perspective.","takeaway":"Weights alone do not specify the variance estimator or make a causal design."},{"title":"Treat nonresponse as a separate stage","body":"The design weight is based on selection, while a response adjustment relies on additional assumptions about who responds. Calibration may align weighted totals with trusted benchmarks, but it cannot guarantee that respondents and nonrespondents have the same outcome within adjustment cells. Publish response rates, coverage limitations, weight construction and design-aware uncertainty. If conclusions may depend on nonresponse assumptions, add a sensitivity analysis rather than claiming that weighting removes all bias.

A response adjustment is conditional on an assumption about nonrespondents, so it should be checked rather than treated as a guarantee. In an illustrative synthetic telephone survey, 80 selected households respond and 20 do not. Within an adjustment cell, suppose respondents’ average weekly hours are 32 hours and the base-weighted target count is 100 households. A simple response-rate adjustment is 100/80 = 1.25; each respondent’s weight is multiplied by 1.25, preserving an estimated 100 households. The resulting 32-hour mean still assumes the 20 nonrespondents would average 32 hours after conditioning on the cell. If they averaged 40 hours instead, the respondent mean would differ from their mean by 8 hours, signaling possible bias. This is synthetic, not observed evidence. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 506 — Sampling Theory and Methods (open course notes)’ in the linked sources.

A useful diagnostic is to separate the weighted respondent estimate from a plausible nonresponse sensitivity range. Suppose, purely illustratively, that a synthetic labour survey targets 70% urban and 30% rural workers, and the respondent means are 35 and 25 hours per week. If the adjustment cells are those two groups, the benchmark-weighted respondent estimate is 0.70×35 + 0.30×25 = 32 hours per week. This is not yet a guarantee: imagine rural nonrespondents would average 31 hours, while rural respondents average 25, with a 50% rural response rate; the implied rural all-selected mean is (0.50×25) + (0.50×31) = 28 hours, so the corresponding population mean becomes 0.70×35 + 0.30×28 = 32.9 hours per week, 0.9 hours above the respondent-based estimate. Urban nonrespondents were assumed equal to urban respondents in this illustration, not observed to be so. Report that assumption and vary it in sensitivity analysis. Finally, do not confuse this bias check with precision: under the lab’s equal-cluster approximation, m = 20 and ρ = 0.20 give DEFF = 1 + 19×0.20 = 4.8, so 600 records represent roughly 600/4.8 = 125 independent observations for variance intuition.

A response adjustment can preserve a weighted count while leaving outcome bias untouched. In a synthetic cell, 60 of 75 selected households respond, so multiplying each respondent’s base weight by 75/60 = 1.25 represents the full cell. If respondents average 28 weekly work hours, the adjusted mean remains 28 hours. That result implicitly assigns 28 hours to the 15 nonrespondents after conditioning on the cell. If a plausible sensitivity scenario assigns them 34 hours, the full-cell mean becomes [60(28) + 15(34)]/75 = 29.2 hours, a 1.2-hour difference. Report this assumption, the response rate, and the sensitivity range separately from selection weighting. See “Penn State STAT 506 — Sampling Theory and Methods (open course notes)”.","takeaway":"Selection, response, calibration and variance estimation are related but distinct parts of survey analysis.","practice":{"question":"A sample has a large number of respondents but oversamples one region by design. What should an analyst check before reporting the raw mean as a national average?","hint":"Ask what each respondent represents and how the regional selection probabilities differ.","solution":"Check the target population and region-specific inclusion probabilities, then use appropriate survey weights and design-aware variance estimation. Also assess coverage and nonresponse assumptions."}}]
data.case_study: A national survey deliberately samples remote districts at a higher rate so that their labour-market conditions can be reported. The raw respondent average therefore does not represent the national workforce by itself. The analyst uses the documented selection weights, retains the strata and primary sampling units for uncertainty estimates, and separately explains nonresponse adjustments.
data.misconceptions:
A weight does not prove that nonresponse bias has been removed.
A large respondent count does not make a convenience sample representative.
Stratification and clustering have different roles and can appear together.
A design effect is tied to an estimator and design; it is not a fixed property of a survey.
