data.title: Survival & Duration Analysis
data.excerpt: Duration analysis studies how long it takes for an event—such as finding work, leaving school or recovering—to happen. Learn how to use follow-up that ends before the event, account for incomplete observations, and describe event rates without treating unfinished cases as failures.
data.objectives:
Represent follow-up time and event status separately.
Interpret right-censoring, risk sets and the Kaplan–Meier survival curve.
Distinguish survival probabilities from hazards and interpret Cox hazard ratios cautiously.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Duration outcomes contain time and status","body":"For an unemployment-spell study, record how long each person is followed and whether re-employment is observed during that period. Someone still searching when the study ends contributes a known spell lasting at least until their last observed date. Their event time is unknown beyond that point, but their observed follow-up is not useless. Preserve the time scale, origin, event definition and status flag for every eligible spell.

A useful data layout keeps duration and status in separate columns. Consider a synthetic study of six households followed from benefit application for 4, 7, 9, 12, 12, and 15 weeks. Suppose three events occur at weeks 4, 9, and 12, while the others are still under observation at week 15. The record for the week-7 case is (7 weeks, status 0), not (0 weeks, status 0); it establishes at least 7 weeks without the event. If status 1 means the event was observed, the event case at week 4 is (4 weeks, 1). This encoding preserves calendar units and supports risk-set calculations. It does not prove why durations differ or make follow-up comparable if entry rules vary. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Schober & Vetter — Survival Analysis and Interpretation of Time-to-Event Data (open-access review)’ in the linked sources.

To see how status and follow-up enter a Kaplan–Meier estimate, use this illustrative synthetic cohort of eight claimants. Suppose re-employment is observed at months 2, 5, 5, and 9; other spells are censored at months 4, 7, 10, and 12. Start with eight people at risk. At month 2, one event gives S(2) = (8−1)/8 = 7/8 = 0.875. The month-4 censoring is removed before the next event time, so six people remain at risk at month 5; two events give S(5) = 0.875 × (6−2)/6 = 0.5833. The month-7 censoring then leaves three at risk at month 9; one event gives S(9) = 0.5833 × (3−1)/3 = 0.3889, or 38.9% estimated event-free. Thus the estimated median duration is 9 months, the first event time at which survival is at most 0.5—not the average observed spell. Censoring at months 10 and 12 does not change S(9). This calculation assumes censoring is unrelated to imminent re-employment, at least conditional on relevant observed information; administrative closure may be plausible, but selective loss from the data system can violate that assumption.

A duration record needs two questions answered independently: how long was the spell observed, and did the defined event occur? Consider a synthetic benefits file with (3 months, 1), (8 months, 0), and (11 months, 1). The first claimant exited to work after 3 months; the second was observed unemployed for at least 8 months; the third experienced the event at 11 months. Coding the middle record as zero months would discard eight months of risk information, while coding it as an event would invent a return to work. Keep the origin, units, event definition, and status coding documented, especially when delayed entry or repeated spells are possible. See “Schober & Vetter — Survival Analysis and Interpretation of Time-to-Event Data (open-access review)”.","takeaway":"A duration outcome combines follow-up time with an event indicator."},{"title":"Right-censoring is partial information, not a zero","body":"Right-censoring occurs when an event has not been observed by the end of follow-up or a person leaves observation. The data tell us the event time exceeds the recorded follow-up. A censored spell should not be coded as if the event occurred at that time or as if the duration were zero. Kaplan–Meier estimation uses those who remain at risk at each event time; censoring reduces later risk sets without causing a downward step in the survival estimate at that instant. Informative loss to follow-up can still bias the result.

Think of censoring as a one-sided measurement. In a synthetic clinic study, a participant is observed for 10 weeks without recovery, then leaves the system. The data support T > 10 weeks, not T = 10 and not T = 0. If another participant recovers at week 6, that record supports T = 6 weeks and status 1. At week 10, the first person contributes 10 person-weeks of observed risk time; after week 10, they contribute none. Treating the censored case as a week-10 recovery would create one false event and shorten estimated duration. The interpretation depends on censoring being plausibly unrelated to unobserved recovery time, conditional on relevant information; administrative closure may be safer than selective dropout. For a fuller treatment, see ‘UCLA OARC — Introduction to Survival Analysis in R (open workshop notes)’ in the linked sources.

Here is a synthetic illustration of why a hazard ratio must be translated through time before discussing risk. Suppose a constant monthly event hazard is λ = 0.04, and follow-up lasts 12 months. The event-free probability is S(12) = exp(−0.04 × 12) = exp(−0.48) ≈ 0.619, so the model-implied probability of an event by 12 months is 1 − 0.619 = 0.381, or 38.1%. If a comparison group has hazard ratio 1.5, its hazard is 0.04 × 1.5 = 0.06 per month; its corresponding survival is exp(−0.06 × 12) = exp(−0.72) ≈ 0.487, implying 51.3% experiencing the event and an illustrative absolute difference of 13.2 percentage points. These are synthetic model calculations, not observed outcomes, and the absolute gap depends on the time horizon and baseline hazard. The calculation also assumes a constant hazard and correctly specified comparison; censoring does not turn the 38.1% or 51.3% into observed proportions unless follow-up and censoring assumptions support that interpretation. A changing hazard would require integrating λ(t), rather than multiplying one rate by time.

Right-censoring can be read as an inequality: a censored customer observed for 14 months without cancellation supplies T > 14 months. In a synthetic risk table, that customer contributes to the risk set through month 14 and disappears afterward; they do not create a downward Kaplan–Meier step at month 14. A customer canceling at month 9 contributes T = 9 with status 1 and does create an event step. If cancellations cause people to leave the database, censoring may be informative because departure relates to the unobserved event time. Administrative study closure is easier to defend than selective loss, but neither assumption should be hidden. See “UCLA OARC — Introduction to Survival Analysis in R (open workshop notes)”.","takeaway":"A censored observation remains informative up to its last known time, subject to censoring assumptions."},{"title":"Read the survival curve and median","body":"The survival function S(t) is the probability that the event time is later than t. The Kaplan–Meier curve estimates this function as a stepwise product of the event-free proportions at observed event times. Its median duration is the first time at which the estimated survival probability reaches one half; if the curve never falls that far during follow-up, the median is not observed within the study horizon. The curve is a probability over time, not a count of events.

Illustrative synthetic example — Suppose an employment service follows 8 jobseekers for 12 weeks from the start of an unemployment spell, recording the week of re-employment or the last week observed. Two find work in week 2, so the Kaplan–Meier estimate becomes (8−2)/8 = 0.75. One person leaves the records in week 4 without a job; that case is censored and is removed from later risk sets, not counted as a re-employment. At week 5, 5 people remain at risk and 1 finds work, giving a factor (5−1)/5 = 0.80. At week 8, 4 remain and 2 find work, giving (4−2)/4 = 0.50. Thus Ŝ(8) = 0.75 × 0.80 × 0.50 = 0.30: the estimated share remaining unemployed beyond 8 weeks is 30%, and the estimated median duration is 8 weeks.

The curve describes event-free duration under the observed follow-up; it cannot by itself establish that a training policy caused faster re-employment, guarantee a future job-finding rate, or reveal what happened after a censored observation. A key assumption is that censoring is plausibly unrelated to the unobserved event time after conditioning on relevant information. Check the risk table and censoring marks, compare censoring patterns across groups when relevant, and consider whether the curve changes implausibly after heavy loss to follow-up. Do not read Ŝ(8) = 0.30 as saying exactly 30% of these named people will find work later, or confuse the median with an average duration. The “UCLA OARC — Introduction to Survival Analysis in R (open workshop notes)” in the linked sources below provides further guidance.

The curve’s vertical reading is conditional on the event-free population represented by the risk sets. In a synthetic example, 10 customers are event-free just before month 3 and 2 close their accounts then, so the factor is (10−2)/10 = 0.80. By month 5, 6 remain at risk and 1 closes, so the factor is (6−1)/6 = 5/6 ≈ 0.833. The estimated survival beyond month 5 is 0.80 × 0.833 ≈ 0.667, or 66.7% on the probability scale. A median is the first time the curve is at or below 0.50; if it stays above 0.50 through 12 months, the median exceeds 12 months or is not observed. This is descriptive, not proof of a treatment effect. For a fuller treatment, see ‘UCLA OARC — Introduction to Survival Analysis in R (open workshop notes)’ in the linked sources.

Use the lab’s smooth curves as a model-to-probability calculation, not as a replacement for the Kaplan–Meier risk table. Suppose, purely illustratively, that a baseline monthly hazard is λ = 0.04 and a comparison group has hazard ratio HR = 1.50. Under the constant-hazard assumption, the comparison hazard is 0.04 × 1.50 = 0.06 per month. At t = 6 months, baseline survival is S₀(6) = exp(−0.04 × 6) = exp(−0.24) ≈ 0.787, so the modeled event probability by six months is 1 − 0.787 = 0.213, or 21.3%. Comparison survival is S₁(6) = exp(−0.06 × 6) = exp(−0.36) ≈ 0.698, giving 30.2% by six months. The hazard ratio is 1.50, but the six-month event-probability ratio is 0.302/0.213 ≈ 1.42, not 1.50; translating hazards requires the time horizon and baseline hazard. Treat these values as synthetic illustrations: real hazards may vary with time, and censoring assumptions and model fit must be checked before interpreting a group contrast.

Read a Kaplan–Meier display horizontally for time and vertically for the estimated event-free probability. In a synthetic curve, suppose the estimate is 0.80 immediately after month 3 and 0.56 after month 7; the vertical drop at month 7 represents events among that month’s risk set, not 24% of the original sample necessarily. If the curve first reaches 0.50 at month 10, the estimated median is 10 months. If it remains above 0.50 through the final month, the median is not observed within follow-up. Censoring marks remove later risk exposure but do not themselves lower the curve. This descriptive reading assumes censoring is plausibly noninformative given relevant information. See “UCLA OARC — Introduction to Survival Analysis in R (open workshop notes)”.","takeaway":"The Kaplan–Meier curve changes at event times and accounts for the changing risk set.","formula":"Ŝ(t) = ∏_{tₖ≤t}(1 − dₖ/nₖ), where dₖ events occur among nₖ units at risk."},{"title":"Hazard is conditional on still being at risk","body":"The hazard describes the instantaneous event rate around time t among units that have not yet had the event. The survival probability is cumulative; it describes the chance of remaining event-free beyond a time. A Cox proportional-hazards model compares hazards over time while leaving the baseline hazard unspecified. Its hazard ratio is a relative rate among the risk sets under the proportional-hazards assumption—not a percentage-point change in the probability of re-employment or an expected number of extra months.

Hazard comparisons use a changing denominator: only people still event-free at that time are eligible for the instantaneous comparison. Suppose a synthetic risk set at week 8 contains 20 people, and 2 events occur during the next one-week interval. A simple interval event proportion is 2/20 = 0.10, or 10% over that week—not a statement that 10 percentage points of the original sample will experience the event. If a second group has 1 event among 20 at-risk people, its corresponding proportion is 1/20 = 0.05, and the ratio is 0.10/0.05 = 2. The ratio describes relative event rates for those at risk, under a suitable time model; it is not two extra weeks, a 10-percentage-point probability increase, or a causal effect. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Schober & Vetter — Survival Analysis and Interpretation of Time-to-Event Data (open-access review)’ in the linked sources.

For a concrete synthetic illustration, suppose an unemployment spell has a constant re-employment hazard of 0.04 per month in a baseline group, and a comparison programme is assigned a hazard ratio of 0.75. First multiply the rate: 0.04 × 0.75 = 0.03 per month. Over 12 months, the cumulative hazards are 0.04 × 12 = 0.48 and 0.03 × 12 = 0.36, so the model-implied survival probabilities are S₀(12) = exp(−0.48) ≈ 0.619 and S₁(12) = exp(−0.36) ≈ 0.698. Thus the corresponding event probabilities are about 38.1% and 30.2%, a difference of roughly 7.9 percentage points; the hazard ratio itself is not 7.9% and cannot be converted to that difference without the baseline hazard and time horizon. This calculation assumes a constant hazard and proportional hazards, with no informative censoring after conditioning on the model’s covariates. In the lab, changing the censoring slider should not move these curves: it represents incomplete observation, not extra re-employment. If censoring is related to unobserved re-employment prospects, the displayed survival interpretation may be biased.

A hazard ratio compares event rates among people who have survived event-free to the comparison time, not among everyone who started. Suppose a synthetic program group has 3 events among 30 people at risk in one interval, while comparison has 2 among 40. The simple interval proportions are 0.10 and 0.05, giving a ratio of 2. That does not mean twice as many original participants will eventually find work, nor does it mean two additional months. The eligible denominator can change after every event or censoring. A Cox interpretation also requires attention to proportional hazards and the time scale. Treat the ratio as a conditional relative rate, not a probability or causal effect. See “Schober & Vetter — Survival Analysis and Interpretation of Time-to-Event Data (open-access review)”.","takeaway":"A hazard ratio is not a risk ratio, a survival-probability difference or a duration difference."},{"title":"Check whether the comparison remains credible over time","body":"The proportional-hazards assumption says that a covariate’s hazard ratio is stable over the modeled time scale. Plot group-specific survival curves, inspect diagnostics and consider time-varying effects if the policy association changes across the spell. State whether time begins at benefit eligibility, spell start or another landmark; delayed entry, competing events and repeated spells may require further methods. Censoring should be plausibly independent of the event time after conditioning on modeled information, or addressed through an appropriate design or sensitivity analysis.

A proportional-hazards check asks whether a relative comparison is reasonably stable across the chosen time scale. In a synthetic example, a program group has an estimated hazard ratio of 0.60 during weeks 1–4 but 1.20 during weeks 5–8. The early ratio suggests a 40% lower hazard (1−0.60 = 0.40), whereas the later ratio suggests a 20% higher hazard (1.20−1 = 0.20); one constant hazard ratio would hide that reversal. Plotting survival curves and inspecting time-varying effects can reveal the problem. These ratios still compare conditional event rates, not causal impacts or guaranteed duration changes. Delayed entry, competing events, and informative censoring can also distort a simple comparison, so the risk-set definition must be stated. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Schober & Vetter — Survival Analysis and Interpretation of Time-to-Event Data (open-access review)’ in the linked sources.

Use the lab’s constant-hazard model to translate a relative hazard into an absolute 12-month comparison. Suppose the illustrative baseline monthly hazard is λ = 0.05 and the comparison hazard ratio is HR = 0.75, so the comparison hazard is 0.05 × 0.75 = 0.0375 per month. Under a constant-hazard and independent-censoring assumption, baseline survival at 12 months is S₀(12) = exp(−0.05 × 12) = exp(−0.60) ≈ 0.5488, while comparison survival is S₁(12) = exp(−0.0375 × 12) = exp(−0.45) ≈ 0.6376. Thus the modeled event risks by month 12 are 1 − S₀ = 45.1% and 1 − S₁ = 36.2%, an absolute difference of about 8.9 percentage points in this synthetic illustration. The HR of 0.75 describes a 25% lower instantaneous hazard (1 − 0.75), not a 25-percentage-point reduction in 12-month event probability. If censoring is related to impending re-employment even after conditioning on modeled information, these curve calculations need sensitivity analysis; censoring is not an event.

A single hazard ratio can conceal a changing comparison. In a synthetic analysis, an estimated ratio of 0.70 in months 1–3 corresponds to a 30% lower hazard, while 1.10 in months 4–6 corresponds to a 10% higher hazard; these are conditional rate comparisons, not percentage-point changes in survival. Plot group-specific curves and inspect whether they cross or separate unevenly. Then state the time origin, delayed-entry rule, competing-event treatment, and censoring mechanism. If the association changes, consider a time-varying effect rather than reporting one average ratio as if it held throughout. The diagnosis does not turn an observational program contrast into a causal result. See “UCLA OARC — Introduction to Survival Analysis in R (open workshop notes)”.","takeaway":"Time scale, risk-set definition and censoring process are part of the estimand."}]
data.case_study: An employment service follows benefit claimants from the start of an unemployment spell. Some return to work during observation; others remain unemployed when the administrative window closes or move out of the data system. A duration analysis can use each person’s observed time without pretending that all censored spells ended in re-employment, while making the follow-up and censoring assumptions explicit.
data.misconceptions:
Censoring does not mean that an event occurred at the last observed time.
A hazard ratio is not a change in the probability of an event by a fixed date.
A Kaplan–Meier curve does not correct for informative loss to follow-up by itself.
A model with a fitted hazard is not automatically a causal evaluation.

data.title: Spatial Dependence & Regional Econometrics
data.excerpt: Outcomes in nearby areas often resemble each other because people, jobs and policies cross local boundaries. Learn how to define neighbourhoods and measure spatial patterns, and distinguish geographic association from evidence that one area’s change caused a change in another.
data.objectives:
Define a spatial weights matrix and a spatial lag.
Interpret global Moran’s I and a spatial-randomization reference distribution.
Distinguish spatially lagged outcomes from spatially correlated errors and assess sensitivity to neighbourhood choices.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"A map is data with a geography","body":"Regional unemployment or house prices are attached to defined spatial units such as districts or grid cells. Before comparing regions, document boundaries, dates, population denominators and whether the values are rates, totals or model residuals. Aggregation can hide variation within a region, and changing the boundary system can change patterns—a version of the modifiable areal unit problem. A visually appealing map is a useful first check, not an inference method.

A map also determines the denominator of a comparison. Suppose, illustratively, that synthetic District A has 2,000 unemployed people out of 50,000 workers, while synthetic District B has 900 out of 15,000. Their unemployment rates are 2,000 ÷ 50,000 = 0.04 = 4%, and 900 ÷ 15,000 = 0.06 = 6%, so B is higher by 2 percentage points, not 2 percent. If a map instead displays counts, A appears larger (2,000 versus 900), even though its rate is lower. The interpretation therefore depends on the research question and a consistent time period; a rate comparison assumes denominators are measured comparably. Neither display reveals within-district inequality or establishes why the rates differ. For a fuller treatment, see ‘GeoDa Center — Global Spatial Autocorrelation workbook’ in the linked sources.

To see why the weights rule is part of the estimand, use an explicitly synthetic four-region example with outcomes measured in percentage points: A = 2, B = 4, C = 8, and D = 10. Suppose C’s rook neighbors are B and D, each with weight 1. Its row-standardized spatial lag is (1×4 + 1×10)/(1+1) = 7 percentage points, meaning the average outcome assigned to C by this rule is 7 pp. Now add diagonal region A with weight 0.5 while retaining B and D at weight 1. The lag becomes (1×4 + 1×10 + 0.5×2)/(1+1+0.5) = 15/2.5 = 6 pp. The one-unit change is produced by the neighbourhood definition, not by new observations or a change in C. If these outcomes are rates, this equal-region average also implicitly gives a tiny and populous region the same influence; population-weighted or distance-based weights would answer a different question. A high lag or positive Moran’s I still describes patterned similarity, not evidence that neighbours caused C’s outcome; causal spillovers require a defensible design and assumptions.

A choropleth’s visual intensity is meaningful only after its numerator and denominator are named. In a synthetic illustration, district A has 1,500 unemployed people among 30,000 workers, or 5%; district B has 700 among 10,000, or 7%. A count map makes A darker because 1,500 exceeds 700, while a rate map makes B darker because 7% exceeds 5%; the difference is 2 percentage points. Changing from districts to smaller neighbourhoods may expose within-district variation, so a pattern can change without anyone’s outcome changing. Record boundary system, date, unit, and denominator before interpreting adjacency. Mapping association does not identify diffusion or causality. See “GeoDa Center — Global Spatial Autocorrelation workbook”.","takeaway":"Geographic units and scale shape what spatial patterns can be observed."},{"title":"Neighbourhoods become a weights matrix","body":"A spatial weights matrix records which locations count as neighbours and how strongly they contribute. Contiguity links touching polygons; distance bands or nearest neighbours suit other settings. Row-standardizing weights makes a spatial lag resemble a weighted average of neighbouring values, but isolated locations and boundary choices still need explicit handling. There is no universally correct neighbourhood rule: it should reflect the substantive process and be tested for sensitivity.

Row standardization changes the units of a spatial lag but not the underlying neighbour choices. Consider an illustrative synthetic index measured in percentage points: region C has neighbours A and B with values 10 and 14. Equal raw weights give a lag of 1×10 + 1×14 = 24 index points before normalization, whereas row-standardized weights are 0.5 and 0.5, giving 0.5×10 + 0.5×14 = 12 percentage points, the neighbours’ average. If C has only B as a neighbour, its standardized lag is 14 percentage points. This calculation assumes the selected links represent relevant exposure and that the index is comparable across regions. It does not show that neighbours influence C, and different distance cutoffs can produce different lags. For a fuller treatment, see ‘GeoDa Center — Global Spatial Autocorrelation workbook’ in the linked sources.

Suppose an analyst uses a distance-informed rule for a synthetic, illustrative rental-inflation index measured in percentage points. For focal district C, four edge-sharing neighbours have values 6, 8, 10, and 12 pp, while four corner neighbours have values 4, 16, 9, and 11 pp; assign raw weight 1 to edge links and 0.3 to corner links. The weighted numerator is (6+8+10+12) + 0.3(4+16+9+11) = 36 + 12 = 48 pp-weight units, and the row total is 4 + 0.3×4 = 5.2 weight units. C’s row-standardized lag is therefore 48/5.2 = 9.23 pp, not the unweighted eight-neighbour average, 76/8 = 9.50 pp. The denominator matters because boundary districts may have fewer links, and changing the diagonal slider changes both numerator and denominator. In the interactive lab, the same normalization idea is applied to standardized synthetic outcomes on a 6×6 grid before the Moran scatter is drawn; its Moran’s I is descriptive for that generated field and has no permutation p-value. Neither lag, nor a high Moran’s I, identifies a spillover without a defensible causal design.

A spatial lag is a constructed summary, not a neighbour’s original observation. Suppose region D has three selected neighbours with index values 8, 12, and 16 percentage points. Equal raw weights produce 36 index points, whereas row-standardized weights 1/3 each produce 12 percentage points, their average. If a distance rule drops the 8-point neighbour, the standardized lag becomes (12 + 16)/2 = 14 percentage points. The change follows the neighbourhood definition, not a sudden economic movement. Inspect isolated locations and whether distance or contiguity matches the mechanism of interest. A higher lag does not prove neighbours caused D’s value; it only summarizes values under the declared weights. See “GeoDa Center — Global Spatial Autocorrelation workbook”.","takeaway":"The neighbour definition is a modeling decision that changes spatial summaries."},{"title":"Moran’s I summarizes global similarity among neighbours","body":"Global Moran’s I compares each region’s deviation from the overall mean with the spatially weighted deviations around it. Positive values indicate that similar values tend to be neighbours; negative values indicate that dissimilar values tend to be neighbours. A permutation reference distribution can show how unusual the observed statistic is under a chosen spatial-randomness null. Neither a large statistic nor a small permutation p-value proves a causal spillover or locates which neighbourhoods drive the pattern.

Illustrative synthetic example (one-year unemployment rates): four districts lie in a line, with rates of 4%, 4%, 8% and 8%. Using a first-order contiguity matrix, district 1 is connected to 2, districts 2 and 3 each connect to their two neighbours with weight 0.5 each, and district 4 connects to 3; these row-standardized weights have S₀ = 4. The mean rate is 6%, so deviations z are −2, −2, 2 and 2 percentage points. The weighted cross-products sum to 8: district 1 contributes 4, the two middle rows cancel, and district 4 contributes 4. The squared-deviation sum is 16, and with n = 4, I = (4/4) × (8/16) = 0.5. This positive value summarizes similar unemployment rates occurring next to one another in this one-year map.

The result can establish spatial association under this chosen weights matrix, not that high unemployment in one district caused high unemployment in its neighbour, nor which particular pair forms a significant local cluster. A useful decision check is to compare 0.5 with a spatial-randomization reference distribution: repeatedly permute the four observed rates across the fixed district locations, recompute I, and report how unusual the observed value is under that null. Also repeat the calculation with a defensible alternative neighbourhood rule, because the conclusion may depend on contiguity, distance or isolated areas. Do not misread positive Moran’s I as proof of policy spillovers or as evidence that every district is alike. See “PySAL esda — Global Spatial Autocorrelation with Moran’s I” in the linked sources below.

A permutation test separates the observed index from a reference built under spatial randomness. In an illustrative synthetic example, suppose five fixed districts have an observed Moran’s I of 0.32. Randomly reassigning the same five annual income-growth percentages to those locations 999 times produces 999 reference values; if 19 are at least 0.32, a one-sided Monte Carlo proportion is (19 + 1) ÷ (999 + 1) = 0.020, or 2.0%. The +1 correction avoids reporting a zero proportion. This indicates the observed association is unusual under the chosen randomization and weights, not that a spillover exists. The test also depends on exchangeability of values under the null and does not identify local causes or clusters. For a fuller treatment, see ‘PySAL esda — Global Spatial Autocorrelation with Moran’s I’ in the linked sources.

A useful diagnostic before interpreting a global index is to compute one local point exactly. Consider an illustrative synthetic focal district with standardized unemployment value zᵢ = 1.5. Suppose its four rook neighbours have z values 1.0, 0.6, 0.2 and 0.8, while its four diagonal neighbours have −0.4, 0.0, 0.2 and 0.4. If rook links have weight 1 and diagonal links have weight 0.5, the row sum is 4 + 4(0.5) = 6. The weighted neighbour total is 2.6 + 0.5(0.2) = 2.7, so the row-normalized spatial lag is 2.7/6 = 0.45. The corresponding Moran-scatter product for this district is zᵢ × lagᵢ = 1.5 × 0.45 = 0.675, a high–high contribution, but it is not a standalone local significance test. If diagonal weight were set to zero, the lag would instead be 2.6/4 = 0.65; the apparent local association changes because the neighbourhood definition changed, not because unemployment data changed. Standardization also means 1.5 and 0.45 are SD units, not percentage points. This is why compare settings and inspect the map before attributing a regional pattern to spillovers.

Moran’s I is best read together with its null and weights matrix. In a synthetic five-region map, an observed I of 0.30 may look positive, but its meaning depends on which pairs are connected and how rows are standardized. If 24 of 999 random permutations produce I values at least 0.30, the one-sided Monte Carlo proportion with the usual correction is (24 + 1)/(999 + 1) = 0.025, or 2.5%. That is unusual under this fixed-location randomization, not evidence that one region transmitted unemployment to another. Repeat with a substantively defensible alternative neighbourhood rule and inspect local patterns separately; a global statistic does not identify the responsible cluster. See “PySAL esda — Global Spatial Autocorrelation with Moran’s I”.","takeaway":"Moran’s I is a global association summary conditional on a specified weights matrix.","formula":"I = (n/S₀) · [ΣᵢΣⱼ wᵢⱼ zᵢzⱼ] / [Σᵢ zᵢ²], with zᵢ = yᵢ − ȳ and S₀ = ΣᵢΣⱼwᵢⱼ."},{"title":"Spatial lag and spatial error tell different stories","body":"A spatial-lag model includes a weighted average of neighbouring outcomes, which may represent an outcome feedback or spillover mechanism. A spatial-error model instead allows unobserved shocks to be correlated across nearby locations. These are different data-generating stories and require estimators designed for spatial dependence; ordinary least squares with a neighbouring-outcome term is generally not a valid shortcut because that term is endogenous. Economic institutions and timing should determine which story is plausible.

A simple comparison clarifies why the two models differ. Suppose, illustratively, a region’s annual output is 200 million currency units and its neighbours’ weighted average is 180 million. A spatial-lag equation might associate a 0.5 coefficient with that lag: 0.5 × 180 = 90 million currency units as the model’s neighbour-linked component, before adding the intercept and other predictors. In a spatial-error story, the same region could instead have an unobserved 12-million-unit shock correlated with nearby shocks; that shock is not an observed neighbouring outcome and should not be interpreted as a 90-million-unit effect. The lag coefficient requires assumptions about simultaneity and identification; correlation in errors does not prove transmission. Neither calculation alone establishes causality. For spatial-lag IV estimation and spatial-error models, see ‘PySAL spreg — Spatial Lag IV Estimation’ and ‘PySAL spreg — Spatial Error ML Estimation’; the esda source below supports the Moran-style calculation.

To see how a global association is assembled, use this illustrative four-region line, not observed data. Suppose standardized rental-growth values are z = (−1, −0.5, 0.5, 1), and each interior region averages its two adjacent neighbours while an endpoint uses its one neighbour. The resulting spatial lags are (−0.5, −0.25, 0.25, 0.5). Using the same row-normalized convention as the lab, the numerator is Σzᵢ(Wz)ᵢ = (−1)(−0.5) + (−0.5)(−0.25) + (0.5)(0.25) + (1)(0.5) = 1.25. The denominator is Σzᵢ² = 1 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 1 = 2.5, so the Moran-style ratio is 1.25/2.5 = 0.50. That positive value says high and low standardized outcomes tend to sit beside similar values under this chosen neighbour rule; it does not say a rail investment transmitted rental inflation. In the site’s 6×6 synthetic grid, changing ρ, diagonal weight, or the local shock changes the computed statistic. A randomization reference would additionally ask whether 0.40 is unusual after shuffling values across fixed locations; without that comparison, the number is descriptive, and edge handling and weights remain substantive assumptions.

Separate an observed neighbour outcome from an unobserved shared shock. In a synthetic model, region output is 140 million currency units and its row-standardized neighbour outcome is 100 million. A lag coefficient of 0.4 contributes 40 million units before the intercept and other terms; this is a model component, not automatically a causal effect. Under a spatial-error story, the region might instead receive an unobserved 8-million-unit shock correlated with nearby shocks, with no observed neighbour outcome entering the equation. Simultaneity makes neighbouring outcomes endogenous, so ordinary least squares with that term is not a safe shortcut. Choose the model from timing, institutions, and identification, not from a map alone. See “PySAL esda — Global Spatial Autocorrelation with Moran’s I”.","takeaway":"A spatial lag in outcomes and spatial correlation in unobserved shocks are not interchangeable."},{"title":"Stress-test the geography and causal claim","body":"Repeat descriptive diagnostics under defensible alternative weights, check influential regions, inspect residual spatial dependence and report how the map was constructed. A cross-sectional pattern can reflect shared industries, sorting, policies or measurement—not necessarily diffusion across borders. To estimate policy spillovers, define exposure to neighbouring treatment and a comparison strategy that addresses interference and common shocks. Keep the geographic estimand local to the units and network represented in the data.

Sensitivity analysis asks whether a conclusion survives reasonable definitions of nearby. Consider illustrative synthetic residuals from a regional regression: with a four-neighbour contiguity matrix, Moran’s I is 0.28; with a 100-kilometre distance band, it is 0.11; with six nearest neighbours, it is 0.20. The difference is 0.28 − 0.11 = 0.17 index points between the first two specifications, not 17 percentage points, because Moran’s I is dimensionless. A stable sign across choices supports a more robust descriptive association, while instability signals dependence on geography. These checks assume each alternative rule is substantively defensible and comparable. They do not turn residual similarity into a causal spillover or solve common shocks, sorting, or interference. For a fuller treatment, see ‘GeoDa Center — Global Spatial Autocorrelation workbook’ in the linked sources.

To move from a global signal to a local diagnostic, work cell by cell rather than calling every high Moran’s I result a cluster. In an illustrative synthetic 6×6 grid, suppose one region has standardized rent-growth residual zᵢ = 1.5 and its four equal-weight rook neighbours have z = 1.0, 0.8, −0.2, and 0.4. Its spatial lag is the weighted mean, (1.0 + 0.8 − 0.2 + 0.4) / 4 = 0.50, so the local cross-product zᵢ × lagᵢ = 1.5 × 0.50 = 0.75: a high value surrounded mostly by high values, despite one less-similar neighbour. Next, hold the residual values and weights fixed, randomly permute the 36 values across cells, and recompute that local statistic many times; the observed value’s rank in this reference distribution is evidence about unusual local concentration, not proof of diffusion. Repeat the diagnostic under a defensible diagonal-weight rule, record which regions change classification, and account for multiple local tests. A local result remains descriptive unless treatment exposure, timing, interference, and a credible counterfactual support a causal spillover claim.

A sensitivity table should show both the spatial rule and the statistic’s scale. In a synthetic residual analysis, contiguity gives Moran’s I = 0.31, a 50-kilometre band gives 0.18, and eight nearest neighbours gives 0.27. The largest difference is 0.13 index points, not 13 percentage points, because I is dimensionless. A stable positive sign supports a repeated descriptive association; the smaller value warns that strength depends on what “nearby” means. Also check whether one large region drives the result and whether residual dependence remains after covariates. None of these checks establishes rail-induced spillovers without an exposure definition, timing, comparison strategy, and interference assumptions. See “GeoDa Center — Global Spatial Autocorrelation workbook”.","takeaway":"Spatial adjustment can describe dependence; causal spillovers still need a research design."}]
data.case_study: A regional analyst studies rental inflation around a new commuter rail line. Neighbouring districts may share housing demand, commuters cross boundaries, and treatment exposure depends on distance as well as contiguity. The analyst starts with a transparent spatial weights matrix, maps the outcome and its spatial lag, checks global autocorrelation, then treats any causal spillover as a separate identification question.
data.misconceptions:
Positive spatial autocorrelation is not evidence that one region caused its neighbour’s outcome.
Moran’s I depends on the chosen weights matrix and data scale.
A spatial-lag coefficient should not be estimated by simply adding neighbouring outcomes to ordinary least squares.
A significant global statistic does not identify which regions form local clusters.

data.title: Bootstrap Inference & Resampling
data.excerpt: Bootstrap inference estimates how much a statistic may vary by repeatedly resampling the data already collected. See how to form standard errors and intervals, choose the right resampling unit for people, places or time periods, and why resampling cannot fix biased data.
data.objectives:
Construct a bootstrap distribution by sampling observed units with replacement.
Use bootstrap variation to describe standard errors and approximate confidence intervals.
Read a resample trace and histogram, and choose a resampling unit that reflects the study design.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Resample the data you have","body":"Choose the statistic that answers the question first: a median wage, a difference in employment rates or a regression slope. The population distribution is unknown, so the ordinary nonparametric bootstrap uses the observed sample's empirical distribution as a stand-in. Penn State STAT 555's process graphic makes the steps visible: sample, empirical-population approximation, computer resamples, then a distribution of the recomputed statistic. Draw n units with replacement, recompute T, and repeat. Reused rows are not new people; bootstrapping cannot repair a biased sample or reveal the unobserved population.

Illustrative synthetic example (weekly labour-market data, March 2026): suppose a survey records hourly wages for six randomly selected workers in one town: £12, £14, £15, £16, £18 and £25 per hour. The question is the town’s median hourly wage. Sort the observations and take the middle pair: (15 + 16) ÷ 2 = £15.50 per hour. To approximate its sampling variation, draw six wages with replacement from these observed values; one replicate might be £12, £15, £15, £18, £25 and £25, whose median is (15 + 18) ÷ 2 = £16.50 per hour. Repeat this resampling, say 5,000 times, and record each median. The resulting bootstrap distribution shows how the reported £15.50 estimate might vary under the observed sample’s empirical distribution.

A bootstrap can describe uncertainty conditional on the observed workers and their sampling process; it cannot establish the town’s true median with certainty, explain why wages differ, or recover workers omitted by nonresponse or an unrepresentative sample. The key decision check is whether the resampling unit matches the design: if workers came from sampled districts, resample districts or use an appropriate clustered procedure rather than treating every row as independent. Inspect the replicate trace for stability and the histogram for skew or extreme tails before summarising spread. Do not misinterpret 5,000 resamples as 5,000 new workers or as proof that the interval covers the parameter. The “Penn State STAT 555, §15.3 — Bootstrapping (sampling-distribution diagram)” in the linked sources below illustrates the workflow.

A useful way to see what replacement changes is to count distinct units, not just rows. Illustrative synthetic example: an original sample has four monthly sales amounts in dollars—$100, $120, $120, and $200. A size-four resample could be $120, $120, $120, and $200: four draws but only two distinct observations, and the mean is ($120 + $120 + $120 + $200) / 4 = $140 per month. The original mean is ($100 + $120 + $120 + $200) / 4 = $135 per month. This difference is sampling variation within the empirical distribution, not new sales. The method assumes the observed units reasonably represent the target process; it cannot correct systematic undercoverage. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 555, §15.3 — Bootstrapping (sampling-distribution diagram)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic lab audit: suppose the control is set to n = 50 and B = 400, and the recorded bootstrap medians have a mean of 20.4 synthetic units with a sum of squared deviations of 806.4 synthetic-units². The bootstrap standard deviation is sqrt[806.4 ÷ (400 − 1)] = sqrt(2.020) = 1.42 synthetic units, so it measures replicate-to-replicate spread, not the standard deviation of the 50 original observations. To form a nearest-rank 95% percentile interval, sort all 400 medians: the lower rank is ceil(0.025 × 400) = 10 and the upper rank is ceil(0.975 × 400) = 390. If those ordered values are 17.8 and 23.6 synthetic units, respectively, the reported interval is 17.8–23.6 synthetic units. The observed median should be marked separately (for example, 19.6 synthetic units); it need not equal the bootstrap mean. Percentile interpolation conventions can move an endpoint slightly, so record the convention and check that increasing B leaves the trace and endpoints broadly stable. This is an illustrative computer calculation, not an observed wage estimate or a guarantee of 95% coverage.

Replacement means a bootstrap replicate can repeat an observation while omitting another. For a synthetic sample of monthly profits $80, $100, $120, and $200, the observed mean is $125. One size-four replicate, $80, $80, $120, and $200, has mean ($80 + $80 + $120 + $200)/4 = $120. Another replicate can differ even though every draw comes from the same four recorded units. Across many replicates, the distribution describes variation conditional on this empirical sample. It does not add omitted firms, repair selection bias, or prove the population mean. If records are clustered by district, resample districts rather than rows. The sample and resampling unit must represent the collection design. See “Penn State STAT 555, §15.3 — Bootstrapping (sampling-distribution diagram)”.","takeaway":"The empirical distribution stands in for an unknown population only under stated sampling assumptions."},{"title":"Read spread and intervals from the bootstrap distribution","body":"The standard deviation of bootstrap estimates is a bootstrap standard error. A percentile interval uses quantiles of the bootstrap distribution as approximate confidence limits. For example, the central 95% interval is bounded by its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. These are methods for estimating uncertainty, not a guarantee that a particular interval contains the population value. Bias, skew, small samples and the chosen interval method can matter; compare a bootstrap interval with a defensible analytic alternative when one is available.

Take five illustrative hourly wages: £10, £11, £12, £13 and £30. Their median is £12. One bootstrap resample draws five entries with replacement—for example, £10, £11, £11, £12 and £30—and its median is £11. Another resample might have median £12. Repeating this many times creates a distribution of resampled medians. Its spread estimates how much the median could vary if the observed sample is a reasonable stand-in for the target population; quantiles of that distribution can form an approximate interval.

The repetitions reuse the same five workers; they do not create new evidence or reveal an unobserved wage group. If the original sample missed the highest-paid workers, a bootstrap cannot put them back. If the data were sampled in districts or observed through time, resampling individual rows may break the design or dependence; resample the appropriate clusters or time blocks instead. The interval also depends on the statistic and bootstrap method. See the NIST Bootstrap Plot and Hesterberg article linked below for practical guidance.

The formula’s units stay attached to the statistic: if each bootstrap estimate is a wage in dollars per hour, the bootstrap standard error is also dollars per hour, while a percentile interval has two dollar-per-hour endpoints. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose five bootstrap medians are £14, £15, £15, £16, and £20 per hour. Their average is (£14 + £15 + £15 + £16 + £20) / 5 = £16 per hour; the standard deviation describes spread in £ per hour, not percent. With many more replicates, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles would define an approximate 95% interval. Five values are too few for reliable tail percentiles, and the interval does not prove a 95% probability that this fixed parameter lies inside it. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Hesterberg (2015) — What Teachers Should Know About the Bootstrap (open access)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose an analyst estimates the median one-way commute time from seven sampled workers: 18, 21, 23, 24, 27, 32 and 46 minutes. The observed median is the fourth ordered value, 24 minutes. For each of B = 1,000 bootstrap replicates, draw seven worker records with replacement and recompute the median; do not divide by 1,000, because each resample still has n = 7. After sorting the medians, the lab’s linear-quantile rule places the lower endpoint at position 0.025(1,000 − 1) = 24.975, between the 25th and 26th ordered medians. If those are 18.4 and 18.5 minutes, the endpoint is 18.4 + 0.975(0.1) = 18.4975 minutes, or about 18.50 minutes. The upper position is 0.975(999) = 974.025; if the 975th and 976th values are 25.8 and 26.1 minutes, it is 25.8 + 0.025(0.3) = 25.8075, about 25.81 minutes. The approximate interval is therefore 18.50–25.81 minutes, conditional on workers being a defensible independent resampling unit. It describes sampling variation in the median, not the share of commuters whose true time lies in that range; clustered workplaces or survey weights require a different design.

The bootstrap lab reports two different summaries: Bootstrap SE of median is the sample standard deviation of the T* values, while the percentile interval uses their lower and upper quantiles. Suppose a synthetic set of five bootstrap medians is £18, £19, £20, £22, and £26 per hour. Their average is £21 per hour, but the standard deviation describes spread in pounds per hour, not percent. With only five replicates, tail quantiles are unstable; use many more repetitions before reading approximate 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. The trace should look stable as replicate number grows, and the histogram should reveal skew or boundary effects. Neither summary guarantees that a fixed population median lies inside the interval. See “NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook — Bootstrap Plot”.","takeaway":"A bootstrap interval is an approximation whose method and assumptions should be reported.","formula":"Bootstrap SE = SD(T*₁, …, T*ᴮ); percentile interval = [Q₂.₅%(T*), Q₉₇.₅%(T*)]."},{"title":"Match resampling to the data structure","body":"Resampling individual rows assumes those rows are exchangeable independent sampling units. If workers were sampled within a small set of districts, resample whole primary sampling units or use design-provided replicate weights rather than treating every worker as independent. For a time series, random row resampling destroys serial order; a block or model-based method may be needed. A bootstrap calculation is only as credible as its representation of how the data were collected.

The resampling unit should preserve the independent variation that generated the data. Synthetic example: two districts each contain three workers, with hourly wages in dollars of District A: 10, 11, 12 and District B: 20, 21, 22. If districts are the sampled units, a cluster bootstrap draws two districts, not six workers independently. Drawing A twice produces six wages—10, 11, 12, 10, 11, 12—and a mean of $11 per hour; drawing A and B once gives total $96 divided by 6 = $16 per hour. Independent row resampling would mix workers in a way the design may not support and can make uncertainty too small. This example assumes districts, rather than workers, were sampled; it does not establish a causal district effect. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke (2009), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 8 — Nonstandard Standard Error Issues’ in the linked sources.

Suppose an analyst has an illustrative, synthetic sample of five hourly wages (dollars per hour): 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16. The sample median is $14/hour. One bootstrap draw keeps size n = 5 but samples with replacement; for example, (13, 13, 15, 16, 16) has ordered middle value $15/hour, while (12, 12, 13, 14, 14) has median $13/hour. Repeating this operation B times creates a distribution of medians, not five new workers or a new wage survey. In a hypothetical run of B = 1,000, suppose the bootstrap medians have sample standard deviation $0.99/hour and percentile limits of $12/hour and $16/hour. Report the point estimate as $14/hour, the bootstrap SE as $0.99/hour, and the approximate percentile interval as [$12, $16] per hour. This interval describes sampling variation under the assumption that these observations reasonably represent independent draws from the target population; it is not a 95% probability statement about this fixed sample’s parameter. With n = 5, the replicate distribution is discrete and can have unreliable percentile coverage, so increasing B improves Monte Carlo smoothness but cannot repair poor representation or dependence.

The independent unit is determined by collection, not by spreadsheet layout. Synthetic example: three sampled districts each contain two wages: A has $12 and $14, B has $20 and $22, and C has $30 and $32. A district bootstrap draws three districts with replacement. Drawing A, B, and A yields six wages totaling $94, so the replicate mean is $15.67 per hour. Row-wise resampling could combine isolated workers from all districts and understate uncertainty when district conditions move together. For a time series, random rows also destroy order; blocks preserve local dependence. Record whether the design sampled people, districts, or time blocks before choosing a bootstrap. Repetitions cannot correct the wrong resampling unit. See “Angrist & Pischke (2009), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 8 — Nonstandard Standard Error Issues”.","takeaway":"The resampling unit follows the sampling design and dependence structure, not the spreadsheet row by default."},{"title":"Choose a bootstrap model and inspect its output","body":"The nonparametric bootstrap resamples observed cases; a parametric bootstrap simulates from a fitted distribution; some semiparametric methods resample and add carefully justified smoothing noise. These are different assumptions, not interchangeable buttons. A trace plot places each replicate's statistic against its replicate number, as in NIST's bootstrap-plot teaching graphic; a histogram then reveals the distribution's shape and tail spread. Check for Monte Carlo instability, skew, boundaries and statistics that depend heavily on unobserved tails. More repetitions smooth computation, not missing information.

Model choice changes what counts as plausible variation. Illustrative synthetic example: observed delivery times are 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 minutes. A nonparametric resample might be 2, 2, 4, 5, and 6, whose mean is (2 + 2 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 5 = 3.8 minutes. A parametric bootstrap fitted with a normal model could generate a value such as 7 minutes, which is not observed but is allowed by that model; the two procedures therefore answer different approximation questions. In a trace, replicate means of 3.8, 4.1, 3.9, and 4.0 minutes suggest little visible movement, whereas a sudden 9.0-minute value merits checking. More replicates reduce simulation noise, not model misspecification or bias. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook — Bootstrap Plot’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose seven independently sampled workers have weekly earnings of 18, 21, 23, 24, 31, 45, and 60 hundred dollars. The observed median is the fourth ordered value, 24 hundred dollars per week. To make one bootstrap replicate, draw seven workers with replacement; a possible draw is 21, 21, 24, 31, 45, 45, 60, whose median is the fourth value, 31 hundred dollars per week. Another draw, 18, 18, 21, 23, 23, 24, 31, has median 23 hundred dollars per week. Repeating this procedure B times creates medians T*. If the resulting synthetic bootstrap distribution has a 2.5th percentile of 21 and a 97.5th percentile of 31 hundred dollars per week, the percentile interval is 21–31 hundred dollars per week; it describes an approximation to sampling uncertainty around the sample median, not a 95% probability that the fixed population median lies inside these particular endpoints. The inference also assumes the observed sample reasonably represents the target population. For a stratified or region-clustered wage survey, resample within strata or resample regions as designed; row-wise resampling can understate uncertainty.

The bootstrap model determines which unobserved values are considered plausible. In a synthetic sample of delivery times 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 minutes, a nonparametric replicate may repeat 3 and omit 7, producing 3, 3, 4, 6, 6 with mean 4.4 minutes. A fitted parametric model might generate 8 minutes, which is not in the sample but could be allowed by its assumed distribution. In the lab, inspect the Bootstrap trace for drift or unstable runs, then use the distribution histogram to assess skew, tails, and boundaries. A smooth trace from more repetitions does not validate the model. Report method, resampling unit, statistic, and limitations. See “NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook — Bootstrap Plot”.","takeaway":"State how the population was approximated; use a trace plot for replicate stability and a histogram for distribution shape."},{"title":"Connect bootstrap intervals to econometric inference","body":"An estimated coefficient or median difference also needs an uncertainty calculation that respects the units and dependence in the study. If policy is assigned at a small number of districts, resampling individuals independently may make the interval too narrow. Angrist and Pischke's discussion of nonstandard standard errors and MIT's applied-econometrics reading list are useful follow-up reading on clustering and serial dependence; bootstrap methods still need their own design justification and do not automatically solve small-cluster inference.

Econometric estimates often combine a coefficient’s units with a dependence structure. Illustrative synthetic example: a policy coefficient is 2.0 percentage points in an employment-rate regression, and a cluster-aware bootstrap produces a standard error of 0.8 percentage points. A comparison is 2.0 / 0.8 = 2.5 standard-error units; that ratio is not a causal conclusion and is not a valid test statistic under few clusters. If four districts contribute many workers each, resampling workers can count thousands of rows as if they were thousands of independent policy assignments, understating uncertainty. Resampling districts respects the assignment level, but four independent districts still provide limited information. The interpretation also depends on a credible design and correctly measured outcome; a wider interval cannot repair confounding. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke (2009), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 8 — Nonstandard Standard Error Issues’ in the linked sources.

Consider an illustrative synthetic sample of six hourly wages, in dollars per hour: $18, $20, $21, $25, $31, and $40. The sample median is (21 + 25) / 2 = $23.00 per hour. One bootstrap resample must contain six draws with replacement; for example, [18, 21, 21, 31, 40, 40] has median (21 + 31) / 2 = $26.00 per hour. Another possible resample, [18, 18, 20, 21, 21, 25], has median (20 + 21) / 2 = $20.50 per hour. Repeating this operation B times gives a distribution of median estimates: its sample standard deviation is a bootstrap estimate of the median’s standard error, while its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles form an approximate 95% percentile interval. That interval describes uncertainty under repeated samples resembling these six observed units; it is not a 95% probability that the fixed population median lies inside this particular interval. The interpretation also relies on the six wages being a defensible independent resampling unit; survey weights, strata, or worker clustering would require a design-matched procedure, and a small sample can make percentile limits unstable.

A confidence interval is only as credible as the resampling unit behind it. Suppose a synthetic policy is assigned to four districts, each containing 50 surveyed workers, and the estimated employment-rate difference is 3 percentage points. Resampling all 200 worker rows independently treats them as 200 independent assignments, which can make uncertainty too small. A district bootstrap draws four districts with replacement, carries along their workers, and recomputes the difference. The worker count describes outcomes, but the independent policy units are districts. With only four clusters, percentile limits may still be unstable. This synthetic calculation is not an empirical finding or causal proof; assignment validity and nonresponse remain separate assumptions. See “Angrist & Pischke (2009), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 8 — Nonstandard Standard Error Issues.”","takeaway":"Clustering-aware inference is a design issue; a bootstrap does not fix too few independent assignment units."},{"title":"Apply it to a regional wage comparison","body":"A labour analyst wants to compare median hourly earnings between two regions, where earnings are skewed and group sizes differ. Resample workers separately within each region, calculate the median difference on every repetition, and summarize the resulting distribution. If workers were selected through a complex survey or grouped by sampled areas, the replication must reflect that design. The interval describes sampling uncertainty conditional on the observed data and assumptions; it does not remove nonresponse or establish why regional wages differ.

For two regions, compute the same contrast in every replicate so the units remain clear. Illustrative synthetic example: Region East has hourly wages of $15 and $21, while West has $12 and $14. The East median is ($15 + $21) / 2 = $18 per hour and the West median is ($12 + $14) / 2 = $13 per hour, so the observed difference is $5 per hour. In one separate-within-region resample, East draws 15 and 15 (median $15), while West draws 12 and 14 (median $13); that replicate difference is $2 per hour. Repeating this yields a distribution of differences, not a distribution of causes. Tiny groups make tail limits unstable, and unequal response or clustered sampling can invalidate simple resampling. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Hesterberg (2015) — What Teachers Should Know About the Bootstrap (open access)’ in the linked sources.

To see why the statistic must be recomputed, consider an illustrative synthetic sample of six hourly wages in one region: $18, $20, $22, $27, $40, and $45. The observed median is ($22 + $27)/2 = $24.50 per hour. A bootstrap replicate draws six values with replacement; for example, $18, $22, $22, $40, $45, $45 sorts to $18, $22, $22, $40, $45, $45, giving T* = ($22 + $40)/2 = $31.00 per hour. Do this B times, store every T*, and calculate the sample standard deviation of those B medians as the bootstrap standard error: SE* = sqrt[Σ(T*_b − mean(T*))²/(B − 1)]. If a synthetic run produced SE* = $3.10 per hour and its central 95% percentile cutoffs were $19.20 and $31.80, report those as approximate uncertainty for the population median under the resampling assumptions—not as a 95% chance that this fixed interval contains the parameter. With only six workers, duplicated draws and unstable tails are expected; preserve survey strata or clusters rather than treating workers as independent when the design says otherwise.

For a regional median comparison, keep the contrast identical through every replicate. Illustrative synthetic data give North wages of $10, $20, and $40 and South wages of $12, $14, and $16. The observed medians are $20 and $14, so North minus South equals $6 per hour. One bootstrap draw might repeat North’s $10, $40, $40, whose median is $40, and draw South’s $12, $12, $16, whose median is $12; that contrast is $28 per hour. Such a change is possible because each group is tiny, not evidence of a real wage shift. Read the replicate distribution as uncertainty about this sample contrast, while checking survey strata, weights, and nonresponse before using a simple bootstrap. The numbers are synthetic, not regional evidence. See “Hesterberg (2015) — What Teachers Should Know About the Bootstrap (open access).”","takeaway":"A useful bootstrap case still needs a clear target population and a defensible sample design.","practice":{"question":"In an ordinary bootstrap for n sampled workers, how is each resample formed?","hint":"Think about the sample size and whether a worker can appear more than once.","solution":"Draw n workers with replacement from the observed sample. A worker may appear multiple times or not at all in a given resample."}}]
data.case_study: A regional labour survey reports a median-wage gap. A bootstrap can show how that median difference varies across resamples, but the analyst must preserve any survey strata or sampled-area clustering and still discuss coverage and nonresponse separately.
data.misconceptions:
A bootstrap does not generate new population information beyond the observed sample.
A percentile interval is not guaranteed to work well for every statistic or small sample.
Resampling individual rows is not appropriate when the design or dependence structure requires resampling clusters or time blocks.
Increasing the number of repetitions cannot remove selection bias or measurement error.
