data.title: Regularization, Cross-Validation & Prediction
data.excerpt: When an economic prediction model has many overlapping predictors, a perfect fit to the historical sample may be a poor guide to the next month. Learn why Ridge and LASSO deliberately shrink coefficients, how cross-validation chooses tuning strength, and how to guard against leakage. An interactive synthetic lab lets you vary the penalty, predictor correlation and sample size while watching training and validation error move. The module also separates predictive success from causal evidence: a model that predicts unemployment well does not, by itself, identify what a policy would change.
data.objectives:
Explain how coefficient penalties trade a little bias for lower prediction variance.
Distinguish Ridge shrinkage from LASSO's ability to set coefficients to zero.
Use validation or cross-validation to choose a penalty without leaking test information.
Explain why a predictive model is not automatically a causal model.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Why a perfect historical fit can fail next month","body":"A model is overfitting when it learns sample-specific noise as if it were a stable economic relationship. Training error measures fit to the observations used to estimate the model; prediction error concerns new observations. Add enough interactions or flexible features and ordinary least squares can fit the training sample extremely closely while becoming unstable outside it. The target of this module is prediction, not a causal coefficient.

Think of forecasting local unemployment with dozens of highly related indicators. A small change in which districts enter the training data may produce large swings in estimated coefficients. First set aside observations that will not be used for fitting or tuning. They are the final test set; looking at them repeatedly turns them into another training resource.

A useful way to see the bias–variance trade-off is to compare repeated predictions, not just one fitted line. Illustrative synthetic example: for four new districts, an unregularized model predicts unemployment changes of 1.0, 5.0, 1.0, and 5.0 percentage points, while the actual changes are 3.0 percentage points in every district. Its squared errors are 4, 4, 4, and 4, so MSE = (4+4+4+4)/4 = 4 percentage-points-squared and RMSE = 2 percentage points. A steadier model predicts 2.5 points each time: every squared error is 0.25, giving RMSE = 0.5 percentage points. The example illustrates variance reduction, not proof that shrinkage always wins or that predictions explain causes. For a fuller treatment, see ‘James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani & Taylor — An Introduction to Statistical Learning (official free book site; linear-model regularization chapter)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic tuning exercise: suppose an agency has 36 monthly training observations and wants a one-month-ahead unemployment-change forecast in percentage points. Reserve the latest 6 months as a final test block, leaving 30 months for fitting and tuning. Within those 30 months, use rolling validation: fit on months 1–18 and score month 19, then fit on months 1–19 and score month 20, continuing through month 30. If λ = 0.00, 0.40, and 0.80 produce validation squared-error totals of 4.00, 2.25, and 3.24 percentage-points-squared across the 12 validation forecasts, their mean validation MSEs are 0.333, 0.188, and 0.270, so λ = 0.40 is selected because 0.188 is smallest; its validation RMSE is √0.188 ≈ 0.433 percentage points. Refit the chosen specification on all 30 tuning-period months, then evaluate the untouched six-month test block once. Standardize each predictor using means and standard deviations computed separately within each fitting window; using the full 36 months would leak future information. This procedure supports a forecast-performance claim, not a causal claim about unemployment policy.

Forecast evaluation must mimic the information available at the forecast date. Imagine a synthetic quarterly unemployment model trained through quarter 8 and evaluated on quarters 9–12. Predictions are 4, 6, 5, and 7 percentage points; actual changes are 5, 5, 6, and 6. Squared errors are 1, 1, 1, and 1, so test MSE is 1 and RMSE is 1 percentage point. Using later revisions or future indicators during preprocessing could report artificially low error because it leaked information. Randomly mixing future quarters into training folds creates a similar problem. Regularization may reduce coefficient instability, but cannot repair contaminated evaluation. These values are synthetic forecast arithmetic, not evidence about an agency or causal policy effect. See “James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani & Taylor — An Introduction to Statistical Learning (official free book site; linear-model regularization chapter).”","formula":"Expected prediction error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise (conceptual decomposition).","takeaway":"A small in-sample error does not tell you how well a model will predict new data.","practice":{"question":"A model has training RMSE 2 and test RMSE 14. What is the immediate warning?","hint":"Compare performance on seen and unseen observations.","solution":"The large gap is consistent with overfitting or a changed test distribution. It is not proof of which cause applies, but the training score alone is not a credible performance claim."}},{"title":"What Ridge and LASSO penalties change","body":"Regularization adds a cost for large coefficients to the usual residual-error objective. Ridge uses the sum of squared coefficients, so it continuously shrinks estimates and generally keeps every predictor. LASSO uses the sum of absolute coefficients; for some penalty strengths it sets some coefficients exactly to zero. Both can stabilize prediction when predictors are numerous or strongly correlated, but their coefficient patterns answer different questions.

Before applying either penalty, scale continuous predictors using information from the training data only. Otherwise the penalty acts on coefficients expressed in different units, so an equivalent economic effect can receive different shrinkage solely because one predictor is measured in dollars and another in a small rate. Standardize continuous predictors using training data only so the penalty operates on comparable predictor scales. The tuning parameter λ sets the strength of shrinkage: larger λ means a stronger penalty. The intercept is usually not penalized.

Suppose predictors have already been standardized using training data, so their coefficients refer to a one-standard-deviation change rather than raw currency units. Illustrative synthetic example: two candidate coefficient vectors are (0.8, −0.6), with RSS 10, and (0.4, −0.3), with RSS 11. At λ = 2, Ridge penalty contributions are 2(0.8²+0.6²)=2(1.00)=2.00 and 2(0.4²+0.3²)=2(0.25)=0.50. Their objectives are therefore 12.00 and 11.50, so Ridge prefers the smaller slopes. LASSO would use 2(|0.8|+|−0.6|)=2.80 versus 2(0.4+0.3)=1.40, and can make a coefficient exactly zero at stronger tuning. These are optimization comparisons, not causal evidence; scaling and the chosen λ matter. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Cunningham — Ridge, LASSO, Elastic Net and Cross-Validation (course notes)’ in the linked sources.

For a forecasting decision, choose λ with time-respecting validation rather than random folds. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose an agency has 12 quarterly observations and compares λ = 0.2 with λ = 0.8. In three expanding-window validation folds, the λ = 0.2 model has mean absolute forecast errors of 1.2, 1.0, and 1.3 percentage points, so its average is (1.2 + 1.0 + 1.3) / 3 = 1.17 percentage points. The λ = 0.8 model gives 1.3, 0.9, and 1.0 percentage points, averaging 3.2 / 3 = 1.07 percentage points; select 0.8 within the training period. In each fold, standardization and any feature screening must be fitted only on that fold’s earlier data, then applied to its later validation quarter. After selecting λ, refit using all pre-test quarters and evaluate once on the untouched future quarter. The lower validation average is evidence for better expected forecast accuracy under this split, not proof that shrinkage improved the economy or that any indicator causes unemployment. A changing regime or few quarters can make the chosen λ unstable.

Ridge and LASSO alter the optimization objective, so compare fit and penalty on the same scaled predictors. In a synthetic example, candidate A has RSS 9 and coefficients (0.7, −0.5); candidate B has RSS 10 and coefficients (0.3, −0.2), with λ = 1. Ridge objectives are 9 + 0.7² + 0.5² = 9.74 for A and 10 + 0.3² + 0.2² = 10.13 for B, so Ridge prefers A despite larger slopes. LASSO objectives are 9 + 0.7 + 0.5 = 10.2 and 10 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 10.5, again preferring A. A larger λ could reverse the choice, and LASSO may set coefficients to zero. Standardization must use training data only; selected variables are predictive choices, not causal discoveries. See “Cunningham — Ridge, LASSO, Elastic Net and Cross-Validation (course notes).”","formula":"Ridge: minimise RSS + λΣβⱼ². LASSO: minimise RSS + λΣ|βⱼ|; the unpenalized intercept is omitted from the sums.","takeaway":"Ridge shrinks all slopes; LASSO can also remove predictors, but neither penalty makes a causal design.","practice":{"question":"With many almost-duplicate labour-market indicators, which penalty is more likely to keep a group of small nonzero coefficients?","hint":"Compare continuous shrinkage with exact zeros.","solution":"Ridge tends to retain and shrink correlated predictors together. LASSO may select a smaller set, but which member of a correlated group survives can be unstable."}},{"title":"Choose the penalty with cross-validation","body":"Cross-validation repeatedly hides part of the training data, fits on the remainder, and scores predictions on the hidden fold. Average the scores across folds for each candidate λ, then choose a value using the stated rule—for example, the minimum average error or a simpler model whose error is close to that minimum. This uses training data efficiently while retaining an untouched test set for one final performance check.

Every learned preprocessing step belongs inside the fold: scaling, imputation, feature screening and dimensionality reduction must be recalculated from that fold's training portion. If you use the full dataset to choose predictors before splitting, information from the held-out outcomes has leaked into model selection. For a time series, use forward or rolling-origin validation rather than randomly mixing future observations into past training folds.

Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data): suppose we want to predict a county's monthly unemployment rate, measured in percentage points, one month ahead. We have 24 consecutive months and three predictors: housing permits per month, job vacancies per month, and the monthly change in retail employment. Keep the final six months untouched as the test period; use the first 18 months for training and three time-ordered validation folds. After standardizing each predictor inside each fold, try three Ridge penalties, lambda = 0.1, 1, and 10. Their average validation mean squared errors are 0.64, 0.49, and 0.56 percentage-points-squared. Choose lambda = 1 because 0.49 is smallest, so the cross-validated RMSE is the square root of 0.49 = 0.70 percentage points. Then refit using all 18 training months and evaluate once on the six-month test period.

A cross-validation result can help choose a penalty for prediction under this stated horizon and loss; it cannot establish that vacancies, permits, or retail employment cause unemployment changes, nor that the selected coefficient is a policy effect. A key diagnostic is whether the validation design respects time: every validation month must be predicted using only earlier training months, and scaling, imputation, and feature screening must be learned anew within each fold. Also compare the chosen model with a simple baseline, such as last month's unemployment rate. Do not interpret the smallest validation error as proof that the model is true or permanently best; it is evidence conditional on the sample, folds, predictors, and future regime. The James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani & Taylor - An Introduction to Statistical Learning (official free book site; linear-model regularization chapter) is named in the linked sources below.

Cross-validation is an estimate of future predictive loss, so the loss must match the reporting unit. Illustrative synthetic example: three validation folds forecast monthly inflation, measured in percentage points, with squared errors 0.36, 0.49, and 0.25 for one candidate λ. The average MSE is (0.36+0.49+0.25)/3 = 1.10/3 = 0.3667 percentage-points-squared; RMSE is √0.3667 ≈ 0.61 percentage points. A competing λ with fold MSEs 0.25, 0.64, and 0.36 averages 0.4167, so the first is preferred under squared-error loss. Each fold must learn scaling and imputation from its training portion only. This comparison does not guarantee future performance if the economic regime changes. For a fuller treatment, see ‘James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani & Taylor — An Introduction to Statistical Learning (official free book site; linear-model regularization chapter)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic calculation (not observed data): suppose two predictors have already been standardized, so one unit means one training-sample standard deviation, and the outcome is next-month unemployment in percentage points. For 100 training observations, let the cross-products be X′X = [[100, 80], [80, 100]] (correlation 0.80) and X′y = [100, 20]. Ordinary least squares solves X′Xβ = X′y, giving β₁ = (10,000 − 1,600)/3,600 = 2.33 and β₂ = (−8,000 + 2,000)/3,600 = −1.67 percentage points per predictor SD. With a Ridge penalty λ = 20 under the objective ||y−Xβ||² + λ||β||², solve (X′X + 20I)β = X′y: the matrix is [[120,80],[80,120]], whose determinant is 8,000, so β₁ = (12,000−1,600)/8,000 = 1.30 and β₂ = (−8,000+2,400)/8,000 = −0.70. The coefficients move toward zero while retaining their signs, illustrating stability under collinearity—not a causal effect. Because penalty scaling conventions differ, compare λ values only within the same implementation, and select it inside the training folds; the untouched test period still supplies the final check.

Cross-validation is a comparison of prediction rules, so define the forecast information set before calculating scores. Illustrative synthetic example: a model predicts quarterly vacancy rates in percentage points using 16 earlier quarters, with four rolling validation origins. Candidate penalties have fold MSEs 0.81, 0.49, 0.64, and 0.36 for one setting, averaging 2.30/4 = 0.575 percentage-points-squared; its RMSE is √0.575 ≈ 0.76 percentage points. A second setting averages 0.64, so the first wins under squared loss. Scaling and imputation must be refit at every origin, and a final future block remains untouched. This is synthetic forecast arithmetic, not an unemployment result or causal estimate. At very weak penalties a flexible model may have low training error but high validation error; stronger shrinkage can reduce instability, while excessive shrinkage eventually adds too much bias. A broad flat minimum is often more informative than a tiny numerical difference between neighbouring tuning values. The choice should also reflect the cost of a complex or unstable model.

Report the outcome, prediction horizon, loss function, split rule, tuning procedure and uncertainty or variation in performance across folds. Compare with a simple baseline such as last month's value or a low-dimensional regression. A sophisticated model is useful only if it beats a reasonable benchmark under a fair evaluation, not because its training fit looks impressive.

A validation curve should be read with its uncertainty and practical costs, not as a command to select the numerically smallest point. Illustrative synthetic example: three penalties produce validation RMSEs of 1.02, 1.00, and 1.01 percentage points for one-month-ahead unemployment forecasts. The middle penalty is lowest, but the spread is only 0.02 percentage points; fold-to-fold variation could easily exceed that difference. If the stronger penalty uses four predictors instead of twelve, it may be a sensible simpler choice when accuracy is effectively tied. Report that the target is a percentage-point forecast, the time horizon is one month, and the score is RMSE. A flat curve supports caution, not a claim that all penalties are identical or that the model is causal. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Cunningham — Ridge, LASSO, Elastic Net and Cross-Validation (course notes)’ in the linked sources.

Use the lab’s stylized equations to make the bias–variance trade-off concrete, while treating every value below as synthetic teaching output rather than observed economic data. With predictor correlation ρ = 0.70 and training size n = 100, the renderer’s noise term is (0.2 + 1.4ρ)(100/n) = (0.2 + 0.98)×1 = 1.18 relative-error units. At λ = 0.55, training error is 0.45 + 0.55λ + 0.08λ² = 0.45 + 0.3025 + 0.0242 = 0.7767, whereas validation error is 0.90 + 0.55λ² + 1.18/(1 + 4λ) = 0.90 + 0.1664 + 1.18/3.20 = 1.4351. Removing the penalty (λ = 0) lowers training error to 0.45 but raises validation error to 2.08; pushing to λ = 1.40 raises validation error again to about 2.16 because bias dominates. On the lab’s 36-point grid, the minimum is λ = 0.48 with validation error 1.4308, so λ = 0.55 is a nearby, practically similar choice—not evidence of a precise optimum. This calculation assumes the stylized curve is the evaluation rule; real tuning must recompute preprocessing and folds inside training data, then use an untouched future test period.

A tuning curve is most useful when its horizontal scale and uncertainty are visible. Suppose, illustratively, that log-penalties −3, −1, and 1 produce validation RMSEs of 2.41, 2.38, and 2.40 percentage points for the same forecast horizon. The middle value is numerically smallest, but the maximum difference is only 0.03 percentage points. If fold variation is larger, the ranking is fragile; choosing the more strongly penalized model may be reasonable if it uses fewer predictors and has nearly equal error. That choice should be reported as a stability or simplicity decision, not as proof that the stronger penalty is true. Compare every candidate with a baseline and preserve the test set. Prefer a stable or simpler choice and report that the minimum is flat."}},{"title":"Keep prediction separate from economic explanation","body":"A predictive model is judged by how well it forecasts outcomes under a defined evaluation design. A causal analysis asks what would happen under an intervention and needs a research design and identifying assumptions. LASSO may be useful for building forecasts or screening a large set of candidate controls, but a selected nonzero coefficient is not automatically an unbiased treatment effect. Selection also changes the uncertainty calculations that would be appropriate for causal claims.

For example, a set of indicators might predict which towns experience employment declines without revealing the effect of a wage subsidy. State the purpose first, keep all feature selection within the training process, and use a causal design—such as a credible experiment, instrument or quasi-experiment—when the question is about policy effects. Revisit the site's causal and IV modules for those design questions.

Prediction and intervention can disagree even when a model forecasts well. Illustrative synthetic example: among 100 applicants, a fitted model labels 20 as high risk of missing a loan payment, and 15 of those actually miss payments; among 80 labeled low risk, 8 miss payments. The observed rates are 15/20 = 75% and 8/80 = 10%, a 65-percentage-point association in this synthetic sample. That gap may help target forecasts, but it does not tell us what would happen if every applicant received a counselling programme: applicants were not randomly assigned, and risk factors may affect both counselling and repayment. A causal effect needs a credible counterfactual design, not merely a selected coefficient or risk gap. For a fuller treatment, see ‘James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani & Taylor — An Introduction to Statistical Learning (official free book site; linear-model regularization chapter)’ in the linked sources.

Consider an explicitly synthetic forecasting calculation with unemployment measured in percentage points and two predictors standardized to one SD: a vacancy-rate index z₁ and a claims index z₂. Suppose the training fit has intercept 5.0 pp and OLS slopes 0.80 and −0.60 pp per predictor SD. To show the algebra cleanly, assume the standardized columns are orthogonal and scaled so X′X = I, and use the ridge objective SSE + λ(β₁² + β₂²), leaving the intercept unpenalized. At λ = 1, each slope becomes β̂/(1+λ): 0.80/2 = 0.40 and −0.60/2 = −0.30 pp per SD. For a region with z₁ = 1.5 and z₂ = −1.0, OLS predicts 5.0 + 0.80(1.5) − 0.60(−1.0) = 6.80 pp, whereas ridge predicts 5.0 + 0.40(1.5) − 0.30(−1.0) = 5.90 pp. The 0.90-pp difference is shrinkage, not a causal claim. With correlated columns, slopes change jointly rather than by this simple factor; choose λ by training-only validation and test the final forecast on a later, untouched period.

A variable can be excellent for forecasting while being unsuitable for an intervention claim. Consider an illustrative synthetic model that predicts next-month electricity demand from weather, calendar indicators, and a utility’s past discount code. If the code improves forecast accuracy, it may proxy for expected demand or operational planning; its selected coefficient does not reveal what demand would be under a new discount policy. The relevant causal question requires a counterfactual assignment design, not merely a nonzero LASSO coefficient. Keep feature selection inside training data, describe the prediction target and horizon, and reserve causal language for a design that supports it. The example is constructed and neither predicts real demand nor estimates a policy effect. data.case_study: An employment agency wants next-quarter regional unemployment forecasts from a large set of correlated indicators. The lesson uses a synthetic example to compare an ordinary least-squares benchmark with shrinkage, selects tuning strength inside training data, and keeps a future test period untouched. The result is discussed as a forecast, not as an estimate of any programme's effect.
data.misconceptions:
A lower training error does not necessarily mean better out-of-sample predictions.
LASSO selection is not proof that the chosen variable is economically causal or uniquely important.
Cross-validation does not remove leakage if preprocessing or feature selection used held-out information.
Random folds do not respect temporal order in forecasting problems.

data.title: Meta-Analysis & Evidence Synthesis for Economics
data.excerpt: A policy can be evaluated in many places and periods, producing a set of estimates rather than one decisive study. Learn how meta-analysis combines comparable effect estimates using their precision, why between-study differences call for a random-effects perspective, and how meta-regression relates effects to study features. The interactive forest-plot lab generates a clearly labelled synthetic evidence set and compares fixed- and random-effects summaries. The lessons also cover publication bias, multiple estimates from the same study, transparent inclusion rules and why counting significant results is not a substitute for synthesis.
data.objectives:
Prepare a study-level dataset of comparable effect estimates and standard errors.
Explain inverse-variance weighting and the difference between fixed- and random-effects summaries.
Describe heterogeneity, meta-regression and dependence among estimates.
Recognize publication bias and avoid vote-counting conclusions.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Start with a question and a study-selection rule","body":"Meta-analysis combines estimates from multiple studies that address a sufficiently similar question. Before collecting numbers, define the population, intervention or exposure, outcome, comparison, follow-up window and eligible study designs. Record how studies were searched for and why each was included or excluded. This prevents a convenient collection of positive results from silently becoming the evidence base.

The working dataset usually has one row per independent estimate, with an effect estimate, its standard error, study identifier and useful design or population features. Extract estimates from published and unpublished sources where possible. A meta-analysis cannot make unlike outcomes comparable merely by placing them in the same spreadsheet; decide which effects can be meaningfully put on a common scale and explain that choice.

Begin by writing the estimand in ordinary language: for example, the change in monthly wages in US dollars 12 months after a training offer, compared with no offer, among unemployed adults. Then apply the same rule to every candidate report. Illustrative synthetic example: Report A measures wages at 6 months, Report B at 12 months, and Report C reports a standardized test score rather than dollars. If the protocol targets 12-month wages, A is excluded or separately classified, B is eligible, and C is ineligible unless a prespecified conversion is defensible. This step prevents a pooled number from mixing units or time horizons. Inclusion rules reduce discretion, but they cannot remove selective reporting or flaws in the underlying studies. For a fuller treatment, see “Chabefer — Statistical Tools for Causal Inference, Chapter 13: Meta-analysis and Publication Bias” in the linked sources.

Apply the eligibility rule at the estimate level, not merely at the report level. Illustrative synthetic example: a single job-training evaluation publishes three numbers—an intention-to-treat (ITT) change in employment of 4.0 percentage points at 12 months with standard error 1.5 percentage points, a 6-month ITT change of 2.0 percentage points, and a 12-month per-protocol change of 6.0 percentage points. If the protocol names the 12-month ITT effect among all people offered training, retain only the first estimate for the primary dataset; classify the other two as secondary or exclude them under the written rule. Do not enter all three as independent studies: they reuse participants, so treating them as separate rows for a pooled analysis would overstate the amount of independent evidence and could give this evaluation excessive influence. Record the study identifier, estimand, follow-up, analysis population, and reason for exclusion, then check whether another report from the same evaluation supplies overlapping participants. This bookkeeping does not make the 4.0-point estimate causal by itself; its interpretation still depends on the evaluation’s design and assumptions.

A review protocol should make an estimate eligible because it answers the target question, not because its sign is attractive. Suppose the target is the effect of a job-search offer on monthly earnings in dollars, measured six months after assignment, among unemployed adults. An illustrative report gives a four-month earnings effect, another gives six-month earnings, and a third gives a six-month standardized wellbeing score. The second matches the target; the first needs a prespecified separate category or exclusion, and the third is not interchangeable without a defensible conversion. Record search dates, eligible designs, population, comparison, outcome units, and follow-up. A pooled number cannot repair mismatched estimands. These examples are synthetic. See “Chabefer — Statistical Tools for Causal Inference, Chapter 13: Meta-analysis and Publication Bias.”","takeaway":"A transparent review question and inclusion rule come before weighting or pooling.","practice":{"question":"Why might a review of job-training programmes record follow-up time as well as an earnings effect?","hint":"The effect may differ between the first year and later years.","solution":"Time horizon changes the estimand and can explain real differences between estimates. Combining short- and long-run effects without a plan can obscure what the pooled quantity means."}},{"title":"Weight estimates by precision, not by significance","body":"An estimate with a smaller standard error typically contains more sampling information than a very noisy estimate. In a simple fixed-effect model, inverse-variance weights are wₖ = 1/SEₖ², and the pooled estimate is the weighted mean of study estimates. This is not a vote: a small study with a large point estimate should not automatically count as much as a precise study. Nor should studies be weighted by whether their p-value falls below a threshold.

The fixed-effect calculation assumes one shared underlying effect and attributes differences among estimates to sampling error. That can be a useful benchmark, but it is often a strong description for policies implemented in different labour markets, institutions or years. Check the study scales and standard errors before interpreting any pooled number.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose three evaluations of job-training programmes report the change in employment rate, measured in percentage points, 12 months after enrolment. Study A estimates +4 percentage points with SE 1; Study B estimates +8 points with SE 2; Study C estimates 0 points with SE 2. Fixed-effect inverse-variance weights are 1/1² = 1, 1/2² = 0.25 and 1/2² = 0.25. The pooled estimate is [1(4) + 0.25(8) + 0.25(0)] ÷ [1 + 0.25 + 0.25] = 6 ÷ 1.5 = +4 percentage points. Study A receives four times the weight of either less precise study because its sampling uncertainty is smaller; this is a calculation for the stated 12-month outcome, not a claim about every programme.

The fixed-effect result can summarize a common underlying effect when the studies measure a sufficiently comparable 12-month employment outcome and their reported standard errors and sampling models are credible. It cannot establish that all settings share one true effect, that training caused the difference if the underlying designs are biased, or that +4 percentage points will occur in a new labour market. Check the effect scale, follow-up window, confidence intervals and forest plot for incompatible definitions or unusually different estimates before pooling. Do not count each significant paper as one vote: significance depends on precision. For further context, see “Haghnejad & Farahati (2024) — An Overview of Meta-Analytic Methods for Economic Research (open preprint)” in the linked sources below.

Inverse-variance weighting can be read as a comparison of information, not importance or quality. Illustrative synthetic example: two studies estimate a rent change in dollars per month: Study X is +$30 with SE $10, and Study Y is +$50 with SE $20. Their weights are 1/10² = 0.01 and 1/20² = 0.0025, so X receives four times Y’s weight. The pooled value is [0.01(30) + 0.0025(50)] ÷ 0.0125 = 0.425 ÷ 0.0125 = $34 per month. This arithmetic assumes a common underlying effect and comparable dollar definitions. It does not prove the estimate is unbiased, nor does precision compensate for a poorly designed study. For a fuller treatment, see “Haghnejad & Farahati (2024) — An Overview of Meta-Analytic Methods for Economic Research (open preprint)” in the linked sources.

A random-effects calculation changes the question from “which estimate is most precise?” to “how should precision be balanced against genuine cross-setting spread?” Illustrative synthetic example: three evaluations report weekly earnings changes, all in dollars per week: Study A is +$12 (SE $3), Study B is +$20 (SE $5), and Study C is −$4 (SE $4). Suppose the analyst sets, rather than estimates, the between-study SD at τ = $6 per week. The random-effects weight is 1/(SE² + τ²), giving A 1/(9+36)=1/45, B 1/(25+36)=1/61, and C 1/(16+36)=1/52. Thus the pooled estimate is [(12/45)+(20/61)−(4/52)] ÷ [(1/45)+(1/61)+(1/52)] = $8.95 per week, approximately $9.00. The added τ² narrows the weight gap: A is only about 1.36 times as heavily weighted as B, not 2.78 times under fixed-effect weights. This summary targets the mean effect across the included settings; its interpretation depends on comparable earnings definitions and a defensible τ, and it does not correct selective publication, dependence, or biased study designs.

Inverse-variance weighting rewards smaller standard errors under a fixed-effect model, but it does not certify study quality. Illustrative synthetic estimates of a common wage change are Study A = $12 per month with SE $3 and Study B = $20 with SE $6. Their weights are 1/3² = 1/9 and 1/6² = 1/36, so A receives four times B’s weight. The pooled value is [(1/9)×12 + (1/36)×20] ÷ [(1/9)+(1/36)] = (48/36+20/36)/(5/36) = 68/5 = $13.60 per month. This arithmetic assumes a shared effect and comparable definitions. A precise but biased design is not rescued by its weight, and significance is not a weighting rule. See “Haghnejad & Farahati (2024) — An Overview of Meta-Analytic Methods for Economic Research (open preprint).”","formula":"Fixed-effect pooled estimate = Σ(wₖ θ̂ₖ) / Σwₖ, with wₖ = 1 / SEₖ².","takeaway":"Precision weighting uses uncertainty; it is not a count of positive or statistically significant papers.","practice":{"question":"Study A estimates +0.2 with SE 0.05; Study B estimates +0.8 with SE 0.40. Which carries more fixed-effect weight?","hint":"Compare the inverse squared standard errors.","solution":"Study A has far greater inverse-variance weight because its standard error is much smaller. This arithmetic does not decide whether a fixed-effect assumption is credible."}},{"title":"Allow effects to vary across settings","body":"A random-effects model allows the underlying effect to differ across studies. A common teaching formulation adds an estimated between-study variance τ² to each study's sampling variance, giving weight 1/(SEₖ² + τ²). When τ² is larger, normalized weights become more balanced: a small or imprecise study can receive a larger share of the pooled mean than under fixed-effect weighting, although adding τ² reduces every study’s raw inverse-variance weight. This is not a universal correction for poor evidence; it changes the model and the target summary.

The pooled mean describes an average across the included distribution of settings, not necessarily the effect in a particular town or future policy. Report a heterogeneity measure and inspect the individual estimates and intervals. A wide range can mean that the average alone is not the most useful policy conclusion.

The between-study variance τ² is measured in squared effect units, so it is added to SE² before inversion. Illustrative synthetic example: effects are annual earnings changes in dollars, with Study A = $100 and SE = $10, Study B = $140 and SE = $20, and τ² = 300 (dollars squared). The random-effects weights are 1/(100 + 300) = 0.0025 and 1/(400 + 300) ≈ 0.00143. The pooled mean is (0.0025×100 + 0.00143×140) ÷ (0.0025 + 0.00143) ≈ $114.6 per year. The added variance makes weights less unequal. This average describes the modeled distribution of included settings; it does not predict every labour market or establish causality. For a fuller treatment, see “Haghnejad & Farahati (2024) — An Overview of Meta-Analytic Methods for Economic Research (open preprint)” in the linked sources.

A useful second question is how much a genuinely new setting could differ from the pooled mean. Illustrative synthetic review: suppose a random-effects summary of standardized annual earnings effects is 0.30 SD, with standard error 0.12 SD, and the assumed between-setting standard deviation is τ = 0.40 SD. First report the average-effect interval: 0.30 ± 1.96(0.12) = 0.30 ± 0.235, or approximately 0.06 to 0.54 SD. Then include heterogeneity when forming a rough 95% prediction interval for one comparable future setting: 0.30 ± 1.96√(0.12² + 0.40²) = 0.30 ± 0.82, giving about −0.52 to 1.12 SD. The wide prediction range says that a positive pooled average can coexist with little effect or a negative effect in some labour markets; it is not evidence that any particular programme will fall in that range. This calculation assumes effects are comparable, the random-effects distribution is a reasonable approximation, and τ is adequately estimated; the interactive lab instead supplies τ as a teaching assumption. If the outcome were in dollars rather than standardized units, every interval endpoint would need dollar units, not percentage points.

Random-effects weighting changes the question from one common effect to an average across a distribution of settings. Take two illustrative synthetic estimates of annual earnings change: Study A is $80 with SE $8 and Study B is $140 with SE $16. If between-study variance is τ² = 256 dollars squared, the weights are 1/(64+256) = 0.003125 and 1/(256+256) = 0.001953125. The pooled mean is (0.003125×80 + 0.001953125×140)/(0.005078125) ≈ $103.1. Without τ², the first study would receive four times the second study’s weight; with it, the ratio is 1.6. The average is not guaranteed for a new labour market, and τ² itself is estimated. See “Haghnejad & Farahati (2024) — An Overview of Meta-Analytic Methods for Economic Research (open preprint).”","formula":"Random-effects weight: wₖ = 1 / (SEₖ² + τ²), where τ² is between-study variance.","takeaway":"A random-effects average summarizes a distribution of settings; it does not make those settings identical.","practice":{"question":"What happens to the relative weights of small and large studies when τ² grows?","hint":"A common variance component is added to every study's sampling variance.","solution":"The precision differences matter less, so weights become more balanced than in the fixed-effect formula. The uncertainty about τ² and the appropriateness of the model still matter."}},{"title":"Explain heterogeneity without overfitting the review","body":"Meta-regression relates study-level effects to recorded study features such as programme length, baseline employment or outcome timing. It can help organize why studies differ, but it uses the number of studies—not the number of participants in the original trials—as its effective information base. With few studies and many moderators, apparently precise stories can be unstable. Study-level associations also do not establish that an individual participant would respond the same way.

Some papers report several outcomes or specifications from the same sample. Those estimates share information and are dependent. Treating them as independent rows can overstate precision. Choose a primary estimate using a rule, combine them appropriately, or use a model that represents their dependence. Describe the choices so another researcher can reproduce the synthesis.

Meta-regression uses studies as its units, so a moderator coefficient describes between-study pattern rather than an individual-level response. Illustrative synthetic example: four independent studies report effects in percentage points, and the fitted difference between programmes lasting 12 weeks and 8 weeks is +2 percentage points. If the 8-week predicted effect is +3 percentage points, the 12-week prediction is 3 + 2 = +5 percentage points. That comparison is based on four study observations, not four participants; adding many outcomes from one sample does not create independent evidence. Correlated estimates should be combined, selected by a prespecified rule, or modeled for dependence. The coefficient may reflect confounding study features and is not a causal return to extending a programme. For a fuller treatment, see “Chabefer — Statistical Tools for Causal Inference, Chapter 13: Meta-analysis and Publication Bias” in the linked sources.

Consider this purely illustrative synthetic calculation. Three comparable studies estimate an effect in standardized units: 0.10 (SE 0.10), 0.40 (SE 0.20), and 0.70 (SE 0.40). Under a fixed-effect model, weights are 1/SE², namely 100, 25, and 6.25; the pooled estimate is (100×0.10 + 25×0.40 + 6.25×0.70) ÷ 131.25 = 0.186. The smallest-SE study therefore dominates. Now suppose, as a teaching assumption rather than an estimate from these three studies, that between-study SD τ = 0.30. Random-effects weights become 1/(SE² + τ²): 10.00, 7.69, and 4.00, giving (10×0.10 + 7.69×0.40 + 4×0.70) ÷ 21.69 = 0.317 (rounded). The corresponding approximate standard error is √(1/21.69) = 0.215, so a normal-approximation 95% interval is 0.317 ± 1.96×0.215, or about −0.10 to 0.74 standardized units. Adding τ² both reduces precision and prevents one very precise study from deciding the average. Because τ is assumed here, changing it changes the estimand’s weighting; it does not prove that the studies share a common causal effect or repair selective reporting or dependence. The interactive lab makes the same structural distinction with synthetic studies, a user-controlled τ, and normal-approximation intervals.

Meta-regression treats studies, not participants, as observations. Suppose five evaluations report employment effects by programme length. A fitted +1.5-percentage-point contrast between 10- and 6-week programmes corresponds, under a linear moderator, to 1.5 ÷ (10−6) = 0.375 points per additional programme week at study level—not an individual dose response. Studies differ in populations and design, so that slope does not predict any participant’s gain from adding a week. If one evaluation contributes four outcomes from the same sample, treating them as four independent studies exaggerates information unless dependence is modeled or one outcome is prespecified. Five studies also limit moderator count. Report study count, dependence handling, and exploratory status. Synthetic values do not show that longer programmes cause employment gains. See “Chabefer — Statistical Tools for Causal Inference, Chapter 13: Meta-analysis and Publication Bias.”","takeaway":"Study features can explain variation, but the review still needs enough independent studies and a defensible dependence model.","practice":{"question":"A review has 12 independent studies and tests 15 meta-regression moderators. What is the main concern?","hint":"The moderator count is large relative to the number of studies.","solution":"The study-level model is likely to be unstable and vulnerable to overfitting. Treat subgroup patterns as exploratory or reduce the moderator set using a prespecified rationale."}},{"title":"Check what the published evidence leaves out","body":"If studies with statistically significant or preferred-direction results are more likely to appear in journals, the observed set can be a selected sample of all analyses performed. Funnel plots and regression-based checks can flag patterns, but they cannot prove publication bias or repair missing evidence by themselves. Small-study effects may also arise because smaller studies differ in design, populations or implementation.

Do not count how many papers are “significant” and call that an average effect: significance depends on sample size and precision. Report the search protocol, small-study diagnostics and sensitivity analyses alongside the pooled estimate. If the evidence remains heterogeneous or selectively observed, say so. A careful synthesis communicates what the available studies can and cannot support.

A funnel diagnostic asks whether effect estimates become systematically different as their standard errors change, but the pattern has several explanations. Illustrative synthetic example: among six small studies with SE 0.30, five report positive employment effects and one negative; among six large studies with SE 0.10, three are positive and three negative. The simple positive proportions are 5/6 = 83.3% versus 3/6 = 50.0%, a 33.3-percentage-point difference. That contrast may signal selective publication, but it could also reflect genuinely different populations, methods, or chance. It is not a probability that a missing study exists, and it does not correct the pooled estimate. Pre-register searches, inspect unpublished evidence, and report sensitivity analyses. For a fuller treatment, see “Chabefer — Statistical Tools for Causal Inference, Chapter 13: Meta-analysis and Publication Bias” in the linked sources.

A useful sensitivity exercise is to ask how much an unobserved null result would matter, without pretending that it exists. Use an explicitly illustrative, synthetic fixed-effect calculation in standardized employment-effect units: three published estimates are 0.30 (SE 0.10), 0.20 (SE 0.20), and 0.10 (SE 0.20). Their inverse-variance weights are 1/0.10² = 100 and 1/0.20² = 25 for each of the other two, so the pooled estimate is (100×0.30 + 25×0.20 + 25×0.10)/(100+25+25) = 37.5/150 = 0.25 SD units. Now posit, purely as a sensitivity scenario, two unpublished null estimates with SE 0.20; each contributes weight 25 and zero to the numerator, giving 37.5/(150+50) = 0.1875, or about 0.19 SD units. The change is 0.0625 SD units, not proof that two studies are missing and not a corrected estimate. Repeat the exercise across plausible numbers and directions of unpublished results, then report the assumed selection scenario separately from the observed-study synthesis. The conclusion should also acknowledge that random-effects weighting and dependence can change the calculation.

Funnel asymmetry is a prompt to investigate, not a mechanical correction. Illustrative synthetic evidence contains eight small studies with SE 0.25 and eight large studies with SE 0.08. Seven small studies report positive effects, while four large studies do. The positive shares are 7/8 = 87.5% and 4/8 = 50%, a 37.5-percentage-point difference. Selective publication could create that pattern, but small studies might also use different populations, weaker designs, or genuinely different interventions; random variation is another possibility. Do not convert the contrast into a probability that studies are missing, and do not count positive papers as votes. Register search rules, seek unpublished evidence, inspect study features, and report sensitivity analyses. These numbers are synthetic, not a publication-bias estimate. See “Chabefer — Statistical Tools for Causal Inference, Chapter 13: Meta-analysis and Publication Bias.”","takeaway":"A pooled estimate is only as credible as the search, comparability and assumptions behind the studies it includes.","practice":{"question":"A funnel plot is asymmetric. Does that prove that journals suppressed null results?","hint":"Think of other reasons that study size and estimated effects may be related.","solution":"No. Asymmetry can be consistent with publication or selection bias but can also reflect genuine differences, design quality or chance. It is a warning to investigate, not a verdict."}}]
data.case_study: A review team compares evaluations of job-training schemes from regions with different labour markets. The worked example uses synthetic effects and standard errors to show how a precise estimate, a heterogeneous distribution and study-level moderators affect the summary. The lesson emphasizes that the target is an average across the review's included settings, not a guaranteed effect for the next programme.
data.misconceptions:
A forest plot is a display, not proof that the included studies estimate the same quantity.
Random-effects weighting does not eliminate publication bias or dependence among estimates.
The number of original-study participants is not the sample size for a meta-regression across studies.
Funnel-plot asymmetry is a diagnostic clue, not a definitive test of publication bias.

data.title: Causal Mediation & Mechanism Analysis
data.excerpt: A programme may change an outcome because it changes an intermediate behaviour, but observing that behaviour does not automatically reveal a causal mechanism. Learn to distinguish total, direct and indirect effects, draw the treatment–mediator–outcome path, and state the assumptions needed to interpret mediation estimates. An interactive linear teaching model lets you vary the pathway and a hypothetical unmeasured mediator–outcome bias. The module explains why randomizing the programme does not randomize the mediator, why the familiar product-of-coefficients is limited, and how sensitivity analysis makes hidden-confounding assumptions visible.
data.objectives:
Represent treatment, mediator and outcome relationships in a causal diagram.
Explain direct and indirect causal-effect questions in counterfactual terms.
State why sequential ignorability is stronger than randomizing treatment alone.
Use sensitivity analysis and careful reporting when mediator–outcome confounding is plausible.
data.lessons:
[{"title":"Ask what pathway a mechanism claim proposes","body":"A mediation question asks whether some of a treatment's effect operates through an intermediate variable. For example, job-search coaching may increase interview practice, which may then affect employment. Draw treatment T, mediator M and outcome Y, with arrows T→M and M→Y; also include a possible direct T→Y path. The diagram makes the proposed pathway explicit, but arrows are hypotheses about causal structure, not findings produced by the drawing.

First estimate or define the total effect of the treatment on Y. Then ask a separate question about how that effect is transmitted. A variable measured after treatment can be part of the mechanism, but conditioning on it in an ordinary regression may change the estimand or create bias. Measurement timing and the causal role of M must be justified before interpreting any decomposition.

A useful diagram distinguishes a proposed mechanism from a statistical shortcut. Suppose an illustrative synthetic coaching study measures practice minutes during week 2 and employment status at month 3. Among 100 offered participants, 60 are employed and among 100 controls, 52 are employed: 60% − 52% = 8 percentage points, a total-assignment comparison. Next, compare practice distributions, such as 180 − 120 = 60 minutes per participant on average; this difference alone does not show that the extra minutes caused employment. A mechanism claim needs timing, a plausible arrow from coaching to practice, and a defensible comparison for the practice-to-employment link. The diagram cannot establish that link or rule out motivation. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Imai, Keele & Tingley — A General Approach to Causal Mediation Analysis’ in the linked sources.

Consider a synthetic, illustrative coaching scenario where T is an offer indicator, M is interview-practice hours during the program, and Y is month-3 earnings measured in hundreds of dollars per month. Suppose the additive path estimates are a = 0.5 hours per offer, observed b = 0.8 hundred dollars per month per practice hour, and direct c′ = 0.4 hundred dollars per month per offer. The naive indirect component is therefore a×b = 0.5×0.8 = 0.4 hundred dollars per month, or $40 per month; adding the direct path gives 0.4 + 0.4 = 0.8 hundred dollars, or $80 per month. Make the lab’s sensitivity assumption explicit: if hypothetical mediator–outcome bias u = 0.2 hundred dollars per month per practice hour, replace b by b−u = 0.6. The adjusted indirect component becomes 0.5×0.6 = 0.3 hundred dollars ($30), and the model total becomes 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7 hundred dollars ($70) per month. These are synthetic calculations, not observed findings. They require linear additivity, no treatment–mediator interaction, and a defensible interpretation of u; varying u shows fragility, not the hidden confounder’s value.

A mechanism claim needs more than a mediator that changes after treatment. Consider a synthetic tutoring offer, weekly practice minutes as M, and a certification outcome as Y. If offered learners practice 30 minutes more on average and certify more often, the diagram may propose T→M→Y, while also allowing a direct T→Y path. Motivation can point to both M and Y, so the practice difference alone is not a causal pathway estimate. First state the total treatment contrast and timing; then explain what intervention on the mediator would mean. Conditioning on a post-treatment variable can alter the target or open bias. The diagram organizes assumptions, not findings. This example is constructed and does not show a tutoring effect. See “Imai, Keele & Tingley — A General Approach to Causal Mediation Analysis.”","takeaway":"A mediator is an intermediate variable in a proposed causal pathway, not simply a variable correlated with treatment and outcome.","practice":{"question":"A coaching offer is randomized, and participants who attend more sessions earn more. Is attendance automatically a mediator with a causal effect?","hint":"Motivation can affect both attendance and later earnings.","solution":"No. Attendance is post-treatment and can be confounded by motivation, time or need. Randomizing the offer does not randomize attendance."}},{"title":"Separate total, direct and indirect effects","body":"Counterfactual notation helps state the comparison. Let M(t) be the mediator value under treatment status t, and let Y(t,m) be the outcome if treatment were t and the mediator were set to m. A natural indirect effect asks how Y would change when the mediator moves from its untreated to treated value while treatment is held fixed; a natural direct effect changes treatment while fixing the mediator at a specified counterfactual value. These contrasts require careful cross-world assumptions because not every person can be observed in both states.

In a simple additive linear model with no treatment–mediator interaction, a familiar decomposition is total effect = direct effect + indirect effect, with the indirect path equal to a×b. In nonlinear models, with interactions, or under other estimands, that equality need not hold. Name the estimand and model rather than presenting a generic “percent mediated” as universal.

Illustrative synthetic example (employment at three months, percentage points, 2026): suppose a randomly offered job-search coaching programme increases interview-practice time by a = 1.5 hours per participant. In a simple additive linear teaching model, one extra practice hour is associated with b = 2 percentage points higher employment at the three-month follow-up, while the treatment’s direct path is c′ = 1 percentage point. The indirect path through practice is therefore a × b = 1.5 × 2 = 3 percentage points. Adding the paths gives a total effect of c = c′ + ab = 1 + 3 = 4 percentage points: an offer would raise employment by four points in this model, with three points attributed to the proposed practice pathway and one point to other direct routes. These are constructed values, not programme estimates.

This decomposition can clarify a stated counterfactual question, but it cannot by itself establish that interview practice caused the employment change, nor that it is the only mechanism. A key check is sequential ignorability: after accounting for credible pre-treatment factors, there must be no unmeasured cause of both practice time and later employment; also check measurement order and overlap, then vary a plausible hidden-confounding value in sensitivity analysis. Do not read 3 ÷ 4 = 75% as a universal “percent mediated,” especially with nonlinear outcomes or treatment–mediator interaction. The product is causal only under its model and identification assumptions. See “Imai, Keele & Yamamoto (2010) — Identification, Inference and Sensitivity Analysis for Causal Mediation Effects” in the linked sources below.

Keep units visible when decomposing effects. In an illustrative synthetic model, an offer raises weekly study time by 2 hours per participant (a = 2 hours per offer), and each additional study hour corresponds to 1.5 percentage points of course completion (b = 1.5 percentage points per hour). The indirect path is 2 × 1.5 = 3 percentage points per offer. If the direct path is 2 percentage points, the additive total is 2 + 3 = 5 percentage points. This arithmetic is a decomposition, not an observed historical estimate. It assumes the additive linear specification and required identification assumptions; it does not prove that study time caused completion or justify saying 60% of the effect was mediated in another model. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Imai, Keele & Yamamoto (2010) — Identification, Inference and Sensitivity Analysis for Causal Mediation Effects’ in the linked sources.

Use the lab’s sensitivity controls as a separate synthetic calculation: let a = 0.7 mediator units per treatment offer, observed b = 0.8 outcome units per mediator unit, direct c′ = 0.4 outcome units per offer, and hypothetical hidden mediator–outcome bias u = 0.2 outcome units per mediator unit. First, the unadjusted product is ab = 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56 outcome units per offer. Next, treat u as a scenario value rather than an estimate: the bias-adjusted mediator association is b − u = 0.8 − 0.2 = 0.6 outcome units per mediator unit. The adjusted indirect path is therefore a(b − u) = 0.7 × 0.6 = 0.42 outcome units per offer, and the corresponding additive total is c′ + a(b − u) = 0.4 + 0.42 = 0.82 outcome units per offer. Thus this scenario reduces the mediated component by 0.14 units (0.56 − 0.42), while leaving the direct path unchanged. The interpretation is conditional: it assumes the additive linear model and a correctly signed, constant bias term; varying u can change both magnitude and even the sign of the pathway, without revealing the actual confounder.

The coefficient-product shortcut is a model-specific decomposition, so keep units attached to every path. In an illustrative additive linear model, an offer increases mentoring sessions by a = 0.8 sessions per person, and one additional session corresponds to b = 3 percentage points of certification; the direct path is c′ = 2 percentage points. The indirect path is ab = 0.8×3 = 2.4 percentage points, and the total is c′+ab = 4.4 percentage points. These values are constructed, not observed. The arithmetic requires the stated linear, additive specification and mediation identification assumptions. With a treatment–mediator interaction or a nonlinear binary outcome, direct and indirect effects must be defined through counterfactual predictions instead of assumed to add this way. See “Imai, Keele & Yamamoto (2010) — Identification, Inference and Sensitivity Analysis for Causal Mediation Effects.”","formula":"In the simple additive linear model only: indirect path = a × b and total effect = direct + indirect.","takeaway":"Direct and indirect effects are counterfactual contrasts; the coefficient-product shortcut depends on model and identification assumptions.","practice":{"question":"If a = 0.5 mediator units and b = 2 outcome units per mediator unit, what is the simple-model indirect path?","hint":"Multiply the two path coefficients, then retain the units.","solution":"The illustrative product is 1 outcome unit per treatment change. It is a causal indirect effect only if the model and mediation identification assumptions are credible."}},{"title":"See why treatment randomization is not enough","body":"Randomly assigning T can remove confounding of treatment assignment, but M is usually not randomized. An unmeasured variable such as motivation U may influence both M and Y, creating a back-door path from mediator to outcome. Sequential ignorability requires adequate control of treatment–outcome and mediator–outcome confounding, alongside consistency, positivity and other design conditions. It also rules out certain treatment-induced confounders of the mediator–outcome relation for common natural-effect definitions.

These assumptions are demanding and cannot generally be verified by checking that a regression fits well. A randomized treatment experiment can therefore identify a total treatment effect while leaving the mechanism uncertain. A mediation analysis should state which confounders were measured before treatment, which were not, and why the remaining assumptions are plausible in the particular economic setting.

Imagine an illustrative synthetic randomized training offer assigned to 200 people, with 100 offered and 100 not offered. Randomization can balance baseline ability on average, so an employment difference such as 58% − 50% = 8 percentage points can estimate the offer’s total effect under usual trial conditions. But suppose among offer recipients, high-motivation people complete 6 practice sessions while others complete 2, and motivation also raises employment by 10 percentage points. Comparing people with 6 versus 2 sessions mixes the session pathway with motivation; the 4-session contrast is not a randomized comparison. Adjustment for measured baseline motivation may help, but post-treatment or unmeasured factors can remain. Thus randomization supports the offer contrast, not automatically the mediator contrast. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Imai, Keele & Yamamoto (2010) — Identification, Inference and Sensitivity Analysis for Causal Mediation Effects’ in the linked sources.

Read the lab’s sensitivity control as a scale check, not as a knob that estimates a hidden variable. In an explicitly illustrative synthetic setting, suppose an offer changes practice by a = 0.7 hours per person, the observed mediator–outcome slope is b = 0.8 employment-probability units per practice hour, the direct path is c′ = 0.4 employment-probability units, and the hypothetical bias is u = 0.2 employment-probability units per practice hour. First, the unadjusted indirect path is a×b = 0.7×0.8 = 0.56 employment-probability units per offer. Next, subtract the assumed bias on b’s scale: b−u = 0.8−0.2 = 0.6, so the sensitivity-adjusted indirect path is 0.7×0.6 = 0.42. The implied model total is c′ + 0.42 = 0.82 probability units, versus 0.96 before sensitivity. The difference, 0.14, equals a×u, which is a useful arithmetic check. Do not subtract 0.2 directly from 0.56: the bias belongs to the mediator–outcome slope, not to the already-multiplied pathway. These constructed values do not identify a real employment effect; the conclusion still requires the additive, no-interaction model and credible mediator–outcome assumptions.

Randomization answers the offer-versus-no-offer question, not automatically the question of receiving a particular mediator level. Suppose a synthetic experiment assigns 150 people to coaching and 150 to control. Employment is 54% versus 48%, a total-assignment difference of 6 percentage points. Within coaching, highly motivated participants attend eight sessions and less motivated participants attend three; motivation also predicts employment. The eight-versus-three comparison is therefore confounded even though the offer was randomized. Sequential ignorability requires stronger control of mediator–outcome confounding, plus defensible timing and overlap. Adjustment for a measured baseline factor may help but cannot certify that no unmeasured factor remains. The percentages are synthetic and do not identify a coaching mechanism. It is not a universal mediation algorithm. Binary outcomes, nonlinear links, treatment–mediator interactions, measurement error and selection into mediator observation can all change the estimand or invalidate a simple coefficient product. Counterfactual simulation or other estimators can accommodate richer models, but they still rely on identification assumptions.

Plan measurement order carefully: observe baseline confounders before treatment, measure the mediator at a defensible point after treatment, and measure the outcome later. Check overlap in mediator values and treatment groups. Report how the model represents interactions and uncertainty, and distinguish the analysis plan from exploratory alternatives tried after seeing the results.

Outcome scale determines what an estimate means. In an illustrative synthetic sample of 1,000 applicants, a programme changes completion from 40% to 46%, which is 6 percentage points, or 0.06 probability units; the relative increase is 6 ÷ 40 = 15%, a different quantity. A logistic model may express paths in log-odds, so multiplying two coefficients does not automatically produce 0.06 probability units. A practical workflow is: define the target scale, fit models consistent with binary completion and treatment–mediator interaction, then use counterfactual predictions to compare predicted probabilities under specified interventions. For example, predicted completion might be 0.46 versus 0.40, giving 0.46 − 0.40 = 0.06. This comparison still depends on correct specification, timing, overlap, and identification; flexibility cannot create missing causal assumptions. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Imai, Keele & Tingley — A General Approach to Causal Mediation Analysis’ in the linked sources.

Consider a synthetic coaching example in which treatment is an offer of coaching (T = 1) versus no offer (T = 0), the mediator is completed practice sessions, and the outcome is employment probability six months later. Suppose the fitted treatment-to-mediator path is a = 0.50 sessions per offer, the observed mediator-to-outcome path is b = 0.12 probability units per session, and the direct path is c′ = 0.08 probability units per offer. The naive indirect component is therefore 0.50 × 0.12 = 0.060 probability units, or 6.0 percentage points; adding the direct path gives 0.140, or 14.0 percentage points, under the model. These numbers are illustrative, not observed data. The calculation supports a causal interpretation only if timing, measurement, overlap, and sequential ignorability are defensible; randomizing the offer alone does not establish that assumption.

Always identify the outcome scale before interpreting a mediation path. In a synthetic binary completion example, predicted probability rises from 0.35 under no offer to 0.41 under an offer. With interactions, calculate specified counterfactual predicted probabilities under the relevant treatment and mediator settings. Report the total effect, the named direct and indirect estimands, the identification assumptions, measurement timing, estimation method and sensitivity range. Avoid claiming that a mediator is “the mechanism” solely because its coefficient is statistically significant. A credible result may be that the total effect is supported while the evidence for a particular pathway remains inconclusive.

Sensitivity analysis can be shown with explicitly defined hypothetical parameters. Suppose an illustrative synthetic analysis estimates an indirect effect of 4 percentage points at u = 0. If a separate scenario parameter u_ind is defined directly on the indirect-effect scale, setting u_ind = 1.5 percentage points gives 4 − 1.5 = 2.5 percentage points; u_ind = 4 gives zero. This is not the lab’s u: the lab defines u on the mediator–outcome slope scale and adjusts the indirect effect through a(b − u). Do not subtract a slope-scale u directly from an indirect effect. These are hypothetical values, not observed data or discoveries about a real confounder. Report the parameter’s meaning, units, range, and whether the total effect changes. A pathway that reaches zero under a plausible scenario is assumption-sensitive; sensitivity analysis cannot identify the hidden variable or prove robustness beyond the scenarios examined. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Imai, Keele & Yamamoto (2010) — Identification, Inference and Sensitivity Analysis for Causal Mediation Effects’ in the linked sources.

Consider an illustrative synthetic coaching study where treatment is an offer (T = 1 versus 0), the mediator M is completed practice sessions, and Y is employment within six months. Suppose the fitted treatment-to-mediator contrast is a = 0.50 sessions per offer, the mediator-to-outcome slope is b = 0.06 employment-probability units per session, and the named direct path is c′ = 0.03 probability units. The naive indirect effect is therefore a×b = 0.50×0.06 = 0.030 probability units, or 3.0 percentage points: the offer-associated increase in practice multiplied by the outcome difference per extra session. If a sensitivity scenario posits u = 0.02 probability units per session of mediator–outcome confounding, replace b by b−u = 0.04; the adjusted indirect effect is 0.50×0.04 = 0.020, or 2.0 percentage points, and the model total is c′ + adjusted indirect = 0.03 + 0.02 = 0.05, or 5.0 percentage points. This arithmetic is interpretable only under the lab’s additive linear, no-interaction setup and a defensible timing and confounding story; it is not evidence that practice caused employment.

Sensitivity analysis is a map of what conclusions require, not a detector for the hidden confounder. Suppose an illustrative mediation calculation gives an indirect effect of 3.2 percentage points when the bias parameter is zero. Under a hypothetical confounding scenario, the adjustment is −0.9 points, giving 3.2−0.9 = 2.3 points; under a stronger scenario, the adjustment is −3.2, giving 0.0 points. Report the parameter’s meaning, units, range, and whether the total effect changes. If a plausible scenario reaches zero, describe the pathway as assumption-sensitive rather than robust. Do not present these scenarios as measured bias or empirical outputs. Separate evidence for the overall treatment effect from evidence for the proposed mediator. data.case_study: A synthetic evaluation of job-search coaching asks whether interview practice could mediate a later employment effect. The diagram includes a plausible motivation variable that affects both practice and employment. The lab decomposes effects only under a simple additive linear teaching model, then varies an explicit hypothetical bias term to show why the mediator–outcome assumption matters.
data.misconceptions:
A randomized treatment does not automatically make the mediator–outcome relationship unconfounded.
A significant mediator coefficient is not proof of a causal mechanism.
The product-of-coefficients decomposition is not universal for nonlinear or interactive models.
Sensitivity analysis describes robustness to assumptions; it does not identify the hidden confounder.
